Once the delta region is expanded, you can view the sequence of all transitions in the
waveform view directly as shown in the following figure:

Chapter 2: Debugging X Values on Signals
Using Temporal Flow View Pane
Using Temporal Flow View Pane
The automatic tracing feature of Verdi allows you to trace X or corruption using the
Temporal Flow View (TFV) using the Trace Active X right-click option. You can access
TFV using the Tools -> Temporal Flow View menu option.
You can also enable TFV from different Verdi panes like source code, waveform window,
signal list, and so on by right-clicking a signal and selecting the Temporal Flow View
option.
For example, in the following figure, the power of the cell is CORRUPT.
When CORRUPT is traced using the Trace This Value option, the automatic tracing
functionality traces the corrupted power supply set to debug the root cause of power
corruption.
In this case, the root cause of power corruption is the power switch that changes from 1
->0 as root-caused by Verdi TFV.
Checking Through Assertions
Automated Assertions

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Chapter 2: Debugging X Values on Signals
Viewing Static Debug Reports
VCS generates automated runtime assertions. These assertions can be used:
• To validate power logic control sequences.
• To ensure specific requirements are met before and after power domain transitions.
• To ensure crossover ports return to its original state when supply source changes its
state from shutdown.
Custom Assertions
UPF also provides a way to add custom assertions using the bind_checker command.
You can write your assertions in a module and then bind that module to the boundary
instances. These assertions can be used:
• To check whether a signal is isolated or not.
• To check whether certain critical registers are properly preserved before entering sleep
and restored correctly upon exiting.
• To monitor power state modes and transitions which might lead to uncertain states.
• To monitor whether the domain enters the sleep mode when triggered by an event and
exits the sleep mode when another event occurs.
Viewing Static Debug Reports
VCS NLP generates multiple compile-time static reports inside the
mvsim_native_reports directory. These reports contain useful information and are
mainly used for debugging purposes.
You can use these reports to check whether the mentioned UPF strategies are correct and
honored by the tool. The following reports are helpful in debugging:
• flop_inference.rpt: Captures the details of the flops which are retained using the
retention strategy specified in the UPF file.
• isolation_association_summary.rpt: Captures the details of the associated isolation
cell instances and their associated isolation strategies.
• srsn_spa_association.rpt: Captures information about SRSN/SPA buffers associated
with a port.
• SDA/SDA_attribute_summary.rpt: Captures information of the set_design_attributes
command specified at the element or model level.

KDB Compile-Time Crash
To collect debug information for compiler crash, following information is required:
1. Code of the stack trace (using engineer build or debug build to reproduce the issue).
2. The process_debug_$PID.csh file (during vlogan/vcs crash, this file is generated
under the current directory).
3. The turbo.log file
a. If vlogan -kdb crash, do setenv TURBO_AU_DIR tmp , rerun the compilation, and
send back tmp/turbo.log to VCS support.
b. If vcs -kdb crash, send back simv.daidir/elabcomLog/turbo.log to VCS
support.
4. Machine resource usage information when the tool runs and is crashed.

Post-Process Verdi Crash
For post-process Verdi crash (%verdi -ssf <fsdb> ), Verdi generates coredump and
sysinfo.log (or sysinfo.tar) files under the Verdi working log directory novasLog/
verdiLog. These files include useful information for debugging.
Also, novas.cmd/verdi.cmd records user steps and helps to find the root cause of crash.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Interactive Flow Verdi Crash
To collect the debug information for Verdi interactive crash (./simv -verdi & ), perform
the following steps:
1. Save verdiLog/sim.log file and send it to VCS support.
Reason: To check if there is any problem in communication with simulator. Check if
there is a simv crash.
2. Save ./novas_dump.log file and send it to VCS support.
Reason: To check if there is any PLI/dumping issue.
3. Save verdiLog/verdi.cmd file and send it to VCS support.
Reason: To check which command/flow causes crash.
4. Copy the Verdi crash call stack from the terminal when crash occurs and send this
information to VCS support.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Verdi Hang
Following are the steps to collect the debug information for Verdi hang:
1. Invoke Verdi in a terminal (for example, in the machine linux1).
2. In another terminal (same machine linux1) start gdb.
3. Get the process ID of Verdi run.
% ps -ef | grep Verdi
4. Start gdb
% gdb - <pid_of_verdi>
%(gdb) cont
(continuing)
(Do Ctrl+c to interrupt the gdb run)
%(gdb) bt
(This displays the stack trace information)
5. Collect the stack trace information and send it to VCS support.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
FSDB Utility Issues
For FSDB Utilities, refer to the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Guide. Following are
some of the FSDB Utilities: fsdbdebug, fsdbreport, fsdbextract, and fsdb2saif.
To collect the FSDB utility crash, perform the following steps:
1. For crash issue:
a. fsdbdebug -info xxx.fsdb >& info.log
b. setenv FFR_SEC_DEBUG_LEVEL 1
c. setenv VPD_DEBUG_ON_BRIEF 1
d. <run your program> >& dmp.log (For example, fsdbreport <other options>
>& dmp.log )
e. Send info.log and dmp.log to VCS support.
2. For performance issue:
a. fsdbdebug -vread_mode -stat -detail novas.fsdb >& stat.log
b. setenv FFR_GATE_COMPUTATON_DETAIL
c. setenv FFR_ENV_MEASURE_PERFORMANCE
d. <run your program> >& per.log (For example, fsdbreport <other options>
>& per.log )
e. Send stat.log and per.log to VCS support.

Overview
Verdi Planner enables you to track a verification project and ensures that all its verification
goals are achieved. It allows you to create a hierarchical verification plan to measure what
is important for each project. A linked and executable verification plan ties every part of the
original written specification and test plan documents to their corresponding verification
goals. The following figure shows how the verification specifications, plans, and data come
together to track progress and status of the verification project:
Links to the specifications ensure that every feature in the specification has a
corresponding feature in the plan. Links to verification data ensure that anything below
target (low coverage, tests failing, etc.) is presented and linked to the corresponding
features to highlight needed actions. For more details on specification linking, see the
Linking Specifications to Features section. The figure below shows specification linking
with the verification plan and data:
The next step is to connect measurable verification targets to the plan. The easiest way
to link coverage and other data sources into features, run some simulations, open the
coverage databases in Verdi, and drag and drop the coverage regions from the Verdi

Chapter 1: Overview

coverage window to each feature. Once you have linked those sources, whenever you run
Verdi with a plan, the scores for linked features are automatically updated.
This document covers the following benefits that you can receive from Verdi Planner:
• Linking Specifications to Features
• Tapeout Goals

Linking Specifications to Features
Linking specifications to a verification plan ensures that the verification plan properly
covers all known requirements and specifications. It allows you to easily identify bugs in
a feature and to track whether all the features are implemented in the plan. Verdi Planner
provides two ways to create a link between a specification and a plan feature. One way is
to select the specification and the feature, and create a link between them. Another way
is to create a feature from the specification by selecting a section of the specification, and
then link that section with the feature.
Verdi Planner enables you to create many-to-many relationships between a specification
and a plan. A single feature may correspond to multiple requirements and multiple
features may support a single requirement. Also, Verdi Planner enables you to track
whether the entire specification is linked to the plan. It provides a specification coverage
metric to quickly measure the percentage of the specification that is linked to the plan.
It highlights all the linked sections of the specification and thereby, provides a visual
review of the specification. For example, the following figure shows that the specification
document, ijuke.pdf, is 96.75% linked to the plan:
You can link a specification to a plan at any time in a project, the earlier the better. The
best technique is to use the specification as the basis for creating a plan. In this case, the
plan is incrementally (feature-by-feature) built by linking it to the specification. In cases
where the plan already exists, you can link the plan with the specification at any time in the
project’s duration.

Tapeout Goals
The most obvious use of Verdi Planner is to achieve tapeout goals. To achieve tapeout
goals, you need to collect data from many sources, such as test results, specification
coverage, code coverage, and functional coverage. Verdi Planer enables you to collect
relevant verification data and compare it with the verification goals.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
peout
goals, you need to collect data from many sources, such as test results, specification
coverage, code coverage, and functional coverage. Verdi Planer enables you to collect
relevant verification data and compare it with the verification goals.
Verification goals are generally set for the entire plan by setting the default goal for each
metric. Each feature in the plan then inherits the default goal. For example, you may set
the following goals as the global goals for a plan:
• ◦ All tests must pass, that is, test.fail <= 0 .
◦ Functional coverage must exceed 99%, that is, Group >= 0.99 .
You can then apply these goals to each feature in the plan as shown in the figure below:
Sometimes, global goals must be adjusted specifically for a feature, so, Verdi Planner
allows you to adjust these goals on a feature-by-feature basis. In the previous example,
you may override the global goals of test.fail <= 0 and Group >= 0.99 to test.fail
<= 3 and Group >= 0.95 respectively for the functionality feature (see the figure
below). Also, it is possible to change the goals for an entire branch of the plan with
a single edit as the goals are hierarchically inherited. In this example, the power_up
and cash sub-features of the functionality feature inherit the new values, that
is, test.fail <= 3 and Group >= 0.95 once these values get updated for the
functionality feature.

Chapter 3: Tapeout Goals

Interim Milestones
Verdi Planner enables you to track the progress of a verification project by setting interim
milestones. These interim milestones typically consist of goals set to lower levels than
the tapeout goals. For example, you may have a 100% tapeout coverage goal, however,
it is not reasonable to set 100% coverage as an interim milestone. Closing on coverage
requires time and effort and occurs gradually as the project proceeds.
Consider the following figure that shows a plan that is annotated in the initial days of a
verification project representing the following tapeout goals:
• All tests must pass, that is, test.pass >= 100% .
• Group coverage must exceed 99%, that is, Group >= 99% .

Chapter 4: Interim Milestones

The annotated plan shows that scores are color-coded to represent whether the feature
has met its tapeout goals. The plan shows many red-coded scores and few green-coded
scores. However, it does not show a useful analysis of the project's progress - when
everything is red you cannot see what is truly behind, and what is on track but not yet
complete.
Now, consider the following figure that shows the annotated plan with the following interim
milestones of the project:
• More than 75% tests must pass, that is, test.pass >= 75% .
• Group coverage must exceed 60%, that is, Group >= 60% .
In the above figure, it is more evident which features are behind the interim milestone
represented by the modified goals.
Also, there may be features of the verification plan that are not yet started at certain
milestones. Verdi Planner allows pruning of these features by adding a user-defined
attribute. Using the attribute values, the planner can prune the features and provide
a concise report for the interim milestones. In the previous example, annotate a new
attribute, milestone, to the plan that defines by when a feature is expected to be verified.

Customization and Templates
Verdi Planner enables you to create a template containing only definitions and high-level
feature structure. You can customize the template to add details as per your requirements.
However, it is not necessary to create the template to start using Verdi Planner. You can
always start using templates later after you identify how they can help your project.
For example, the figure below shows a template plan that defines all the following
requirements yet contains no details:
• Supports user-defined attributes, such as owner or priority, on each feature.
• Contains user-defined metrics, such as bug_rate or cpu_cycles.
• Supports reference-specific metric types per feature.
• Conforms to a common high-level feature structure.
This plan is embodied in a single .hvp language text file, template.hvp, which is shown
below:
plan your_project_here; metric real bug_rate;
aggregator = average;
goal = (bug_rate < 0.1); endmetric
metric integer cpu_cycles; aggregator = sum;
goal = (cpu_cycles > 0);
endmetric
attribute integer priority = 0; feature safety;
endfeature

endplan

There is no need to understand these language constructs to use Verdi
Planner. However, it is good to know that everything you see in Verdi has a
corresponding language construct that you can edit, if required.
You can customize the template plan by adding lower-level feature details, measurement
sources, and attribute values. For example, the following figure shows the subfeatures
added to safety and functionality features along with the value to the priority

The template plan provides the framework to add references to verification data sources,
such as covergroups and test results. For example, the following figure shows two

Once the plan is populated with measures and sources, the actual verification data is
loaded and annotated to the plan. For example, the following figure shows annotated
results in the columns to the right of the features:
In the above figure, the features that reference covergroups have a score in the Group
column. In addition, the features that reference tests have scores in the following three
“test” score columns:
• test.pass%: Reports the percentage of tests that are passed.
• test.completion: Reports the number of tests that are executed compared to the
number of tests that are expected to be written irrespective of the actual test result.
This column tracks the progress towards writing the expected number of tests.
• test pass/fail/other/missing : Reports an absolute count of the number of tests
that fall into the four categories, namely pass, fail, other, and missing.

Project Reviews and Audits
Often a verification project is reviewed, where stakeholders get the opportunity to ask
questions about how a project is being verified and understand its coverage model. These
reviews are performed more effectively when they are organized at the plan level. A basic
hierarchical descent through the plan allows the review team to drill down through the
areas of interest. Also, using interim goals, as discussed in the Interim Milestones section,
makes it easy to follow the path of the features not meeting their goals by hierarchically
traversing down features with red scores. The review team can quickly reach even to the
lowest level of detail to resolve issues by reviewing code or applying exclusions/waivers.
For example, consider the following figure that shows the
jukebox.functionality.power_up feature whose score is 50%, which is below its goal:
To look for the reason for its low coverage score, double-click into it to expand its
Sources and Regions , as shown in the figure below. The figure shows that the

affecting the overall coverage score:

implemented but not yet hit. For example, consider the following figure that shows the
jukebox.media.cd_handler feature has not reached 100% coverage:

Missing Verification Sources
Missing verification sources are unmatched sources, such as covergroups, bins, and tests,
which are mentioned as sources in the plan but not found in the generated verification
data. Verdi Planner enables you to plan for these sources by specifying their name before
they are implemented. You can use wildcards to collect these sources. Your own naming
convention can make this easier. For example, to verify the queue flush feature using
covergroups whose names begin with qflush, specify qflush* in the relevant feature's
source string.

Verdi Planner provides the following two techniques to find missing sources of the

1. Missing Source Markers
Verdi Planner uses "!" to mark features that have unmatched sources (see the figure
below).

Chapter 7: Missing Verification Sources

Now, double-click the power_up feature to find the reason for the missing source.
Double- clicking the feature shows the reset_deassert covergroup is missing (see
the figure below):
2. Scores for Missing Sources
To ensure that missing sources are not missed by your analysis and review, Verdi Planner
assigns the worst possible score to them. This way the overall score of the higher-level
verification plan is lower than the expected score. In the above figure, you can see that
the reset_deassert covergroup is assigned 0% due to which the score of power_up is
50%, and hence, the overall score of jukebox becomes 72.92%.
Linkage of the plan to verification data can occur at any time during the project. You can
even define links to verification data that is not yet produced. If you want to link objects
to the plan that do not yet exist in the database, you can enter their names as sources in
the plan. When they are added to the design in later iterations, Verdi automatically finds
them and annotates their scores in the design. For example, you can use the name of a
covergroup that will be written later as a source. You can also use wildcard expressions,
so if you have a naming convention for sources, you can have Verdi automatically find any
matching sources.
Note:
If you have a design hierarchy, groups or asserts, or tests, you can easily drag
and drop source regions into the Plan pane to create features to measure them.
Also, Verdi GUI provides indication whether the design hierarchy, groups or
asserts, or tests are already used in the current plan.

Subproject Reports
Verdi Planner enables you to create reports as per your requirements. You can create a
report for a feature as well as for the entire plan. To generate a feature-specific report, you
can either create a user-defined attribute for the feature or use a built-in attribute. After
this, use filters on the attribute to generate the required report as explained in the Interim
Milestones section.
For example, the following figure shows the report generated using filters on the user-
defined attribute, priority and the built-in attribute, owner:

is usr2.

Reuse
Just as good testbench and RTL code is reused in future projects, verification plans can
also be reused using Verdi Planner. Reusing verification plans is critical to the productivity
and efficiency of a verification project. Plan reuse involves reusing features and sub-blocks
in derivative plans from the parent plan. Any plan can reference a subplan. The scores
aggregated to the top of the subplan are passed on to the parent plan.
It is possible to parameterize subplans like IP and RTL. You can design a master-top
plan that contains features that are optionally turned on and off as they are instantiated
in the top plan. For example, you can have a union plan that contains every feature and
configuration of the IP. Then, the parent plan selects which features are activated in the
subplan by setting its parameter values when instantiated from the parent plan.
For example, the LP_Plan verification plan in the figure below is reused as a sub-plan
twice. You can also parameterize owner and priority attributes in the plan based on
your requirements.

Chapter 9: Reuse

Traceability
Verdi Planner allows you to trace user requirements and verification details as verification
plans are linked to the original written specification, test plan documents, and verification
goals. Linked and executable plans track progress and status of a verification project
along with low-level verification details. Verdi Planner allows you to interactively trace
between requirements and low-level verification results and vice versa.
Verdi Planner provides a complete traceable verification plan by linking specifications,
verification plans, and verification data. It provides the following benefits:
• Traces from a requirement defined in the specification to the actual verification metrics
that are used to verify the requirement.
• Analyzes whether the requirement is adequately tested.
• Traces failed tests and low coverage to the requirements that rely on them.
• Identifies gaps in the verification environment.
For example, to trace the details of the low score feature, Power Domain (D) , double-click
the feature in the plan. Double-clicking opens the specification and highlights the feature in
the specification (see the figure below).

Tactical Responses
A well-organized verification data helps in taking quick decisions in critical times. Verdi
Planner helps you to organize the data into a hierarchical plan, which enables you to
provide tactical responses. If a project already has all its verification data organized into a
plan, then you can easily create the urgently required information and depict it as per your
requirements.

Reallocation of Resources
As the verification data is organized into a hierarchical structure, it is easier for you to
determine features that are ahead of their schedule and the features that are behind.
Using this statistics, you can temporarily reallocate resources to the features that are
behind the schedule. Also, you can use filters and goal overrides to focus on the actual
problem areas and know the features of the project that can benefit from reallocation of
resources.

Business and Market Responses
Often a chip is intended to serve multiple markets or needs. Networking and
communications chips often should support a wide range of protocols or features that are
not needed by all customers. For example, consider three ISPs, A, B, and C that require
different feature subsets of a modem chip. To indicate features for different ISPs, you can
tag a verification plan with different attributes based on the required features. If ISP B
does not require the modem chip, you can use filters in the verification plan to keep only
features required by A and C.

Communication With Customers
Verdi Planner allows you to share verification data with customers as per their
requirements. Filters and various other reporting options allow you to control what
information appears in the collateral shared with customers. For example, customers
may not be interested in internal milestones, therefore, you may mask the attribute
corresponding to the milestones in the report prepared for the customers.

Identifying Simulation Performance Issues and Improving Performance 5

Improving Compilation and Simulation
Performance by Identifying Performance
Bottlenecks
This document describes the available compilation and simulation profiler capability to
identify performance bottlenecks and to enable corrective actions. The document includes
the following sections:
• Identifying Compilation Performance Issues and Improving Performance
• Identifying Simulation Performance Issues and Improving Performance
Identifying Compilation Performance Issues and Improving
Performance
Compilation performance issue shows up either as a capacity issue or as a compilation
issue. In case of capacity issues, analyze (vlogan or vhdlan) or elaboration (vcs) stage
consumes a significant memory that needs to be investigated. In case of compilation
issues, analyze and elaboration stage takes significantly longer time.
You can improve compilation performance by reviewing the command line and identifying
any compilation option that leads to performance bottleneck. You can regenerate the
performance number after removing any such options present in the command line. You
can also identify the stages and the modules where time is consumed to debug the actual
issue. You need to work with Synopsys support to narrow down such compiler issues.
Improving Compilation and Simulation Performance by Identifying Performance Bottlenecks
Y-2026.03-SP2

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Chapter 1: Improving Compilation and Simulation Performance by Identifying Performance
Bottlenecks
Identifying Simulation Performance Issues and Improving Performance
Identifying Simulation Performance Issues and Improving
Performance
You can improve simulation performance issues by reviewing the command line and
identifying if any options used in the command line are not needed and leading to
simulation bottleneck. For example:
• Do not use the +rad option as it can slow down the performance. Use this option only if
the design under investigation is a gate-level design and has no timing specified. There
are several technologies under radiant that are enabled using the +rad option. If the
slowdown occurs, you can investigate and find out which technology is causing the
slowdown.
• Use the -hsopt=gates option only if the design is a gate-level design, which
significantly improves the performance on RTL.
• Use only the required debug capabilities and do not turn on the debug capability on the
entire design, if you do not need it.
VCS uses unified profile report to identify the bottlenecks in the design. You need to run
the simprofile option for time and memory separately because running them together
can cause skewed results and longer simulation time. You should pass the -simprofile
compilation option during elaboration. This generates raw performance data inside the
simprofile_dir directory, which needs to be processed using the $VCS_HOME/bin/
profrpt script to generate either a text or an HTML report.
The profrpt profile report generator script supports several options and you can use
different combinations of these options to generate customized reports. Also, use the
inbuilt help message to understand the different combinations.
You can use the following commands:
• To elaborate the design with profile instrumentation, execute the following command
during compilation:
% vcs -simprofile test.v
• To simulate with time profile to generate raw data under the simprofile_dir directory,
execute the following command at simulation:
% simv -simprofile time
• To simulate with memory profile to generate raw data under the simprofile_dir
directory, execute the following command at simulation:
% simv -simprofile mem

Introduction
VCS MX allows you to enable access (ACC) capabilities throughout your design and
specify ACC capabilities for specific parts of your design. It also enables you to specify
selected ACC capabilities using a PLI tab file. Enabling ACC capabilities impacts
performance, VCS MX allows you to enable only the ACC capabilities that you need.
PLI is the Programming Language Interface (PLI) between C/C++ functions and VCS MX.
It helps to link applications containing C/C++ functions with VCS MX, so that they execute
concurrently. VCS MX supports PLI 1.0 and PLI 2.0 routines for the PLI. Therefore, you
can use VPI and ACC routines to write the PLI application.
Access capabilities (read, write, force, and callback) can be enabled by the PLI application
using the following methods:
• Module-Based PLI
• Instance-Based or Signal-Based PLI
This document describes the methods to enable the access capabilities to improve the
compile/runtime performance.
Improving Simulation Performance Using PLI
Y-2026.03-SP2

Module-Based PLI
This method enables the module-level ACC capability. This capability is applied to the
complete design wherever the modules are connected. Therefore, this capability is also
applied to the unwanted design hierarchies and affects the compile/runtime performance.
To improve the performance in module-based PLI, you can restrict the ACC capabilities
using learn PLI.
Enabling Module Level PLI Learn
Use the +vcs+learn+pli runtime option to instruct VCS MX to learn the access
capabilities (signal at module level) that are used by the modules in your design and write
them into a secondary PLI tab file named pli_learn.tab. You can use this tab file to
recompile your design so that subsequent simulations use only the ACC capabilities that
are required.
Recompile your design using the +applylearn compile-time option and run the
simulation.
By default, VCS MX selects the pli_learn.tab file.
Use Model
% cat pli.tab
acc+=frc:dut //Enable force capability on signals/ports of "dut" module.
% vcs -P pli.tab <design file>
% . /simv +vcs+learn+pli //learn the debug capability on module-level PLI
% vcs -P pli.tab +applylearn+pli_learn.tab <design File>
Enabling Signal PLI Learn at Instance Level
Use the +vcs+learn+pli+sigpli +vcs+learn+pli+instpli runtime option to instruct
VCS MX to learn the access capabilities (signal at instance level) that are used in the
simulation and write them into a secondary PLI tab file named, pli_learn.tab.
Recompile your design using the +applylearn -instpli -sigpli compile-time option
and then run the simulation. By default, VCS selects the pli_learn.tab file.
Improving Simulation Performance Using PLI
Y-2026.03-SP2

Instance-Based or Signal-Based PLI
ACC capabilities are required only for few signals in a module. Enabling ACC capabilities
on the entire module creates a significant performance overhead that can be eliminated
using the instance/signal PLI (instpli/sigpli) constructs.
The instpli/sigpliconstructs allow ACC capabilities to be specified for module signals
instead of entire modules. This allows VCS MX to learn the capability by instance/signal
based PLI.
Use Model
% cat pli.tab
acc+=frc:top.dut.a // Enable force capability on the signals of
the
"top.dut.a" module.
% vcs -P pli.tab <design file> -sigpli -instpli // Enable debug
capability on
a signal at instance level
%. /simv

Overview
The document briefly describes the compilation flows, such as incremental flow and
partition compile flow. The document includes the following sections:
• Introduction
• Managing Cross-Module References
• Scenarios Causing a Recompilation of a Partition
Introduction
Partition compile flow allows you to compile portions of the design and get significantly
faster turnaround time during the iterative process of compile and recompile. There are
two modes of using partition compile flow. They are as follows:
• Autopartitioning
• Manual Partitioning
Autopartitioning
Autopartitioning is the default mode in partition compile flow where partitioning is decided
by VCS by simply enabling the partition compile flow using the -partcomp compile-time
option. Autopartitioning automatically partitions the design and the testbench. You do not
need to specify yourself what parts of the design and testbench are in which partitions.
VCS creates optimal number of partitions to get better performance and the typical
compile time of each partition is 3-4 minutes. Further, the partitioning is regularly updated
based on the incremental changes done in the design to get optimal recompile time.
Autopartitioning automatically takes care of the cross-partition limitations across partitions
and re-adjusts the partitioning to avoid any cross-partition errors.
The use model for autopartitioning is easy to adopt partition compile flow.
To use partition compile flow with autopartitioning, use the following command in VCS two-
step flow:
% vcs -partcomp top <other vcs elaboration options>

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Chapter 1: Overview
Managing Cross-Module References
You can change the autopartitioning threshold using the following option:
-partcomp=autopart_[low|medium|high]
The option applies autopartitioning to both modules and packages with a low, medium
and high threshold. By default, the option applies autopartitioning to both modules and
packages with a medium threshold.
Manual Partitioning
When you want to create a separate partition for a specific block that is under debugging
or development, then you can use the manual partition to create a separate partition along
with autopartitioning.
You can specify manual partition using the following command:
% vcs -partcomp top +optconfigfile+pc.cfg <other vcs elaboration options>
Here, +optconfigfile is a simple text file. You can specify a partition in the
+optconfigfile files with a line beginning with the partition keyword. The cell keyword
specifies that the partition is for all instances of the module name or the program block
name that follows.
For example:
// +optconfigfile configuration file cfg.txt
partition cell test;
partition cell dut;
This configuration file specifies:
• one partition for program block test.
• one partition for both instances of module dut.
VCS honors manual partitioning mentioned in the configuration file as well as enables
autopartitioning for the remaining portion of the design.
Managing Cross-Module References
When your design is partitioned, there is a chance that there are cross-module references
(XMRs) across partitions. That is, signals and variables from one partition are accessed
from another partition.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Chapter 1: Overview
Scenarios Causing a Recompilation of a Partition
You can manage XMRs using the partition compile flow as follows:
• If there is no change in XMRs, you do not need any extra option or any change in
configuration file for the partition compile flow.
• If the XMR changes, use the -partcomp=noxmrconfig option, so that only the
changed partition is recompiled or it might cause some runtime slowdown. If you do not
use any option, both the referrer and the referee partitions are recompiled.
Scenarios Causing a Recompilation of a Partition
The following scenarios causes recompilation of a partition:
• ◦ ▪ Changes in module definition.
▪ Changes in vcs command-line option or in the synopsys_sim.setup or
+optconfigfile configuration file.
▪ Changes to the global design property, such as adding $dumpvars to a partition.
This retriggers recompilation of all the partitions.
▪ Changes to the $unit scope: Any change (addition of new signal, type, module,
interface) to the $unit results in recompilation of all the partitions associated
with this $unit scope.
▪ Changes to an interface require the recompilation of all modules connected to
that interface.
▪ Changes to a shared package. In this case, recompilation is required for all the
partitions sharing this package.
Note:
Complete list of scenarios that triggers recompilation of a partition is available in
the Partition Compile section of the VCS/VCS MX LCA Features Guide.

Introduction
When you are debugging or developing a block in the design, then you end up spending
lot of time compiling the entire design for a small piece of change in the block in your
design.
To improve compile-time performance in VCS/VCS MX, you can use the default
incremental compilation method or enable the partition compilation method and save
on the overall compile turnaround time (TAT) during the process of debugging or
development.
Incremental compilation is the default method in VCS/VCS MX. During incremental
compilation, VCS/VCS MX analyzes and compiles only those design units that are
changed since last compilation.
However, when the design is complex and you want further optimized compile
performance, then you can use the partition compile flow. Partition compile flow allows you
to decide on how to partition your design so that you can fine tune the recompile behavior.
The partition compile can significantly reduce the compilation turnaround time by allowing
you to recompile only the changed partitions (portions of the design) and reuse the
partitions for the unchanged portions of the design that are already compiled earlier. You
can enable partition compile flow using the -partcomp compile-time option.

Incremental Compile Flow
Incremental compile flow works for both two-step and three-step flows and it recompiles
only the modified files. It is enabled by default to give optimized compile-time performance.
You do not need to pass any extra option to the regular VCS commands. However,
incremental compile might trigger recompilation of the design under the following
conditions as the nature of change has global impact:
• Change in the command-line options
• Change in the target of a hierarchical reference
• Change in the ports of a design unit
• Change in the functional behavior of the design
• Change in a compile-time constant such as a parameter/generic

Partition Compile Flow
Partition Compile is a VCSMX feature that compiles only the changed partitions (portions
of the design) and get significantly faster turnaround time during the iterative process of
compile and recompile. With partition compile flow, VCS creates partition in your design
and recompiles only the modified partitions in the subsequent compiles. It provides you
with the flexibility to fine tune the partitioning (if needed) and get the most efficient compile
performance.
Some of the partition compile features or benefits are as follows:
• The partition compile flow provides simplified use model and enable partition compile
flow by simply adding the -partcomp option at compile time.
• You can also compile partitions in parallel by using the -fastpartcomp option and
improve compile turnaround time further.
• It also supports for cross-module references (XMRs) across partitions.
• Partition Compile reduces disk space usage across multiple partitions.

Loading FSDB Without KDB
Use Model to Load Single FSDB File
% verdi -ssf <fsdbfile_name> -nologo &
Use Model to Load Multiple FSDB Files
% verdi -ssf <fsdbfile_name1> -ssf <fsdbfile_name2> -nologo &
You can only view the instance/signal value in the waveform. You can add the required
signal to the waveform using the Signal > Get Signal option.

Introduction
VCS Native Low Power (NLP) has the Native Verdi integrated, which can be used
for debugging low power simulations. Verdi supports IEEE 1801 UPF. It allows you to
visualize, trace, and analyze the source of low power events. It simplifies low power debug
by allowing you to visualize the power intent (UPF) and supports features to determine
whether an unexpected design behavior is caused by the functional logic or a power
event.
This document describes the low power debug using Verdi in the following sections:
• Use Model
• Low Power Debug Features
• Signal Shading
• List of Default Static Debug Reports Dumped by VCS NLP

Use Model
For VCS and Verdi databases to be consistent for accurate debugging, VCS NLP
instruments the low power objects in HDL design to mimic the power intent specified in the
UPF. Verdi allows you to debug low power objects instrumented by VCS NLP.
The following is the syntax to compile the low power design:
% vcs -sverilog <design_file> -upf <upf_file> -power_top <design_top>
-kdb -debug_access+all <compile_options>
The following is the syntax to invoke Verdi GUI:
% verdi -sverilog <design_file> -upf2.0|-upf1.0 <upf_file> -ssf file.fsdb
Example:% verdi -sverilog *.v -upf2.0 *.upf -ssf demo.fsdb
To dump the power-related signals that include the power supply nets and power-domain
states (upf_simstate), you must use the +power or +allin the $fsdbDumpvars system
task as follows:
$fsdbDumpvars("+power");

Low Power Debug Features
The Power Aware Debug support is integrated with the main nTrace window. The power
related panes are opened in the main window after importing the UPF power file into
the Verdi platform. Also, you can select the Power Debug Mode work mode from the
Welcome page or select the Window > Power Debug Mode command to open the power
related panes.
The following figure illustrates an example of Power Aware Debug panes:
The following sections describe the Power Aware Debug panes:
• Power Domain Hierarchy Pane

• Power State Table Pane
• Power State Annotation in nSchema

Power Domain Hierarchy Pane
The Power Domain Hierarchy pane displays all the power domains defined in the design.
This pane is docked to the same pane location as the design browser as a new tab. Each
domain is marked with a different color.
The power states for all power domains are represented by different icons. For example,
the icon represents the Normal Power Domain On and the icon represents the Normal
Power Domain Off. Use the Help > Legend menu command and select the Power
Manager tab to check all the icons.
Power Source Code Pane
The Power Source Code pane consists of HDL Source Code View tab that displays the
HDL source code and UPF Code View tab that displays the UPF code. The UPF Code
View tab is displayed by default. Click the HDL Source Code View tab to view the HDL
source code.
You can double-click an element in the Power Domain Hierarchy pane to view its
definition in both UPF Code View and HDL Source Code View of the Power Source Code
pane.
The HDL Source Code View annotates power information from UPF. The instance
hierarchy list is color coded and each color represents a power domain. The signal list
annotates the type of protection cells by which each signal is impacted. Moving the mouse
on a signal opens a tooltip box with information on its policy.

Power State Table Pane
The Power State Table pane shows the power state table of the design. The table is

Power > Show Power State Table (if UPF file is loaded).

Temporal Flow View Pane
Temporal Flow View Pane
The Temporal Flow View (TFV) pane supports power aware debugging. The Temporal
Flow View contains the complete unrolled path of the low power hierarchy. The TFV
window also supports power domain highlight and RET/ISO annotation for retention/
isolation latches and flip-flops.

Viewing Power Objects in nWave

nWave Get Signals form under the design scope. This feature is also supported with the

List of Default Static Debug Reports Dumped by
VCS NLP
The following reports can be used for debug purpose. These reports are dumped under
the mvsim_native_reports directory.
Report Name Description
hierarchical_flop_inference.rpt Compile-time static report for Verilog. Captures
the details of the inferred retention registers.
hierarchical_flop_inference_vhdl.rpt Compile-time static report for VHDL. Captures
the details of the inferred retention registers.
isolation_association_summary.rpt Captures the details of the associated isolation
cell instances and their associated isolation
strategies
library_mapping.rpt Captures the cell information.
library_match.rpt Captures the matching/non-matching cell
information.
library_mapping_after_upf.rpt Captures the port-based corruption information
of a cell.
SDA/SDA_attribute_summary.rpt Captures information of the
set_design_attributes command specified at
element or model level.
srsn_spa_association.rpt Captures information about the SRSN and SPA
buffers associated with a port
upf_state_machine.rpt Captures the objects with legal/illegal
states/transitions being covered.
upf_control_port_coverage.rpt Captures the functional coverage on the control
ports/signals of a power switch, isolation
strategy, and retention strategy.
upf_powerswitch_mapping.rpt Captures the associated/Unassociated Power
Switch Instances information

Chapter 5: List of Default Static Debug Reports Dumped by VCS NLP

Report Name Description
upf_supply_set_power_state.rpt Captures information on all the power states of
all the Supply Sets in the design.
undefined_db_cell.rpt Lists the cells modules which are defined within
`celldefine and `endcelldefine, but not
having a corresponding matched liberty db cell.
upf_supply_source_rsd.rpt Captures information on all the type of supply
sources like root supply of a supply source and
net/ports connected the source.
upf_construct_statistics.rpt Captures information on the number of low
power constructs used in the UPF file.

Verdi Database
Verdi platform provides the following two databases. All analysis engines and visualization
tools use these databases.
• Knowledge Database (KDB): As it compiles the design, the Verdi platform uses
its internal synthesis technology to recognize and extract specific structural, logical,
and functional information about the design and stores the resulting detailed design
information in the KDB.
• Fast Signal Database (FSDB): The FSDB stores the simulation results, including
transaction data and logged messages from SVTB or other applicable languages in an
efficient and compact format that allows you to access data quickly. Synopsys provides
the object files that can be linked to common simulators to store the simulation results
in FSDB format directly. You can generate FSDB either from the provided routines or
after reading and converting your VCD file. In addition, FSDB read/write API routines
are provided for customers and partners to use.

Overview
Low power assertions are the simulation messages that capture the power events
during the simulation. These messages are automatically issued by the tool as per the
simulation behavior.
This document describes low power assertions in the following sections:
• Low Power Messaging Format
• Message Control

Low Power Messaging Format
Following is the format of the low power simulation messages:
[time] [severity] [message_id] <Message>
Where, severity can be one of the following:
INFO | WARNING| ERROR|FATAL
[0][INFO][LP_PD_INIT_STATE] Power domain 'testbench/inst/Island_VDD'
started in 'NORMAL' state.
[500][INFO][LP_PD_STATE_CHANGE] Power domain 'testbench/inst/Island_VDD'
state changed from 'NORMAL' to 'CORRUPT'.

Message Control
The following two modes of message control are supported:
• Simulation Configuration File
• Function Calls from Testbench
The options specified through the runtime configuration file are used for initialization. The
function calls from the testbench overrides these initial settings. The following message
control options are supported:
• Choice of message logging modes
• Turn ON/OFF all/selected messages
• Override default severity of messages
• Filter messages based on severity
Simulation Configuration File
Use the -power <config_file> runtime option to specify the simulation configuration file.
The following topics describe the options supported in the configuration file:
• Set Low Power Message Log Mode
• Turn ON/OFF Messages
• Override the Default Severity of Messages
• Filter Messages Based on Severity
Set Low Power Message Log Mode
Use the following command to set the low power message log mode:
set_lp_msg_log_mode <DEFAULT/CUSTOM/DEFAULT_CUSTOM>
-file {filename}

Chapter 3: Message Control
Simulation Configuration File
Where,
DEFAULT — All the messages are logged into the simulation log file specified with the -l
runtime option. Without -l, messages are displayed on the console.
CUSTOM — All the messages are logged into the log file specified using -file with
set_lp_msg_log_mode.
DEFAULT_CUSTOM — All the messages are logged into the simulation log file specified with
the -l runtime option and -file with set_lp_msg_log_mode.
set_lp_msg_log_mode CUSTOM -file {test.log}
All the low power messages are dumped in the test.log file.
Turn ON/OFF Messages
Use the following command to turn ON/OFF low power messages:
set_lp_msg_onoff <ON/OFF> -msg {msgList}
• Default value is ON for all the messages.
• -msg is optional. Not specifying -msg results in the ON/OFF value being applied to all
the messages.
• msgList is the list of space separated messages.
Turn OFF all the messages:
set_lp_msg_onoff OFF
Turn ON specific message ID:
set_lp_msg_onoff ON -msg { LP_SS_INIT}
Turn OFF specific message ID:
set_lp_msg_onoff OFF -msg { LP_ISOGN_INIT}
Turn OFF multiple message IDs:
set_lp_msg_onoff OFF -msg {LP_SS_INIT LP_PST_INIT_ILLEGAL
LP_PSW_CTRL_INIT_INVALID}

Chapter 3: Message Control
Function Calls from Testbench
Override the Default Severity of Messages
Use the following command to override the default severity of low power messages:
set_lp_msg_severity <INFO/WARNING/ERROR/FATAL> -msg {msgList}
Severity must be one of
INFO|WARNING|ERROR|FATAL.
set_lp_msg_severity ERROR -msg {LP_SS_INIT}
set_lp_msg_severity INFO -msg {LP_ISOEN_INVALID}
set_lp_msg_severity WARNING -msg {LP_ISOGN_OFF}
Filter Messages Based on Severity
Use the following command to filter low power messages based on severity:
set_lp_msg_log_severity <INFO|WARNING|ERROR|FATAL>
All the messages with severity less than the specified severity value are filtered.
INFO — Default severity level. No messages are filtered.
WARNING — Messages with severity INFO are filtered.
ERROR — Messages with severity INFO and WARNING are filtered.
FATAL — Messages with severity FATAL are ON and the rest are filtered.

Chapter 3: Message Control
Function Calls from Testbench
Override the Default Severity of Messages
Use the following command to override the default severity of low power messages:
set_lp_msg_severity(input string msgIds, input string sev);
msgids — string type, space separated message IDs
sev — string type, one of INFO|WARNING|ERROR|FATAL
set_lp_msg_severity(" LP_ISOGN_INIT", "WARNING");
Turn ON/OFF Messages
Use the following command to turn ON/OFF low power messages:
set_lp_msg_onoff(input string msgIds, input string value);
msgids — string type, space separated message IDs
value — string type, must be either ON or OFF
set_lp_msg_onoff("LP_SS_INIT", "OFF");
Filter Messages Based on Severity
Use the following command to filter low power messages based on severity:
set_lp_msg_log_severity(input string sev);
sev — string type, must be one of INFO|WARNING|ERROR|FATAL
Example:
set_lp_msg_log_severity("WARNING");

Overview
There are several RTL and gate-level design strategies for reducing power. This document
describes the power reduction methods in the following sections:
• Power Gating
• Multi-Voltage Design (Multi-VDD)
• Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling
• Adaptive Body-Biasing (ABB)
• Multiple-Vt Library Cells

The following topics describe the low power techniques in detail:
• Power Gating
• Multi-Voltage Design (Multi-VDD)
• Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling
• Adaptive Body-Biasing (ABB)
• Multiple-Vt Library Cells
Power Gating
Power gating is a power-saving technique in which portions of the chip are shut down
temporarily during periods of inactivity, as illustrated in the following figure:
This technique reduces the leakage power of the chip. Power gating with state retention
involves switching off an area of a design when its functionality is not required, then
restoring power when it is required.
For example, in a cell phone chip, the block that performs voice processing can be shut
down when the phone is in standby mode. When the user places a call or receives an
outside call, the voice processing block must “wake up” from its powered-down state.

Chapter 2: Low Power Techniques
Power Gating
Power gating has the potential to reduce overall power consumption substantially because
it lowers leakage power as well as switching power.
Shutdown
In this technique, the power supply of the entire design is shut off when the circuit is not
in use. Such designs do not require data to be retained in registers or latches used in the
design. Functional verification of the design is still required to make sure that the position
of designs that are awake function properly and to ensure that the system would work
when power is restored in the sleeping part of the device.
Isolation
When the power is shut off, each power domain must be isolated from the rest of the
design, so that it does not corrupt the downstream logic. Power shutdown results in
slow output from the power gated blocks. These outputs spend a significant time at the
threshold voltage, causing large crowbar currents in the always on blocks. Isolation cells
are used to prevent these crowbar currents. The isolation cells are placed between the
outputs of the power gated blocks and inputs of the always on blocks.
In a design with power gating, an isolation cell is required where each logic signal crosses
from a power domain that can be powered down to a domain that is not powered down.
The cell operates as a buffer when input and output sides of the cell are both powered up,
but provides a constant output signal during times that the input side is powered down. An
enable input controls the operating mode of the cell. An isolation cell is illustrated in the

Multi-Voltage Design (Multi-VDD)
Multi-Voltage Design (Multi-VDD)
In this technique, critical paths and blocks in the design are given access to maximum
voltage for the process and the specification, but voltage is reduced for those blocks that
need less power.
Different parts of a chip might have different speed requirements. For example, the CPU
and RAM blocks might need to be faster than a peripheral block. As mentioned earlier,
a lower supply voltage reduces power consumption, but also reduces speed. To get
maximum speed and lower power at the same time, CPU and RAM can operate with a
higher supply voltage while the peripheral block operates with a lower voltage, as shown in
the following figure:
Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling
In this technique, supply voltage and clock frequency is reduced based on workload that
results in a quarter of the power consumption. Voltage scaling techniques can be of the
following types:
• Dynamic - Here, a larger number of voltage levels are dynamically switched to follow
changing workloads.
• Adaptive - Here, a closed loop feedback system is used to adjust the voltage.

Adaptive Body-Biasing (ABB)
The following figure illustrates dynamic voltage and frequency scaling:
Adaptive Body-Biasing (ABB)
This technique is used to control the leakage current during stand-by and active mode.
Reverse body bias is used for stand-by mode and zero body bias is used for active mode.
ABB method reduces the leakage current exponentially. When body-to-source junction is
reversed biased, the voltage threshold increases, thus reducing the leakage.
Multiple-Vt Library Cells
Some CMOS technologies support the fabrication of transistors with different threshold
voltages (Vt values). In that case, the cell library can offer two or more different cells to
implement each logic function, each using a different transistor threshold voltage. For
example, the library can offer two inverter cells: one using low-Vt transistors and another
using high-Vt transistors.
In this technique, a low-threshold-voltage library is used for a first pass through synthesis
to get maximum performance and meet timing goals. Thereafter, the critical paths in the
design, that is, the path or paths in the design that require the highest performance, are
determined. Later, areas that do not require low-threshold-voltage cells are located and

Introduction
In many designs, it is important to analyze and report on the performance of a shared
resource utilization. The shared resource may be a bus, a memory, a DMA channel or any
other design element that is used by more than one initiator over a period of time.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
designs, it is important to analyze and report on the performance of a shared
resource utilization. The shared resource may be a bus, a memory, a DMA channel or any
other design element that is used by more than one initiator over a period of time.
As a generic VMM package, the Performance Analyzer (PAN) is not based on nor requires
specific shared resources, transactions or hardware structures. It can be used to collect
statistical coverage metrics relating to the utilization of a specific shared resource.
Performance is analyzed based on user-defined atomic resource utilization called tenures.
A tenure refers to any activity on a shared resource with a well-defined starting and ending
point. A tenure is uniquely identified by an automatically-assigned identifier. A tenure may
also identify a specific initiator or a specific target or both an initiator and a target.
For example, a tenure on a SoC bus could represent a write transaction from a specific
master to a specific slave.
Tenures may overlap if the shared resource can handle more than one operation
concurrently. Usually, tenures are mutually exclusive but can be suspended and later
resumed to allow a higher-priority tenure to access the shared resource.
Performance data is stored in an SQL database, one database per simulation run.
Performance metrics can then be subsequently generated from the SQL database.
Performance metrics can be reported for a single simulation only or they can be generated
from a database merged from multiple databases from other simulations. Please refer to
SQL Schema for a detailed description of the SQL schema used to store performance
data.

Analyzing Performance of a Resource
This chapter describes how to measure the performance of a resource. The examples
shown in this chapter are taken from the example that can be found in ${VMM_HOME}/
sv/perf/examples/tl_bus. The classes used to implement the measurement are
specified in Performance Analysis Support Classes.
Defining Performance
The first thing you need to know is exactly what you are analyzing. You can use the VMM
Performance Analysis package to measure and analyze many different performance
aspects of a design. At its core, it is a simple data collection engine that gives you the
ability to perform post-simulation statistical analysis and plotting of the collected data. It is
your decision what this data represents and how it conveys an analysis of a performance
aspect of the design.
Performance is measured for a specific resource (e.g. the entire design, a specific arbiter,
a memory or a bus). Individual transactions, requests or transformations are performed
on that resource. These individual transactions, requests or transformations are called
"tenures". The performance for the resource may be how it is utilized by the combination
of all the tenures performed on it. The performance may also be how fast the resource is
able to perform the combination of all the tenures.
For example, measuring the performance of an on-chip bus would involve measuring
how long it takes for each bus access. A tenure would thus correspond to a READ or
WRITE cycle on that bus. When measuring the performance of an arbiter, a tenure would
correspond to a request-grant operation.
Data is collected for each individual tenure that is performed on the resource whose
performance is being measured. Performance is analyzed in a post-processing step, using
the collected data to compute a specific metric (such as an average) or plot a specific
graph (such as latency vs arrival rate).

Data Collection
Collected Data
For each tenure, the Performance Analysis package collects the following data:
• Start and end time
• Who initiated it and who was the target
• How long it was active (end time minus start time minus time spent suspended)
• If it was aborted or completed
For an on-chip bus, the start and end time would correspond to the time the READ or
WRITE was started and eventually completed, respectively. The initiator identity would be
an integer identifying the bus master. The target identity would be an integer identifying the
targeted slave.
For an arbiter, the start time would correspond to the time when the request line is
asserted. The end time would correspond to the time when the corresponding grant line
is asserted or the request is removed. The latter might be marked as an aborted tenure.
The initiator identity would be an integer identifying the requestor. There would not be any
specific target identified as the target is the arbiter in all cases.
Data Collection
Data collection is the first step when analyzing the performance of a resource. Data is
collected for each resource in a separate instance of the vmm_perf_analyzer class. It is a
good idea to locate these instances in the extension of the vmm_env class implementing
your verification environment. These instances should be allocated in the build phase.
For example, two instances of the vmm_perf_analyzer class would be required to analyze
the performance of the on-chip bus and arbiter in the same design.
Example 1 Per-Resource Analyzer

vmm_sql_db_sqlite db;
vmm_perf_analyzer bus_perf;
vmm_perf_analyzer arb_perf;

this.db = new("perf_data.db");
this.bus_perf = new("Bus", this.db);
this.arb_perf = new("Arb", this.db);
endfunction: build

Tenures
Operations that consume the resource must be mapped into individual tenures. There
must be one instance of the vmm_perf_tenure class for each operation that is performed
on the bus. Tenures are associated with the instance of the vmm_perf_analyzer class that
corresponds to the resource operated on.
The start and end times of a tenure is identified by calling the
vmm_perf_analyzer::start_tenure() and vmm_perf_analyzer::end_tenure() methods
respectively.
How and where a tenure is created and updated depends on the capabilities of the
verification environment and of the transactors it contains. Much like functional coverage
sampling, they can be created and updated by monitoring channels, notifications or
callbacks.
For example, a tenure on an on-chip bus can be tracked by grabbing the bus
transaction descriptor at the exit of the transaction generator then waiting for the
vmm_data::STARTED and vmm_data::ENDED indications.
Example 5 Creating and Managing a Tenure

bus_tr tr,
ref bit drop);
vmm_perf_tenure tenure = new();
env.bus_perf.start_tenure(tenure);
tr.notify.wait_for(vmm_data::ENDED);
env.bus_perf.end_tenure(tenure);
end
endtask: post_inst_gen

SQL Schema
An instance of the vmm_perf_analyzer class will store all performance data collected
during a single simulation in a single data table.
When instantiating a performance analyzer object, you choose which database the data
table will be created in by specifying an instance of the vmm_sql_db class. The data table
will be created in the database associated with the access class specified at the creation
of the performance analyzer object. As illustrated in Figure 1, a single simulation can thus
create multiple tables (one per vmm_perf_analyzer instance) in one or more databases
(one per vmm_sql_db instance).
Figure 1 Simulations and Databases

Data tables are named after the name of the vmm_perf_analyzer class instance with
which they are associated. Care must be taken that data tables be uniquely named within
the same database. If a different database is used for each data table, care must be taken
that the databases be uniquely named across different simulation running concurrently on
a CPU farm.

SQL Schema
Merging operations will likely be easier if a single database is used for all of the data
tables for a single simulation run.
Runs Table
The SQL access layer creates in each database a table named "vmm_runs" that contains
one row for each simulation run whose data is included in the database. There is only one
runs table in a database. The runs table is the top-level table that is used to navigate the
performance data stored in a database. The following table describes the schema used for
the runs table.
Table 1 Runs Table Schema
Name Type Description
hostname VARCHAR(255) Hostname where simulation was run.
utime INTEGER Unix timestamp of the system real clock time when
the first DB was opened, specified as the number
of seconds elapsed since 00:00:00 on January 1,
1970 (UTC)
systime VARCHAR(30) The local system real clock time when the first
DB was opened formatted as "YYYYMMDD
HH::MM::SS".
tzone SMALLINT Decimal representation of the HHMM (e.g. -730
for -7:30) offset between local time and UTC
[-1200..1200].
seed INTEGER Initial seed used.
tables VARCHAR(255) Name of the data table list table
When merging database data from different runs, the content of the individual runs tables
should be concatenated into a single runs table.
Data Table List Table
The SQL access layer maintains a table in each database that enumerates the names of
all the data tables created during a specific run in that database. The name of the data
table list table is implementation-specific and can be obtained from the runs table entry
corresponding to the run. The following table describes the schema used for the data table
list table.

SQL Schema
Table 2 Data Table List Table Schema
Name Type Description
tblname VARCHAR(255) Data table name.
datakind TINYINT 0x00=Performance Data, other values are
user-defined.
When merging database data from different runs, the merged set of data table list tables is
composed of all the data table list tables in each database.
vmm_perf_analyzer Data Table
Each instance of the vmm_perf_analyzer class creates a data table containing a record of
the performance data for each terminated tenure. The name of the data table is specified
by the user when vmm_perf_analyzer::new() is called and can be obtained from the data
list table. The following table describes the schema used for the data table.
Table 3 Performance Analyzer Data Table Schema
Name Type Description
tenureID INTEGER Tenure identifier.
initiatorID INTEGER Tenure initiator identifier. -1 if none.
targetID INTEGER Tenure target identifier. -1 if none.
start BIGINT Absolute time of tenure start.
end BIGINT Absolute time of tenure completion.
active BIGINT Amount of time tenure was active.
aborted TINYINT 0: Tenure completed normally. Was aborted
otherwise.
user user Additional user-defined columns, as defined in
vmm_sql_db::create_table()
When merging database data from different runs, the merged set of data tables is
composed of all the data tables in each database.

Linking SQL with VCS
Linking SQL with VCS
There are many different implementations of SQL-compatible databases. The VMM SQL
interface currently supports SQLite. Instruction for installing and using the appropriate SQL
implementation are provided in this section.
If neither of these SQL implementation is readily available, a simple-minded ASCII

interface currently supports SQLite. Instruction for installing and using the appropriate SQL

If neither of these SQL implementation is readily available, a simple-minded ASCII
database implementation is available without requiring any SQL code in your VCS
simulation. See vmm_sql_db_ascii for more details.
SQLite
If you use the vmm_sql_db_sqlite class, it is necessary to include the required SQLite
code in your VCS simulation.
This version of the VMM Performance Analysis package has been developed and tested
using SQLite 3.3.16 and should also work on slightly older versions. A binary or source
distribution can be obtained at:
http://www.sqlite.org/download.html
Follow the instructions included in the distribution to compile and install SQLite. Ensure
that the options used to build SQLite match the configuration of the VCS installation you
will be using. For example, the -m32 option will be required if a 32bit VCS installation is
used on a 64-bit machine.
The environment variable SQLITE3_HOME should be set to the absolute path of the SQLite
installation. This will make it easier to relocate an environment to a different network where
the location of the SQLite installation may be different
% setenv SQLITE3_HOME /path/to/sqlite3
The following files must then be available:
${SQLITE3_HOME}/include/sqlite3.h
${SQLITE3_HOME}/lib/libsqlite3.so
The path ${SQLITE3_HOME}/lib must be added to your LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment
variable:
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH ${SQLITE3_HOME}/lib:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH}
When invoking VCS, you must specify the following command-line options:
% vcs $VMM_HOME/shared/src/vmm_sqlite_interface.c \
-CFLAGS -I${SQLITE3_HOME}/include

User Data
ASCII Database
If you use the vmm_sql_db_ascii class, it is necessary to include the required
implementation support code in your VCS simulation.
When invoking VCS, you must specify the following command-line options:
% vcs $VMM_HOME/shared/src/vmm_sqltxt_interface.c
User Data
If required, it is possible to add user-defined data to the SQL database. Data that is valid
for the entire simulation can be added as a user-defined table. Data that is valid for a
specific tenure can be added to the performance data table.
User-Defined Data Table
A user-defined table can be created in a SQL database to store information that pertains
to the entire simulation. For example, DUT configuration information could be stored in a
user-defined table.
A user-defined table is created using the vmm_sql_db::create_table() method. The user-
defined table will be added to the Data Table List Table. The data type and name of each
column must be defined as a string of comma-separated names and types.
Example 6 Creating a User-Defined Data Table
vmm_sql_db_sqlite db = new();
vmm_sql_table cfg_data = db.create_table("cfg",
"num_masters INTEGER, num_slaves INTEGER");
Data can be added to the table by using the vmm_sql_table::insert() method. This
method can be called repeatedly to add new rows in the user-defined data table. A table
containing configuration information would typically contain only one row. The data is
added as a string of comma-separated formatted values corresponding to each column
defined at the time of the table creation.
Example 7 Adding Data to a User-Defined Data Table
cfg_tbl.insert($psprintf("%0d, %0d", this.cfg.bus.n_masters,
this.cfg.bus.n_slaves));
When creating a table, it is a good idea to ensure that its name will be unique when
merged with other databases.

User-Defined Tenure Data
User-defined data can be added to the performance data for each tenure. This user-
defined data is then stored in the SQL database and resides in the same table row as
the other performance data for that tenure. For example, a clock cycle count timestamp
information could be stored with each tenure.
User-defined tenure data must be defined when the instance of the vmm_perf_analyzer
class is created. The data type and name of each additional performance data column
must be defined as a string of comma-separated names and types.
Example 8 Adding User-Defined Performance Data

vmm_sql_db_sqlite db;
vmm_perf_analyzer bus_perf;
vmm_perf_analyzer arb_perf;

this.db = new("perf_data.db");
this.bus_perf = new("Bus", this.db);
this.arb_perf = new("Arb", this.db, , , , "stamp BIGINT");
endfunction: build

endclass: tb_env
Additional tenure data must be specified when the vmm_perf_analyzer::end_tenure()
method is called. The data is specified as a string of comma-separated formatted values
corresponding to each additional column defined at the time of the performance analyzer
creation.
Example 9 Specifying User-Defined Performance Data
this.env.arb_perf.end_tenure(tenure, $psprintf("%0d", cycle_count));
In the Verification Methodology Manual (VMM) package, Performance Analyzer
(PAN) supports Universal Verification Methodology (UVM), Open Verification
Methodology (OVM), and third-party class types. Use PAN to measure and analyze
different performance aspects of your design. PAN uses Object Policy classes and
parameterization to extend support to UVM, OVM, and other custom class libraries.
The main element in policy-based design is a class template named the host class. You
provide several type parameters to this template. You select types for these parameters,

called policy classes. Each policy class defines a specific method, known as a policy. Each
policy class controls a separate aspect of the host class’s behavior.
By providing a host class and several ready-made policy implementations, you can create
many behavior combinations. Resolve these combinations at compile time. Select the
behavior you need by mixing and matching different policy classes when you instantiate
the host class template. If you need a behavior not included in the library, write a custom
policy implementation. Use this approach to support situations the library designer did not
anticipate.

Performance Analysis Support Classes
This appendix provides detailed information about the classes that are used to implement
and support performance analysis.
The OpenVera and SystemVerilog classes have identical functionality and features.
Therefore, this appendix documents this information together. The heading used to
introduce a method uses the SystemVerilog name. The OpenVera name will be identical
except for the few cases where a _t suffix is appended to indicate that it may be a
blocking method.
Usage examples are usually specified in a single language. However, that should not deter
users of the other language as they would be almost identical. This appendix provides
more, different examples instead of nearly identical examples in each language.
The classes are documented in alphabetical order. The methods in each class are
documented in a logical order, where methods that accomplish similar results are
documented sequentially. A summary of all available methods with cross references to
the page where their detailed documentation can be found is provided at the beginning of
each class specification.
Class Summary
• vmm_perf_analyzer
• vmm_perf_tenure
This class is a performance analyzer for a single shared resource and a single simulation.
There must be an instance of this class for each shared resource whose performance is to
be independently analyzed. For example, in a SoC design with two busses, two instances
should be used if the performance of each bus is to be independently analyzed.
For guidelines on using this class, see Analyzing Performance of a Resource.

vmm_perf_analyzer::new()
Create a new instance of a performance analyzer.
function new( string name,
vmm_sql_db db,
int unsigned max_n_iniators = 0,
int unsigned max_n_targets = 0,
int unsigned max_n_concurrent = 1,
string user_schema = "")
task new( string name,
vmm_sql_db db,
integer max_n_iniators = 0,
integer max_n_targets = 0,

integer max_n_concurrent = 1,
string user_schema = "")
Create an instance of a performance analyzer for a specific shared resource with the
specified name. The specified name will be used as the name of the table that will contain
the performance data collected by this instance. It must be unique within a simulation but
similar across different simulation for the same resource. The specified name is also used
as the instance name of the message interface found in the vmm_perf_analyzer::log class
property.
A maximum number of tenure initiators, tenure targets and concurrent tenures can also be
specified. By default, only one tenure can exist from an unlimited number of initiators on
an unlimited number of targets. If a maximum number of initiators or targets is specified,
an error will be issued if tenures associated with this performance analyzer identify more
initiators or targets than the analyzer supports. This is an absolute maximum number of
initiators or targets, not the maximum value for the initiator or target identifiers.
Specifying 0 as the maximum number of initiators, targets or concurrently active tenures
specifies no maximum number.
Additional user-defined data columns can be added to the table schema. They are
appended to the pre-defined columns (see SQL Schema ) and are specified as additional
comma-separated creation definitions (see vmm_sql_db::create_table()). If additional
user-defined data columns are specified, data for these columns must be specified when
calling vmm_perf_analyzer::end_tenure().
Example 10
vmm_perf_analyzer arbitor_perf;
this.arbitor_perf = new("ARBITOR", db, 0, 0,
this.masters.size(), "");

vmm_perf_analyzer::now()
Get current time for the resource.
virtual function time now();
virtual function bit[63:0] now();

Return the current absolute time used to measure resource usage. Can be simulation time
(the default), or any other user-defined time measure, such a clock cycle count.
By default, returns the current simulation time.

string str;
$swrite(str, "Report generated at Time : %t", ad_bus_perf.now());

vmm_perf_analyzer::suspend_tenure()
Specify the suspension of a tenure.
function void suspend_tenure( vmm_perf_tenure tenure);
task suspend_tenure( vmm_perf_tenure tenure);
Indicates that the specified tenure has been suspended. A suspended tenure no longer
utilizes the shared resource but is not yet completed. Suspending a tenure will not shorten
its start-to-end duration measurement. Suspending a tenure will reduce the utilization of
the shared resource. A suspended tenure must eventually be resumed to be completed.

Other tenures may be started while a tenure is suspended without affecting the suspended
tenure. A suspended tenure does not count toward the maximum number of concurrently
active tenures on the shared resource.
If the specified tenure is not currently active on the shared resource, an error is reported.
A write transaction that is interrupted by a retry status may be specified as suspended and
will resume once it is retried.
A DMA channel access that is interrupted by a higher priority request may also be
specified as suspended and will resume once access is regained.
Example 14
vmm_perf_tenure tenure = new(gen.stream_id,
if (tr.status == bus_tr::RETRY)
this.env.ad_bus_perf.suspend_tenure(tenure);
end

Indicates that the specified tenure has been completed. A completed tenure no longer
utilizes the shared resource and cannot be suspended nor resumed.
A completed tenure no longer counts toward the maximum number of concurrently active

If the specified tenure is not currently active on the shared resource, an error is reported.

vmm_perf_analyzer::abort_tenure()
Specify the premature end of a tenure.

function void abort_tenure( vmm_perf_tenure tenure,
string more_data = "");
task abort_tenure( vmm_perf_tenure tenure,
string more_data = "");
Indicates that the specified tenure has been aborted. An aborted tenure represents a
wasted use of a shared resource and is tracked separately from completed tenures. An
aborted tenure no longer utilizes the shared resource and cannot be suspended nor
resumed.
An aborted tenure no longer counts toward the maximum number of concurrently active
tenures on the shared resource.
If additional user-defined columns in the SQL table associated with this performance
analyzer instance were specified (see vmm_perf_analyzer::new()), a string of suitable
comma-separated data value images must be provided.
If the specified tenure is not currently active on the shared resource, an error is reported.
Note:
For VMM Performance Analyzer, if no tenures are aborted, the value reported
for the same in the text report will be marked as -1.
Example 17
vmm_perf_tenure tenure = new(gen.stream_id,
if (tr.status == bus_tr::IS_OK)
this.env.ad_bus_perf.abort_tenure(tenure);
end
