Create a human-readable report of simple performance metrics (minimum, maximum and
average tenure durations and percentage of utilization) for the shared resource associated
with this instance of the performance analyzer, for this simulation.
If a filename is specified, the report is written to the specified file instead of the standard
output.
If an initiator and/or target identifier is specified, metrics are provided for that initiator and/
or target.
To open the report in append mode, the third argument should be a which enables the file
in write mode.
The report includes all performance data collected so far. Subsequent reports will contain
this data and any data subsequently collected.

vmm_perf_tenure::new()
Create a new instance of a tenure descriptor
function new( int unsigned initiator_id = 0,
int unsigned target_id = 0,
vmm_data tr = null);
task new( integer initiator_id = 0,
integer target_id = 0,
rvm_data tr = null);
Create an instance of a tenure descriptor. The identity of the initiator or target of the
tenure may be optionally specified. A transaction descriptor describing the transaction
corresponding to the utilization of the shared resource may also be associated with the
tenure descriptor to ease traceability and debugging.
The mapping of initiator or target identifier to actual hardware structures (such as a bus
master or slave) or software thread (such as an interrupt service routine) is left to the user.
A performance analysis for a specific resource may limit the maximum number of unique
initiators or targets. This limits the absolute number of different initiator or slave identifiers,
not their identifier values. This is designed to catch usage errors in pre-defined hardware
structures. For example, a specific SoC has a pre-determined number of bus masters
or bus slaves. It is thus impossible to have tenures with more unique initiator or target
identifiers than bus master or slaves, respectively.

SQL Database Support Classes
This appendix provides detailed information about the classes that are used to implement
and support a generic interface to one or more SQL databases.
The OpenVera and SystemVerilog classes have identical functionality and features.
Therefore, this appendix documents this information together. The heading used to
introduce a method uses the SystemVerilog name. The OpenVera name will be identical
except for the few cases where a _t suffix is appended to indicate that it may be a
blocking method.
Usage examples are usually specified in a single language. However, that should not deter
users of the other languages as they would be almost identical. This appendix provides
more, different examples instead of nearly identical examples in each language.
The classes are documented in alphabetical order. The methods in each class are
documented in a logical order, where methods that accomplish similar results are
documented sequentially. A summary of all available methods with cross references to the
page where their detailed documentation exists is provided at the beginning of each class
specification.

interpreted using a PERL script to reconstruct the content of individual tables.

Overview
This document describes how to declare equivalent Verilog packed and unpacked arrays/
vectors in VHDL.
In general, VHDL has no pre-defined two dimensional or multidimensional unpacked
arrays. You must specify these packed/unpacked arrays/vectors when required. To specify
these packed/unpacked arrays/vectors, define the type keyword. When type is defined,
you can declare the new signal, variable, or constant using the data type as shown in
the following code:
type arr_typ is array (0 tO 7) of std_logic_vector (7 downto 0);
<--- Unpacked dimensions---> <--- Packed dimensions--->
signal x : arr_typ ;
Arrays in Verilog language constitute of multidimensional arrays both in packed and
unpacked dimensions. The dimensions declared before the object name are referred to as
the vector width/packed dimensions. The dimensions declared after the object name are
referred to as the array dimensions/unpacked dimensions as shown in the following code:
reg [7:0 ] x [0:7] ;
<--Packed dimensions--> <--Unpacked dimensions-->

Introduction
In VCS Native Low Power (NLP), gate-level netlist simulations are not the same as RTL
simulations. In addition to the design (gates and models) and the UPF, VCS NLP also
needs .db files for library cells and the corresponding behavioral model for the cell. This
document describes non-PG netlist simulation flow with VCS NLP.

Using Library Files for Simulation
Following is the use model to use the library files for simulation. The library files contain
library cell information.
Use the following search path and link library command in the configuration file. You can
specify this file as an argument to the -power_config <file_name> compile-time option.
db_search_path = {path of db files}
db_link_library = {.db files}
Following is the syntax to run the testcase:
% vcs <design_files> -v <behavioral_model_file> -upf file.upf
-power_config lp_config

Database (DB) Cell Matching Criteria
The following conditions must be satisfied for the cell definition in the .db file to be termed
as matched to the RTL behavioral model:
• Name of the Verilog model and the DB cell must match
• All RTL ports must match the cell logic pins in name and width
• Any RTL port matching DB PG pin must not have width greater than 1
Cell information is captured in the mvsim_native_reports/library_mapping report file.
Matched/Non-matched cells are listed in the mvsim_native_reports/library_match
report file.

Power Aware and Non-Power Aware Models
The model for a cell may or may not include PG pins. A model which does not contain PG
pins is referred to as a “non-power aware” model. If PG pins are present in a model, they
must exactly match what is present in the .db representation, otherwise VCS NLP treats it
as a non-power aware model.
In a power aware model, the PG pins can be:
• input/output ports of the model
• reg/wire
• supply_net_type
• supply0/supply1 type

Simulation Behavior for Power Aware Models
If a model is recognized as power aware, it means that the model itself completely
describes the power behavior. That is, VCS NLP does not corrupt anything inside the
model; it only drives the appropriate supply values to the PG pins of the cell. The model
takes care of corruption.
For example, in the following power aware model, the output pin Z is corrupted to x when
the PG pin VDD is turned off.
module BUFFD0HVT (I, Z, VDD, VSS);
input I, VDD, VSS;
output Z;
assign Z = (VDD) ? I : 1'bx;
endmodule
To force VCS NLP to corrupt the ports for all cells even when the models are power aware:
set_design_attributes -attribute \
SNPS_override_pbp_corruption TRUE

Simulation Behavior for Non-Power Aware
Models
If a model is recognized as non-power aware, VCS NLP corrupts the following:
• Output ports of the cell based on the power-down function
• Input ports of the cell based on related power and ground pins
If there is no power-down function, VCS NLP uses the related_power_pin attribute
to corrupt the ports. You can override the above default behavior by using the following
set_design_attributes commands.
To force VCS NLP not to corrupt the ports for all cells even when the models are non-
power aware:
set_design_attributes -attribute \
SNPS_override_pbp_corruption FALSE

Implicit Supply Net Connections
The UPF may have connect_supply_net (CSN) commands to the PG pins of various
cells. If there is no CSN in the UPF, then the PG pin is assumed to be connected to the
primary power or the primary ground of the domain containing the cell.
The isolation cells (ISO/ELS) and the retention cells are exceptions to this rule. If the
UPF contains isolation strategies, VCS NLP tries to match isolation strategies with the
implemented ISO and ELS cells in the netlist. Once an ISO cell is matched with a strategy,
isolation_power_net and isolation_ground_net specified in the strategy are implicitly
connected to the PG pins of the ISO cell.

In the Synopsys low power flow, explicit CSN is required for the level shifter cells, else the
level shifter cells are treated as always-on cells, and no implicit connections are made to
the PG pins.
If there is an explicit CSN, that connectivity is honored. Similarly, if there is a retention
strategy, VCS NLP tries to associate the retention cell with a strategy. If there is no explicit
CSN, the retention power/ground nets in the strategy implicitly drive the backup PG pins of
the retention cell.
For the blocks that are not bias enabled using the enable_bias design attribute,
unconnected bias PG pins (pwell/nwell) are tied to domain supplies implicitly; pwell is tied
to the primary ground, and nwell is tied to the primary power of the domain. To keep the
unconnected bias PG pins ON, use the -power=unconnected_bias_pins_on compile-
time option.

Basic Information to be Shared With the
Synopsys Support Center to Expedite a Case
Resolution
This document lists the basic information that needs to be shared with the Synopsys
Support Center to expedite a case resolution. The document includes the following
section:
• Providing Basic Information to the Synopsys Support Center
Basic Information to be Shared With the Synopsys Support Center to Expedite a Case Resolution

Providing Basic Information to the Synopsys
Support Center
The information that needs to be provided to Synopsys support center depends on the
issues or queries that are reported by the user. These information helps in expediting the
root cause of the problem and suggesting the appropriate solution quickly.
For any errors or problems, mention the criticality of the problem and impact at your end
explicitly along with the following information. This helps in attributing the right priority to
your issue.
• Provide the mandatory information as follows:
◦ For any problem related to VCS, provide the VCS release version. Run the
following command to provide the VCS release version:
% vcs -id or
% vcs -full64 -id (for 64-bit)
VCS generates the following information:
vcs script version: M-2017.03
machine name = xxxxxx
machine type = linux
machine os = Linux 2.6.32-642.13.1.el6.x86_64
The FLEXlm host ID of this machine is "101f742f9512 101f742f9510
101f742f9526 101f742f9524"
Compiler version = VCS M-2017.03
VCS Build Date = Feb 15 2017 20:40:41
If you need to renew your license, please email this information
to your Account Manager. To obtain contact information for your
Account Manager please email pass@synopsys.com
◦ Similarly, for any problem related Verdi tool, provide the Verdi release version. Run
the following command to provide the Verdi release version:
% verdi -id or
% verdi -full64 -id (For 64-bit)
Verdi generates the following information:

machine name = vgintwm222

machine os = 2.6.32-642.13.1.el6.x86_64
Product version = Verdi_M-2017.03 (RH Linux x86_64/64bit)

Product Build Date = Mon Feb 13 04:07:59 PDT 2017
Build type = opt

If you need to renew your license, please email this information
to your Account Manager. To obtain contact information for your
Account Manager please email pass@synopsys.com
◦ Provide all the VCS compilation and simulation command lines and compilation and
simulation log files to understand the exact usage. You should use the -l and -V
option to generate the log file during compilation or simulation as follows:
% vcs -V -l comp.log <other compilation switches>
% simv -l run.log <other runtime switches>
Provide the complete test case along with the proper README.txt file (that provides
all the relevant information related to the test case). You can provide the test
case as an attachment or upload the test case to Synopsys FTP site (see https://
solvnet.synopsys.com/retrieve/036451.html ). This helps the support center to recreate
the problem at their end, analyze the problem, and provide a suitable solution.
If it is not possible to share the complete test case, provide the source file or the
snippet of the code within the source file on which the error is reported.
Basic Information to be Shared With the Synopsys Support Center to Expedite a Case Resolution

Chapter 2: Providing Basic Information to the Synopsys Support Center

• Along with the above information, you can also provide information pertaining to
specific scenarios as follows:
◦ For tool crashes (compilation or simulation) or segmentation faults, provide the
complete log file and the complete command line or provide the complete context

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
rmation, you can also provide information pertaining to
specific scenarios as follows:
◦ For tool crashes (compilation or simulation) or segmentation faults, provide the
complete log file and the complete command line or provide the complete context
information followed by the stack trace. Whenever a tool crashes, it provides a
stack trace preceded by some context information regarding the crash as shown:
◦ For simulation time or memory performance issues, try the simulation profiler
at your end and analyze. For further assistance and analysis, share the
profileReport files. To generate the profile reports, use the following commands:
% vcs -simprofile <other compilation switches>
% simv -simprofile <'mem' OR 'time'>
The commands generates the profileReportdirectory and profileReport.*
files.
◦ For coverage related issues, provide the URG/Verdi command line along with the
coverage database (.vdb) information. Also, for any GUI related issues in coverage,
provide the relevant snapshots along with specific steps or action to recreate the
problem and analyze the same at our end.
◦ For issues related to Verdi, provide the relevant snapshots along with the specific
steps or actions to recreate the problem and analyze the same at our end. Also, for
FSDB or KDB related issues, share the Verdi logs.
Basic Information to be Shared With the Synopsys Support Center to Expedite a Case Resolution

Chapter 2: Providing Basic Information to the Synopsys Support Center

◦ If it is not possible to share the above information, remote access is another
option. The remote access can be a dedicated VPN access provided to Synopsys
support center or using a View Connect session (https://solvnet.synopsys.com/
retrieve/903285.html) or a WebEx session based on your availability. The preferable
option between WebEx and View Connect, is using a View Connect session
as it requires users’ intervention only for establishing the connection. Once the
connection is established, users’ desktop need not be occupied while Synopsys
debug the problem unlike WebEx.

Recommendations to Solve X-Related Issues
From RTL to GLS
This document discusses the features provided in VCS MX to identify X-related issues.
This document includes the following sections:
• Introduction
• Using the X-Propagation Technology
• Initializing Verilog Variables, Registers, and Memories
Introduction
Designers use RTL constructs to describe hardware behaviors. However, certain RTL
simulation semantics are insufficient to accurately model the hardware behaviors.
Therefore, simulation results are either too optimistic or pessimistic than the actual
hardware behaviors.
This is one of the reasons to run the netlist simulation. The netlist simulation helps you to
identify issues related to uninitialized registers and timing amongst others.
Debugging issues at netlist level is tedious and time consuming. To minimize the time
spent during Gate-Level Simulation (GLS) qualification, VCS MX provides features to
identify such X-related issues in RTL.
Using the X-Propagation Technology
Standard RTL simulations ignore the uncertainty of X-valued control signals and assign
predictable output values. Thus, RTL simulations often fail to detect design problems
related to the lack of
X-Propagation. However, the same design problems can be detected during GLS.
The simulation semantics of Verilog and VHDL control constructs is insufficient to account
for the ambiguity of statements executed under X control. A more accurate simulation
model to handle indeterminate control signals is to execute the design with a 0 and 1
control signal and then merge the results.
Recommendations to Solve X-Related Issues From RTL to GLS
Y-2026.03-SP2

Chapter 1: Recommendations to Solve X-Related Issues From RTL to GLS
Initializing Verilog Variables, Registers, and Memories
The VCS MX Xprop simulator provides the above mentioned simulation model that allows
Xprop problems to be exposed by standard RTL simulations.
You can specify various Xprop behaviors using a configuration file. In the Xprop
configuration file, you can specify the top-level module of a Design Under Test (DUT) and
enable Xprop on the DUT instance tree. The Xprop technology is targeted for designs
simulating actual hardware (synthesizable RTL code).
The Xprop usage model compiles the design in Xprop mode and execute the simv
executable. The -xprop compile-time option is used to enable Xprop and to specify the
merge mode at runtime. By default, VCS MX uses the tmerge merge mode. However, you
can specify a different merge mode at either compile time or runtime.
For more details on X-propagation, please refer to “Using X-Propagation” chapter in the
VCS/VCS MX User Guide.
Initializing Verilog Variables, Registers, and Memories
VCS MX provides a way to initialize all the design nodes with random or fixed values
at time 0. This can help you to detect if the design can be reset properly and can be
recovered from a random state.
You can use one of the following compile-time options to initialize Verilog variables,
registers and memories in a design:
• +vcs+initreg+random
This option enables initialization for an entire design.
• +vcs+initreg+config+config_file
This option enables initialization for the selective parts of a design.
For more information on the +vcs+initreg option, refer to the “Elaborating the Design”
chapter in the VCS/VCS MX User Guide.

Recommended Debug Settings for a New Project
Y-2026.03-SP2

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
VCS Settings
Set the VCS_HOME environment variable to the path where VCS MX is installed:
% setenv VCS_HOME <VCS_installation_path>
Set the UNIX PATH variable to $VCS_HOME/bin:
% set path = ($VCS_HOME/bin $path)
Recommended Debug Settings for a New Project
Y-2026.03-SP2

Verdi Settings
Set the VERDI_HOME environment variable to point to the installation directory:
% setenv VERDI_HOME < Verdi_installation_path>
Set the UNIX PATH variable to $VERDI_HOME/bin:
% set path = ($VERDI_HOME/bin $path)
Recommended Debug Settings for a New Project
Y-2026.03-SP2

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Debug Mode Settings
You can debug the simulation using Verdi in the following modes:
Interactive Simulation Debug Mode
This debug mode allows you to debug your design interactively.
The recommended debug option for interactive debug is -debug_access+all.
For example:
% vcs -debug_access+all -kdb <other compile-time options> <design file>
% ./simv -gui=verdi <other runtime options>
Post-Processing Debug Mode
This debug mode allows you to debug your design using a database (FSDB).
The recommended debug option for post-process debug is -debug_access.
% vcs -debug_access -kdb <other compile-time options> <design file>
% ./simv <other runtime options> // FSDB file is generated when design
has "$fsdbDumpvars"
% verdi -ssf <fsdb file> -nologo &
Note:
FSDB file must be generated using the $fsdbDumpvars system task or the
UCLI dump command.

Methodology to Verify Timing Constraints at RTL
With VCS SDC
Modern SOC designs demand aggressive timing closure strategies to meet performance
targets without architectural redesign. Design teams increasingly rely on timing exceptions
—multi-cycle paths (MCPs) and false paths defined in Synopsys Design Constraints
(SDC)—to achieve convergence without over-designing combinational logic or adding
pipeline stages. Yet these same exceptions, when functionally unverified, creates critical
silicon escape risks that result in costly respins, schedule delays, and loss of market
opportunities.
Traditionally, timing exceptions have been verified through timing-annotated gate-level
simulations. This approach has three significant limitations:
• Simulation speed is 10–100× slower than RTL.
• Complex bring-up, requiring gate netlists and timing libraries.
• Debugging challenges that obscure root causes under layers of synthesis
transformations.
These limitations result in inadequate coverage of exception corner cases and heightened
risk of bugs escaping to silicon, where debug costs escalate exponentially.
The industry needs RTL-level SDC verification that combines simulation speed with
timing-aware checking. This application note presents the VCS SDC dynamic verification
solution, which brings timing intent validation into the RTL domain. It examines critical
failure modes that zero-delay RTL simulation cannot detect, including MCP endpoint
violations, false path activations, and timing-functional mismatches; and demonstrates
how automated checker insertion and metastability modeling expose these bugs during
standard regression testing.
This application note contains the following sections:
• Motivation
• Verification Hierarchy for SDC
• SDC Lint/Static Checks
• Formal Verification

Motivation
• Dynamic Verification
• False Paths: Proving Functional Impossibility
• Debug
• Coverage: Measuring SDC Verification Completeness
• Conclusion
Motivation
SDC verification failures manifest across multiple dimensions, each with distinct silicon risk
profiles. The following categories describe the most critical failure modes that RTL- level
verification must address to prevent costly downstream escapes.
• Mismatch Between RTL Intent and Timing Constraints
RTL designers implement functional logic assuming specific timing relationships, while
timing engineers apply SDC constraints that might misinterpret that intent. When these
diverge—such as a three-cycle RTL protocol marked as a four-cycle MCP—the design
simulates correctly but fails in silicon. Traditional zero-delay simulation cannot detect
this class of errors because both the RTL and the SDC are independently correct in
their respective domains.
• Early Detection of Timing Issues
Timing violations discovered during post-synthesis analysis trigger expensive design
iterations: RTL modifications, re-synthesis, static timing re-closure, and regression re-
runs. Each iteration consumes days to weeks of schedule. Identifying incorrect MCP
specifications or missing false path declarations during RTL verification—when design
changes cost hours instead of weeks—compresses convergence cycles and reduces
project risk.
• Constraint Coverage and Completeness
Incomplete SDC specifications create silent failures. A missing false path declaration
forces timing tools to over-constrain a path that never functionally activates, wasting

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
ce cycles and reduces
project risk.
• Constraint Coverage and Completeness
Incomplete SDC specifications create silent failures. A missing false path declaration
forces timing tools to over-constrain a path that never functionally activates, wasting
area and power on unnecessary buffering. Conversely, a missing MCP on a legitimate
multi-cycle protocol creates a setup violation that synthesis cannot fix without
microarchitectural changes. Verification must prove that all timing-critical paths carry
appropriate constraints and those constraints align with functional behavior.
• Functional and Timing Consistency
Zero-delay RTL simulation validates functional correctness under ideal timing
assumptions—all signals propagate instantaneously, setup and hold times are
irrelevant, and multi-cycle relationships collapse to single-cycle behavior. This creates

Verification Hierarchy for SDC
a critical verification gap: designs pass all functional tests yet fail when timing-realistic
delays reveal race conditions, metastability windows or setup violations. Bridging this
gap requires injecting timing awareness into RTL simulation without sacrificing debug
efficiency.
• Design Robustness and Quality
Late-stage constraint fixes—discovered during gate-level simulation, or, worse,
in silicon—cascade into multiple verification domains. A corrected false path may
invalidate formal proofs, change power profiles, or expose functional bugs previously
masked by timing optimizations. Catching constraint errors early improves design
quality by ensuring that all downstream verification flows (formal, power, and synthesis)
operate on timing-accurate assumptions from the start.
Verification Hierarchy for SDC
Comprehensive SDC verification relies on a three-pronged approach, with each aspect
targeting distinct failure classes:
• Lint/Static Analysis: Validates the syntactic and structural integrity of SDC files in
conjunction with the design topology; clock definitions, constraint syntax, hierarchical
path validity.
• Formal Verification: Proves timing intent for bounded designs through exhaustive
state exploration, generating incremental SDC for paths that exceed capacity limits.
• Dynamic Verification: Simulates timing-aware behavior during Register Transfer
Level (RTL) regression, detecting violations through checker insertion and metastability
modeling.

SDC Lint/Static Checks
Figure 1 SDC Verification Workflow
Figure 1 illustrates this verification workflow alongside the corresponding Synopsys tool
solutions: SpyGlass CDC (Clock Domain Crossing) for static analysis, VC Formal/Timing
Constraints Manager (TCM) for formal verification, and VCS SDC for dynamic simulation.
This application note focuses on the dynamic verification domain, where timing intent must
be validated against functional stimulus under realistic corner cases that formal methods
alone cannot scale to address.
Note:
This RTL-level verification flow integrates into a broader SDC management
methodology that includes back-end correlation (ensuring synthesis applies
constraints correctly) and incremental constraint refinement.
SDC Lint/Static Checks
Just as RTL code undergoes lint checking for coding violations and structural hazards,
SDC files require analogous validation. SDC defines timing intent through constraint

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
SDC Lint/Static Checks
commands that reference design objects (pins, ports, clocks) and specify relationships
(clock groups, exceptions, input/output delays). Syntactic errors—malformed commands,
invalid clock periods, non-existent pin references—prevent downstream tools from
correctly interpreting intent. Structural errors—conflicting constraints, incomplete clock
definitions, missing clock group declarations—creating ambiguous timing scenarios that
synthesis resolves unpredictably.
Detecting these errors during RTL development, alongside regular code checks, ensures a
correct-by-construction constraint methodology. You can integrate SDC lint into continuous
integration flows, apply waiver management to known issues, and enforce constraint
quality standards before functional verification begins.

Clock Domain Crossing (CDC) Considerations
Clock domain crossing verification intersects with SDC validation, especially for clock
relationship declarations. CDC checkers validate that asynchronous clock domain

Formal Verification
boundaries employ proper synchronizers and that set_clock_groups -asynchronous
declarations align with synchronizer placement. Specific CDC issues include the following:
• Metastability Risks at Synchronizer Boundaries: Data launched from one clock
domain and captured in another without proper synchronization.
• Missing Synchronizers: Structural CDC paths lacking the required flip-flop stages to
resolve metastability.
• Data Coherency Violations: Multi-bit buses crossing clock domains without gray-
coding or valid-based protocols.
• Reconvergence Hazards: Synchronized signals reconverging through different delay
paths, potentially causing transient glitches.
Note:
These checks are important; however, they are outside the scope of this
application note. For more information, see the SpyGlass VC CDC product
documentation.
Formal Verification
Formal methods provide an exhaustive proof of timing intent correctness across all
reachable design states. For bounded design partitions, formal SDC verification can
mathematically prove that no input sequence violates multicycle path (MCP) setup/hold
requirements or activates false paths.
However, formal verification faces two main scalability challenges:
• Capacity Limits: State space explosion leads to more conservative runtime and
capacity limits as design size grows.
• Constraint Complexity: Formal tools require precise environmental constraints to
avoid false positives.
The Synopsys Timing Constraints Manager (TCM) solution addresses these challenges
with a hybrid approach. It formally verifies the maximal provable subset, then generates
incremental SDC for paths that cannot be proven.
The formal-to-dynamic handoff creates a verification partition strategy:
• Formal Proves: Control-intensive logic and complex state machines.
• Dynamic Verifies: Data path-heavy logic, large state spaces, and stimulus-dependent
corner cases.

Multi-Cycle Paths: The Invisible Mismatch Problem
The challenge: RTL implements a three-cycle data transfer protocol. The timing team
declares a four-cycle multi-cycle path (MCP) to ease place-and-route convergence.
Traditional RTL simulation cannot detect this kind of mismatch—at zero-delay, both
interpretations appear correct. Yet, in silicon, the additional cycle causes the destination to
sample stale data, leading to critical failures.
Why MCPs are Hard to Verify: Unlike functional bugs (incorrect data) or timing bugs
(late data), MCP bugs are invisible mismatches—the RTL and SDC are each correct in
isolation, and are fundamentally incompatible. VCS SDC exposes this by injecting timing
awareness into zero-delay simulation.
Multi-cycle paths relax timing constraints for logic that cannot meet single-cycle setup and
hold requirements. The SDC file explicitly specifies setup and hold cycle counts:
Multi-Cycle Path Declaration in SDC
# Allow 3 cycles for data propagation from FF1 to FF2
set_multicycle_path -setup 3 -from [get_pins FF1/Q] -to [get_pins FF2/D]
set_multicycle_path -hold 2 -from [get_pins FF1/Q] -to [get_pins FF2/D]

Stable Endpoint MCPs: When Protocol Meets Timing
Figure 2 shows the canonical stable MCP pattern. The dvalid signal strobes every three
cycles, creating a microarchitectural protocol that enforces the multi-cycle relationship.
Even in zero-delay simulation, the design functions correctly because dvalid controls
when FF2 samples.
Figure 2 MCP With Stable Endpoint
What the Figure Shows:
• FF1/Q changes data when dvalid pulses (every three cycles).
• FF2/D samples only when dvalid is high.
• The combinational logic between them has a three-cycle MCP declared in SDC.
• At zero delay, dvalid ensures correct operation, independent of SDC .
Potential Issue: What if the SDC specifies four cycles but dvalid implements three
cycles?

Figure 3 MCP With Stable Endpoint: Design Bug Missed
Figure 3 illustrates the critical failure case:
• RTL Reality: dvalid strobes every three clock cycles
• SDC Declaration: set_multicycle_path -setup 4 (timing team relaxed to ease
convergence)
• Zero-Delay Simulation: Passes completely—dvalid protocol ensures correct three-
cycle sampling
• Silicon Failure: Timing tools optimized assuming four-cycle capture. On cycle 4, FF2
samples while FF1 is transitioning → metastability
Why Traditional Simulation Misses This: The functional protocol dvalid is correct. The
timing assumption (four-cycle) is never tested because zero-delay simulation treats all
paths as instantaneous.

Figure 4 MCP With Stable Endpoint - Bug Detected Using VCS SDC
Figure 4 demonstrates the detection mechanisms of VCS SDC overlaid on the same
waveform:
What VCS SDC Adds:
• Setup Checker (Red Marker): Triggers at the point where the source changes within
four cycles of the destination sampling.
◦ What it detected: FF1/Q changed at cycle 3, but FF2 sampled at cycle 0 (only
three cycles prior; SDC requires ≥4)
◦ Message:
MCP Setup Violation: Source changed 3 cycles after destination
captured (expected ≥4)
• X-Injection (Purple Shaded Region): Shows where VCS SDC injected X-values at
the input of FF2
◦ Duration: Cycles 1–3 (modeling the uncertainty window)
◦ Purpose: Forces downstream logic to prove it does not depend on early data arrival
• Checker Firing Point (Red Arrow): Cycle where the violation was detected and
logged
Reading the Waveform (Top to Bottom):
• Clock: Reference timing
• dvalid: Strobes every three cycles (RTL protocol).
• FF1/Q: Source data changes aligned with dvalid.

• FF2/D (Zero-Delay Simulation): Shows what traditional simulation observes - where
data arrives instantly.
• FF2/D (VCS SDC): Shows X-injection modeling the four-cycle constraint.
• Checker Status: Shows when the setup violation was detected.
A key point in Figure 4 is that X-injection does not just detect the bug—it models what
silicon does. Any downstream logic depending on cycle-3 data now fails explicitly
(assertions trigger, and X-propagation causes mismatches), enabling rapid debug.
Debugging Workflow:
• Test fails with Unexpected X in downstream logic.
• Designer opens Figure 4-style waveform in Verdi.
• The VCS SDC annotation identifies the X-injection source.
• Click annotation → navigates to SDC constraint (four-cycle MCP).
• Compares against dvalid timing (three-cycle strobe).
• Realizes mismatch, and corrects SDC to -setup 3.
Metastable Endpoint MCPs: No Safety Net
Figure 5 MCP With Metastable Endpoint
Figure 5 shows the critical difference; no control signal guards the path.

What is Missing:
• No dvalid strobe.
• No enable signal.
• No architectural indication; this is a multi-cycle path.
• FF1/Q connects directly to FF2/D through combinational logic.
What the Figure Reveals:
• In zero-delay simulation, FF1/Q → FF2/D propagate in the same cycle (instant).
• The design works because timing is abstracted away.
• The three-cycle MCP exists only in the SDC, based on static timing analysis showing
that the combinational path cannot meet single-cycle timing.
Why This Is Critical: There is no RTL clue that this path has special timing. Verification
must prove timing correctness without architectural hints.
Figure 6 MCP With Metastable Endpoint: Design Bug Miss
Figure 6 demonstrates why traditional simulation completely misses metastable MCP
bugs:
• RTL Assumption: Pipeline designer assumes three-cycle propagation from ALU result
(FF1) to write back (FF2).
• SDC Reality: Timing team applied four-cycle MCP after discovering that the path does
not close at three cycles.

• Zero-Delay Waveform Figure 6:
◦ FF1/Q changes at cycle 0.
◦ FF2/D shows data at cycle 0, instant propagation.
◦ Downstream logic expects data at cycle 3, but gets it at cycle 0 in simulation.
◦ No functional failure occurs because zero-delay makes everything fast enough.
The Silicon Reality (Not Shown in Traditional Sim):
• FF1/Q changes at cycle 0.
• Combinational delay actually takes 3.5 cycles.
• SDC state that FF2 samples at cycle 4 (per four-cycle MCP).
• However, downstream hazard logic expects data ready at cycle 3.
• This results in pipeline stalls, hazard unit failure, and instruction corruption.
Why Figure 6 shows a Missed Bug: Every signal looks normal. no X-values, no violations,
no failures. The timing assumption mismatch is completely invisible.

Figure 7 shows the same scenario with VCS SDC enabled. The transformation is
dramatic:
What VCS SDC adds:
• X-Injection Window (Purple Shaded Region): Cycles: 1–3 (MCP-1 cycles)
◦ Behavior: FF2/D shows X values instead of data.
◦ Duration: For a four-cycle MCP, inject X for cycles 1–3; allow real data only at cycle
4.
◦ Purpose: Models the entire timing uncertainty window—downstream logic cannot
rely on data arriving before cycle 4.
• Source Stability Checker (Red Marker): Fires if FF1/Q changes within four cycles of
FF2 sampling.
◦ What it detected: FF1 changed at cycle 0, FF2 sampled at cycle 3 (only three
cycles, violates four-cycle requirement).
◦ Message:
MCP Stability Violation: Source changed 3 cycles before destination
capture (expected ≥4).
• X-Propagation Trail (Dashed Lines): Shows how X-values propagate through
downstream pipeline.
Reading the Waveform (Top to Bottom):
• FF1/Q: Source changes at cycle 0.
• FF2/D (Traditional): Would show data immediately (dotted gray line).
• FF2/D (VCS SDC): Shows X-injection for cycles 1–3, data at cycle 4.
• Pipeline Hazard Unit: Sees X instead of expected data at cycle 3 → assertion fires.
• Checker Status: Violation logged with precise cycle information.
The critical insight from Figure 7:
The X-injection does not just flag a problem—it forces all downstream consumers to
correctly handle the four-cycle delay. If pipeline stage two assumes data arrival at cycle-3,
it now sees X and fails explicitly.
Debugging Workflow:
1. Pipeline assertion fires; Unexpected X in hazard detection logic.
2. Designer opens waveform (Figure 7 view in Verdi).

3. Traces X backward to FF2/D.
4. Sees VCS SDC annotation: “4-cycle MCP X-injection active”.
5. Reviews pipeline documentation; assumes three-cycle propagation.
6. Discovers mismatch: either fixes the pipeline to handle four cycles or verifies that the
path can meet three cycles and corrects SDC.
The Optimization: Debug scan chains are structurally connected to mission-mode data
paths. The test_mode signal ensures these domains are mutually exclusive—the path
never activates during normal operation. Declaring it false prevents timing tools from
wasting resources on an impossible scenario.
The Risk: If the test_mode logic has a bug, you have told timing tools to ignore a live
path. Silicon timing fails.
The role of VCS SDC: Verifies that the “never activates” guarantee is correct by
monitoring for any source-to-destination propagation.
Figure 8 False Path
Figure 8 illustrates a canonical false path scenario.
What the Figure Shows:
• Structural Path: FF1/Q → Mux → FF2/D; the arc exists in netlist.
• Control Logic: test_mode (signal dvalid in Figure 8) selects between scan data
(FF1, when test_mode=1) and mission data (alt_data, when test_mode=0).

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
• SDC Declaration: set_false_path -from FF1/Q -to FF2/D (assumes
test_mode=0 during mission mode).
• Architectural Guarantee: The mode controller ensures test_mode=0 during functional
operation.
Why This Matters:
• If test_mode=0: Mux selects alt_data; FF1→FF2 arc is structurally present; however,
it is functionally inactive.
• Timing tools skip optimizing this arc (per false path declaration).
• Area, power, and timing resources focus on active mission-mode paths.
The Assumption Being Verified: test_mode never glitches to 1 during mission mode.
Figure 9 False Path: Design Bug Missed
Figure 9 demonstrates how traditional simulation misses false path activation:
What the Figure Shows:
• Cycle 0–1: Normal operation, test_mode=0 (signal dvalid in Figure 9), alt_data
flows to FF2.
• Cycle 2: A bug occurs—test_mode glitches to 1 (shown in red).
◦ The Mux switches to select FF1/Q.
◦ The scan data of FF1 propagates to FF2/D.
• Cycle 3+: test_mode returns to 0, and operation resumes.

Zero-Delay Simulation Behavior:
• FF1/Q data reaches FF2/D instantly during the glitch.
• If FF1/Q happens to hold stable, the correct data is captured, as shown in Figure 9—
stable value.
• FF2 samples during cycle 2 and, by coincidence, gets the expected value.
• No functional failure is observed; all downstream checks pass.
Why Bug Miss: The test shows the path did activate (test_mode glitch), but because:
• Zero-delay propagation was fast enough.
• FF1 happened to hold the right data.
• No functional checker specifically monitors test_mode stability.
The bug passes verification completely.
Silicon Reality (Not Visible in Figure 9):
• The same glitch occurs during power-on sequence.
• The FF1→FF2 path was never optimized (declared false).
• Path delay = 850 ps, but clock period = 500 ps.
• FF2 samples during metastability window.
• Random data corruption during every power-on.
Figure 10 False Path - Design Bug Detected

text:
Figure 10 shows the transformation when VCS SDC monitors the same scenario:
What VCS SDC Adds:
• Activation Detection (Red Alert Icon): Fires at cycle 2 when a test_mode glitch
(signal dvalid in Figure 10) causes FF1→FF2 propagation.
◦ Trigger: Source transition (FF1/Q) is correlated with destination change (FF2/D)
during the test_mode=1 window.
◦ Message:
False Path Activation: FF1/Q → FF2/D activated via test_mode @ cycle
• X-Injection at Destination (Purple Shading): Cycles 2–4
◦ Behavior: Replaces FF2/D with X values upon detecting activation.
◦ Duration: Extends beyond the glitch to model the metastability window.
◦ Purpose: Models unpredictable behavior of an unoptimized path.
• X-Propagation Downstream (Dashed Purple Lines): Shows how corruption spreads.
◦ The power sequencer FSM receives X instead of a valid init_done signal.
◦ FSM assertion fires: “Unexpected X in state transition logic”.
Reading the Waveform (Top to Bottom):
• test_mode: Shows glitch at cycle 2 (root cause).
• FF1/Q: Scan data value.
• FF2/D (Traditional): Would show scan data (dotted gray line).
• FF2/D (VCS SDC): Shows X-injection starting at cycle 2.
• Power Sequencer: X-propagation causes assertion failure.
• Activation Checker: Violation logged with test_mode as the through-path.
The Key Difference Between Figure 9 and Figure 10:
• Figure 9: Everything looks normal, bug invisible.
• Figure 10: Explicit failure through X-injection, clear root cause (test_mode), and rapid
debug.

Debugging Workflow from Figure 10:
1. Assertion fires in the power sequencer: “Unexpected X”.
2. Designer opens the Verdi waveform (Figure 10 view).
3. Traces X backward to FF2/D.
4. Sees VCS SDC annotation: "False path activated through test_mode @ cycle 2".
5. Examines the test_mode waveform and discovers a glitch during the reset sequence.
6. Reviews reset controller RTL and finds an asynchronous reset logic race condition.
7. Fixes the reset sequencing and re-verifies with VCS SDC monitoring.

Key Takeaways From the Figures
Multi-Cycle Paths:
• Figures 2–4 (Stable): Look for protocol signals. If present, verify they match SDC
cycle counts.
• Figures 5–7 (Metastable): When no protocol signal exists, X-injection is the only way
to model timing at RTL.
• Critical Observation: Compare Figure 3 versus Figure 4, or Figure 6 versus Figure 7
—VCS SDC makes the invisible visible.
False Paths:
• Figures 8–10: The difference between simulation and reality is activation detection.
• Figure 9: The bug is invisible because coincidental factors align (stable data, zero
delay).
• Figure 10: X-injection removes coincidence, forcing explicit failure.
Universal Pattern Across All Figures:
1. Before figures (3, 6, 9): Shows traditional simulation—everything looks fine.
2. After figures (4, 7, 10): Shows VCS SDC—violations explicit, X-values propagate,
checkers fire.
3. Debug acceleration: Waveform annotations link violations directly to SDC constraints.
• Recommended Actions
◦ Review the MCP and false path constraints of your design.
◦ Identify which category your paths fall into (use Figures 2, 5, 8 as templates).
◦ Enable VCS SDC on a representative testbench.
◦ Examine waveforms for X-injection patterns (Figures 4, 7, and10 as reference).
◦ Investigate all checker violations—each represents a potential silicon escape.
Debug
Modeling and checking timing annotations during RTL simulations addresses the detection
problem. However, this capability must be paired with good debug aids to truly improve
user productivity.

Debug
The following three layers of debug support are covered in more detail in the upcoming
sections:
• Simulation log output.
• Visual waveform debug with Verdi.
• Automated root cause analysis.
Simulation Logs
The first level of error detection is typically the simulation log. In such cases, getting
an appropriate checker message that regression tools can detect as an error allows
the simulation to end at or close to the point of failure, thus improving overall compute
efficiency. Additionally, the checker messages provide a focused starting point for debug
that greatly speeds up debug and improves verification productivity. The following is an
example of one such early capture error.
Example 1 Sample Checker Message: Early Capture Error
EARLY-CAPTURE-VIOLATION @ Time: 275000 ps. TO test.u_ddie.u_dest_reg.dout
|--> FROM test.u_ddie.u_source_reg.dout (Clock: test.u_ddie.clk_one
(sdc_clk_one:test.sdc:3)) changed @ Time: 270000 ps.
Observed 1 cycle delay, expected 2 cycle delay (set_multicycle_path
test.sdc:6)
VCS SDC prints the path that is being violated (source and destination) along with the
source of the constraint in the SDC file, enabling direct traceability from the violation to the
specific SDC command that declared the timing relationship.
Violation messages are categorized by type through prefixes (example: MCP, FP and so
on.), enabling automated triage at the user level.
Compile-Time Diagnostics
Beyond runtime violations, VCS SDC generates a suite of diagnostic log files during
compilation that serve as the first line of defense against SDC quality issues:
• Summary Log: Reports parse statistics (commands parsed versus failed), expanded
path counts, and per-command validation summaries with cross-references to any
errors or warnings.
• SDC Errors Log: Consolidates parsing errors, missing source or destination warnings,
unmatched path alerts, and unsupported construct notifications into a single file for
systematic review.

Coverage: Measuring SDC Verification Completeness
• Clock Log: Lists all identified clocks, their periods, and the flops connected to each,
enabling quick verification that SDC clock definitions align with the design's clock
architecture.
These diagnostics catch many classes of SDC errors—such as typos in signal names,
missing clock definitions, paths without valid endpoints—before simulation even
begins, preventing wasted runtime on fundamentally broken constraints.
Visual Debug With Verdi Integration
VCS SDC integrates with Verdi to overlay timing intent on waveforms:
• X-injection markers showing metastability modeling.
• Checker violation indicators (clickable).
• Constraint overlays on signals.
In addition to the tool-provided checkers, some failures because of additional X-injection
and modeling are detected by traditional test checkers and monitors. In these cases, it is
helpful and sometimes crucial to have the modeled intent visible for effective debug.

Coverage: Measuring SDC Verification Completeness
Dynamic verification operates across vast state spaces, making coverage measurement
essential to proving completeness. While traditional code coverage and functional
coverage quantify design exercise, SDC verification requires additional metrics specific to
timing exceptions. Critically, these metrics must be aggregated across entire regression
suites to prove comprehensive verification closure.
The Regression Coverage Challenge
Unlike a single test that exercises one scenario, SDC verification closure requires
demonstrating that:
• All declared constraints were activated across the complete regression suite.
• Each relevant false path is exercised in all operational modes (normal, debug, low-
power, and so on).
• Diverse stimulus toggled MCP endpoints under varied conditions (data patterns, clock
relationships, reset scenarios).
• Corner cases were explored (rapid transitions, back-to-back MCPs, simultaneous false
path candidates).

Conclusion
Key Insight: A single test might exercise only 5–10% of SDC constraints. Verification
closure requires aggregating coverage data across hundreds or thousands of regression
tests to achieve the targeted constraint coverage goals.

Coverage-Driven Test Generation
• Directed tests targeting untested exceptions.
• Constraint randomization biasing stimulus.
• Formal-driven corner-case sequences.
• Incremental SDC focus from formal overflow.
Typical closure: 95%+ constraint coverage before tapeout.
Conclusion
As designs scale in complexity and performance targets tighten, the traditional reliance
on gate-level simulation for SDC verification is no longer tenable. The combination
of prohibitive runtimes, cumbersome debug, and incomplete coverage creates an
unacceptable risk of silicon escapes.
VCS SDC addresses this gap by bringing timing intent verification into the RTL domain
through:
• Automated Checker Insertion: Eliminates manual assertion development.
• Timing-Aware Modeling: Exposes functional dependencies on timing.
• Integrated Debug: Reduces debug turnaround time.
• Coverage-Driven Closure: Provides measurable completeness metrics.

Conclusion
When combined with upstream lint/static checks and formal verification for bounded
proofs, dynamic SDC verification completes the verification triad. This enables design
teams to achieve comprehensive verification of timing constraints at RTL speed,
significantly reducing the risk of late-stage timing failures and costly silicon respins.

General Guidelines
VHDL
VHDLcoding styleeffect on simulation speed
coding style is the most important factor affecting simulation speed. VHDL is a
behavioral language, so you can write a model many different ways. How you write
your VHDL design models can affect the performance of both the VHDL Analyzer and
simulator.
This chapter describes the general coding guidelines for the following topics:
• VHDL Coding Style
• VHDL Value and Character Limits
This chapter does not attempt to teach VHDL coding rules and practices in general. For
information about writing design descriptions in VHDL, see the IEEE Standard VHDL
Language Reference Manualor any of the quality books related to designing with VHDL.
VHDL Coding Style
This section provides general guidelines to produce maximum simulation speed. Cycle
simulation refers to simulating a complete or partial design description in VCS cycle mode.
The guidelines are as follows:
• Use the highest level of abstraction as possible to code your design. The higher the
level of abstraction of the modeling style, the faster the simulation run. Thus, RTL style
simulates faster than gate-level and behavioral style simulates faster than RTL.
• Use variables rather than signals, especially when modeling memory contents.
Variables require much less memory and overhead which yields to faster simulation.
• Group functionality into processes according to the signals that activate that
functionality. VCS cycle frequently groups related processes as part of the overall
cycle optimization techniques. However, in event simulation, this task remains for the
designer to accomplish.
• Use commonly accepted synthesis coding templates. For sequential processes, only
include the clock and any required asynchronous control signals in the sensitivity
list. Use the synthesis accepted style for synchronous and asynchronous controlled
sequential processes (see the “Templates for Register Inference” appendix).

Chapter 1: General Guidelines
VHDL Coding Style
• Use complete sensitivity lists for combinational processes. If you leave out signals
that are read in a combinational process, event simulation might run faster. However,
incomplete sensitivity lists can cause mismatches between simulation and synthesis, or
between event simulation and cycle simulation.
VCS cycle automatically completes an incomplete sensitivity list in a combinational
process just as synthesis does.
• Limit the use of text input and output in your code. Try not to use Read and Write
routines often, especially when working with LINE-type variables. This applies whether
you are reading from or writing to a file.
• Use subprograms for large processing blocks. Using subprograms for small and simple
blocks of code slows down the simulation.
The subprograms in the standard libraries (Std., IEEE, and Synopsys) are optimized by
VCS.
For user-defined subprograms, each call can add significant simulation overhead
especially when signal class parameters are used. When you create subprograms for
reusable code, consider both the simulation overhead. Also, consider the amount of
work the subprogram does to make the best choice.
• Use the following IEEE standard VHDL types:
◦ std_logic
◦ std_logic_vector
◦ std_ulogic
◦ std_ulogic_vector
◦ numeric_std signed and unsigned
◦ std_logic_arith signed and unsigned
• Avoid Bit-Blasting. Do not break vector signals into single bits to process them one
by one and then combine them again. Instead, work with the whole vector signal
whenever you can. Use vector-level operations and manipulations.
• Perform operations only when needed. For example, do not convert a value to a
string unless you need to report an exception. Convert the value to a string only if the
exception actually happens.

Chapter 1: General Guidelines
VHDL Coding Style
• “For” loops in VCS are unrolled during simulation. If the loop has many iterations and
complex operations, this can create large code and slow down performance. To reduce
the size of the unrolled “for” loop code,
◦ Reduce the number of iterations (if possible). For example, use vector operations or
slice assignments instead of bit-level operations and assignment.
◦ Keep code that is loop-invariant outside the loop.
◦ Reduce operations and calculations inside the loop. For example, eliminate
common expressions by using temporary variables.
• Structure branch logic optimally to avoid unnecessary expression evaluation. For
example, the following code is inefficient as both condA and condB are always
evaluated:
if condA then
target <= valueA;
if condB then
target <= valueB;
It is more efficient to write the code as follows:
if condB then
target <= valueB;
elsif condA then
target <= valueA;
condA is evaluated only when condB is false. For if-then-elsif statements, place
the most likely TRUE conditions first. This helps synthesis tools create efficient priority
encoders.
• Minimize signal assignments in a process. Signal assignments are simple to write,
but they use more processing resources. This extra processing does not happen for
combinational signals in cycle simulation. The following is an example of an inefficient
description:
S <= default;
case sel is
when "00" => S <= valA;
when "01" => S <= valB;
when "10" => S <= valC;
when others => null;

Chapter 1: General Guidelines
VHDL Value and Character Limits
This description shows that two signal assignment statements are executed in three
out of four cases. To improve clarity, use variables to store the values first. Then,
assign these values to the signals at the end. Refer to the following example:
var := default;
case sel is
when "00" => var := valA;
when "01" => var := valB;
when "10" => var := valC;
when others => null;
S <= var;

Testbench Guidelines
This chapter presents a number of coding rules and guidelines for testbenches. These
guidelines help you construct VHDL testbenches that are efficient for VCS in event and
cycle mode.
This chapter describes the testbench coding guidelines for the following topics:
• General Testbench Guidelines
• Clock Generation from the Testbench
• Clock Generation from the Main Clock
• Reset Generation
• Data Generation
• Stimulus and Response Files
• Message Files
In general, a testbench to be simulated in VCS cycle is limited to the same VHDL
constructs as synthesis and the design being simulated in cycle mode. In addition to the
synthesis policy, the cycle testbench supports the use of behavioral style wait statements,
assert statements, and TEXTIO constructs.
General Testbench Guidelines
VCS automatically detects and identifies processes that are to be simulated in cycle
mode and fit the testbench guidelines (as presented in this chapter) as cycle testbench
processes.
The presence of a behavioral wait statement indicates a cycle testbench process.
Although you can use behavioral wait statements to model other design functionalities,
such as a PLL, cycle simulation identifies the process as a cycle testbench process and
report this information in the elaboration output.
A testbench process is shown in Example 1.

General Testbench Guidelines
Example 1 Sample Testbench Process
architecture behavior of TB is
CLOCK: process
CLK <= '0';
wait for 50 ns;
CLK <= '1';
wait for 50 ns;
end process CLOCK;
end behavior;
For a cycle testbench, use processes with behavioral
wait statements
wait statements to create timing
in the testbench and to model asynchronous activity. Behavioral wait statements do not
conform to the synthesis policy. For example, “wait for time” is a behavioral wait statement.
Thus, these processes are identified as testbench processes (see above).
Do not use the
after clause
“after” clause to produce delays or timing in your models, cycle simulation
ignores the after clause.
The only statement that causes a delay to occur in cycle simulation is the “wait for time”
statement. Most of the wait statements supported by cycle simulation are shown in bold in
Example 2.

--Process with explicit "wait for time" statement
--This is a testbench process
process

wait for 50 ns;
RESET <= '1';
wait for 50 ns;
RESET <= '0';
wait;

Clock Generation from the Main Clock
Ideally, you must only use
wait statements

in cycle mode. In some cases, you might want to
clock generation
create a clock that is synchronized to
another clock or the main clock. Examples of these derived clocks include clock dividers,
clock multipliers, and phase lock loops.
Creating a clock from another clock usually causes a delta delay between the main clock
and the derived clock. These delta delays can cause undesirable behavior if both the main
clock and the derived clocks are used in the design. Thus, use the following guideline for
properly generating derived clocks when using cycle simulation (you can simulate the
testbench in cycle or event mode).
When deriving clocks from a main clock, use only the derived clocks in the design. The
main clock must be restricted to the processes that create the other clocks.
Example 6 shows a process that generates a
clock divider
clock divider.
Example 6 Creating a Clock Divider
divider: process
clk50 <= '0';
clk100 <= '0';
clk200 <= '0';
loop -- forever
for j in 1 to 2 loop
for k in 1 to 2 loop
wait on clk;
clk200 <= not clk200;
clk100 <= not clk100;
clk50 <= not clk50;
end process divider;
Note that the clock (clk200) has the same frequency as the main clock (clk), but it is
delayed by a delta cycle. The derived clocks occur simultaneously and are the ones used
by the design.

Reset Generation
Reset Generation
This section provides rules and guidelines for
reset generation
creating resets from the testbench. These
rules and guidelines apply to asynchronous resets because cycle simulation treats resets
and clocks the same way. You can also generate synchronous resets using the same
guidelines. These guidelines also apply to modeling other asynchronous signals such as
interrupt signals.
In general, apply the same rules to reset signals that you apply for clocks. For instance,
use minimum number of buffers or temporary signals for connecting the reset signal to the
registers.
Always pulse the reset signal to the active state from the inactive state. Asynchronous
resets in cycle simulation are edge triggered even if in the registers they appear to be level
sensitive. To ensure the registers are reset properly, always create a reset process that
toggles the reset condition value. Example 7 creates a pulse for an active-low reset.
Example 7 Generating Reset from a Testbench
reset: process
RST<= '1';
RST<= '0';
wait for 100 ns;
RST<= '1';
wait;
When simulating the design in cycle simulation (with the testbench in either cycle or
event), model asynchronous resets as you do clocks, that is, generate resets globally from
a testbench process. Use a wait statement with no condition or time to indefinitely suspend
the processes that contain the reset.

Avoid using
subprograms
multiple subprograms or repeatedly calling the same subprogram from
a process when simulating in cycle mode. This applies to user-defined subprograms
(procedures or functions) and not to the subprograms already analyzed into the Synopsys
supplied design libraries.
Subprograms are inlined in cycle simulation (including testbench processes simulated
in cycle mode), causing the virtual size of the process to increase. Heavy use of
subprograms can create virtual processes so large that they significantly affect
performance. This can lead to very long elaboration times and can cause an out-of-
memory error during elaboration.
To avoid creating large
virtual processes
virtual processes, follow these guidelines:
• Use the pre-analyzed Synopsys supplied subprograms from packages in IEEE and
Synopsys libraries whenever possible.
• Avoid using large complicated subprograms that call other subprograms.
• Use a modeling style that has few calls to subprogram that are not supplied by
Synopsys.
• Use multiple processes instead of one big procedural based process.
• Reduce the number of calls to a subprogram. For example, by performing an operation
once instead of multiple times outside a for-loop when the parameters do not depend
on the loop iteration or replace multiple calls in two or more conditional branches by
one call made unconditionally (even if the results of the subprogram call are not always
needed).
• Replace calls to user-defined type conversion functions with type qualification,
especially when used in “for” loops.
Example 12 shows how you can use multiple subprogram calls. Example 13 shows a
subprogram that is only called once after the case statement and not in each branch of the
case statement.

Stimulus and Response Files
This section provides guidelines for reading and writing stimulus files from the
VHDL testbench by using TEXTIO.
The most common method of reading data from files is using VHDL TEXTIO files.
Other methods of reading data include using (binary) file I/O, using memories with the
load_memory command, or using C models via the VHDL PLI.
Saving response is done most efficiently by using the VCS trace (dump) command. This
command efficiently saves data for later viewing in the waveform viewer. You can use
TEXTIO to store the results, but because the data is in text format, files are larger and thus
less efficient. Also, you lose the benefit of being able to easily turn off or restrict the output
when using TEXTIO.
VCS supports the standard VCD output format in addition to the VCD+ format.
When simulating the testbench in cycle mode, access “line” types using the read
procedures defined in the TEXTIO and std_logic_textio packages. The analyzer restricts

Stimulus and Response Files
most uses of the “line” access types such as indexing when simulating in cycle mode. You
can determine the length of a “line” using the
’length attribute
’length attribute.
Example 14 shows a method of skipping blank and
comment lines
comment lines in a file that fails
analysis for cycle simulation. Example 15 shows a successful method of skipping blank
and comment lines.
Example 14 Indexing a Line Fails Analysis (Not Recommended)
variable L : LINE;

--Skip Blank/Comment Lines
while not endfile ( infile ) loop
readline(infile, L );
if L'length = 0
or L(1) = '#' then next; -- ERRORS
Example 15 Indexing a String (Recommended Coding)
variable L : LINE;

--Skip Blank/Comment Lines
while not endfile ( infile ) loop
readline(infile, L );
if L'length = 0 then next;
read(L,st(1 to L'length));
if st(1) = '#' then next;
Example 16 shows an alternate method of using
TEXTIO file
TEXTIO. This procedure reads a string
from the file you pass to it and returns both a string that contains the next line of the file
and the length of the string, which contains good text. When using a temporary string
variable, the unused characters of the string are filled with blanks.
Example 16 Procedure to Read a Variable Length String
procedure my_read_line (variable infile : in text; lin :
out string; line_length : out integer) is
variable line_from_file : string(1 to 80) :=
(OTHERS => ' ');
variable L : LINE;
readline(infile, L);
line_length := L'length;
read(L, line_from_file(1 to L'length));
lin := line_from_file;
return;

user-defined procedures

Message Files
During simulation, you might want to
printing messages
print messages for failures or to record other
information.
Use TEXTIO instead of assert statements to print messages. TEXTIO supports most
data types and allows writing to multiple files. Asserts are limited to strings only, and data
types must be converted to strings by inefficient functions. Example 21 shows the use of
TEXTIO for printing messages.
Example 21 Using TEXTIO to Print Messages
if (S1 /= ADATA) then
write(L, string'("Signal S1 (" ));
write(L, S1);
write(L, string'(") Data is incorrect" ));
writeline (outfile, L);

Message Files
Control the severity levels of assertions to reduce the amount of assertion output when
using assertions. VCS provides assertion filtering capabilities with the following two
simulation environment variables:
• ASSERT_IGNORE Controls which user-defined assertions are ignored based on
severity level.
• ASSERT_IGNORE_OPTIMIZED_LIBS Controls the filtering of assertion messages
generated from within the optimized libraries (for example, IEEE.Numeric_Std,
IEEE.Std_Logic_1164).
By carefully planning the severity level of your assertions and by setting these simulation
environment variables, you can filter out informational and non-error warning messages.
This improves your simulation performance and reduces the volume of data in the
simulation results which must be checked for true design errors.
Use
assert statements
assert statements for printing text messages to avoid performance degradation.

Design Guidelines
VCS cycle mode is designed to provide the best possible capacity and performance for
simulating synthesizable, register-transfer level descriptions of synchronous circuits.
However, as your VHDL code departs from the coding style recommended for cycle
simulation, a gradual degradation in simulation performance occurs.
This chapter describes coding guidelines that allow you to get the maximum advantage of
the inherent speed and capacity from cycle simulation. These guidelines will also improve
the quality of your synthesis results.
This chapter describes the design coding guidelines for the following topics:
• Pullups and Pulldowns
• Vectorization and Loops
• Combinatorial Logic
• Sequential Logic
• Clock Generation
• Gate-level Modeling
For more information about design coding styles, see the VHDL Compiler Reference
Manual.
Pullups and Pulldowns
This section provides guidelines for modeling pullups and pulldowns.
Use only the strong corresponding states (0, 1, X, Z) of the standard types to model
pullups and pulldowns. Cycle simulation maps weak states to strong ones, it maps ’H’
states to ’1’, ’L’ to ’0’. For example, in cycle mode ’H’ and ’0’ states are resolved to ’X’,
because the ’H’ is really a ’1’.

Vectorization and Loops
Remove weak state pullups and pulldowns from the design, because they do not simulate
correctly. Use the types defined in the standard IEEE.std_logic_1164 package to model
pullups and pulldowns. For pullups, use the tri1 and tri1_vector types. For pulldowns, use
the tri0 and tri0_vector types.
In Example 22, pu_bit is resolved to ’1’ and pu_bus is resolved to “1101”.
Example 22 Defining A Pullup
signal pu_bus : tri1_vector(3 downto 0);
signal pu_bit: tri1;
p1 : process

pu_bit <= 'Z';
pu_bus <= "ZZZZ";

end process p1;

p2 : process

pu_bit <= 'Z';
pu_bus <= "ZZ01";

end process p1;
If the pullup or pulldown functionality is implemented in an I/O PAD, it is best to simulate
the PAD cells in event simulation and only partition the DUT into cycle simulation mode.
Most designs are already organized hierarchically where the PAD cells are instantiated at
or above the level of hierarchy containing the DUT instance. Therefore, it is usually easy to
leave the PADs in the event partition.
There might be other reasons for PAD cells to remain in event. For example,
signal assignments with after clauses which cannot be modeled easily as cycle
testbench processes and for which the delays are necessary to ensure correct
results.
Vectorization and Loops
The guidelines for vectorization and loops are presented in this section.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Vectorization and Loops
Use
vectorsassignments
vector assignments and operations wherever possible. Vectorization improves
runtime performance because cycle simulation maps vector operations to word operations
on the target computer.
Use vectorization to make your code more compact and readable. For example, you can
set an entire array of arrays to zero (such as arrays representing a RAM) as shown in
Example 23.
Example 23 Using Vectorization
ram_array := (others => (others => '0'));
Do not use
for loops
“for” loops to iterate over an array index, you lose the compactness and
performance advantages of vectorization. Example 24 shows a slow method for
computing a bitwise XOR. The vectorized version in Example 25 produces a faster runtime
performance.
vectorsfor loopsarray index
Example 24 Using Bitwise XOR with FOR loop (Not Recommended)
function SLOW_XOR(bbit : std_logic;
avec : std_logic_vector)
return std_logic_vector is
variable cvec : std_logic_vector(avec'range);
for I in avec'range loop
cvec(I) := avec (I) XOR bbit;
return(cvec);
Example 25 Using Bitwise XOR with Vectorization (Recommended Coding)
function FAST_XOR(bbit : std_logic;
avec : std_logic_vector)
return std_logic_vector is
variable cvec, temp : std_logic_vector(avec'range);
temp := (others => bbit);
cvec := avec XOR temp;
return(cvec);
The cycle elaborator unrolls “for” loops for maximum runtime efficiency. Long “for” loops
increase the size of the code generated for cycle and the time it takes to elaborate. The
elaborator issues a warning when it encounters an excessively long for loop.

correctly and efficiently.
Use complete
sensitivity lists

cause a mismatch between cycle simulation (and synthesis) and event simulation, as
shown in Example 26 and Figure 3.
Example 26 shows a VHDL process that yields an OR gate when synthesized and

complies with strict VHDL semantics and does not propagate changes on signal B through
the gate until signal A changes.

In “case” and “if” statements, be sure to cover all possible conditions, and for each
condition, specify what happens to all output signals. Incomplete specifications, such as in
Example 27, can lead to the inference of unwanted latches in cycle simulation (and VHDL
Compiler).
statementscasecase statementsstatementsifif statementslatchesinferencestatementsincomplete
In general, case statements execute faster than multiple if statements. Use if-then-else-
endif constructs only when you need priority encoding.

Sequential Logic
Example 27 Using Incomplete if and case Statements (Not Recommended)
process (A, B) begin
if (A = '1') then
Q <= B;
end if; --missing "else" clause!

process (C) begin
case (C) is
when '0' => Q <= '1'; P <= '0';
when others => Q <= '0'; --missing assignment
--to signal P
Do not insert VHDL assertion statements in combinatorial logic, although they are
supported in cycle simulation. Using assertion statements in combinatorial logic can result
in assertion message mismatches between cycle and event simulation. The order in which
combinatorial processes are executed is not guaranteed in cycle simulation. Nor does
cycle simulation guarantee that combinatorial processes are even executed during a given
evaluation cycle.
Do not use feedback loops that do not include a single register element. They can degrade
both simulation performance and synthesis results. The cycle elaborator detects and
reports warning for such loops.
The cycle elaborator attempts to break combinatorial feedback loops by inserting the
equivalent of a register. This might or might not result in correct functionality during
simulation. Therefore, it is best to avoid combinatorial loops.
Sequential Logic
This section provides guidelines that ensure your sequential logic simulates correctly and
efficiently.
Do not explicitly instantiate registers (flip-flops and latches) in the source code, instead,
let VCS infer them. This method can help you to meet the design requirements without
adhering to a particular technology.
Certain VHDL templates
templatesdefinition
imply (by VCS and the synthesis tools) a particular register type.
Example 28 shows a template for a sequential process. A full catalog of templates is
provided in the Templates for Register Inference appendix.

Clock Generation
There are three different ways to generate a clock signal: global, gated, or combinatorial.
In cycle mode, global clocks generated from a central place such as the testbench
produce the highest performance, and combinatorial clocks produce the lowest
performance. For information about coding testbench-driven global clocks, see Testbench
Guidelines chapter.
This section presents the guidelines for coding design-driven gated clocks.
Keep the gated clock process in a separate architecture, and make the clock as global as
possible. Example 29 shows the gated clock architecture in bold.
Example 29 Using Separate Architecture for Gated Clocks
Architecture RTL of Gated_clock is
CLK_GATE <= (GATING_LOGIC);
end RTL;
p1: process ( CLK_GATE ) BEGIN
if (CLK_GATE'EVENT and CLK_GATE='1') then

if (CLK_GATE'EVENT and CLK_GATE='1') then

device to model the gated logic, or replace the gated clock with a synchronous load if the
clock and gate signals are both generated from the same logic and they occur at the same

If the clock and gate signals occur at a different time, the gated clock will function properly.
