Do not use clock buffering because clock buffering can break up processes into separate
functions. Use one trigger function for each clock region.
Gate-level Modeling
Cycle simulation ignores timing delays, except when modeled using a testbench style. (For
more information, see the Testbench Guidelines chapter). Therefore, VITAL components
are simulated in cycle using only their functionality. All timing information for VITAL
components is discarded when simulated in cycle mode. These components include Wire
Delays, Path Delays, and Timing Checks, It is referred to as functional VITAL simulation.
Functional VITAL simulation is automatically enabled. It cannot be disabled in cycle
simulation. If a design is dependent on accurate timing, it cannot be simulated in cycle
mode. It is a natural consequence of functional VITAL simulation that no SDF back-
annotation can be performed.
You can enable functional VITAL simulation of all VITAL models in a design in an event
simulation. To do so, specify the –novitaltiming option on the simv command line.

Gate-level Modeling
Guidelines
• Do not use gate-level simulation in cycle mode as it degrades simulation performance.
However, sometimes, it is necessary to use some gate-level models. In this case, cycle
simulation can handle VITAL Level 1 compliant models in functional mode. For correct
results, the design and the VITAL component should not depend on accurate timing
from the VITAL component.
• The coding style of the VITAL Level 0 compliant models should closely follow that
required for Level 1 compliant models. This includes all the timing areas (Wire Delay,
Path Delay, and Timing Checks) that the model includes.
There are no rules and guidelines for the architecture's coding style in a Level 0
compliant model. Therefore, VCS might not correctly ignore and only ignore the timing
aspects of a Level 0 model. Level 0 architectures should follow, as closely as possible,
the style of Level 1 architectures. This ensures that VCS correctly identifies the timing
aspects of the model.
If you encounter problems in simulating Level 0 compliant VITAL models in the
functional VITAL or cycle mode, contact the Synopsys Technical Support Center for
help on the coding style.
All VITAL Level 1 compliant models are also Level 0 compliant. Therefore,
this guideline applies only to those models which are only Level 0 compliant
and not Level 1 compliant.
• Use VITAL models that conform to the VITAL ’95 standard. VCS does not support
VITAL 2000.
• The GTECH library can be used for gate-level modeling with cycle simulation. The
GTECH library is compiled for cycle simulation.
• Use the –novitaltiming option to simv to enable fast functional event simulation with
VCS. Use this option only if the design is not dependent on accurate timing through the
VITAL components.

Memory Model Guidelines
This chapter presents several rules and guidelines for coding ROM and RAM memory
models. These guidelines show examples of coding both synchronous and asynchronous
memory models. The examples also show how to use the mem_api package to create
efficient sparse memory models and the byte enable procedure. VCS provides the best
simulation performance when you use these guidelines.
This chapter describes coding rules and guidelines for the following topics:
• General Memory Guidelines
• Sparse Memory Models
• Dual Port Memories
• Writing a Byte into Memory
VCS provides two basic types of memory models: sparse and dense. In general, use the
sparse memory model for larger memories (100 KB and larger). For smaller memories,
use a dense model. The dense model refers to using a VHDL variable or signal for the
memory element. For both sparse and dense memories, a synchronous coding style
is recommended whenever possible. The mem_api package provides optimal runtime
performance for your sparse memory models. For more information about the mem_api
package, see the “Synopsys Standard Packages” chapter in the VHDL Simulation User
Guide.
General Memory Guidelines
This section provides one rule and several guidelines for coding memory models.
Do not use multi-dimensional arrays to model the memory, as shown in Example 30. VCS
cycle does not support multi-dimensional arrays. Instead, use an array of arrays as shown
in Example 31.
Example 30 Using Two-Dimensional Arrays (Not Supported)
type ram9x4 is array(511 downto 0, 15 downto 0)
of std_logic;

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
General Memory Guidelines
Use arrays of std_logic_vector type to load and dump memories. VCS does not support
loading arrays of integers. Example 31 shows the use of std_logic_vector type in bold.
Example 32 shows, in bold, the use of arrays of integers that is not recommended.
Example 31 Using Arrays of std_logic_vector Type for Loading and Dumping Memories
(Recommended Coding)
type ram9x4 is array (511 downto 0)
of std_logic_vector (15 downto 0) ;
Example 32 Using Arrays of Integers for Loading Memories (Not Recommended)
type ram9x4 is array (511 downto 0)
of integer;
In general, use synchronous memory models when possible. Synchronous memories
usually provide faster simulation performance compared to asynchronous memories.
Clear dense memories by using a vector assignment and “others” clauses instead of “for”
loops. Example 33 shows, in bold, how to properly clear a memory at reset.
Example 33 Using Synchronous Memory Models (Recommended Coding)
mem5: process( clk, rst)
type ram_t is array( 0 to 15) of
std_logic_vector( 15 downto 0);
variable rama : ram_t;
if (rst = '0') then
rama := (others => (others => '0'));
if (we = '0') then
rama (conv_integer(addr)) := datain;
dataout <= rama (conv_integer(addr));
For asynchronous memories, use variables in the memory process. With asynchronous
memory models, you can use multiple enables or clocks. Example 34 shows an
asynchronous memory model that contains a reset, write enable, read enable, and chip
select.

Sparse Memory Models
Note, this memory modeling style (multiple clocks, enables, resets, and the wait
statement) results in the cycle elaborator identifying the process(es) as testbench
process(es). While this degrades the performance, it is the best method for modeling
certain types of memories such as dual port RAMs.
Example 34 Using Asynchronous Dense Memory Models (Recommended Coding)
architecture async of ram is
mem: process
variable rama : ram_t;
wait on we, re, cs, rst;
if (cs = '0') then
if (rst = '0') then
rama := (others => (others => '0'));
if (we = '1') then
rama(conv_integer(waddr)) := datain;
if (re = '1') then
dataout <= rama(conv_integer(raddr));
Sparse Memory Models
This section provides examples for coding sparse (approximately 100KB and larger)
memory models.
Use functions and procedures in the mem_api package to model sparse memory models.
Example 35 and Example 36 show a sparse ROM and a RAM modeled using the
mem_api package. Basically, you use the previous dense memory examples, but you
only replace the variable assignments with the signal assignment that calls the mem_init
function. The reading and writing to the memory is done using the mem_read and
mem_write procedures defined in the mem_api package.
Example 35 Using a Sparse ROM (Recommended Coding)
Library IEEE;
Use IEEE.mem_API.all;
entity ROM is
generic (n_addr : natural; n_data : natural);
port(addr : in std_logic_vector(n_addr - 1 downto 0);
data : out std_logic_vector(n_data - 1 downto 0);
rclk : in std_logic );

Instantiating Verilog or VHDL in Your Design
This chapter describes the following instantiation processes:
• Instantiating a Verilog Design in a VHDL Design
• Instantiating a VHDL Design in a Verilog Design
Both these processes are closely connected to the analysis process described in the
Chapter, “Analyzing Your Design” in the VCS User Guide. The analysis and instantiation
processes overlap in many of the situations discussed in this chapter.
You can add a Verilog module to your VHDL design by declaring it as a component. Then,
use a component instantiation statement to include it in your design. This process works
the same way as instantiating a VHDL component.
You can declare component ports in any order. However, it is recommended to use the
same port order as in your Verilog module.
Use the following data types to specify ports in the component declaration:
• bit
• std_logic
• std_ulogic
• bit_vector
• std_logic_vector
• std_ulogic_vector
• boolean
• buffer
buffer type is supported only when a Verilog module instantiates a VHDL component.
• User-defined types and subtypes, if the basic type of the element type is in std_ulogic
bit and boolean.

• Unconstrained vector VHDL port
• Function call at VHDL port size expression
• VHDL signed/unsigned to Verilog wire signed
You can use vector data types for vector ports in the Verilog module. VCS includes built-in
data type conversion to convert VHDL data types to Verilog data types.
In addition, you can instantiate a Verilog module having port of type signed in a VHDL
design unit (architecture). See Signed and Unsigned Type Support.
If a module defines parameters, the related component declaration specifies generics that
match the parameter names. Refer to the following example.
Example 39 shows a Verilog module definition that instantiates in a VHDL design.
Example 40 shows the VHDL component declaration that you use to instantiate the Verilog
module.
Example 39 Verilog Module Definition
module vlog(topin,topout);
parameter topdelparam=6;
input topin;
output [7:0] topout;
vlogbot #(topdelparam) vlogbot1(topin,topout);
.
.
.
Example 40 Corresponding VHDL Component Declaration
component vlog
generic (topdelparam : integer := 6);
port (topin : in STD_LOGIC;
topout : out STD_LOGIC_VECTOR (7 downto 0));
end component;
After declaring this component, you enter a component instantiation statement, for
example
vloginst1 : vlog generic map (7) port map (a,b);
If the Verilog design unit contains parameters, declare them as generics for corresponding
component declaration. Actual mapping for those generics is optional in instantiation.
VCS also allows you to instantiate a VHDL design in another Verilog design. For
information on instantiating a VHDL design in a Verilog design, refer Instantiating a VHDL
Design in a Verilog Design. This Verilog design can be further instantiated in a VHDL
design. This is commonly called a mixed-HDL “donut” design. There is no limit to the
number of layers of VHDL and Verilog source code in the design.

Signed and Unsigned Type Support
Mixed-HDL simulation supports signed and unsigned types at the mixed HDL boundary
without restriction. This means you can instantiate a Verilog module, containing a port
of type signed, into a VHDL design unit (architecture). While Verilog does not have any
explicit unsigned types, all wire types are effectively unsigned. VHDL explicitly supports
signed and unsigned types.
Example 41 shows a Verilog adder module with signed and unsigned types followed by
the part of the VHDL testbench design instantiating the Verilog module.
Example 41 Instantiating Verilog Signed and Unsigned Types into VHDL
Verilog module:
`timescale 1 ns/ 1 ns

module VL_FULL_ADD4(a, b, cin, sum);
input signed [3:0] a;
input [3:0] b;
input cin;
output signed [3:0] sum;

assign sum = a + b + cin;

USE STD.textio.all;

use IEEE.std_logic_arith.all;

entity tb is
end tb;

architecture tb_a of tb is

You can use the command line to assign generics at any layer in a design. For example:
e (VHDL)
-->uut (VHDL)
-->convert (VHDL instance of Verilog implementation)
-->z_1 (Verilog instance at VHDL implementation for z_1)
You can specify the value of generic g1 as shown below. Note that the VHDL portion of
the hierarchy is case insensitive, while the Verilog portion (module, instances) is case-
sensitive.
Assignment Syntax Comment

Mapping Verilog Ports to VHDL Ports
The port names in the VHDL component declaration must match the port names in the
Verilog module definition.
The mode or direction of the in, out, or inout ports in the VHDL component declaration
must match the type of input, output, or inout port declaration in the Verilog module
definition.
The size or bit-width and the bit values used to specify the bit-width, of the ports in
the VHDL component declaration must match the bit-width and bit values in the port
declarations in the Verilog module definition.
In Example 39, port topin is a scalar input port and in Example 40, port topin is also a port
of mode in with a scalar data type. In Example 39, port topout is an eight bit vector output
port with the bits numbered from 7 to 0 and in Example 40, port topout is also an eight bit
vector port of mode out with the bits numbered from 7 down to 0.
In Example 40, port topin has the STD_LOGIC data type because this is a valid data type
for converting values from VHDL to Verilog and port topin is a scalar port. Similarly, in

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Example 5-2, port topout has the STD_LOGIC_VECTOR data type because this is also a
valid data type for converting values from Verilog to VHDL and port topout is a vector port.
Instantiating a Verilog Module With Parameterized Ports
In Verilog, a port can be parameterized so that its bit-width is specified using a parameter.
This allows you to get ports with different bit-widths by passing different parameters to
different instances of the same module.
Example 42 shows a module definition with a parameterized port.
Example 42 Verilog Module With A Parameterized Port
module dev (inport, outport);
parameter portsize = 1;
input inport;
output [portsize + 1 : 0] outport;
.
.
.
To instantiate a module with a parameterized port, use a generic in the component
declaration that corresponds to the parameter in the module definition. This generic must
have the integer data type or a subtype with data type integer. Example 43 shows such a
component declaration.
Example 43 Component Declaration for a Module With a Parameterized Port
component dev
generic (portsize : integer := 1);
port (inport : in std_logic;
outport : out std_logic_vector
((portsize + 1) downto 0));
end component;
You can then use the generic map in the component instantiation statement to pass a new
value to the generic and thus a new size to the port.
Using a Configuration Specification to Resolve Verilog Instances
You can bind the instances of Verilog designs within configuration. The syntax is:
for instance_label : component_name
use entity library.Verilog_Module_identifier;
end for;
You cannot specify “configuration” instead of “entity”. Also, since the Verilog design does
not have an architecture, you need not specify any architecture along with the entity.

For example,
for vlogtopinst1 : vlogtop
use entity LIB.vlogtop;
end for;
Names and Identifiers
The names (formally called identifiers) of design objects such as components, entities,
architectures, ports, or signals are not case-sensitive in VHDL but they are in Verilog. For
this reason, in the Verilog module that you instantiate in the VHDL design, the names of
Verilog modules, ports, and parameters must be unique without regard to case, unless you
use extended identifiers.
For example, in Verilog you can specify the following two input port names: in1 and IN1,
but not in VHDL. Therefore, you must change one of the port names if the port is in the
top-level module of the Verilog design that you are instantiating in your VHDL design. You
cannot use VHDL keywords as the names of modules, ports, or parameters in the top-
level Verilog module, unless you use extended identifiers.
You must follow the rules for VHDL identifiers in the names of modules, ports, or
parameters in the top-level Verilog module. Valid VHDL identifiers consist of upper or
lowercase letters, numbers, and the underscore. The first character must be a letter,
and the last character cannot be the underscore character (_), unless you use extended
identifiers.
Using Extended Identifiers
You can use extended identifiers (similar to Verilog escaped identifiers) to fulfill the rules
for VHDL identifiers, for example,:
• You can specify ports \in1\ and \IN1\ in the component declaration.
• You can specify an entity named \component\.
• You can begin a name with a number and end with an underscore, such as an
architecture named \1comparch_\.
Module Header Port List Restrictions
The port list in the module header for the instantiated module cannot contain either of the
following:
• Unconnected ports
• Jumpered ports

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
An unconnected port is an empty space between commas in the port connection list, for
example:
module vlogtop (portia, , portib);
A jumpered port is a port that appears more than once in the port list, for example:
module vlogtop (portia, portia);
Mapping VHDL Bit/Logic Vector Generics to Verilog Parameters
VCS allows you to map
bit_vector
bit_vector and
std_[u]logic_vector

Ordered Vector
A vector can have an ascending range ([0:4] or (0 to 4) ) or a descending range
([4:0], (4 downto 0) ) in both VHDL and Verilog. However, when mapping VHDL
generics to Verilog parameters, the ranges are irrelevant, and the mapping always occurs
from right to left. For example, if you want to map all combinations in Example 44.
Example 44 Design Example
COMPONENT vector
GENERIC (
G_DOWN : std_logic_vector(4 downto 0);
G_UP : std_logic_vector(0 to 4));
PORT (
top_in : IN std_logic;
top_out : OUT std_logic
);
END COMPONENT

Generics:
G_DOWN : std_logic_vector(4 downto 0) := "11100";
G_UP : std_logic_vector(0 to 4) := "11100";
Parameters:
parameter [4:0] P_DOWN = 5'b00000;
parameter [0:4] P_UP = 5'b00000;
Following are the results of mapping Generics to Parameters:
Mapping Result
G_DOWN->P_DOWN 11100
G_DOWN->P_UP 11100
G_UP->P_DOWN 11100
G_UP->P_UP 11100
The same applies to parameters having no explicit range. For example:
parameter no_range = 5'b00000; //5-bit vector

Mapping Result
G_DOWN->no_range 11100
G_UP->no_range 11100
Underflow/Overflow
Mapping to Parameters with Explicit Ranges
If the Verilog parameter is constrained by a range, then the range is preserved, and the
VHDL generic is truncated or padded as necessary. For example, consider the following
generics and parameters:
Generics:
LONG : std_logic_vector(5 downto 0) := "111000";
SHORT : std_logic_vector(3 downto 0) := "1100";
Parameters:
parameter [4:0] top_address = 5'b00000;
Following is the mapping output, if you map both of the above generics to top_address:
Mapping Result
LONG ->top_address 11000 (truncated from left)
SHORT->top_address 01100 (0's padded on left)
Mapping to Parameters with No Range

Consider the case where the Verilog parameter has no range, and is given an initial value
of a 5-bit vector. For example,
parameter no_range = 5'bxxxxx; //5-bit vector
In this case, the parameter takes the range of the VHDL actual assigned to it. For
example:
Mapping Result
LONG ->no_range 111000 (now 6 bits)
SHORT->no_range 1100 (now 4 bits)
Mapping to Integer Parameters
If the Verilog parameter has no range, but has an initial value of type integer, then
the updated value takes the size and value of the VHDL generic. For example, if you

Typed Parameters
If the parameter has an explicit type, then the size of that type is preserved. The type used
implies that the parameter uses either 2-state or the 4-state logic, and the appropriate
mapping from Table 4. The following data types accept values from the VHDL data types
listed in Table 2.
integer, shortint, longint, int, bit, logic, and byte
In this case, the range is considered explicit, and therefore the resulting parameter takes
the size of the Verilog data type. For example, a parameter of type byte will also be 8-bits
long. The actual generic is padded or truncated appropriately.
Limitations
• Unpacked and multi-dimensional packed arrays are not supported.

You can instantiate the VHDL

design entity (entity and architecture) within a Verilog
design in the same way that you instantiate a Verilog module: with a module instantiation

In the module instantiation statement you can specify either of the following:
• The entity name of the top-level design entity, see Example 45 and Example 46. You

• The configuration name of the configuration that specifies the entity and architecture of

VCS also allows you to instantiate a Verilog design in a VHDL design. For information

in a VHDL Design. This VHDL design can be further instantiated in a Verilog design as
described above. This is commonly called a mixed-HDL “donut” design. There is no limit to
the number of layers of VHDL and Verilog source code in the design.
The ports declared in the top-level entity are limited to the following data types:
• The built-in bit and boolean data types
• The IEEE std_logic, std_logic_vector, std_ulogic and std_ulogic_vector data
types
• The IEEE std_logic_arith and numeric_bit defining signed and unsigned types
The generics in the top-level entity are limited to the integer, real, string, bit,
boolean and time generic data types.

Passing Parameter Values to VHDL GenericsVHDLinstantiating top-level design entitypassing parameter values to generics
The part of the module instantiation statement that passes and assigns parameters, is
located between the module identifier and the instance name and resembles a delay
specification. In Example 46, it is this part: #(15,"myInst"). It is in this part of the
statement that you can pass new values to the VHDL generics in the top-level VHDL
entity. You pass new values to these generics in the order in which they are declared in
that entity. Passing new values to these generics is optional.
In addition to passing parameter values directly, you can also use name-based parameter
passing to pass a value to a generic. To do this, you must include the
+v2k+v2k[v2k]
+v2k compile-time
option that enables name-based parameter passing. Example 49 shows an instantiation
statement that passes and assigns a valid name-based parameter.
Example 49 A Valid Parameter Passing Assignment Part

The top-level entity can have generics of type real, integer, string, bit, boolean, and
TIME.
You can pass an integer to bit and boolean generics. A 0 (zero) value is a 0 value to a
bit generic and a false value to a boolean generic. Any other value is a 1 value to a bit
generic or a true value to a boolean generic.
Pass a Verilog string to a TIME generic. The TIME type has both a value and a unit so
include both in the string, for example:
vhdltop #(.myTIME("10 ns")) vhdltopinst (rega,wireb);
You can pass delay values to the VHDL design using integer or real generic types in
combination with a TIME generic. The VHDL design multiplies the integer or real value
with the TIME value to calculate the delay value. In Example 45, generic p1, of the
integer type, with the default value of 10, is used as a delay value for a concurrent signal
assignment statement. In the module instantiation statement in Example 46, a new value
of 15 is passed to generic p1 as a parameter.
Important:
You cannot use a Verilog defparam statement to pass values to a VHDL
generic.
Connecting Verilog Signals to VHDL PortsVHDLinstantiating top-level design entityconnecting Verilog signals to VHDL ports
You can use name-based or order-based syntax for connecting signals to the instance of
the VHDL design entity. In order-based syntax, you list the signals that connect to the ports
in the VHDL top-level entity in the same order that you declare the ports in the entity.
In name-based syntax you can connect the Verilog signals to the VHDL ports in any order.
Example 50 shows valid order based and name based connection lists.
Example 50 Valid Order Based and Name Based Connection Lists
vhdltop #(15,"myInst") vhdltopinst (rega,wireb);
vhdltop #(15,"myInst") vhdltopinst (.pb(wireb),.pa(rega));
In the second, name-based, connection list in Example 5-11, the VHDL ports are not listed
in the order in which they are declared in the VHDL entity (although they could also be
validly listed in that order).
VHDL is not case-sensitive so the following name based connection list would also work:
vhdltop #(15,"myInst") vhdltopinst (.PB(wireb),.Pa(rega));

Instantiating a Signed or Unsigned VHDL Design Entity
You can instantiate a VHDL entity having a port or generic of type signed or unsigned in a
Verilog module. VHDL explicitly supports signed and unsigned types, and Verilog supports
arithmetic and arithmetic shift operations on signed vectors of arbitrary length. Further,
though Verilog does not have any explicit unsigned types, all wire types are effectively
unsigned. VHDL explicitly supports signed and unsigned types.
The following example shows a VHDL adder design with signed and unsigned types
followed by the part of the Verilog testbench design instantiating the VHDL module.

use IEEE.STD_LOGIC_1164.all;
use IEEE.std_logic_arith.all;

port (A: in signed(7 downto 0);
B: in unsigned(7 downto 0);
CIN: in std_logic;
SUM: out signed(7 downto 0));
end FULL_ADD8;

architecture FOR_GENERATE of FULL_ADD8 is

process (A, B, CIN)
SUM <= A + B + CIN;
end FOR_GENERATE;

configuration CFG_fulladder of FULL_ADD8 is
for FOR_GENERATE
end for;

// vhdl: signed + unsigned

reg signed [7:0] A;
reg [7:0] B;

FULL_ADD8 i1(A, B, CIN, SUM);

A = 4'b0;
B = 4'b0;
CIN = 1'b0;
#1 A = -4'sh3;
B = 4'b0011;
#1 A = 4'b0010;
B = 4'sh7;
.
.

end

Modeling Your Design
Verilog coding style is the most important factor that affects the simulation performance
of a design. How you write your design can make the difference between a fast error-free
simulation, and one that suffers from race conditions and poor performance. This chapter
describes some Verilog modeling techniques that will help you code designs that simulate
most efficiently with VCS.
This chapter covers the following topics:
• Avoiding Race Conditions
• Race Detection in Verilog Code
• Optimizing Testbenches for Debugging
• Avoiding the Debugging Problems From Port Coercion
• Creating Models That Simulate Faster
• Case Statement Behavior
• Precedence in Text Macro Definitions
• Memory Size Limits in VCS
• Using Sparse Memory Models
• Obtaining Scope Information
• Avoiding Circular Dependency
Avoiding Race Conditions
A race condition is defined as a coding style for which there is more than one correct
result. Since the output of the race condition is unpredictable, it can cause unexpected
problems during simulation. It is easy to accidentally code race conditions in Verilog. For
example, in Digital Design with Verilog HDL by Sternheim, Singh, and Trivedi, at least two
of the examples provided with the book (adder and cachemem) have race conditions. VCS
provides some tools for race detection. For details, see Race Detection in Verilog Code.

Avoiding Race Conditions
Some common race conditions and ways of avoiding them are described in the following
sections.
Using and Setting a Value at the Same Time
In this example, the two parallel blocks have no guaranteed ordering, so it is ambiguous
whether the $display statement will be executed.
module race;
reg a;
a = 0;
#10 a = 1;
end
#10 if (a) $display("may not print");
end
The solution is to delay the $display statement with a #0 delay:
#10 if (a)
#0 $display("may not print");
end
You can also move it to the next time step with a non-zero delay.
Setting a Value Twice at the Same Time
In this example, the race condition occurs at time 10 because no ordering is guaranteed
between the two parallel initial blocks.
module race;
reg r1;
initial #10 r1 = 0;
initial #10 r1 = 1;
#20 if (r1) $display("may not print");
The solution is to stagger the assignments to register r1 by finite time, so that the ordering
of the assignments is guaranteed. Note that using the nonblocking assignment (<=) in both
assignments to r1 would not remove the race condition in this example.

Avoiding Race Conditions
Flip-Flop Race Condition
It is very common to have race conditions near latches or flip-flops. Here is one variant in
which an intermediate node a between two flip-flops is set and sampled at the same time:
module test(out,in,clk);
input in,clk;
output out;
wire a;
dff dff0(a,in,clk);
dff dff1(out,a,clk);
module dff(q,d,clk);
output q;
input d,clk;
reg q;
q = d; // race!
The solution for this case is straightforward. Use the nonblocking assignment in the flip-
flop to guarantee the order of assignments to the output of the instances of the flip-flop
and sampling of that output. The change looks like this:
q <= d; // ok
Or add a nonzero delay on the output of the flip-flop:
q = #1 d; // ok
Or use a nonzero delay in addition to the nonblocking form:
q <= #1 d; // ok
Note that the following change does not resolve the race condition:
#1 q = d; // race!
The #1 delay simply shifts the original race by one time unit, so that the intermediate node
is set and sampled one time unit after the posedge of clock, rather than on the posedge of
clock. Avoid this coding style.

Avoiding Race Conditions
Continuous Assignment Evaluation
Continuous assignments with no delay are sometimes propagated earlier in VCS than in
Verilog-XL. This is fully correct behavior, but exposes race conditions such as the one in
the following code fragment:
assign x = y;
y = 1;
#1
y = 0;
$display(x);
end
In VCS, this displays 0, while in Verilog-XL, it displays 1, because the assignment of the
value to x races with the usage of that value by the $display.
Another example of this type of race condition is the following:
assign state0 = (state == 3'h0);
state = 0;
if (state0)
// do something
end
The modification of state may propagate to state0 before the if statement, causing
unexpected behavior. You can avoid this by using the nonblocking assignment to state in
the procedural code as follows:
state <= 0;
if (state0)
// do something
This guarantees that state is not updated until the end of the time step, that is, after the
if statement has executed.
Counting Events
A different type of race condition occurs when code depends on the number of times
events are triggered in the same time step. For instance, in the following example, if A
and B change at the same time, it is unpredictable whether count is incremented once or
twice:
always @(A or B)
count = count + 1;
Another form of this race condition is to toggle a register within the always block. If
toggled once or twice, the result may be unexpected behavior.

The solution to this race condition is to make the code inside the always block insensitive
to the number of times it is called.
Time Zero Race Conditions
The following race condition is subtle but very common:
always @(posedge clock)
$display("May or may not display");
clock = 1;
forever #50 clock = ~clock;
end
This is a race condition because the transition of clock to 1 (posedge) may happen before
or after the event trigger (always @(posedge clock) ) is established. Often the race is not
evident in the simulation result because reset occurs at time zero.
The solution to this race condition is to guarantee that no transitions take place at time
zero of any signals inside event triggers. Rewrite the clock driver in the above example as
follows:
clock = 1'bx;
#50 clock = 1'b0;
forever #50 clock = ~clock;
end

• Dynamic Race Detection Tool - Finds the race conditions during simulation.
• Static Race Detection Tool- Finds the race conditions by analyzing source code
during compilation.

Introduction to the Dynamic Race Detection Tool
The dynamic race detection tool finds two basic types of race conditions during simulation:
• Read - Write Race Condition
• Read
• Write
• Write - Write Race Condition
• Write-Write
Read - Write Race Condition
The Read - Write race condition occurs when both Read and Write on a signal take place
at the same simulation time.
Example:
#5 var1 = 0; // write operation on signal var1

#5 var2 = var1; // read operation on signal var2
Read
Procedural assignment in any one of the always or initial block, or a continuous
assignment samples the value of signal var1 to drive signal var2.
Write
Procedural assignment in another always or initial block, or another continuous
assignment assigns a new value to signal var1.

In the above example, at the simulation time 5, there is both read and write operation on
signal var1. When simulation time 5 is over, you do not know if signal var2 will have the
value 0 or the previous value of signal var1.
Write - Write Race Condition
The Write - Write race condition occurs when multiple writes on a signal take place at the
same simulation time.
Example:
#5 var1 = 0; // write operation on signal var1

#5 var1 = 1; // write operation on signal var1
Write-Write
Value of the signal var1 is non-deterministic when there are multiple concurrent procedural
assignments on the same variable at the same simulation time.
In the above example, at simulation time 5, different initial blocks assign 0 and 1 to signal
var1. When simulation time 5 is over, you do not know if var1 signal value is 0 or 1.
Finding these race conditions is important because in Verilog simulation you cannot
control the order of execution of statements in different always or initial blocks, or
continuous assignments that execute at the same simulation time. This means that a
race condition can produce different simulation results when you simulate a design with
different, but both properly functioning Verilog simulators.
Even worse, a race condition can result in different simulation results with different
versions of a particular simulator, or with different optimizations or performance features of
the same version of a simulator.
$dumpvars can also expose races.
Also, sometimes modifications in one part of a design can cause hidden race conditions to
surface even in unmodified parts of a design, thereby causing different simulation results
from the unmodified part of the design.
The indications of a race condition are the following:
• When simulation results do not match when comparing simulators
• When design modifications cause inexplicable results
• When simulation results do not match between different simulation runs of the same
simulator, when different versions or different optimization features of that simulator are
used

Therefore, even when a Verilog design appears to be simulating correctly and you see
the results you want, you should look for race conditions and remove them so that you will
continue to see the same simulation results from an unrevised design well into the future.
Also, you should look for race conditions while a design is in development.
VCS can help you find these race conditions by writing report files about the race
conditions in your design.
VCS writes the reports at run time, but you should enable race detection at compile-time
with a compile-time option.
The reports can be lengthy for large designs. You can post-process the report to generate
another shorter report that is limited, for example, to only part of the design or to only
between certain simulation times.
Enabling Race Detection
When you compile your design, you can enable race detection during simulation for your
entire design or part of your design.
The -race compile-time option enables race detection for your entire design.
The -racecd compile-time option enables race detection for the part of your design that is
enclosed between the 'race and 'endrace compiler directives.
The -race and -racecd compile-time options supports dynamic race detection
for both pure Verilog and SystemVerilog data types.
The Race Detection Report
While VCS simulates your design, it writes race detection reports to the race.out and
race.unique.out files.
The race.out file contains a line for all race conditions that it finds at all times throughout
the simulation. If VCS executes two different statements in the same time step for several
times, the race.out file contains a line for each of these times.
The race.unique.out file contains only lines for race conditions that are unique, and
which have not been reported in a previous line.
The race.unique.out is automatically created by the PostRace.pl Perl script
after the simulation. This script needs a perl5 interpreter. The first line of the
script points to perl at a specific location, see Modifying the PostRace.pl Script.
If that location at your site is not a perl5 interpreter, the script fails with syntax
errors.

The report describes read-write and write-write race conditions. The following is an
example of the contents of a small race.out file:
Synopsys Simulation VCS RACE REPORT

Z z 0
W x 0
L 0 0
H 1 1
- x 0
Examples
The following sections describe the examples of this feature.
• Ordered Vector
• Underflow/Overflow
• Typed Parameters
Ordered Vector
A vector can have an ascending range ([0:4] or (0 to 4) ) or a descending range
([4:0], (4 downto 0) ) in both VHDL and Verilog. However, when mapping VHDL
generics to Verilog parameters, the ranges are irrelevant, and the mapping always occurs
from right to left. For example, if you want to map all combinations in Example 44.
Example 44 Design Example
COMPONENT vector
GENERIC (
G_DOWN : std_logic_vector(4 downto 0);
G_UP : std_logic_vector(0 to 4));
PORT (
top_in : IN std_logic;
top_out : OUT std_logic
);
END COMPONENT

Generics:
G_DOWN : std_logic_vector(4 downto 0) := "11100";
G_UP : std_logic_vector(0 to 4) := "11100";
Parameters:
parameter [4:0] P_DOWN = 5'b00000;
parameter [0:4] P_UP = 5'b00000;
Following are the results of mapping Generics to Parameters:
Mapping Result
G_DOWN->P_DOWN 11100
G_DOWN->P_UP 11100
G_UP->P_DOWN 11100
G_UP->P_UP 11100
The same applies to parameters having no explicit range. For example:
parameter no_range = 5'b00000; //5-bit vector

Mapping Result
G_DOWN->no_range 11100
G_UP->no_range 11100
Underflow/Overflow
Mapping to Parameters with Explicit Ranges
If the Verilog parameter is constrained by a range, then the range is preserved, and the
VHDL generic is truncated or padded as necessary. For example, consider the following
generics and parameters:
Generics:
LONG : std_logic_vector(5 downto 0) := "111000";
SHORT : std_logic_vector(3 downto 0) := "1100";
Parameters:
parameter [4:0] top_address = 5'b00000;
Following is the mapping output, if you map both of the above generics to top_address:
Mapping Result
LONG ->top_address 11000 (truncated from left)
SHORT->top_address 01100 (0's padded on left)
Mapping to Parameters with No Range

Consider the case where the Verilog parameter has no range, and is given an initial value
of a 5-bit vector. For example,
parameter no_range = 5'bxxxxx; //5-bit vector
In this case, the parameter takes the range of the VHDL actual assigned to it. For
example:
Mapping Result
LONG ->no_range 111000 (now 6 bits)
SHORT->no_range 1100 (now 4 bits)
Mapping to Integer Parameters
If the Verilog parameter has no range, but has an initial value of type integer, then
the updated value takes the size and value of the VHDL generic. For example, if you
instantiate the following module in your VHDL code:
module intp #(INT=0);
$display("%m:INT is %b, integer value: %0d, size=%0d",
INT, INT, $bits(INT));
and map the following code to INT:
LONG : std_logic_vector (5 downto 0) := "111000";
The output of the module is:
test.i3:INT is 111000, integer value: 56, size=6
Even if the VHDL generic is greater than 32 bits (default size of parameter), the new value
and size is taken.
If you pass the following VHDL vector to a parameter:
constant very_long : std_logic_vector(127 downto 0) :=
X"DEADBEEF_DEADBEEF_01010101_DEADBEEF";
The output is:
test.i4:INT is 1101111010101101101111101110111111011110101011011011111011
1011110000000100000001000000010000000111011110101011011011
111011101111, integer value:
295990755083049101696546033211796209391, size=128
Consider the following VHDL constants:
constant bitv : bit_vector(7 downto 0) := "01010101";
constant unsig : unsigned(7 downto 0) := "11111111";
constant signe : signed(7 downto 0) := "11111111";

constant integ : integer := 64;
constant boole : boolean := TRUE;
Following is the mapping output. It shows the resulting size of INT for the above VHDL
constants.
Mapping Result
bitv->INT INT is 01010101, integer value 85, size=8
unsig->INT INT is 11111111, integer value 255, size=8
signe->INT INT is 11111111, integer value 255, size=8
integ->INT INT is 00000000000000000000000001000000,
integer value 64, size=32
boole->INT INT is 1, integer value 1, size=1
Typed Parameters
If the parameter has an explicit type, then the size of that type is preserved. The type used
implies that the parameter uses either 2-state or the 4-state logic, and the appropriate
mapping from Table 4. The following data types accept values from the VHDL data types
listed in Table 2.
integer, shortint, longint, int, bit, logic, and byte
In this case, the range is considered explicit, and therefore the resulting parameter takes
the size of the Verilog data type. For example, a parameter of type byte will also be 8-bits
long. The actual generic is padded or truncated appropriately.
Limitations
• Unpacked and multi-dimensional packed arrays are not supported.
VHDLinstantiating top-level design entity
You can instantiate the VHDL
design entityinstantiating
design entity (entity and architecture) within a Verilog
design in the same way that you instantiate a Verilog module: with a module instantiation
statement.
In the module instantiation statement you can specify either of the following:
• The entity name of the top-level design entity, see Example 45 and Example 46. You
don’t specify the architecture when you specify the entity. During elaboration, the vcs
compiler uses the most recently compiled architecture for the entity. In VCS, VHDL
elaboration happens when you compile the Verilog part of the design.
• The configuration name of the configuration that specifies the entity and architecture of
the top-level design entity, see Example 47 and Example 48.
VCS also allows you to instantiate a Verilog design in a VHDL design. For information
on instantiating a Verilog design in a VHDL design, refer Instantiating a Verilog Design

in a VHDL Design. This VHDL design can be further instantiated in a Verilog design as
described above. This is commonly called a mixed-HDL “donut” design. There is no limit to
the number of layers of VHDL and Verilog source code in the design.
The ports declared in the top-level entity are limited to the following data types:
• The built-in bit and boolean data types
• The IEEE std_logic, std_logic_vector, std_ulogic and std_ulogic_vector data
types
• The IEEE std_logic_arith and numeric_bit defining signed and unsigned types
The generics in the top-level entity are limited to the integer, real, string, bit,
boolean and time generic data types.
Instantiating By Entity Name

entity vhdl_en is
generic (p1 : integer := 10;
INSTNAME : string := "I1");
port ( a : in bit;
b : out bit);
end vhdl_en;

architecture vhdl_enarch of vhdl_en is

vhdl_en #(15,"myInst") vhdl_eninst (rega,wireb);
In Example 46, the module identifier vhdl_en matches the entity name of the top-level

attach to the VHDL ports a and b.

Passing Parameter Values to VHDL GenericsVHDLinstantiating top-level design entitypassing parameter values to generics
The part of the module instantiation statement that passes and assigns parameters, is
located between the module identifier and the instance name and resembles a delay
specification. In Example 46, it is this part: #(15,"myInst"). It is in this part of the
statement that you can pass new values to the VHDL generics in the top-level VHDL
entity. You pass new values to these generics in the order in which they are declared in
that entity. Passing new values to these generics is optional.
In addition to passing parameter values directly, you can also use name-based parameter
passing to pass a value to a generic. To do this, you must include the
+v2k+v2k[v2k]
+v2k compile-time
option that enables name-based parameter passing. Example 49 shows an instantiation
statement that passes and assigns a valid name-based parameter.
Example 49 A Valid Parameter Passing Assignment Part
vhdltop #(.instname("myInst")) vhdltopinst (rega,wireb);

The top-level entity can have generics of type real, integer, string, bit, boolean, and
TIME.
You can pass an integer to bit and boolean generics. A 0 (zero) value is a 0 value to a
bit generic and a false value to a boolean generic. Any other value is a 1 value to a bit
generic or a true value to a boolean generic.
Pass a Verilog string to a TIME generic. The TIME type has both a value and a unit so
include both in the string, for example:
vhdltop #(.myTIME("10 ns")) vhdltopinst (rega,wireb);
You can pass delay values to the VHDL design using integer or real generic types in
combination with a TIME generic. The VHDL design multiplies the integer or real value
with the TIME value to calculate the delay value. In Example 45, generic p1, of the
integer type, with the default value of 10, is used as a delay value for a concurrent signal
assignment statement. In the module instantiation statement in Example 46, a new value
of 15 is passed to generic p1 as a parameter.
Important:
You cannot use a Verilog defparam statement to pass values to a VHDL
generic.
Connecting Verilog Signals to VHDL PortsVHDLinstantiating top-level design entityconnecting Verilog signals to VHDL ports
You can use name-based or order-based syntax for connecting signals to the instance of
the VHDL design entity. In order-based syntax, you list the signals that connect to the ports
in the VHDL top-level entity in the same order that you declare the ports in the entity.
In name-based syntax you can connect the Verilog signals to the VHDL ports in any order.
Example 50 shows valid order based and name based connection lists.
Example 50 Valid Order Based and Name Based Connection Lists
vhdltop #(15,"myInst") vhdltopinst (rega,wireb);
vhdltop #(15,"myInst") vhdltopinst (.pb(wireb),.pa(rega));
In the second, name-based, connection list in Example 5-11, the VHDL ports are not listed
in the order in which they are declared in the VHDL entity (although they could also be
validly listed in that order).

Modeling Your Design
Verilog coding style is the most important factor that affects the simulation performance
of a design. How you write your design can make the difference between a fast error-free
simulation, and one that suffers from race conditions and poor performance. This chapter
describes some Verilog modeling techniques that will help you code designs that simulate
most efficiently with VCS.
This chapter covers the following topics:
• Avoiding Race Conditions
• Race Detection in Verilog Code
• Optimizing Testbenches for Debugging
• Avoiding the Debugging Problems From Port Coercion
• Creating Models That Simulate Faster
• Case Statement Behavior
• Precedence in Text Macro Definitions
• Memory Size Limits in VCS
• Using Sparse Memory Models
• Obtaining Scope Information
• Avoiding Circular Dependency
Avoiding Race Conditions
A race condition is defined as a coding style for which there is more than one correct
result. Since the output of the race condition is unpredictable, it can cause unexpected
problems during simulation. It is easy to accidentally code race conditions in Verilog. For
example, in Digital Design with Verilog HDL by Sternheim, Singh, and Trivedi, at least two
of the examples provided with the book (adder and cachemem) have race conditions. VCS
provides some tools for race detection. For details, see Race Detection in Verilog Code.

Avoiding Race Conditions
Some common race conditions and ways of avoiding them are described in the following
sections.
Using and Setting a Value at the Same Time
In this example, the two parallel blocks have no guaranteed ordering, so it is ambiguous
whether the $display statement will be executed.
module race;
reg a;
a = 0;
#10 a = 1;
end
#10 if (a) $display("may not print");
end
The solution is to delay the $display statement with a #0 delay:
#10 if (a)
#0 $display("may not print");
end
You can also move it to the next time step with a non-zero delay.
Setting a Value Twice at the Same Time
In this example, the race condition occurs at time 10 because no ordering is guaranteed
between the two parallel initial blocks.
module race;
reg r1;
initial #10 r1 = 0;
initial #10 r1 = 1;
#20 if (r1) $display("may not print");
The solution is to stagger the assignments to register r1 by finite time, so that the ordering
of the assignments is guaranteed. Note that using the nonblocking assignment (<=) in both
assignments to r1 would not remove the race condition in this example.

Avoiding Race Conditions
Flip-Flop Race Condition
It is very common to have race conditions near latches or flip-flops. Here is one variant in
which an intermediate node a between two flip-flops is set and sampled at the same time:
module test(out,in,clk);
input in,clk;
output out;
wire a;
dff dff0(a,in,clk);
dff dff1(out,a,clk);
module dff(q,d,clk);
output q;
input d,clk;
reg q;
q = d; // race!
The solution for this case is straightforward. Use the nonblocking assignment in the flip-
flop to guarantee the order of assignments to the output of the instances of the flip-flop
and sampling of that output. The change looks like this:
q <= d; // ok
Or add a nonzero delay on the output of the flip-flop:
q = #1 d; // ok
Or use a nonzero delay in addition to the nonblocking form:
q <= #1 d; // ok
Note that the following change does not resolve the race condition:
#1 q = d; // race!
The #1 delay simply shifts the original race by one time unit, so that the intermediate node
is set and sampled one time unit after the posedge of clock, rather than on the posedge of
clock. Avoid this coding style.

Avoiding Race Conditions
Continuous Assignment Evaluation
Continuous assignments with no delay are sometimes propagated earlier in VCS than in
Verilog-XL. This is fully correct behavior, but exposes race conditions such as the one in
the following code fragment:
assign x = y;
y = 1;
#1
y = 0;
$display(x);
end
In VCS, this displays 0, while in Verilog-XL, it displays 1, because the assignment of the
value to x races with the usage of that value by the $display.
Another example of this type of race condition is the following:
assign state0 = (state == 3'h0);
state = 0;
if (state0)
// do something
end
The modification of state may propagate to state0 before the if statement, causing
unexpected behavior. You can avoid this by using the nonblocking assignment to state in
the procedural code as follows:
state <= 0;
if (state0)
// do something
This guarantees that state is not updated until the end of the time step, that is, after the
if statement has executed.
Counting Events
A different type of race condition occurs when code depends on the number of times
events are triggered in the same time step. For instance, in the following example, if A
and B change at the same time, it is unpredictable whether count is incremented once or
twice:
always @(A or B)
count = count + 1;
Another form of this race condition is to toggle a register within the always block. If
toggled once or twice, the result may be unexpected behavior.

The solution to this race condition is to make the code inside the always block insensitive
to the number of times it is called.
Time Zero Race Conditions
The following race condition is subtle but very common:
always @(posedge clock)
$display("May or may not display");
clock = 1;
forever #50 clock = ~clock;
end
This is a race condition because the transition of clock to 1 (posedge) may happen before
or after the event trigger (always @(posedge clock) ) is established. Often the race is not
evident in the simulation result because reset occurs at time zero.
The solution to this race condition is to guarantee that no transitions take place at time
zero of any signals inside event triggers. Rewrite the clock driver in the above example as
follows:
clock = 1'bx;
#50 clock = 1'b0;
forever #50 clock = ~clock;
end
VCS provides the following race detection tools:
• Dynamic Race Detection Tool - Finds the race conditions during simulation.

follows:
clock = 1'bx;
#50 clock = 1'b0;
forever #50 clock = ~clock;
end
VCS provides the following race detection tools:
• Dynamic Race Detection Tool - Finds the race conditions during simulation.
• Static Race Detection Tool- Finds the race conditions by analyzing source code
during compilation.
The above two tools are described in the following sections:

The Dynamic Race Detection Tool
This section consists of following topics:
• Introduction to the Dynamic Race Detection Tool
• Enabling Race Detection
• The Race Detection Report
• Post Processing the Report
• Debugging Simulation Mismatches
Introduction to the Dynamic Race Detection Tool
The dynamic race detection tool finds two basic types of race conditions during simulation:
• Read - Write Race Condition
• Read
• Write
• Write - Write Race Condition
• Write-Write
Read - Write Race Condition
The Read - Write race condition occurs when both Read and Write on a signal take place
at the same simulation time.
Example:
#5 var1 = 0; // write operation on signal var1

#5 var2 = var1; // read operation on signal var2
Read
Procedural assignment in any one of the always or initial block, or a continuous
assignment samples the value of signal var1 to drive signal var2.
Write
Procedural assignment in another always or initial block, or another continuous
assignment assigns a new value to signal var1.

In the above example, at the simulation time 5, there is both read and write operation on
signal var1. When simulation time 5 is over, you do not know if signal var2 will have the
value 0 or the previous value of signal var1.
Write - Write Race Condition
The Write - Write race condition occurs when multiple writes on a signal take place at the
same simulation time.
Example:
#5 var1 = 0; // write operation on signal var1

#5 var1 = 1; // write operation on signal var1
Write-Write
Value of the signal var1 is non-deterministic when there are multiple concurrent procedural
assignments on the same variable at the same simulation time.
In the above example, at simulation time 5, different initial blocks assign 0 and 1 to signal
var1. When simulation time 5 is over, you do not know if var1 signal value is 0 or 1.
Finding these race conditions is important because in Verilog simulation you cannot
control the order of execution of statements in different always or initial blocks, or
continuous assignments that execute at the same simulation time. This means that a
race condition can produce different simulation results when you simulate a design with
different, but both properly functioning Verilog simulators.
Even worse, a race condition can result in different simulation results with different
versions of a particular simulator, or with different optimizations or performance features of
the same version of a simulator.
$dumpvars can also expose races.
Also, sometimes modifications in one part of a design can cause hidden race conditions to
surface even in unmodified parts of a design, thereby causing different simulation results
from the unmodified part of the design.
The indications of a race condition are the following:
• When simulation results do not match when comparing simulators
• When design modifications cause inexplicable results
• When simulation results do not match between different simulation runs of the same
simulator, when different versions or different optimization features of that simulator are
used

Therefore, even when a Verilog design appears to be simulating correctly and you see
the results you want, you should look for race conditions and remove them so that you will
continue to see the same simulation results from an unrevised design well into the future.
Also, you should look for race conditions while a design is in development.
VCS can help you find these race conditions by writing report files about the race
conditions in your design.
VCS writes the reports at run time, but you should enable race detection at compile-time
with a compile-time option.
The reports can be lengthy for large designs. You can post-process the report to generate
another shorter report that is limited, for example, to only part of the design or to only
between certain simulation times.
Enabling Race Detection
When you compile your design, you can enable race detection during simulation for your
entire design or part of your design.
The -race compile-time option enables race detection for your entire design.
The -racecd compile-time option enables race detection for the part of your design that is
enclosed between the 'race and 'endrace compiler directives.
The -race and -racecd compile-time options supports dynamic race detection
for both pure Verilog and SystemVerilog data types.
The Race Detection Report
While VCS simulates your design, it writes race detection reports to the race.out and
race.unique.out files.
The race.out file contains a line for all race conditions that it finds at all times throughout
the simulation. If VCS executes two different statements in the same time step for several
times, the race.out file contains a line for each of these times.
The race.unique.out file contains only lines for race conditions that are unique, and
which have not been reported in a previous line.
The race.unique.out is automatically created by the PostRace.pl Perl script
after the simulation. This script needs a perl5 interpreter. The first line of the
script points to perl at a specific location, see Modifying the PostRace.pl Script.
If that location at your site is not a perl5 interpreter, the script fails with syntax
errors.

Sometimes race conditions exist, such as write-write race to a signal at the same
simulation time, but the two statements that are assigning to the signal are assigning the

the end of the line for the race in the race.out file.

text:
Post Processing the Report
VCS comes with the PostRace.pl Perl script that you can use to post-process the
race.out report to generate another report that contains a subset of the race conditions in
the race.out file. You should include options on the command line for the PostRace.pl
script to specify this subset. These options are as follows:
-hier module_instance Specifies the hierarchical name of a module instance. The
new report lists only the race conditions found in this instance and all module instances
hierarchically under this instance.
-sig signal Specifies the signal that you want to examine for race conditions. You
can only specify one signal, and must not include a hierarchical name for the signal. If
two signals in different module instances have the same identifier, the report lists race
conditions for both signals.

-minmax min max Specifies the minimum (or earliest) and the maximum (or latest)
simulation time in the report.
-nozero Omits race conditions that occur at simulation time 0.
-uniq Omits race conditions that also occurred earlier in the simulation. The output is the
same as the contents of the race.unique.out file.
-f filename Specifies the name of the input file. Use this option if you have changed the
name of the race.out file.
-o filename The default name of the output file is race.out.post. If you want a different
name, specify it with this option.
You can enter more than one of these options on the PostRace.pl command line.
If you enter an option more than once, the script uses the last of these multiple entries.
Unless you specify a different name with the -o option, the report generated by the
PostRace.pl script is in the race.out.post file.
The following is an example of the command line:
PostRace.pl -minmax 80 250 -f mydesign.race.out -o
mydesign.race.out.post
In this example, the output file is named mydesign.race.out.post, and reports
the race conditions between 80 and 250 time units. The post-process file is named
mydesign.race.out.
Modifying the PostRace.pl Script
The first line of the PostRace.pl Perl script is as follows:
#! /usr/local/bin/perl
If Perl is installed at a different location at your site, you must modify the first line of this
script. This script needs a perl5 interpreter. You can find this script at the following location:
vcs_install_dir/bin/PostRace.pl
Debugging Simulation Mismatches
A design can contain several race conditions where many of them behave the same in
different simulations, so they are not the cause of a simulation mismatch. For a simulation
mismatch, you must find critical races. Critical races are the race conditions that cause the
simulation mismatch. This section describes how to do this.
Add system tasks to generate VCD files to the source code of the simulations that
mismatch. Recompile them with the -race or -racecd options and run the simulations
again.

When you have two VCD files, find their differences with the vcdiff utility. This utility
is located in the vcs_install_dir/bin directory. The command line for vcdiff is as
follows:
vcdiff vcdfile1.dmp vcdfile2.dmp -options > output_filename
If you enter the vcdiff command without arguments, you see the usage information
including the options.
Method 1: If the Number of Unique Race Conditions is Small
A unique race condition is a race condition that can occur several times during simulation,
but only the first occurrence is reported in the race.unique.out file . If the number of
lines in the race.unique.out file are smaller than the number of unique race conditions,
then for each signal in the race.unique.out file:
1. Look in the output file from the vcdiff utility. If the signal values are different, you have
found a critical write-write race condition.
2. If the signal values are not different, look for the signals that are assigned the value of
this signal, or assigned expressions that include this signal (read operations).
3. If the values of these other signals are different at any point in the two simulations,
note the simulation times of these differences on the other signals, and post-process
the race.out file looking for race conditions in the first signal at around the simulation
times of the value differences on the other signals. Specify simulation times before and
after the time of these differences with the -minmax option. Enter:
PostRace.pl -sig first_signal -minmax time time2
If the race.out.post file contains the first signal, then it is a critical race condition, and
must be corrected.
Method 2: If the Number of Unique Races is Large
If there are many lines in the race.unique.out file and a large number of unique race
conditions, then the method of finding the critical race conditions is to do the following:
1. Look in the output file from the vcdiff utility for the simulation time of the first
difference in simulation values.
2. Post-process the race.out file looking for races at the time of the first simulation value
difference. Specify simulation times before and after the time of these differences with
the -minmax option. Enter:
PostRace.pl -minmax time time2

3. For each signal in the resulting race.out.post file:
◦ If the simulation values differ in the two simulations, then the race condition in the
race.out.post file is a critical race condition.
◦ If the simulation values are not different, check the signals that are assigned the
value of this signal or assigned expressions that include this signal. If the values of
these other signals are different, then the race condition in the race.out.post file
is a critical race condition.
Method 3: An Alternative When the Number of Unique Race Conditions is Large
1. Look in the output file from the vcdiff utility for the simulation time of the first
difference in simulation values.
2. For each signal that has a difference at this simulation time:
a. Traverse the signal dependency backward in the design until you find a signal
whose values are same in both simulations.
b. Look for a race condition on that signal at that time. Enter: PostRace.pl -sig
signal -minmax time time2 If there is a race condition at that time on that signal,
then it is a critical race condition.
The Static Race Detection Tool
It is possible for a group of statements to combine and form a loop, so that the loop is
executed once by VCS and more than once by other Verilog simulators. This is a race
condition.
These situations arise when level-sensitive sensitivity lists (event controls which
immediately follow the always keyword in an always block, and which do not contain
the posedge or negedge keywords) and procedural assignment statements in the
always blocks combine with other statements such as continuous assignment or module
instantiation statements to form a potential loop. It is observed that these situations do
not occur if the always blocks contain delays or other timing information, non-blocking
assignment statements, or PLI calls through user-defined system tasks.
You can use the
+race=all+race=all[race=all]
+race=all compile-time option to start the static race detection tool.
The
+race=all+race=all[race=all]
+race=all compile-time option supports only pure Verilog constructs.
After compilation, the static race detection tool writes the file named race.out.static
which reports the race conditions.
