Derived Test Metrics
You can use the following derived built-in test metrics to track verification progress:
• Percent Metric for Test Metric
• test.completion Metric
Using these metrics, you can gather the percentage of tests with different status and test
completion percentage in a verification plan.

Percent Metric for Test Metric
The built-in test metric of enum type reports integer count for sub-metrics: test.pass,
test.fail, test.warn, test.unknown, and test.assert. For example,
test = 6;
test.pass = 3;
test.fail = 3;
The test metric reports the basic number of tests passing, failing, unknown, with warning,
and asserts in the HVP annotated report. It does not display the percentage of these
scores. The test metric score is computed by collecting the scores of measures in the
current feature, its sub-features, and subplans.
For the built-in test metric of enum type, Verification Planner reports percentage for each
enum value of the enum metric. This enables you to get the percentage of tests that pass,
fail, warning, unknown, or assert. The following is the list of the percent sub-metrics:
•
test.percent.pass
test.percent.pass
•
test.percent.fail
test.percent.fail
•
test.percent.warn
test.percent.warn
•
test.percent.unknown
test.percent.unknown
•
test.percent.assert
test.percent.assert
The percent metric is the percentage of the tests with different status (that is the enum
value of pass/fail/warn/unknown/assert) and the total number of tests in that feature.
For example, if test.x is the existing count of the enum value and test is the total count,
then the percentage is computed as follows:
(test.x / test)*100
For example, if
test.pass = 8
test.fail = 2
test = 10
then, the value of test.percentage.pass = 8/10 and is reported as 80%.
Following is the example for the usage of percent metrics:
Example 1 Usage of Percent Metrics
feature f1;
test.percent.pass = test.percent.pass > 60%;
measure test, test.percent.pass m1;
source = "testname*";

Consider the following example,
feature parent:
test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:50.00%
feature block1
test:5[pass:3 fail:2 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:60.00%
feature block2
test:1[pass:0 fail:1 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ] test.percent.pass:
0.00%
In this example, the test.percent.pass score in feature parent is calculated from the
test score of:
feature parent test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0] 50%,
which is equal to 3/6. The score of feature parent is the sum of the scores of feature
block1 and feature block2 .
test.completion Metric
The test metric provides information about the test pass/fail rate that are already written.
By using the test.completion metric, you can protect against verification plan results
that appear better than reality. For example, if a feature requires 4 tests and only 2 tests
are written and these two tests pass, the test.pass result is shown as 100%. Whereas,
if the expected tests are set as 4 in the plan, the test.completion metric for the same is
shown as 50%. This is because the test.completion metric is calculated with reference
to the actual number of tests (2 pass tests) against the expected tests (4).
The score of the
test.completion
test.completion metric is the ratio of total count of all sub-metrics of
the test metric (test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.assert, test.unknown) and
the expected number of tests in a plan/feature. The expected number of tests should be
set using the
test.expected
test.expected attribute.

total_test_count=test.pass+test.fail+test.warn+test.assert+test.unknown

URG Report
When you add the percent metric in an HVP plan, a new column is displayed in all score
tables of hvp hierarchy page and detail page.
When the test.expected number is defined in the hvp plan, the test.completion
column is displayed in all plan and feature score tables, both in hvp hierarchy page
and detail page. Figure 3 displays the URG report with test.completion and percent
metric for Example 1.

Figure 3 Percent Metrics and test.completion Metrics in the URG Report
The percent metric column is only displayed when there is a score for these metrics.
The color is based on the goal of percent metric and no goal is based on percent score
value.
Excel XML Plan
To view the percent metric, add a new column for percentmetric and the percent metric
is explicitly displayed in the metric list of measures.
If you add a new column for test.completion, this metric does not get added in the
metric list of measures. You can set the expected number in the test.expected column,
in the original plan. The test.completion score are shown in the test.expected
column. The score of test.completion is only valid at a feature/plan level, and not at a
measure level.
Figure 4 shows the XML plan.
Figure 4 Excel XML Plan
Limitation
The scores of test.completion are displayed in the $test.expected column when the
value of test.expected is set in the XML plan. These scores are displayed when the test
score is present even when the test.completion column is not added.
Figure 5 shows its Excel annotated report.

Figure 5 Excel Annotated Report
Metric Types and Aggregators
Verification Planner supports six metric types: ratio, percent, integer, real, enum, and
aggregate. It also has five operators: max, min, sum, average, and uniquesum aggregator.
An aggregate metric type is not an aggregator.
There are five available aggregators, but you cannot apply every aggregator to every
metric type. In other words, not all the combinations of aggregators and metric types
produce valid results. The following table summarizes the meaningful combinations:
Table 5 Metric Types and Aggregators
Metric Type
Aggregator ratio percent integer real enum aggregate
sum X X OK OK OK X
average OK OK OK OK X X
min X X OK OK X X
max X X OK OK X X
uniquesum X X OK OK OK X
uniquesum
If a test is referenced by multiple features, each feature contributes to the count of test in
the top module, that is, the count of test status (pass/fail) is more than actual number of
tests. Using the uniquesum aggregator enables you to merge the duplicate tests status of
different features. Thus, the number of tests match the total count of pass/fail and ensures
that exact analysis is made.

In the following example, you can see two user-defined metrics uniq and nouniq. They
are identical, except for uniq uses the uniquesum aggregator and nouniq uses the basic
sum. In the plan, both features A and B reference test1. Note that metric nouniq, test1
is counted twice at the top plan level and you can see that uniq < nouniq and uniq.pass
< nouniq.pass.
Example 4 Using the uniquesum aggregator
File name: test_uniq.hvp
plan ex_uniq;
metric enum {pass, fail} uniq;
aggregator = uniquesum;
goal = (uniq.fail <= 0);
metric enum {pass, fail} nouniq;
aggregator = sum;
goal = (nouniq.fail <= 0);

feature A;
measure uniq, nouniq m1;
source = "test1";
feature B;
measure uniq, nouniq m1;
source = "test*";
File name: test_uniq.usd
HVP metric = uniq, nouniq
test1 = pass, pass
test2 = fail, fail
test3 = pass, pass
Command Line:
% urg -userdata test_uniq.usd -plan test_uniq.hvp

ratio
Verification Planner stores the ratio type metric as a (numerator, denominator) pair.
The purpose of this type is to provide meaningful aggregation of two coverage metrics.
A coverage metric of type ratio can use the numerator to store the number of covered
items, and the denominator to store the total coverable items under test. When two
coverage metrics are aggregated by an average operator, Verification Planner adds all the
numerators and the denominators separately. The ratio of the final numerator over the final
denominator represents the coverage ratio.
percent
Verification Planner stores the percent type metric as a double in the range 0.0 to 1.0.
Like the ratio type, the percent type metric supports only average aggregator. When two
or more percent values are aggregated, Verification Planner makes an arithmetical mean
of the percent values.
In the following example, a feature fa has two child features, fa1 and fa2,which both
contain two metrics of type ratio and percent:
plan metdef_example;
metric ratio metric_ratio;
aggregator = average;
metric percent metric_percent;
aggregator = average;

Identifiers in goal expressions must be valid metric names, enum names or metric-
name.enum names. The metric name is replaced with the actual score of the metric. If the
metric is a ratio type, it is automatically converted to a percentage value while evaluating
the goal.
The following are examples of valid goal expressions:
test = test > 10 && test.fail == 0;
test = (pass + warn / test) > 80 % ;
Line = Line >= 30%
Measure Specification
You can use measure specifications to declare which metrics to annotate a feature from
the verification database. Measure specifications do not specify how values are extracted
from the verification database. In general, a metric represents the declaration of a type,
while a measure contains the actual instance of the source to be annotated. You should
declare a measure specification within a feature (see Feature Declaration). Also, you must
declare all metrics used in a measure specification in the same plan, except for built-in
metrics.
Verification Planner typically attaches measure statements to the lowest level of a feature
hierarchy. Metric values for high-level features are computed by aggregating metric values
from lower-level child features.
The syntax to declare a measure is as follows:
measure metric-reference-list measure-name-identifier;
source = source-list;

measure-name-identifier ::= identifier
metric-reference-list = metric-identifier [, ]
metric-identifier ::= identifier

source-list = "string" [, ]

The syntax to declare a source for Synopsys functional coverage metric,
• For group coverage is:
"[keyword]: scope_name[::]covergroup name"
• For coverpoint, cross, or bin coverage is:
"[keyword]: scope_name[::]<covergroup_name>.<full_hierarchy path
separated by dots>"
• For covergroup instance or coverpoint/cross of a covergroup instance is:
"[keyword]:<full_hierarchy path separated by dots>"
For example:
source = "module : module_name"
source = "instance : dut.hierarchy"
source = "tree : dut.hierarchy"
source = "group : covergroup_name"
When both coverpoint label and coverpoint name are used in Verilog code,
specify the source in HVP plan using the coverpoint label and not the
coverpoint name as shown in the following example:
source = "group: top::cg.cp1";
// here cp1 is the coverpoint label.

covergroup cg @(posedge clk);
cp1:coverpoint a{
bins b1 = {[0:3],[7:10]};
}
cp2:coverpoint b{
bins b1 = {10};
}
endgroup

The easiest way to get the right region hierarchy name after the keyword is to refer to the
URG reports:
• URG hierarchy report – shows existing DUT hierarchy
• URG assert report – shows existing property name with full DUT hierarchy
• URG group report– shows existing covergroup, coverpoint and bin names
You can copy and paste the hierarchy after the right keyword.
In order to match multiple regions in a measure, you can enumerate multiple source
strings separated by commas, as follows:
measure Line, Cond m1;
source = "tree: top.dut.u1", "tree: top.dut.u2",
"tree:top.dut.u3";

Verification Planner Source Expressions
The Verification Planner supports several types of source expressions that allow you to
match a large number of coverage objects with minimal effort. The source strings may
contain wildcards and regular expressions to reference multiple items from the coverage
database or user data files. In addition, you can also provide a "removal" expression that
allows you to subtract specific elements from a wildcard match.
Wildcards
Verification planner supports the simplified wildcards “?”, “*”, and “**”. The “?” and “*”
wildcards work much like they do within the ordinary Unix shell commands. The “?”
wildcard matches any single character and “*” matches a string of characters. The “*”
wildcard is limited to matching only within a single hierarchical level when referencing
objects within the VCS coverage database. To match the spanning across hierarchical
levels, you can use the “**” wildcard.
Source Name Pattern Matching Examples Non-Matching Examples
tree: top.dut.u? top.dut.u1 top.dut.u2
top.dut.uN
top.dut.u11 top.dut.u
tree: top.dut.* top.dut.u1 top.dut.nnn top.dut.u1.sub1
top.dut
tree: top.dut.*.sub1 top.dut.u1.sub1 top.dut.u1.u2.sub
tree: top.dut.** top.dut.u1
top.dut.u1.u2
top.dut
Regular Expressions
Regular expressions are used in the source strings for greater match precision.
Verification Planner supports POSIX 1003.2 extended regular expressions. In order to use
a regular expression in a source expression, insert the tag `r` into the string.
For example, the following source expression matches the strings that begin with u1.u2
and end with either ohio or iowa:
source = "tree: u1.u2.`r`(ohio|iowa)";
Note that, some characters have special meanings and are interpreted as a regular
expression operator instead of a literal string. In particular, the dot “.” character means
“match any character”. As dot is also used as a hierarchical separator in Verilog it is easily
overlooked.
For example, consider this expression:
source = "tree: `r`u1.u2.resetbank[0-2]";

This matches u1.u2.resetbank0, u1.u2.resetbank1, and u1.u2.resetbank2 as
expected. But, it also matches u1Xu2Xresetbank0.
To prevent such unwanted matches, do one of the following:
• Escape the dot with a backslash:
source = "tree: `r`u1\.u2\.resetbank[0-2]";
• Move the `r` tag further to the right:
source = "tree: u1.u2.resetbank`r`[0-2]";
You can also use the tag `n` to turn off the regular expression usage and revert to normal
wildcards, as shown:
source = "tree: u1.u2.resetbank`r`[0-2]`n`.u88.planty";
In the earlier example, only the substring "[0-2]" is interpreted as a regular expression.
It is possible to form a source expression that is a hybrid of normal wildcards
and regular expressions. This provides the flexibility of full regular expressions
when you need it and simplified wildcards (or literal strings) when regular
expressions get in the way. For example, interpreting dot as a wildcard.

Removal Expressions
Often, it is useful to specify a region of source objects by selecting a large set with a
wildcard or regular expression and then excluding a subset of those items selected.
The source expressions discussed so far can be considered as "positive expressions" in
the sense that they select source objects that are added to the measure statement.
In Verification Planner source expression syntax, an optional "removal expression"
is denoted with the `-` tag. The basic structure is <positive expression>[`-`<removal
expression>]. The syntax of optional removal expressions is the same as the required
positive expression.
The behavior of the following removal expression can be visualized as shown in Figure 8.
source = "mod*`-`mod1*";

Figure 7
Taking this example a little further, you can even fill in the donut hole by combining multiple
source expressions:
source = "mod*`-`mod1*", "mod152*";
Figure 8
In Figure 8, mod1* creates the hole and mod152* fills in the hole.
You can freely combine wildcards and regular expressions with the removal syntax. For
example, the last expression could be written as:
source = "`r`mod.*`-`mod1*", "mod152*";
or
source = "mod*`-`mod1`r`.*", "mod152*";
or
source = "mod*`-`mod1*", "mod152`r`.*";
Note that the effect of the `r` does not span the `-` operator, nor does its opposite `n`.

Data Regions in External User Data Sources
You can specify source strings without keywords for non-Synopsys coverage metrics for
which the data sources are userdata files. For a source without keywords, region strings
have no hierarchy but is simply flat. Dots in the strings are not hierarchical separators.
Therefore, you can use “?” wildcards to match single characters and “*” wildcards to match
multiple characters in the strings.
The following are some examples using each of the wildcards:
Source name pattern Matching examples
/test/block1/read_write* /test/black1/read_write_rand_123/test/blac
k1/read_write/rand_123
top.u1.* top.u1.sub1 top.u1.sub1.read1
Note that the “*” wildcard matches regardless of the dot scope.
Performance Tip
While Verification Planner internally traverses and annotates given data regions in the
Synopsys coverage database and the HVP userdata file, it tries to match the current
region path with every single source string in your verification plan. For example,
suppose that your coverage database has 100,000 hierarchy regions including instances,
assertions, coverpoints, bins, and so on. Also, suppose that your verification plan has
1,000 source strings in leaf node measures overall. Then Verification Planner tries to string
match 100,000 * 1,000 times. More source strings result in longer loading times.
You can reduce the number of source strings by using wildcards in measures. For
example, instead of using four source strings as in the following:
source = "tree: top.dut.u1", "tree: top.dut.u2",
"tree: top.dut.u3", "tree: top.dut.u4";
You can use a single pattern, for example:
tree: top.dut.u?
or
tree: top.dut.u*
Using Attributes in Source Specifications
You can also specify a source using attributes and annotations. For example:
plan cache_plan;
attribute string root_mod = "";
feature cache1;

root_mod = "top.";
measure Line cov;
source = "instance: ${root_mod}level2"
feature cache2;
measure Line cov;
source = "instance: ${root_mod}level2"
In the earlier example, the attribute of root_mod in feature cache1 is "top.", so
Verification Planner interprets the source of measure cov in feature cache1 as
instance:top.level2. Because the attribute root_mod in feature cache2 is a null string,
the source measure cov of feature cache2 is instance:level2.
You can also use integer and real type attributes, which are replaced by their decimal
values in the measure source string, but their numeric formats are different.
You can use a reserved variable, ${objpath}, to retrieve the full path of the current
measure hierarchy in the source string. For example:
plan cache_plan;
feature cache1;
measure bugcount mBug;
source = "${objpath}";
In the earlier example, the ${objpath} variable in measure mBug *is replaced with
cache_plan.cache1.mBug at compile time.
The Assert metric supports selection of assertions by category and severity value
masking. To set mask values, use the 24-bit hexadecimal number in either property
categorymask 'h### or property severityMask 'h### source.
The SnpsAvg built-metric is an aggregate type which consists of Line, Cond, FSM,
Toggle, Assert, and Group built-in metrics, so you can use any source format listed in

Feature groups are a group of Hierarchical Verification Plan (HVP) features and may be
spread across a plan and need not be under the same feature subtree in the subplan.
Let’s look at how to specify feature groups within a subplan. For this, define locally-scoped
attributes for the three feature groups, namely, grpA, grpB, and grpC as follows:
attribute integer grpA = 1;
attribute integer grpB = 1;
attribute integer grpC = 1;
Note that all features are enabled, by default, by assigning them value as 1. Now,
designate the groups to which the feature does not belong instead of designating groups

to which a feature belongs. For example, the single_reads feature is a member of Group
A only, therefore, Group B and Group C should be turned off as follows:
feature single_reads;
grpB=0;
grpC=0;

measure Group,Assert,Line,Cond snps;
source="property: ${root_mod}read";
Similarly, if a feature, say code, is a member of Group A and Group B, Group C should be
turned off as follows:
feature code;
grpC=0;
measure Group,Assert,Line,Cond snps;
source="module: sram";
If a feature is a member of all three groups, then do not override any of the group. These
features inherit the default of 1 from the attribute.
Now, let’s instantiate subplan instances and disable various feature groups. Consider the
following example:
feature memory0;
subplan cache_plan #(root_mod="memsys_test_top.dut.u0.", grpA=0);

feature memory1;
subplan cache_plan #(root_mod="memsys_test_top.dut.u1.", grpB=0);

feature memory2;
subplan cache_plan #(root_mod="memsys_test_top.dut.u2.", grpC=0);

feature memory3;
subplan cache_plan #(root_mod="memsys_test_top.dut.u3.", grpA=0, grpB=0);
In the example, grpA, grpB, and grpC are turned off in group features memory0, memory1,
and memory2 respectively. In the memory3 group features, grpA and grpB are turned off.

Remove the turned-off feature groups using the filter-remove statement in the
rm_grps_mod.hvp modifier file as follows:
filter rm_grps;
remove feature where (grpA == 0 && grpB == 0 && grpC == 0);
Apply the modifier file via the -mod command-line argument to URG as follows:
urg -plan -dir simv.vdb -grp_enab_top.hvp -mod rm_grps_mod.hvp

Plan Modifiers
You can modify a verification plan hierarchy outside of the verification plan definition files
using plan modifiers: override and filter (each plan definition is encapsulated in a
planendplan block). Verification Planner-enabled applications first process the entire
verification plan in the HVP language, and then apply modifiers after the plan hierarchy is
loaded. Furthermore, Verification Planner-enabled applications apply multiple override
and filter modifiers sequentially in the order they are given.

Modifiers are useful to create derivatives or alter plans based on a common master plan.
For example, use the override modifier to relax goals during early phases of a project
and then gradually tighten those goals later as tests are created and improved.
Use the filter modifier to generate reduced views for specific purposes of a large master
plan. For example, apply a filter to limit the results to only those features assigned to
phase 2 of a project.
This section discusses the following topics:
• The override Modifier
• filter
• Enabling Feature Filtering With keep and remove
The override Modifier
The override modifier changes values of attributes, annotations, or goal expressions in
metrics for one or more features in a verification plan. It also enables you to change the
value of user-defined attributes in a measure. Apply the override modifier to attribute
values, annotation values, and metric goal expressions only. The modifiers use an XMR-
style full path name to reference an attribute, an annotation, or a metric, and override it
with a different value or goal expression:
plan.subplan-or-feature. … .attribute = value;
plan.subplan-or-feature. … .annotation = value;
plan.subplan-or-feature. … .metric = expression
Encapsulating one or more override statements within an overrideendoverride
block enables Verification Planner to execute each statement sequentially. Verification
Planner passes the override values (or goal expressions) down the plan hierarchy to
override attribute assignments (or goal expressions) in the hierarchy sub-trees.
The BNF for override is:
override-specification ::=
override override-identifier;
( override-assignment )

override-assignment ::=
attribute-full-identifier = attribute-value-literal; |
annotation-full-identifier = annotation-value-literal; |
metric-full-identifier = goal-specification;

override-identifier ::= identifier

attribute-full-identifier ::= plan-identifier.((plan- identifer |
feature_identifer).)*attribute-identifer

annotation-full-identifier ::= plan-identifier.((plan- identifer |
feature_identifer).)*annotation-identifer

Verification Continuum™
text:
Use the following override statements in the modifier file to override the count value of the
measure:
override toOverride;
myplan.module.m1.count = 3;
After applying the modifier, the count value of the measure myplan.module.m1 is
overridden with '3'.
You can use wildcard patterns in an overrideendoverride block to specify scope
names such as plans and features, but not attribute names. Table 8 lists the available
wildcard characters:
Table 8 Using Wildcards to Specify Plans and Features
Wildcard Meaning
? Matches a single occurrence of any character in the name.
* Matches zero or more consecutive characters in a single hierarchy
(between two “.” hierarchy separators).
** Matches zero or more consecutive characters regardless of hierarchy.
Examples
top.*.weight = 2;
top.**.weight = 2;
top.u?.weight = 2;
filter
Specify filterendfilter block outside the plan definition to extract a set of features.
This is useful when you want to view part of the HVP reports pertaining to a sub-project
only. The BNF for filter modifier is as follows:
filter-specification ::=
filter filter-identifier;
(filter-statement)

filter-identifier ::= identifier

filter-statement ::=
keep feature where filter-expression; |
remove feature where filter-expression;
filter-expression ::= expression

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
The filter-expression consists of the keywords feature where followed by an
attribute or an annotation name, and an expression. Any identifier other than an attribute
or annotation name is not interpreted.
The following example shows a filter my_view which defines specific criteria for a given
collection of feature attributes.
filter my_view;
remove feature where phase > 2;
keep feature where phase == 5;
keep feature where router_fabric == "N1" || router_fabric ==
"N2";
Initially, all the features in my_view are selected by default. After applying the filtering
operations: remove and keep, the selection changes as follows:
• The first filter expression removes features whose phase values are greater than 2.
• The second filter expression keeps features whose values are equivalent to 5, even if
they were removed by the first filter expression.
• The last expression keeps all features whose router_fabric attribute is either "N1" or
"N2", even if they were removed by the first filter expression.
If a feature is filtered out, Verification Planner excludes the corresponding measure score
of the feature from propagating through the entire plan hierarchy.
You can also include the following operators in filter expressions:
> < >= <= ==
+ - * / !=
|| && ( )
Currently, Verification Planner does not support the following expressions:
phase inside {1:10 }
match (owner, "bo*")
Filters with spreadsheet flow do not remove the features completely from the
annotated spreadsheet XML file as URG or Verdi does. The features for which
the filters are applied are not annotated with coverage score. You can find these
features reported in “cyan” color in the annotated spreadsheet XML. Note that
the features with missing sources are also reported in “cyan”.

text:
For details on the three new built-in metrics, Group.grp_count, Group.cvp_count, and
Group.bin_count, see the following sections:
• When Used With Covergroup Definitions
• When Used With Covergroup Instances
• When Used in Goal Expressions
When Used With Covergroup Definitions
When the source target is a covergroup definition or variant, then the hit bins and excluded
bins number of the matched group object is returned. This number is not affected by the
number of instances.
For details, see the following sections:
• Source With Group Definition
• Source With Group Variant

• Source With Group Coverpoint
• Source With Group Bin
Source With Group Definition
If the source target is covergroup definition, the matching group objects are group variant.
For example:
measure Group, Group.grp_count, Group.cvp_count, Group.bin_count
Measure_1;
source = "group: bot::cg";// group definition
Its URG report is as follows:
Group.bin_count is the sum of Group.covered_count and
Group.uncovered_count. Group.bin_count does not include
Group.excluded_count.
Source With Group Variant
If the source target is covergroup definition, the matching region is the specific covergroup
variant. For example:
measure Group, Group.grp_count Group.cvp_count Group.bin_count Measure_1;
source = "group: top.b1::cg*";
Its URG report is as follows:

Source With Group Coverpoint
If the source target is covergroup definition, the matching region is a coverpoint. For
example:
measure Group, Group.grp_count Group.cvp_count Group.bin_count Measure_1;
source = "group: top.b1::cg::SHAPE{p=1}.cp1";
measure Group, Group.grp_count Group.cvp_count Group.bin_count Measure_1; source
= "group: top.b1::cg::SHAPE{p=1}.cp1"; endmeasure
Its URG report is as follows:
In the report, Group.grp_count is 0 as the matching object is the coverpoint,
top.b1::cg::SHAPE{p=1}.cp1.
Source With Group Bin
If the source target is covergroup definition, the matching region is a group bin. For
example:
measure Group, Group.grp_count Group.cvp_count Group.bin_count Measure_1;
source = "group bin: top.b1::cg::SHAPE{p=1}.cp1.c1";
Its URG report is as follows:

In the report, the score of Group.grp_count and Group.cvp_count is 0 as the matching
object is the group bin, top.b1::cg::SHAPE{p=1}.cp1.c1.
When Used With Covergroup Instances
When referencing a single instance of a covergroup, Group.cvp_count returns the sum
of the number of coverpoints defined within the group. For example, for an instance of
A::B, Group.cvp_count returns 3. If a wildcard is used to match 4 instances of A::B, then
Group.cvp_count returns 12.
If a source target references multiple instances then the number of bins returned is the
sum of the bins in all of the matches instances.
measure Group, Group.grp_count Group.cvp_count Group.bin_count Measure_1;
source = "group instance: bot::cg";
Its URG report is as follows:

When Used in Goal Expressions
There is no default goal for Group.grp_count, Group.cvp_count, or Group.bin_count.
Group.grp_count, Group.cvp_count, and Group.bin_count are used just like any other
metric in goal expressions. For examples:
Group.cvp_count = Group.cvp_count > 3;

Group.cvp_count = (Group.cvp_count > 0) &&
(Group.cvp_count < 1000000);
As these metrics return integer values, errors are generated if compared against constants
of the different types, such as percent, ratio, string, and so on.
Showing Instance-Based Scores for Coverpoints and Crosses
The Instcov mode score is also available in HVP. Refer to the Showing Instance-Based
Scores for Coverpoints and Crosses section in the Verdi Coverage User Guide and
Tutorial to learn more.
Usage of the -group instcov_for_cp_score Option
Add the -group instcov_for_cp_score option in the Verdi Coverage command line as
given below:
%> verdi -cov -covdir <simv.vdb> -group instcov_for_cp_score
Viewing New Plan Scores
With the -group instcov_for_cp_score option, if you toggle the preference item for
HVP regions scores, a dialog box pops up to enable you to recalculate and view the new
plan scores.

Verification Planner supports measuring individual objects in line and toggle coverage in a
module or an instance.
The syntax to measure line and toggle coverage objects is as follows:
source = "
module
module: <module name>@<object name>";
source = "
instance
instance: <instance name>@<object name>";
source = "tree: <instance name>@<object name>";
The "?", "*", and "**" wildcards are supported with module, instance and object names.
If the "@" symbol is not specified followed by the object name in the source string, the
coverage metric is reported for the entire module or instance.
• Measuring Toggle Coverage Objects
• Measuring Line Coverage Metric
• Limitations
Measuring Toggle Coverage Objects
Toggle coverage objects are measured using signal names. Bit-select or part-selects is
used to select bits of vector signals. The special strings, [0->1] and [1->0], are used to
address individual toggle directions. For more details, see the examples illustrated in the
following section.
Wildcards are not supported in bit selection and signal transitions [0->1] or
[1->0].

Limitations
The following are the limitations with this feature:
• Wildcards are not supported for signal transitions, [0->1]/[1->0].
• Wildcards are not supported for bit selection, [*]/[*:0].
• Bit selections and transitions— [0->1] and [1->0]— are not supported for MDA
signals as shown in the following HVP plan:
measure Toggle m1;
source = "module: m@a[0][2]"; // one bit selection is not supported
source = "module: m@a[0][3:0]";// one bit selection is not supported
source = "module: m@a[0][2:1]";// one bit selection is not supported
source = "module: m@a[1]"; // one bit selection is not supported
source = "module: m@a[1:0]"; // one bit selection is not supported
source = "module: m@a[1:0][2]"; // one bit selection is not
supported
source = "module: m@a[0->1]"; // Transition is not supported
Empty Features Score
A leaf feature with no measure was not assigned any score. Without any measure
statement, it became difficult to decide which metrics should be computed for a leaf
feature.
A Hierarchical Verification Plan (HVP) now adds a zero score for a leaf feature which has
no measure, by default. An HVP enables you to determine a metric for the feature. It also
enables you to determine the denominator N for the 0/N score for a ratio-type metric. In a
ratio-type metric, the denominator must be greater than zero.

having a zero score for its leaf features that have no measure:

• Determining a Metric for an Empty Leaf Feature
• Determining the Denominator N for a Ratio-Type Metric
Determining a Metric for an Empty Leaf Feature
To determine a metric for an empty leaf feature, an HVP measures all metrics that are
defined in its sibling features in a current plan. For example, consider the following code
snippet that shows EmptyFeature as an empty leaf feature:
Example 13 The New_Plan Plan
'include "New_subplan_1.hvp

plan New_Plan;

measure Line, Cond, FSM, Toggle, Branch, Assert,
SnpsAvg Measure_1;
source = "tree: test_jukebox", "tree: test_jukebox.fifo1",
"module: coin_fsm", "module: jukebox";

Empty Features Score
measure Line, Cond, FSM, Toggle, Branch,
Assert, SnpsAvg Measure_1;
source = "module: kp_fsm";
measure Line, Cond, Toggle, Group Measure_2;
source = "group: test_jukebox.cd1::song";
feature NoSourceFeature;
measure Line, Cond, FSM, Toggle, Branch, Group Measure_1;
measure Line, Cond, FSM, Toggle, Branch, Assert, Group,
FVAssert Measure_2;
feature EmptyFeature
subplan sub_plan;
In the example, all metrics that are defined and used in the plan are the metrics that are
defined and used in sibling features in a current plan. Therefore, all these metrics are
measured for EmptyFeature:
Line, Cond, FSM, Toggle, Branch, Assert, Group, SnpsAvg, FVAssert
If an empty leaf feature is in a subplan, all metrics that are defined and used in the sibling
features of an empty feature in the subplan are considered for determining the metrics for
the empty feature. For example, consider the following subplan of the New_Plan plan:
Example 14 Subplan of the New_Plan Plan
plan sub_plan;

measure Group Measure_1;
measure Group Measure_2;
source = "group: test_jukebox::instruction::ticksgroup",
"group: test_jukebox.cd1::song";
feature NoSourceMeasure;

Empty Features Score
In the example, NoSourceMeasure is an empty feature and only Group metric is measured
for this feature. Note that the following metrics of the top plan are not applied to the
NoSourceMeasure feature of the subplan:
Line, Cond, FSM, Toggle, Branch, Assert, Group, SnpsAvg, FVAssert
Determining the Denominator N for a Ratio-Type Metric
For determining the denominator N for a ratio-type metric, calculate average of the direct
siblings of a feature. The direct siblings include features, subplans, and total measure
scores in the current plan. For example, consider the following code snippet that shows
feature siblings:
Example 15 Feature Siblings
plan New_Plan;

measure Line, Cond, Branch Measure_1;
source = "tree: test_jukebox", "tree: test_jukebox.fifo1",
"module: coin_fsm", "module: jukebox";
feature NoSourceFeature;
measure Line, Toggle, Cond Measure_2;
feature NoMetricNoSource;
To determine the denominator for the Feature_1 feature, the score is calculated for line,
condition, and branch coverage as follows:
Line covered/Total Line coverable
Condition covered/Total condition coverable
Branch covered/Total branch coverable
The valid sibling of the NoSourceFeature feature is Feature_1. The score for the
NoSourceFeature feature is calculated as follows:
Line: 0/(line coverable of feature_1)
Condition: 0/(cond coverable of feature_1)
Toggle: 0/1
To determine the denominator for the NoMetricNoSource feature, the score is calculated
as follows:
Line: 0/(line coverable of feature_1)
Branch: 0/(branch coverable of feature_1)

Compiler Directives
Condition: 0/(condition coverable of feature_1)
Toggle: 0/1

Compiler Directives
Unlike Verilog modules which are instantiated separately from their declarations, feature
instantiations in a verification plan appear where the declarations exist. However, you
can move feature declarations using compiler directives. For example, use the‘include
compiler directive to accept a file containing feature declarations.
Verification Planner compiler directives allow simple macro definition similar to the Verilog
Standard, IEEE Std. 1364-2001.
For example:
`define foo \
feature my_feature; \
…. \

Adding Comments
Verification Planner supports the following compiler directives which have the same
definition as in Verilog:
`undef macro_name

`include "file_name"

`ifdef macro-identifier
group-of-lines
{`elsif macro-identifier
group-of-lines }
[`else
group-of-lines ]

`ifndef macro-identifier
group-of-lines
{`elsif macro-identifier
group-of-lines }
[`else
group-of-lines ]
Note that the 'include "file_name" compiler directive searches the file_name based
on the current file directory.

Adding Comments
There are two methods to introduce comments using the HVP language: the line
comments and the block comments. You can use double forward slashes "//" to denote the
start of a line comment which stops at the end of the line. For a block comment, the block
starts with "/*" and ends with "*/". A block comment which spans multiple lines may not be
nested. A line comment token "//" has no meaning inside a block comment.
Using HVP Files
You can use HVP plan and modifier files with URG for annotation and Verdi for editing.
Also, you can pass modifier files into Verification Planner spreadsheet annotator with
plan sheets. For additional information, see Coverage Technology User Guide and Verdi
Coverage User Guide and Tutorial.
Viewing Plan Metadata
A saved plan records the following save-time metadata:
• hvp_version: The HVP or plan version.
• tool_version: The version or build of the tool that actually wrote the file.

Viewing Plan Metadata
• tool_name: Which product or command path last wrote the output; for example, Verdi,
URG, hvpexport, HVP utilities (Doc Plan Generator or HVP gendoc, HVP genxls, HVP
annotate), HVP dump, and reports.
• options: Comma-separated relevant save or export options.
The metadata is saved in the following file formats:
• Native HVP
• Plan XML
• DOC XML
• Excel XML
Example 16 Metadata in a Native HVP Plan
//@hvp_meta hvp_version "Y-2026.03-SP1-1"
//@hvp_meta tool_version "Y-2026.03-SP1"
//@hvp_meta tool_name "verdi"
//@hvp_meta options "save"
plan top_plan;

Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator
This chapter describes how to use the Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator
application, how to tag spreadsheets, and the annotation command-line options.
This chapter contains the following topics:
• Introduction to Spreadsheet Annotator
• Getting Started With Spreadsheet Annotator
• Using the HVP Spreadsheet Meta-Tags
• Using the Spreadsheet Annotator Commands
• Generating Standard HVP Excel XML Plans
• Generating Loadable HVP Excel XML Reports
• XML Doc Plan Generator
• Using the HVP_ARCH_OVERRIDE Variable
• Troubleshooting
Introduction to Spreadsheet Annotator
The following are the methods used to describe verification plan:
• Using the Synopsys proprietary HVP language is the most straightforward method (for
additional information on how to create a plan, see Using the HVP Language).
• Describe an implicit verification plan using spreadsheets which are properly formatted
with the inclusion of identifying meta-tags.
To take the implicit verification plan approach, you need to use either MS Excel or
OpenOffice 2.0 or later to edit the HVP spreadsheets for back-annotation purpose. The

Introduction to Spreadsheet Annotator
back-annotation process is accomplished via the Spreadsheet Annotator. Figure 13
depicts the usage model of the Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator:
Figure 13 Verification Planner-Enabled Application: Spreadsheet Annotator
The purposes for spreadsheet annotation application are to provide:
• Reasonably simple hooks in MS Excel compliant spreadsheets to interface with
Verification Planner-enabled applications.
• Enough degrees of freedom in formatting spreadsheets to promote reusability.
Verification Planner uses the same spreadsheets as a verification plan and annotation
files. You can use spreadsheet formatting features such as font, attributes, insertion
of images, and cell attributes. This allows you the flexibility to design spreadsheets for
conventional documentation purposes.
• A mechanism for using the features of Verification Planner by means of tagging
spreadsheets with reserved meta-tags.

Getting Started With Spreadsheet Annotator
Getting Started With Spreadsheet Annotator
The following steps describe the basic usage model of the Verification Planner
Spreadsheet Annotator:
1. Create spreadsheets to capture a verification plan.
The verification plan contains at most one HVP Plan Sheet, an optional HVP Metric
Sheet, and an optional HVP Attribute Sheet. Label columns and rows of each
spreadsheet with meta-tags which are interpreted by Verification Planner (see Using
the HVP Spreadsheet Meta-Tags on how to tag a spreadsheet).
2. Save spreadsheets as XML file format.
If you are using Excel 2007 and you want to be able to load the saved spreadsheets
into Excel 2003, choose the XML Spreadsheet 2003 option to Save As, not the XML
Data option.
3. Execute the hvp annotate command with the appropriate options, for example:
% hvp annotate -plan=mySpreadsheetPlan.xml
For additional information, see Using the HVP Spreadsheet Meta-Tags.
4. Examine the back-annotated spreadsheets. The annotated spreadsheets are almost
the same as the original ones except for the cells that are annotated with metrics and
color-coded according to goal values.
After annotation, an annotated cell is highlighted in green if the corresponding goal
value of the cell is met, otherwise the cell is highlighted in red. If no goal is specified,
Synopsys coverage and test scores are annotated with various colors as shown in
Figure 15.
Figure 14 shows an example of an original spreadsheet versus an annotated
spreadsheet.

After you apply the hvp annotate command, the corresponding annotated cells
are highlighted in green when goals are met, and in red otherwise, provided that the
goals of metrics are specified. If you do not specify goals, the annotated cells are not
highlighted.
However, for a ratio or percent type metric or test metric, even if no goal is given, the
cell is highlighted in one of six colors from red (low) to green (high) depending on the
metric’s percentage value, as shown in Figure 15.
Figure 15 Color Legend for Coverage Metrics
For the test metric, the cell color is based on the (pass count)/(total test
count) percentage.
5. In an annotated spreadsheet, a cell for a measure source or feature may have a pop-
up window that shows details of its scores and matched region. The information in the
pop-up window is useful in determining the exact matching region strings and scores, if
the source string contains wildcards or if there are multiple sources in the cell.
For example, Figure 16 shows the pop-up window for the source string /cfg1/CPU1/
L1CACHE/* and seven matched test cases, with an annotated score of total=7

pass=6 fail=1 . The pop-up window illustrates details about how this score was
aggregated.
Figure 16 Pop-up Window for a Source String and With Matches

If the number of matched regions is too large, you can set a filter, for example,
to see only the test cases with pass or warn. Then, for example, you can use
-ss_show_sources test pass+warn at the command line. For more information
about using the -ss_show_sources switch, see Using the Spreadsheet Annotator
Commands.
6. If you use the -report urg-report-path switch, you see hyperlinks at source
and feature cells. Clicking one of those hyperlinks opens the URG (Unified Report
Generator) report in your Web browser, so you can see details in the URG/HVP report.
See Using the Spreadsheet Annotator Commands and the Unified Coverage Reporting
User Guide for details about using the -report switch.

Table 9 Plan Definition and Spreadsheet Types (Continued)
HVP Plan Sheet
HVP Plan Sheet describes the feature hierarchy of a verification plan. A verification plan
in spreadsheet format consists of, at most, one HVP Plan Sheet. Figure 17 illustrates a
simple HVP Plan Sheet.
Figure 17 An HVP Plan Sheet

This section contains the following subsections:
• hvp plan plan-name
• plan
• feature
• subplan
• $attribute-name, $annotation-name
• skip
• goal.metric-name
• measure measure-name.source
• value measure-name.metric-name
• include

hvp plan plan-name
In Figure 17, the cell which contains the hvp plan plan-name meta-tag identifies this
sheet as an HVP Plan Sheet. The row and column corresponding to this cell are called tag
row and tag column, respectively. In the example, the meta-tag cell uniquely specifies the
verification plan as my_plan and row 2 is the tag row.
plan
The “plan” tag is located in the tag column, while all the other tags are located in the tag
row. The row with the “plan” tag is used to set attribute or goal values at the plan level, and
to annotate plan-level scores. Figure 18 uses row 2 for plan-level hierarchy.
Figure 18 Location of the “plan” Tag in the Tag Row

feature
The columns with a meta-tag feature indicate a feature/child feature hierarchy level. Each
HVP Plan Sheet can have one or more feature columns. The order of these columns from
left to right represents feature hierarchy level from top to bottom. In Figure 17, “system” is
the top-level feature, and it consists of two child features, “block1” and “block2”.
The corresponding feature cells of the same row are mutually exclusive. In other words,
you can have at most one feature value for any given row. If a row does not have any
feature name, the row is automatically a child feature row to the row above.
In Figure 19, rows 6,7 and 8 do not have any feature values. (Internally, Verification
Planner Spreadsheet Annotator creates a dummy feature value for each of these rows).
By default, these three rows automatically become child features to the row above, that is
instance1.test_jukebox_total.st0_total.

Figure 19 HVP with Meta-Tag: feature

The HVP language allows alphabetical characters, numbers, white spaces, special
characters and underscores (_) in identifiers such as feature names. For example:
feature "feature name can contain special characters & punctuation."

If a feature name conflict occurs, hvp annotate shows the locations of the features for
which the conflict occurs. You must change one of the feature names to eliminate the
feature name conflict.
subplan
The feature or child feature column can also have a subplan name instead of a
feature name as a child feature. To put a subplan name in a cell, enter subplan planname
and add the subplan file name in the column with the include meta-tag in the plan
spreadsheet. You can put the include file name in any row in the "include" column (for
additional information, see include).
In the following example, cache_plan was defined in cache_plan.xml, and was used as
a subplan in myplan.

Figure 20 cache_plan embedded as a subplan in myplan
When you embed a subplan, you can override attribute values in the subplan using
#(attribute-name=value, ) syntax. This is useful if you want to change attribute
values in the subplan without editing the spreadsheet plan file. The overridden attribute
must already have been defined in the subplan.
Figure 21 Overriding root_mod and weight attribute values in cache_plan
$attribute-name, $annotation-name
Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator interprets any meta-tag that starts with the “$”
character as an attribute or annotation. For example, in Figure 22, $phase is an attribute.
You must define all attributes used in the HVP Plan Sheet, except for the built-in owner
attribute and the built-in description and weight annotations.

Figure 22 An HVP Plan Sheet Showing Meta-tag: skip
skip
Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator interprets the meaning of every row and
column in your spreadsheet plan file. However, it is often useful to include non-HVP
information in the spreadsheet plan file. For example, a column or a row might be used
for adding comments or description that helps you interpret the annotated report easily.
You can use the skip keyword in the first cell of such column or row to make the HVP
annotator to ignore that column or row.
In Figure 22, the skip keyword is added for the “Cntlr” feature along with its child
features. So, in the generated annotated spreadsheet plan file, this feature does not have
any coverage score annotated as shown in Figure 23.

Figure 23 Effect of Meta-tag: skip
goal.metric-name
To override the goal of a metric, enter a Boolean expression in the corresponding cell of
the column containing the goal meta-tag. The new goal expression is inherited by the
entire hierarchy similar to attributes. For example, column J in Figure 24 contains the
goal of a Group metric to be 80 percent or higher. If you do not specify goals in the HVP
Plan Sheet, Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator uses goals defined in the metric
definition by default.
You must define a metric in the HVP Metric Sheet before you can use it in a goal
expression except for Synopsys built-in metrics: Line, Cond, FSM, Toggle, Assert, Group,
SnpsAvg, and test. The section, Goal Specification, describes the syntax and rules for
goal expression.
Figure 24 An HVP Plan Sheet Showing Meta-Tag: goal

measure measure-name.source
This meta-tag column contains cells which identify sources for measure measure-name .
You can specify one or more source names or patterns, which can include wildcards: "?",
"*", and **. In Figure 24, the cell content top.d* in column M indicates that top.d* is the
source of measure top_cov .
You can also enter more than one source in a single cell using the “,” character as a
delimiter, for example, test1, test2, test3 in column H. Notice that the measure-name is

title: 50.00 50.00 0 1 2 top.b1::cg::SHAPE{p=1}.cp1
text:
op.d* in column M indicates that top.d* is the
source of measure top_cov .
You can also enter more than one source in a single cell using the “,” character as a
delimiter, for example, test1, test2, test3 in column H. Notice that the measure-name is
a user-defined name and should be unique within a plan sheet (for details, see Measure
Specification).
If the source of a measure is not given, Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator
annotates the corresponding value cell with the aggregated value of its child features (for
details, see value measure-name.metric-name).
value measure-name.metric-name
This value meta-tag column contains values to be back-annotated by the given metric
metric-name to the corresponding sources for each measure measure-name . Notice
that cells in measure measure-name.source column provide sources for the metric
metric-name . For example, jukebox is a source for measure m1 . Verification Planner
Spreadsheet Annotator associates each source and value using the measure-name in a
spreadsheet.
In Figure 25, cell D2 of measure m1.source column does not have a source value,
therefore, the value 65.41% in cell E2 is the aggregated value of 7 child features, namely
cells E3 to E9. Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator computes the aggregation
result (E2) based on the aggregator in its metric definition. If you do not want Verification
Planner to annotate a particular value cell, enter the keyword blank in the corresponding
source cell.

Figure 25 An HVP Plan Sheet Showing Meta-Tag: value
include
To use other spreadsheets as subplans, enter the spreadsheet plan file names in the
include meta-tag column. The external file name can have a relative path from the
current file path. Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator ignores all other cells in the
row which has an include file except for the cell in the include column.
You can put multiple files in a single cell separated by commas. For example:
sub1/JukeST0_2.xml, sub2/JukeST3_4.xml
You can have a plan definition to be used as subplan in HVP language format, not
in spreadsheet format. You can also include the HVP file and use the plans from a
spreadsheet.
If you use ralgen to generate SystemVerilog files based on your RAL register description,
you get HVP files from ralgen automatically. The HVP files can be included in your
spreadsheet verification plan, and the plan in the HVP file can be used as a subplan.
You can include common metric and attribute definition sheets, as well as, plan
spreadsheet files. If you have a list of metric and attribute definitions that are used across
multiple plans, and you do not want to copy and paste them in multiple spreadsheet plan
files, you can create a common metric and attribute definition spreadsheet, and simply
include it. Then the metric and attribute definitions are automatically integrated into the
current plan (for more information, see HVP Metric Definition Sheet and HVP Attribute
Definition Sheet).

Figure 26 HVP Plan Showing Meta-Tag: include
HVP Metric Definition Sheet
Metrics are values annotated to a verification plan from the verification database. Metric
declarations specify the name, type, goal and aggregator for each metric. Descriptions of
Verification Planner metrics and how they are aggregated for multiple scores are provided
in Metric Declaration.
Figure 27 illustrates an example of an HVP Metric Definition Sheet:
Figure 27 HVP Metric Definition Sheet
This section contains the following topics:
• hvp metric plan-name
• name
• type
• aggregator

• goal
• skip
hvp metric plan-name
The cell in a worksheet containing hvp metric plan-name meta-tag identifies this
worksheet as an HVP Metric Definition Sheet. The row and column corresponding to this
cell are tag row and tag column, respectively. In Figure 29, my_plan is the name of this
verification plan. Use the same plan name as specified in the HVP Plan Sheet and HVP
Attribute Definition Sheet to refer to the same verification plan.
If you have multiple plans and they share the same metric definitions, you can create a
worksheet that only contains hvp metric without a plan sheet. You can also add hvp
attribute. To define common HVP metrics, the hvp metric tag should not have plan
name. The worksheet can be included in other plan spreadsheets, and the metrics are
integrated automatically.
Figure 28 Location of the “plan” Tag in the Tag Row

name
Use the name meta-tag column to define user-defined metrics. You must define all metrics
used in HVP Plan Definition Sheet in this column, with the exceptions of Synopsys built-in
metrics.
type
Use the type meta-tag column to specify value types. The available types for user-defined
metrics are integer, real, ratio, percent, enum, and aggregate.
aggregator
Use the aggregator meta-tag column to specify aggregation operators. The available
aggregation operators are sum, max, min, average, and uniquesum(for more information,
see Metric Declaration).

goal
Use the goal meta-tag column to define the default goal expression of a given metric.
Refer to Goal Specification for more details on how to describe a goal expression.
skip
Use the skip meta-tag to ignore a column or row.

hvp attribute plan-name
The cell in a worksheet containing hvp attribute plan-name meta tag identifies this
worksheet as an HVP Attribute Definition Sheet. The row and column corresponding to
this cell are called tag row and tag column, respectively. In Figure 29, my_plan is the
name of the verification plan. Use the same plan name as in the HVP Plan Sheet and HVP
Metric Definition Sheet to refer to the same verification plan.
Just as you can create a common HVP metric definition sheet, you can also create a
common HVP attribute definition sheet. Normally, common HVP metric and attribute
sheets can reside in the same spreadsheet, which can be included by other plan
spreadsheets.
An unqualified hvp attribute tag without a plan name in the HVP attribute definition
sheet makes attributes to be present in all plans. Qualifying an hvp attribute plan-
name tag with a plan name makes attributes to be present in only the named plan and not
in the other plans in the spreadsheet. Consider an example in which there are two plans:
plan1 and plan2 in a spreadsheet:
Figure 30 Example: plan1 and plan2
Figure 31 shows that the hvp attribute plan2 tag is used in the
attribute_definition worksheet. This implies that only plan2 gets attribute definition.
Figure 31 Example: Attribute Definition Sheet

If you make the attribute_definition worksheet unqualified by removing plan2 from
cell A1 of the worksheet, then both plans get attribute definition.
name
Use the name meta-tag column to specify user-defined attributes. You must define all
attributes used in HVP Plan Definition Sheet in this column, with the exceptions of
Synopsys built-in attributes and annotations.
type
Use the type meta-tag column to specify value types. The available types for user-defined
attribute annotation are integer, real, string, and enum.
propagate
Use the propagate meta-tag column to specify the permission for attribute values to
propagate down to child features. A value of yes indicates that a child feature without an
explicit attribute value automatically inherits the parent’s attribute value. However, if the
child feature has an explicit attribute value, the parent value cannot override it. A value of
no indicates that a child feature takes the default regardless of the parent’s attribute value.
default
Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator automatically annotates the value specified
in the default meta-tag column to a feature if neither its parent nor itself has an attribute
value in the verification plan. If a feature has no explicit value and the respective attribute
value has no permission to propagate, the feature takes the default regardless of the
parent’s attribute value. Note that a parent attribute value has precedence over the
default meta-tag value if a child attribute value is not specified.
For an enum type attribute, a default is mandatory.
Applying Modifiers
Verification Planner spreadsheet annotator supports both override and filter modifiers
written in the HVP language format, not in the spreadsheet (for more information, see Plan
Modifiers).
You can pass modifier files with the -plan and -mod options. Based on your modifiers, part
of scores, which are in disabled features, are excluded in score aggregation.
If you use a modifier file to override a goal, attribute, or annotation value, the
original value is still shown in the annotated spreadsheet, not the modified
value.

When you apply a modifier using the -mod option with the hvp annotate or hvp genxls
-report command, Verification Planner automatically appends modifier status rows to the
generated XML plan. These rows appear at the end of the first sheet and confirm that the
modifier files were successfully loaded.
For example, the first sheet ends with a rows similar to the following:
HVP modifier file modifier_set.hvpmod was successfully loaded.
HVP modifier file top_mod.hvpmod was successfully loaded.
These status messages provide a clear indication of which modifier files were recognized
and applied during plan generation.
Activating or Deactivating Modifiers
You can activate or deactivate the modifiers to apply or remove their effects on your plan.
To activate or deactivate a modifier, do the following:
1. Locate the modifier item in your plan.
2. Toggle the check box in front of the modifier item.
◦ Select the check box to activate the modifier. The modifier applies to the plan.
◦ Clear the check box to deactivate the modifier. The modifier is removed from the
plan.
Figure 32 Activating Modifiers
The modifier file item acts as a master control check box for its child items. Selecting or
clearing this check box activates or deactivates all child items at once. This applies in both
file-based and database modes.
When you activate a modifier instruction group, the group applies to the plan, even if the
master check box is not selected. Only deactivated local modifier groups and their child
items appear disabled. The local modifier file and its child items appear disabled if all child
groups are deactivated.

The syntax for Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotator commands is as follows:
hvp annotate -plan xml-in-file [-mod mod-file]
[-plan_out xml-out-file]
[-feature "hierarchies"|-featurefile txt-file]
[-dir covdb-path | -f txt-file]
[-userdata vedata-file | -userdatafile txt-file]
[-group ratio] [-group merge_across_scopes][-v]
[-show ratio][-show_incomplete][-q]
[-userdata_out out-vedata] [-metric_prefix metric-prefix]
[-hvp_disable_wildcards_in_cgshapeparam]

%hvp annotate -h

text:
Example 1
% hvp annotate -feature "myplan.feat1.play*" -dir \ cov1.vdb -feature
"myplan.feat1.rec*" cov2.vdb -plan \ <myplan.xml>
Where, "myplan.feat1.play*"expands to:
myplan.feat1.play1
myplan.feat1.play2
myplan.feat1.play3
The scores of myplan.feat1.play1, mplan.feat1.play2 and myplan.feat1.play3are
annotated with cov1.vdb
Similarly, "myplan.feat1.rec*" expands to:
myplan.feat1.rec1
myplan.feat1.rec2
myplan.feat1.rec3
The scores of myplan.feat1.rec1, mplan.feat1.rec2and myplan.feat1.rec3 are
annotated with cov2.vdb.
Example 2:
% hvp annotate -dir global.vdb -feature \ "myplan.feat1.play*" -dir
cov1.vdb -feature \ "myplan.feat1.rec*" cov2.vdb -plan <myplan.xml>
The scores of the matching regions of the play feature is the average aggregator of
cov1.vdb and global.vdb. Similarly, the scores of the matching regions of the rec
feature is the average aggregator of cov2.vdb and global.vdb.
-featurefile=feature-database mapping file
Specifies a text file that contains a list of hierarchy feature paths. Verification Planner puts
a feature path on separate lines of the feature-database mapping file . For example,
a feature-database mapping file with three feature paths would be arranged as
shown in the following example.
Example 1:
The following example shows the contents of a text feature file with three feature
hierarchies:
a.b.c
a.b.d
a.b.e
The feature-database mapping file is used in conjunction with the -dir switch to
provide a list of feature paths inline without being required to specify each feature. For

example, assume the map1 file contains the previous feature hierarchy, and then when you
invoke:
% hvp annotate -featurefile map1 -dir cov1.vdb -plan \
<myplan.xml>
This command effectively expands to:
% hvp annotate -feature "a.b.c a.b.d a.b.e" -dir cov1.vdb\
-plan <myplan.xml>
Here, the scores of a.b.c, a.b.d and a.b.e are annotated with cov1.vdb.
Example 2:
% hvp annotate -dir global.vdb -featurefile map1 -dir \
cov1.vdb -dir cov2.vdb -plan <myplan.xml>
This command effectively expands to:
% hvp annotate -dir global.vdb -feature "a.b.c a.b.d \
a.b.e" -dir cov1.vdb -dir cov2.vdb -plan <myplan.xml>
Example 3:
% hvp annotate -userdatda myfile1 -feature a.b.c -dir
cov3.vdb -userdata myfile2 -plan <myplan.xml>
The annotated score of feature a.b.c for userdata is the aggregator of myfile1 and
myfile2.
To make the -feature and -featurefile options work effectively, always specify the
-feature and -featurefile options followed by the -dir switch and the coverage
database.
-dir=covdb-path
Specifies one or more coverage database directories. To specify multiple coverage
directories, use at least one white space as a delimiter between them and enclose them
with the double quotation marks ("") characters. For example,
-dir "simv.vdb wb_dma.vdb"
-f=list-of-covdb-paths
Specifies one text file that contains a list of coverage .db directories. This command is
optional.
-userdata=userdata-file

title: 50.00 50.00 0 1 2 top.b1::cg::SHAPE{p=1}.cp1
text:
Specifies one or more HVP userdata files. To specify multiple HVP userdata files, use
at least one white space as a delimiter between them and enclose them with the double
quotation marks ("") characters. For example:
-userdata "data1.txt data2.txt"
-userdatafile=list-of-userdata-files
Specifies one text file which contains a list of paths for multiple userdata files. This
command is optional.
-elfile=exclusion-file
Specifies the exclusion file, used to exclude specific coverage objects from coverage
scores. This exclusion is performed at the UCAPI layer.
-map=mapped-module
Specifies the mapped module name. See the Unified Coverage Database API User Guide
and the Unified Coverage Reporting User Guide for details about module mapping.
-mapfile=map-file-path
Specifies the path to the map file. See the Unified Coverage Database API User Guide
and the Unified Coverage Reporting User Guide for details about module mapping.
-group ratio
Allows you to aggregate Group score as ratio metric type (numerator/denominator) rather
than the default, percent type.
-group merge_across_scopes
Merges the group score across scopes. For more information, see section “Merge
Covergroups Across Scopes” in the Coverage Technology Reference Manual.
-show_ratio
Displays ratio type score in the format of ratio instead of percentage.
-show_incomplete
Displays incomplete scores with the [inc] notation.
-log=logfile
Specifies the logfile in which all screen output messages are to be saved.
-report=urg-report-path
Generates hyperlinks to the given URG report path at feature and measure source cells.
The urg-report-path must exist in the path of the annotated spreadsheet.

-runurg
Automatically run URG to generate a URG report at the path specified by the -report
switch after the Verification Planner process is finished. If the -report switch is not given,
a URG report is generated in the default urgReport subdirectory in the working directory.
To add additional URG-specific options, such as -lca, -plan, -mod, -userdata,
-feature, -dir, and so on, while invoking URG, use the -urgopt <urg options> option
along with the -runurgoption. For example, consider the following command that invokes
URG using -runurg after hvp annotate and passes additional options, such as -xmlplan
and -format, to provide additional functionality:
hvp annotate -plan test.hvp.xml -userdata test.data -runurg -urgopt
"\-xmlplan \-format both"
The URG command for this example is as follows:
urg -xmlplan -format both -plan test.hvp.xml.hvp -userdata test.data
-report urgReport
When URG runs, some Verification Planner switches such as -plan, -mod, -userdata,
-map, -mapfile, -elfile, -trend, and -report are bypassed to URG.
If the VCS_HOME environment variable is not set, URG in the VCS deployment for
Verification Planner is used. You might want to set a different VCS_HOME to choose a
different URG path.
-trend sub-arguments
This switch only works when the -runurg switch is also given. When URG runs, it triggers
the trend chart feature. All -trend arguments are bypassed into URG.
-v
Shows progress status messages.
-q
Enables the quiet mode to suppress all warning messages.
-userdata_out out-userdata-file
Dump annotated scores of all measures into the userdata file specified by out-userdata-
file.
-metric_prefix metric-prefix
You prepend the given prefix to the metric name in the output HVP userdata file specified
with -userdata_out.
-ss_show_sources metric enum1+enum2+

Set enum entries that you want to appear in the measure source cell pop-up. If the
-ss_show_sources entry option is not set, all matching sources appear in the pop-up.
For example:
-ss_show_sources test warn+fail
-hvp_no_score_missing
Stops unmatched coverage sources from affecting the plan scores. From the top plan
score, you can analyze the part of plan which has a problem.
The -hvp_no_score_missing option produces no scores in the following scenarios:
• The sources do not match any object in the .vdb database
• The measure statements have no sources
• The sources match an object in the .vdb database, but when no metric is measured.
feature f2;
measure Line m1;
source = "tree: u1.u2";
Where, “u1.u2” exist in the .vdb database. However, line coverage was not turned on
during simulation.
In the spreadsheet XML plan flow, the measure cells should not be empty and you
should add the source string (for example, TBD- To Be Decided) and then add this
switch to get no coverage.
This switch is applicable to both URG and HVP annotate.
% hvp annotate -plan myplan.xml -dir simv.vdb \
-hvp_no_score_missing

% urg -plan myplan.hvp -dir simv.vdb \
-hvp_no_score_missing
-hvp_score_missing
Annotates 0% coverage for unmatched coverage sources, thereby decreasing the overall
plan score.
The behavior of this switch is made default. You do not need to explicitly specify this
switch in the command line to include unmatched coverage scores. If you do not want
unmatched coverage scores to be taken into account, use the -hvp_no_score_missing
option.

-hvp_disable_wildcards_in_cgshapeparam
This switch disables “*”, “/” and “?” wildcards in an expression of a covergroup shape.

this.arg12_0_cg_init)=3,(this.arg13_0_cg_init **
this.arg14_0_cg_init)=1,(this.arg1_0_cg_init **
this.arg2_0_cg_init)=1,(this.arg3_0_cg_init *
this.arg4_0_cg_init)=2,(this.arg5_0_cg_init **
this.arg6_0_cg_init)=1,(this.arg7_0_cg_init *
this.arg8_0_cg_init)=2,(this.arg9_0_cg_init **
this.arg10_0_cg_init)=2}.*
Inside the expression of test::cg::SHAPE none of the "*" are treated as wildcards.
However, the “*” that is provided after the covergroup shape expression is treated as
wildcard.
-hvp_feature_vertical_aggregation
Enables vertical aggregation for user-defined custom aggregate metrics in both Verdi
Coverage and URG. This option ensures that aggregate metric scores are calculated
using the vertical method, providing a more balanced and accurate representation of

Coverage Mapping and Aggregation at the Feature Level in URG
Coverage supports the annotation of each feature with only the coverage data from one or
more specified coverage databases. It provides the ability to map a feature to one or more
coverage databases, and then use only those databases when computing the scores of
that feature.
URG annotates each feature with only the coverage data from one or more specified
coverage databases, see the following command:
% urg -feature feature-name -dir simv1.vdb -plan \ <myplan.hvp>
The following command takes a list of features in feature-database mapping file :
% urg -featurefile feature-database mapping file \ -dir simv1.vdb -plan
<myplan.hvp>
URG annotates these features with only the coverage data from one or more specified
coverage databases.

Example 1:
% urg -featurefile map1 -dir cov1.vdb -plan <myplan.hvp>
where, map1 contains the list of features. This command effectively expands to the
% urg -feature "FeatA FeatB FeatC" -dir cov1.vdb -plan \ <myplan.hvp>
Here, the scores of FeatA, FeatB, and FeatC are annotated from cov1.vdb.
Example 2:
% urg -feature FeatA -dir cov1.vdb -feature FeatB -dir \ cov2.vdb
cov3.vdb -plan <myplan.hvp>
In the example, the coverage data from cov1.vdb is annotated onto FeatA, and the
merged coverage data from cov2.vdb and cov3.vdb is annotated onto FeatB. URG uses
the merged result of all three VDB directories to write its main report.
If there are coverage directories that should not be used for any feature annotation, they
have to be specified with the regular -dir option.
% urg -dir cov4.vdb -feature FeatC -dir cov5.vdb -dir \ cov6.vdb -plan
<myplan.hvp>
In the earlier example, the score of FeatC is the average of cov4.vdb, and the cumulative
coverage of cov5.vdb and cov6.vdb.
This affects both coverage databases from VCS and user-supplied data. You can provide
other information for annotation into the plan, such as number of test failures/successes.
If the -userdata option is given after the -feature option, then the associated user data
is annotated to the immediately preceding feature. In the following example, FeatD is
annotated with userdata, myfile2 and cov7.vdb:
% urg -feature FeatD -dir cov7.vdb -userdata myfile2 \
-plan <myplan.hvp>
Example 3:
% urg -userdata myfile1 -feature FeatB -dir cov3.vdb -userdata myfile2
-plan <myplan.hvp>
The annotated score of the FeatB feature for userdata is the aggregator of myfile1 and
myfile2.
Use the hvp genxls command to convert an HVP plan into standard Excel XML format for
the spreadsheet annotator workflow. This is the original one-way export: it captures plan

structure, metrics, attributes, and subplans for annotation, but it does not support VMS server mode or round-trip import. For round-trip conversion, VMS server mode, and richer reporting, use the extended loadable report format produced by hvp genxls -report . That format is a superset of this standard output; see Generating Loadable HVP Excel XML Reports. The standard Excel XML plan supports the following elements of the HVP plan: • Top plan sheet (plan, attribute, annotation, feature, measure, and goal) • Attribute definition sheet • Metric definition sheet • Subplan sheets • Use Model • Example • Scoring in Subplans • Retaining Original Measures in HVP Excel XML Export/Import You can use the following HVP command to generate an HVP plan in the excel XML format: % hvp genxls -plan hvpfile -outdir dirname where, • plan hvpfile is a plan file in an HVP language. • outdir dirname is the output directory to place the generated excel XML files. • -merge_measures <1|0> controls whether measures with the same metric types are merged into shared Excel columns. Default is 1. Input: An HVP Plan in the HVP Format: plan topplan; feature feautre1; measure Line,Cond m1; source="module: kp_fsm"; Output: The HVP Plan in the Excel XML Format: hvp plan topplan feature value m1.Line value m1.Cond measure m1.source feautre1 module: kp_fsm
Scoring in Subplans Scoring in subplans is generally the same as scoring at the top plan level, but there are some exceptions. If your top-level plan does not include any measures or sources, annotation scores are shown only in the subplans. The top-level tree does not show an average score in the annotation XML, as shown in the following figure: Figure 34 Score Annotation Behavior in Topplan Versus Subplan Levels However, the GUI calculates and displays the average of subplan scores at the top level, as shown in the following figure: Figure 35 Average of Subplan Scores at Top Level The annotation XML displays only the scores for the defined metrics. If a plan or subplan does not contain any measured metrics, the sheet does not display a score. To include the total and per-metric scores in your annotated report, generate the report using the loadable report format (hvp genxls -report ). This format provides the total score and the scores for each defined measure. For more information about the hvp genxls -report option, see Generating Loadable HVP Excel XML Reports. Retaining Original Measures in HVP Excel XML Export/Import By default, when multiple measures within the same feature share identical metric definitions, the export process from an HVP file to an Excel XML format merges these measures into a single entry in the Excel XML file. Use the hvp genxls -merge_measures option to control whether measures with the same metric types are merged in the Excel output. For a summary of this option, see Controlling Measure Merging in Excel Export. • -merge_measures 1 (default): Merge measures using the same metrics into shared columns. • -merge_measures 0 : Keep each measure as a separate entry with its own score columns, even if multiple measures use the same metric types (for example, Group). Use this when you need to display separate coverage scores for each measure in the generated Excel plan. To export your HVP file to Excel XML format while retaining all original measures, even if they share the same metrics, run the following command: hvp genxls -plan HVP_Example.hvp.xml -merge_measures 0 You can also run hvp genxls --help for command-line option details. For example, with the default behavior, the value . columns of features, kp_fsm, coin_fsm, and jukebox are merged into value m1.Line and value m1.Toggle. Figure 36 Default Behavior of Merging Measures With Identical Metric Definitions The annotate results look like this: If the -merge_measures 0 option is added in the hvp genxls command line, the value . columns are not merged as the following: Figure 37 Behavior of Merging Measures With the -merge_measures 0 Option It uses the generated XML to annotate the coverage score. You get the results of separated coverage scores for each measure. Generating Loadable HVP Excel XML Reports For more information about HVP annotation, refer to Introduction to Spreadsheet Annotator. Generating Loadable HVP Excel XML Reports The loadable report format extends the standard hvp genxls Excel XML output described in Generating Standard HVP Excel XML Plans. It adds worksheets and metadata needed for round-trip conversion between HVP plans and Excel XML or XLSX reports in both file mode and Verification Management System (VMS) mode. Compared with the standard Excel XML plan, the loadable report is more readable, supports VMS mode, and can be imported back into Verdi coverage or HVP with hvp annotate. Verdi coverage can also save reports in this format by setting Loadable to Yes when using Save report. • Expanded Report Format • Using the HVP Utility to Generate and Convert Reports Expanded Report Format The loadable report format extends the original XML report with additional content to support round-trip conversion. The expanded report contains the top plan and all subplans.
