Expanded Report Format
The loadable report format extends the original XML report with additional content
to support round-trip conversion. The expanded report contains the top plan and all
subplans. Each top plan and subplan includes the following sheets:
Both hvp genxls -report and hvp annotate use the same worksheet naming
conventions when generating or reading loadable reports. User-defined metrics, attributes,
and feature-type definition sheets use the naming conventions [index]_metrics,
[index]_attributes, and [index]_featuretype, respectively. The [index] matches
the hierarchy index of the corresponding plan contents sheet.

Generating Loadable HVP Excel XML Reports
Worksheet Naming Example
For a top plan named myplan with subplans FeatureA and FeatureB, the report contains
worksheets such as:
• 0_myplan, 0_metrics, 0_attributes, and 0_featuretype
• 1_myplan_FeatureA_subplan, 1_metrics, 1_attributes, and 1_featuretype
• 2_myplan_FeatureB_subplan, 2_metrics, 2_attributes, and 2_featuretype
Plan Contents Sheet
The plan contents sheet naming convention depends on whether the sheet represents the
top plan or a subplan:
• Top plan: [index]_[plan_name]
• Subplan: [index]_[top_plan_name]_[subplan_name]_subplan
The subplan sheet name includes the top-level plan name as a prefix to ensure unique
worksheet names across the report.
Each plan contents sheet contains the following information:
• Hierarchy index
• Plan, feature, measure, or source name
• Score of metrics with annotated data
• All selected columns, including goal of metrics and attributes
• Measure metrics that record the reference metrics of each measure
In VMS mode, feature names use the format [feature_name] or
[feature_type]:[feature_name] when the feature type is not "common".
User-Defined Metrics Definitions Sheet
The metrics definitions sheet uses the naming convention [index]_metrics and captures
the same information as the hvp genxls metrics output. It contains the following columns:
Table 10 User-Defined Metrics Definitions
Column Description
Name The name of the user-defined metric.
Type The type of the metric (for example, percent, ratio, real, or enum).

Generating Loadable HVP Excel XML Reports
Table 10 User-Defined Metrics Definitions (Continued)
Column Description
Aggregator The aggregation method used for the metric.
Apply The scope or context to which the metric applies.
Goal The target goal value for the metric.
User-Defined Attributes Definitions Sheet
The attributes definitions sheet uses the naming convention [index]_attributes
and captures the same information as the hvp genxls attributes output. It contains the
following columns:
Table 11 User-Defined Attributes Definitions
Column Description
Type The data type of the attribute.
Propagated Status Indicates whether the attribute is propagated.
Name The name of the user-defined attribute.
Default Value The default value assigned to the attribute.
Feature-Type Definition Sheet
The feature-type definition sheet uses the naming convention [index]_featuretype and
contains the following columns:
Table 12 Feature-Type Definitions
Column Description
Name The name of the feature type.
Attribute Limit The maximum number of attributes allowed for this feature type.
Child Limit The maximum number of child elements allowed for this feature
type.

Generating Loadable HVP Excel XML Reports
Using the HVP Utility to Generate and Convert Reports
The HVP utility provides command-line options for converting between HVP files and
report XML/XLSX files. You can generate a report from an existing HVP plan, or convert a
report back into HVP files.
Converting HVP to Report XML
Use the hvp genxls command with the -report option to generate an extended report
XML file from an HVP plan.
File mode:
hvp genxls -plan <input_hvp> -report
VMS server mode:
hvp genxls -hvp_server <web_server_url:port> -hvp_proj <project_name>
-plan <plan_hier_name> -report
The following table describes the command arguments:
Table 13 hvp genxls -report Arguments
Argument Description
-plan <input_hvp> Specifies the input HVP plan file (file mode) or the plan hierarchy
name (VMS server mode).
-report Outputs the report in the extended XML format.
-hvp_server <server_url:port> Specifies the VMS server URL and port for VMS server mode.
-hvp_proj <project_name> Specifies the VMS project name for VMS server mode.
The output file uses the default name [hvp_fileName].xml.
Converting Report XML to HVP
Use the hvp annotate command to convert a report XML file back into annotated report
and HVP files for the top plan and all sub-plans.
hvp annotate -plan <input_report_hvp.xml>

This command produces the following output files:
• Report XML with annotated scores, using the default name
[report_fileName].ann.xml
• HVP files for each plan, using the default name [report_fileName].
[plan_name].hvp
To generate only the HVP files without the annotated report, add the -gen_hvp_only
option:
hvp annotate -plan <input_report_hvp.xml> -gen_hvp_only
The following table describes the command arguments:
Table 14 hvp annotate (Report XML to HVP) Arguments
Argument Description
-plan <input_report_hvp.xml> Specifies the input report XML file to convert.
-gen_hvp_only Generates only the HVP files without producing an annotated
report XML.
For more information about saving a plan as a loadable report in Verdi Coverage and
loading a previously saved report into Verdi Coverage, see “Saving and Loading Reports
in Verdi Coverage” in the Verdi Coverage User Guide and Tutorial.
Verification Planner Doc Plan Generator provides a way to convert verification plans in the
HVP language format to the Word Doc XML plan format. The Doc Plans generated from
the Word Plan generator is given to the Verification Planner word annotator to annotate
scores. This application currently supports MS Word 2003 and later versions only.
It helps you to generate an annotated report in the MS Word format.

The output Doc XML plan contains only a skeleton of feature hierarchy. You might want
to add more additional contents, such as pictures or descriptions, into the documents to
make the plan as a complete verification report before adding it into the annotation flow.
This section consists of the following topics:
• Use Model
• Process Flow
• Command Arguments
• Converting the HVP Language to the Doc XML
• HVP Plan
The use model of the Verification Planner Doc Plan generator is as follows:
• Syntax: hvp gen -plan <Top Plan HVP file> .
• One HVP file must contain one plan. For example, MyTopPlan.hvp is converted to
MyTopPlan.xml. A plan can include other plans as subplan, in that case, the HVP files
for subplan is included using the `include syntax.
• One Doc XML file is generated for each HVP plan file. If multiple HVP files are involved
in the given top plan, multiple Doc XML files are generated accordingly.
• If any included files are not found, hvp gendoc skips the missing HVP file with warning.
The generated top-plan Doc XML might not work with Doc annotation flow due to the
missing file.
All the Doc XML files are generated in the same directory as the associated HVP files. Doc
XML files could also be generated in a different path if involved HVP files are located in the
different path. When the -outdir <path> option is given, all the output Doc XML files are
generated in the given path. In this case, include file path in the Doc XML is reconfigured,
so the generated XMLs can work with the Verification Planner annotator without additional
editing.
Figure 38 shows the use model of the Verification Planner doc plan generator.

Figure 38 Verification Planner Doc Plan Generator Use Model
Process Flow
The process flow of the Verification Planner Doc Plan generator is as follows:
1. Captures a verification plan in the HVP language using the Verification Planner GUI
editor, Verification Planner Spreadsheet annotator, or manual editing in Text Editor.
2. Supports one plan in one HVP file.
3. Syntax: hvp gendoc -plan <top plan HVP file> [-outdir <output path>]
4. Open the generated Doc XML files in MS-Word 2003 or later, then edit them if required.
5. Apply Doc XML files to the Verification Planner Doc annotator.
The Doc Plan Generator flow is not fully interoperable with Verdi HVP edit.
This means that you cannot generate a doc, add more comments, diagrams,
and other details to the doc, generate .hvp and then edit that HVP in Verdi.
If you do so, you may lose your added comments, diagrams, and other
details as these are not recorded in the .hvp file.

Command Arguments
This section consists of the following topics:
• Syntax
• Options
hvp gendoc -plan TopPlan.hvp [-outdir output_path]
Options
-h
Shows the help message.
-plan TopPlan.hvp
Specifies the top plan HVP file. For example:
-plan myplan.hvp
-outdir outpath
Generates the output path for the Doc XML files. It must exist before run.
Converting the HVP Language to the Doc XML
Basically, the Doc XML is using predefined styles in the Doc Plan template, so generated
files look similar to the Doc XML Plan for the Verification Planner doc annotator.
For more details about the Doc XML format, see the Verification Planner User Guide.
HVP Plan
The syntax of the HVP plan is as follows:i
plan myplan;endplan
At the first page of Doc XML, the name of plan should be in the HVP Plan style as follows:

• HVP Include Files
• HVP Metric Definitions
• HVP Attribute/Annotation Definition
• HVP Feature/Subplan
• HVP Measure Statement
• HVP Assignment and Description
• Contents Summary
HVP Include Files
The syntax of HVP include files is as follows:
`include "subplan_sub1.hvp"`include
"subplan_sub2.hvp"plan MyPlan; endplan
At the last page of Doc XML, the following table is added:

The text in the first cell of table is HVP Include File and style is not specified. The
include files are listed from the second row: one in each cell.
HVP Metric Definitions
The syntax of HVP metric definition is as follows:
metric integer bug_count; aggregator = sum; goal = bug_count == 0; endmetric metric
enum{reviewed, ongoing, completed} proj_progress; aggregator = sum;endmetric
At the last part of Doc XML plan, the following tables are added.
Each metric definition is defined in a separate table. The first row is composed of single
column cell, which contains HVP Metric <name> . From the second row, each row is
composed of two columns. The left column has a keyword and the right cell has its
corresponding value string. The style of the text is not specified.
HVP Attribute/Annotation Definition
The syntax of HVP attribute/annotation definition is as follows:
attribute integer phase = 1; attribute enum{orange, apple, apricot} fruit =
orange;annotation string comment = "";
At the last part of Doc XML plan, the following tables are added:

Each attribute/annotation definition is defined in a separate table. The first row is
composed of single column cell which contains HVP Attribute <name> or HVP
Annotation <name> . From the second row, each row is composed of two columns. The
left column has a keyword, and the right cell has its corresponding value string. The style
of the text is not specified.
HVP Feature/Subplan
The text of the HVP feature/subplan hierarchy uses HVP Feature1 to HVP Feature9
depending on the depth of hierarchy. A feature under plan definition is Level 1. A new
page is always followed by Level-1 features.
plan Wishbone; feature InputOutput; feature ReadIO; endfeature feature WriteIO; endfeature
endfeature endplan
This might look simple, because there is nothing between the features. Normally, between
two features, there are measure tables, attribute/goal assignment tables, or some
descriptions for features.

If an object of hierarchy is a subplan instead of a feature, the title is subplan <name> as
follows:
`include “ReadIO.hvp”`include “WriteIO.hvp”plan Wishbone; feature InputOutput; subplan
ReadIO; subplan WriteIO #(phase=2, owner=”Verification Group”); endfeature endplan
You must define ReadIO and WriteIO plans in included HVP files before they are used as
subplans.
As subplan ReadIO is at Level 2, it uses the HVP Feature 2 style.
HVP Measure Statement
A measure statement is described in a table. The first row is composed of single column
with the HVP Measure <name> text. The first row is followed by a few two-column rows with
source at the left cell. The source rows are followed by other two-column rows with metric
name in the left cells.
feature ReadIO; measure Line, Cond mReadComponent source = “tree:
top.Wishbone.Video.read”, “tree: top.Wishbone.Audio.read”; endmeasure

HVP Assignment and Description
The HVP language allows you to assign attribute/annotation values and a goal expression
for metric at an each level of plan/feature hierarchy. These value assignments are
described in a table with HVP Assignment in the first cell. The name of an attribute or a
metric and its associated values are followed in the next row: one assignment at each row.
One exception is the description built-in annotation value. If the description value
is assigned, it appears at the right next line of feature title in the HVP Description style
instead of the HVP Assignment table.
feature ReadIO; description = “This feature is testing Read interface of Wishbone chipset.”
owner = “Verification Group” phase = 2 Line = Line > 95%; Group = Group > 90%;
Contents Summary
At the second page of Doc XML, a summary of hierarchy appears (see the figure below).
This summary contains the plan title, features, metric/attribute definition, and include file
information if they exist.
When the doc XML is generated, the page number and hyperlinks are not resolved
completely because they cannot be determined in Verification Planner. As you see in the
following figure, the page numbers show up as # instead of real numbers except a plan.

To resolve them, you can right-click, click Update Field from the menu, and then select
Update Entire Table.
The right page number shows up as follows:

Troubleshooting
Perform the following if you do not see coverage information annotated to the spreadsheet
after using -dir covdb-path, where covdb-path is your coverage directory:
1. Use the Synopsys Unified Report Generator (URG) to verify that the coverage
information exists. For example:
%urg -dir wb_dma.vdb
2. If the coverage information exists, contact your Synopsys Applications Consultant for
assistance.

HVP Interactive Editor
This chapter provides you the basic steps required to create a new verification plan using
HVP Interactive Editor. Verdi (verdi -cov ) provides you a direct interface to create and
edit a verification plan with coverage data in the Verdi coverage GUI. This feature allows
you to:
• Create a plan
• Drag and drop coverable objects from the coverage hierarchy
• Show the annotated results
• Check for incompleteness or errors in the plan
This chapter describes the following topics:
• Overview of the Basic Verdi Panes for Verification Planner
• Creating a Verification Plan
• Incompleteness Checks
• Displaying Override in the HVP Detail Pane
• Descriptions for Attribute and Metric Definitions
Overview of the Basic Verdi Panes for Verification Planner
The Verdi platform also provides the Verification Planner feature to help you focus on a
hierarchical verification plan and manage the specification for higher coverage.
The verification planner (HVP planner) in Verdi Coverage allows you to create a specific
plan to measure what is important for each design and also allows for accountability,
so that what gets measured gets done. Plans should be created as early as possible
to determine the important metrics; therefore, as the design progresses, the important
features in the plan are not forgotten. Verification plans can be saved into a readable
format, for you to present to management, which keeps everyone informed about the
coverage plan.
Before staring the HVP planner, you need to change Verdi Coverage to Plan mode. Use
the Window > Plan Mode command to invoke the Plan mode. As shown in the following

Creating a Verification Plan
figure, the Summary, Hierarchical Verification Plan (HVP), Hierarchical Verification Plan
Detail, Message, and Exclusion Manager panes are displayed in the main window:
For more details, see Chapter, "Using Verification Planner" in the Verdi Coverage User
Guide and Tutorial.
Creating a Verification Plan
The follow steps illustrates how to create a basic verification plan.
Step 1. Invoking Verdi
Invoke verdi -cov on the command line. You can also use the -covdir command line
argument to specify the coverage databases to load. For example,
verdi -cov -covdir simv1.vdb
Use the -plan command-line argument to specify the HVP plan to open. For example,
verdi -plan myplan.hvp
Use both the -plan and -covdir switches together as follows:
% verdi -cov -covdir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb -plan myplan.hvp
Click Plan > Open/New Plan to open or create a verification plan.
For more details, see Chapter, "Using Verification Planner" in the Verdi Coverage User
Guide and Tutorial.

Incompleteness Checks
Incompleteness Checks
Verdi contains a feature that allows you to compare your verification plan against actual
coverage data. By comparing the two, you can determine whether there are any errors or
inconsistencies that need to be corrected. Examples of errors and inconsistencies are:
• Typos in metric source names.
• Wrong source type selected.
• Unimplemented functional coverage checks. For example, a covergroup was expected
to be implemented, but not yet coded in the testbench or DUT code.
• Coverage objects not referenced in the plan. These coverage objects could be
uncovered and not affect the plan results at all.
Incompleteness checks are automatically turned on when you load a verification plan,
and at least one coverage database or user-defined metric file. You can see the effects
of the incompleteness checks in the form of orange-red marks placed to the far left of the
navigation panes.
In the main editor pane, a red-orange exclamation mark (!) indicates that something is
wrong with the definition of a feature. You can expand that feature’s child feature and
measure nodes to isolate which nodes are causing the warning. If you hold the pointer

Descriptions for Attribute and Metric Definitions
Descriptions for Attribute and Metric Definitions
Verification Planner provides two types of attributes and metrics: Built-in and User-
defined. Built-in attributes and metrics are implicitly computed during annotation for every
verification plan and you cannot customize them. On the other hand, you can create your
own user-defined attributes and metrics based on your requirements.
Verification Planner allows you to add a description to your user-defined attributes and
metrics. The feature works as follows:
• You can add descriptions to all attribute types, that is, integer, real, string, enum,
and set. Also, this option is applicable to all metric types, that is, integer, enum, real,
and percent.
• You can specify more than one line as a description.
• You can use special and escape characters in the description.
This section explains how the description feature works with the following interfaces:
• HVP
• URG
• Limitation
This section describes the following:
• Limitation
HVP
To add a description to an attribute definition in a plan, use the following syntax:
<att_name>.description = <enquoted_description_string>
For example, to add a description to the definition of a user-defined attribute
Attr_Integer, use the following in the plan:
attribute integer Attr_Integer = 1;
Attr_Integer.description = "This is an integer-type attribute. \n This is
a user-defined attribute.";
To add a description to a metric definition in your plan, use the following syntax:
metric metric-type identifier;
goal = goal-specification;
aggregator = aggregator-specification;
description = <enquoted_description_string>;

Descriptions for Attribute and Metric Definitions
For example, to add a description to a user-defined metric color, use the following in the
plan:
metric enum {red, yellow, green, purple, black} color;
goal = (color.green >=4);
aggregator = sum;
description = "This is a color metric. \nThis is a user-defined
metric.";

plan. To do so, add a new column for the description in its attribute and metric definition
sheet as follows:

Limitation
The feature has the following limitation:

Introduction to VC Formal
VC Formal
VC Formal is a comprehensive high performance and high capacity solution for functional
verification. Formal mathematical techniques are used to prove properties or assertions to
ensure correct operations of RTL design.
VC Formal can be used throughout the design and verification process, from specification
validation, white box and black box property checking, to pre-silicon and post-silicon
debugging. To use the tool for property checking, the assertion-based verification
methodology is recommended.
VC Formal consists of the following major components:
• GUI activity viewer
• VC Formal schematic viewer
• Front-end parser to build a netlist model that is common to all VC Static platform
applications
Additionally, there is a formal model builder, formal engines, engine orchestration, and
a built-in netlist simulator used to set up the initial condition and trace replay. A result
database is also an essential part of the components, where results are accessible either
from the activity view or from the vcf Tcl command interface.

This section explains how VC Formal coverage is integrated with the Verdi coverage
reporting flow. The two primary links between Verdi and VC Formal display VC Formal
results in Verdi, and link VC Formal results into your verification plan using Verdi Planner.
The section describes how Verdi coverage can be used to display and link to VC Formal
results.
• Collecting VC Formal Results in the Coverage Database
• Measuring VC Formal Assert Status in HVP
Collecting VC Formal Results in the Coverage Database
To display VC Formal results in the coverage report, you must first have set the VC_STATIC_HOME
VC_STATIC_HOME environment variable. For example:
setenv VC_STATIC_HOME /tools/synopsys/vcst
Here, VC_STATIC_HOME is an environment variable that must be set to point to the
installation directory for VC Formal.
To start the VC Formal tool, use the following command:
vcf
vcf -f test.tcl -verdi
where, vcf is a command to start the VC Formal tool with an interactive shell. The vcf
shell is a new shell that calls vc_static_shell internally. The vcf shell supports all the
options that vc_static_shell supports. The vcf shell automatically runs in the 64-bit
mode, unless you explicitly specify the -mode32 option. For details on vc_static_shell,
see the VC Formal Verification User Guide.
-f indicates your VC Formal execution script

You provide your own Tcl script to run VC Formal. To enable collection and display of
coverage data in Verdi, there are the following two commands that must be included in
that script:
1. The command to run VC Formal must include the -cov all flag. If you want assertions
to be targeted (not just cover properties), you should also include -cm assert as a flag
to VCS:
read_file -cov all -format verilog -sva -top $top -vcs "-cm assert
-sver ilog $testDir/test.v -sva"
2. You must include a command to save the results to the coverage database, for
example, my_covdb:
save_covdb -name my_covdb -cov assert+cover
This section consists of the following two subsections:
• Verdi GUI for VC Formal
• VC Formal Coverage in Verdi
Verdi GUI for VC Formal
To display the Verdi GUI for VC Formal (see Figure 45), use the vcf command with the
-verdi option.
Figure 45 Verdi GUI for VC Formal
The properties are categorized according to usage fields in VC Formal as:
• assert: The property specifies an assertion to be solved. Its values are proven,
inconclusive, vacuous, and falsified.
• assume: The property specifies as a constraint.
• cover: The property specifies as a cover property. Its values are covered, inconclusive,
and uncoverable.
• unused: The property is disabled.

VC Formal Coverage in Verdi
To load the coverage database generated with VC Formal in Verdi, use the following
command:verdi -cov
verdi -cov -covdir my_covdb.vdb
where,
-cov: Starts Verdi in the coverage mode.
-covdir: Opens the coverage database.
my_covdb.vdb: The name of the coverage database that gets opened. This is specified
in the test.tcl script with the save_covdb command. The command generates the
following window:
Figure 46 Verdi Coverage Assert Pane

The VC Formal information is displayed in the Assert tab in the columns: FVtype,
FVstatus, and FVdepth. This information should be same as VC Formal results.
The green color represents Proven or Covered, the red color represents Falsified,
Uncoverable, or Vacuous, and the yellow color represents Inconclusive.
FVtype indicates the usage field. The value in this column can be either Assert, Cover, or
Assume.
FVstatus indicates the run status of VC Formal. Its possible values depend on FVtype:
• If FVtype is Assert, the value of FVstatus can be Proven, Inconclusive, Falsified, or
Vacuous.
• If FVtype is Cover, the value of FVstatus can be Covered, Inconclusive, or
Uncoverable.
The FVdepth column is interpreted as follows:
• If FVstatus is Proven, Vacuous, or Uncoverable and its value is -1, it represents infinite
depth.
• For other FVstatus, N>=0 represents the depth of the trace.

2. Add measures with property type sources and reference the FVAssert metric.

The new FV Assert built-in metric is added to keep the score of FV Assert status
against users’ expectation. If FVstatus is same as fvassert_expected_status, then
the assertion/property is considered to be covered.
For example:
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: top.a1*";
3. Calculate FVAssert metric scores.
After finding the matching region in the coverage database, the covered/coverable
status is extracted from that database and added as a ratio for the FVAssert metric
score. For the FVAssert metric, you can get FVstatus from FV annotations in the
coverage database and compare fvassert_expected_status, which is set in
fvassert* attributes.
If FVstatus is same as fvassert_expected_status, then the assertion/property is
considered to be covered.
For example, the matching property top.a11: FVtype=assert and
FVstatus=Proven. If expectation is fvassert_expected_status = Proven , the
FVAssert metric score becomes 1/1. If expectation is fvassert_expected_status
= inconclusive and fvassert_expected_depth = 60 , the FVAssert metric score
becomes 0/1.

Overview
VCS’s C language interface lets you interact, control, and communicate with the simulation
environment and pass information to and from the internal data structures of the simulator.
The interface is based on the VHDL Procedural Interface, an ANSI C interface
specification that is being standardized by the IEEE to become part of the IEEE-1076
standard.
The C language interface is an implementation of the VHDL Procedural Interface
VHPI interface
(VHPI).
The procedural interface is also referred to as VHDL PLI or VhPLI.
VHPI is based on the definition of a VHDL information model. The information model
represents the static and dynamic VHDL data that is accessible by the procedural
interface. VHPI is also based on a small set of functions that operate on the information
model to access data, make queries about some particular piece of information, modify
data, interact with the simulator, and provide utilities such as printing, checking errors, and
so on.
The VCS VHDL C interface lets you interact with the simulator and the simulation
environment using VHPI functions by creating and using foreign C based models and
applications.
• Naming Conventions
• Information Model
Naming Conventions
VHPIinformation model
The following naming convention is used to refer to the VHPI information model data and
the VHPI functions:
1. All standard functions, classes, types, relationship tag names, and enumeration
constants defined by the interface start by the prefix vhpi.
2. The VHPI standard function names are lower case characters and have an underscore
between each word. All other names (classes, relationship tags, enumeration constant
identifiers) cannot have underscores, and each word after the vhpi prefix must start
with an upper case letter followed by lower case letters for the remainder of the word.

3. All defined VHPI types must end in a capital T.
4. One to many relationship tag names have an s (lower case) at the end.
5. VHPI uses some shorthand name conventions. For example, decl for declaration, stmt

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
letters for the remainder of the word.

3. All defined VHPI types must end in a capital T.
4. One to many relationship tag names have an s (lower case) at the end.
5. VHPI uses some shorthand name conventions. For example, decl for declaration, stmt
for statement, conc for concurrent, seq for sequential, subp for subprogram, and so on.
6. All VHPI class kind names end with the letter K.
7. All VHPI property names end with the letter P.
The VHPI information model is based on an object oriented representation of the VHDL
post-elaboration and simulation runtime data. It partitions VHDL data into VHPI classes
that are connected by relationships. A VHPI class contains methods and properties. An
instance of a VHPI class is called an object.
VHPI lets you access object properties or traverse relationships between classes of
objects. The relationships can be one-to-one or one-to-many. An example of a one-to-one
relationship is the enclosing region (scope) of a declaration, and an example of one-to-
many relationship is the declaration within a region.
• VHPI Handles
• Information Model Classes
• Regions
VHPI Handles
VHPI functions access VHDL data using an abstract object reference called a handle.
A VHPI handle is an opaque reference to a VHDL object that operates within the VHPI
interface. A VHPI handle is used to reference any VHDL object that is defined in the
information model that is identifying static or dynamic data. When you want to access any
VHDL object such as a component instance or a signal, a handle to the object is returned.
Access to a VHDL object is always given with respect to the handle representing the
object.
The C language type of the handle (vhpiHandleT) is defined in the header file
vhpi_user.h. The vhpi_user.h file also contains all of the VHPI function prototypes,
properties, and relationships. The vhpi_user.h file is included in the software installation
tree under the $SYNOPSYS_SIM/$ARCH/sim/include directory.

All VHPI non-standard functions prototypes are declared in a header file called
vhpi_snps.h. This file exists in $SYNOPSYS_SIM/$ARCH/sim/include directory.
Handle Management Functions
VHPI functions create and manipulate handles. This section describes how handles to
objects denoted by the information model are allocated and freed.
All access navigation functions such as vhpi_iterator(), vhpi_scan(),
vhpi_handle(), vhpi_handle_by_name() and vhpi_handle_by_index() create and
return handles. VCS VHDL C language interface does not share handles between various
applications, and it returns a different handle each time the same object is accessed from
a different application.
There are two kinds of data: static and dynamic. Static data is data that was statically
elaborated. Static data exists until the VHDL session ends. Dynamic data is data that was
dynamically created either by the effect of dynamic elaboration or by simulation.
A handle to static data exists until you explicitly release the handle, the application that
requested the handle finishes, or the session ends. Generally, handles to static VHDL data
exist for the lifetime of the VHPI application. You can request to release a handle using the
vhpi_release_handle() function. After a handle is released, do not make any reference
to that handle, also you cannot assume that the handle still exists nor that it refers to the
same object.
Handles to dynamic data become invalid when the data disappears (for example, when
a subprogram call completes or when a restart or reset occurs). Using an invalid handle,
can cause an undefined behavior. Obtain handles to dynamic data only when the data
exists. For example, obtain handles to declared items within a subprogram only when the
subprogram is executing because of a subprogram call.
The navigation functions describe how handles to objects are obtained during traversal.
Iterator handles are handles defined by the interface to access many objects of the same
class type. Iterator handles are used to traverse one-to-many relationships that connect
classes. Iterator handles are slightly different in the sense that they cannot be shared
between applications because they hold the state of the current iteration. The property
vhpiKindP of an iterator handle is of vhpiIteratorK class kind.
Two different handles can identify the same VHPI object. The vhpi_compare_handles()
function can compare two handles and returns true if the handles refer to the same object,
returns false otherwise.
Information Model Classes
Before you start using the VHPI functions to access the VHDL objects, you need
to understand the different classes in the information model and their properties

and relationships. All of the classes properties and relationships are defined in the
vhpi_user.h header file.
The general categories of classes defined by the information model as follows:
• Regions
• Declarations
• Types
• Expressions
• Drivers
This section introduces you to a sample class and the class properties and relationships
from each of the categories. For a complete listing of all the information model classes,
see VHPI Information Model.
The regions category includes the following classes:
• CompInstStmt - Component instantiation concurrent statement
• RootInst - Special class corresponding to the design root
• PackInst - Package instance class. Each package is instantiated once
• IfGenerate - Class corresponding to “if generate” concurrent statements
• ForGenerate - “for generate” concurrent statement class
• BlockStmt - Block statement concurrent statement class
• ProcessStmt - Process statement class
• ArchBody - Architecture design unit class
• CompConfig - Component configuration specification class
• ConfigDecl - Configuration design unit class
• EntityDecl - Entity design unit class
• PackBody - Package body design unit class
• PackDecl - Package design unit class

The CompInstStmt class has the following properties:
• vhpiKindP - Returns the kind of any handle.

The CompInstStmt class has the following properties:
• vhpiKindP - Returns the kind of any handle. In this case, the return value is
vhpiCompInstStmtK.
• vhpiLineNoP - (event only) Returns the line number corresponding to this component
instance statement.
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns the kind of any handle as a string. In this case, the return
value is “vhpiCompInstStmtK”.
• vhpiFullNameP - Returns the VHDL pathname for the component instance and in
general the VHDL pathname for supported classes.
• vhpiFullCaseNameP - Returns the VHDL pathname for this component instance and
in general the VHDL pathname for supported classes. This and vhpiFullNameP return
the same string.
• vhpiNameP - Returns the VHDL simple name for the component instance and in
general the VHDL simple name for supported classes.
• vhpiCaseNameP - Returns the VHDL simple name for the component instance and in
general the VHDL simple name for supported classes. There is no difference between
this property and the vhpiNameP property, they both return the same string.
• vhpiCompNameP - (event only) Returns the name of the component specified in a
configuration specification. If there is no configuration specification, returns NULL.
• vhpiFileNameP - (event only) Returns the name of the VHDL file in which this
statement appears.
The CompInstStmt class has the following one-to-many relationships:
• vhpiInternalRegions - Returns all the regions instantiated within this component
instance. Use this is the mechanism to work down the design hierarchy.
• vhpiStmts - (event only) Returns the statements within the component instance.
The statements are concurrent statements that can be process statements, block
statements, component instance statements, and if or for generate statements.
• vhpiCompInstStmts - Similar to vhpiStmts with the result being a subset of regions
that is only the component instances within the component instance.
• vhpiBlockStmts - Similar to vhpiStmts, but only block statements within the
component instance.
• vhpiDecls - Returns all the declarations within the component instance.

• vhpiGenericDecls - Specialized form of vhpiDecls, returns only generic declarations
through the iterator handle.
• vhpiSigDecls - Returns the set of all signal declarations within the component
• vhpiConstDecls - Returns the set of all constant declarations within the component
• vhpiPortDecls - Returns the set of all port declarations within this component
• vhpiAttrDecls - (event only) Returns the set of all attribute declarations within the
component instance.
• vhpiAttrSpecs - (event only) Returns the set of all attribute specifications within the
component instance.
The CompInstStmt class has the following one-to-one relationships:
• vhpiConfigSpec - (event only) Returns the configuration specification corresponding
to the component instance.
• vhpiUpperRegion - Returns the upper region within which this component
instance is instantiated. This relationship coupled with the one-to-many relation
vhpiInternalRegions can be used to traverse the design hierarchy.
• vhpiDesignUnit - Returns the secondary design unit that the component instance is
bound to.

Static Design Access
Static design access refers to accessing post-elaboration design data. For example,
accessing design hierarchy navigating object types.
VHPI provides two types of static design access:
• Single or one-to-one relationship - Accessing a handle of some class type from a
reference handle of a given class type.
• Multiple or one-to-many relationship - Accessing a list of handles of the same class
type from a reference handle of a given class type.
To perform these operations, you can use the following two functions: vhpi_handle()to
traverse one-to-one relationships, and vhpi_iterator() in conjunction with
vhpi_scan()to traverse one-to-many relationships.
• Simple Property Access Functions
• Single Relationship Traversal Function
• Access by Name Lookup
• Iteration Functions
Simple Property Access Functions
VHPI provides functions to access class properties. There are three classes of properties:
boolean or integer valued properties, string valued properties, and real valued properties.
The interface provides a function to query about boolean or integer valued properties
vhpi_get(), a function to retrieve the string value of a string property vhpi_get_str(),
a function to get the value of a real valued property vhpi_get_real(), and a function
to get physical value properties vhpi_get_phys(). These functions take a handle to an
object, the property of interest and return an integer, a string, a real, or a physical value
respectively.

Simple Property Access Functions
Integer or Boolean Valued Properties
The vhpi_get() function returns the value of an integer or boolean property of the
specified handle.
vhpiIntT vhpi_get(vhpiIntPropertyT propertyTag, vhpiHandleT handle);
propertyTag: Specifies the tag name of the integer or boolean property.
handle: Specifies a handle to an object in the information model that must possess this
property. If the object does not support this property, the interface generates an error,
which you can check by using vhpi_chk_error().
vhpiIntPropertyT: Is an enumerated standard type of all the integer and boolean properties
defined by the interface.
vhpiIntT: Is a VHPI typedef, that represents the entire range of VHDL integers.
The function returns an integer constant corresponding to the value of the requested
property for the given handle, or 0 if an error occurred.
Specific values are defined for each integer property. For instance, the vhpiModeP
property can return the following values vhpiIn, vhpiOut, vhpiInout, vhpiBuffer, or
vhpiLinkage.
typedef enum {
vhpiIn,
vhpiOut,
vhpiInout,
vhpiBuffer,
vhpiLinkage
} vhpiModeT;
For example, to check whether the mode of a port of a component instantiation is an input
port, write your C code as the following fragment:
if (vhpi_get(vhpiModeP, port1[ID]) != vhpiIn) {
vhpi_get_str(vhpiFullNameP, port1[ID]));
}
Since some integer properties might return 1 as a valid return value, it is not possible
in all cases to determine that an error occurred by looking at the returned values. In
these cases, use the error checking functions or register a callback on error to check the
occurrence of an error.

Simple Property Access Functions
String Valued Properties
The vhpi_get_str() function returns the value of a string valued property of the specified
handle such as vhpiNameP or vhpiFullNameP.
const char * vhpi_get_str(vhpiStrPropertyT propertyTag, vhpiHandleT
handle);
propertyTag: Is the tag name of a string property.
handle: Specifies a handle to an object which possesses the string property.
For example to get the full name of a port of a component instantiation for printing error
messages about the port, write your C code as the following fragment:
if (vhpi_get(vhpiModeP, port1[ID]) != vhpiIn) {
vhpi_get_str(vhpiFullNameP, port1[ID]));
}
The function returns a pointer to a static string buffer owned by VHPI that was updated
with the string value of the property successfully retrieved. A return value of NULL
indicates that an error occurred. This can happen if the requested property does not apply
to this object class kind.
• The next call to vhpi_get_str()overwrites the previous string value.
• Since VHDL identifiers can contain special and graphic characters, you must
be cautious when using the C string library functions or C printf functions
when manipulating VHDL strings for name properties. The name property of
an extended identifier contains the starting and ending \ character.
Real Valued Properties
The vhpi_get_real() function returns a double. Use this function to get
vhpiFloatLeftBound and vhpiFloatRightBound of a floating range. You must use the
error checking functions or register a callback on error to determine if an error occurred.
Physical Valued Properties
The vhpi_get_phys function returns a physical value. Use this function to get
vhpiPhysLeftBoundP and vhpiPhysRightBoundP for physical ranges. You can also use it
for the vhpiPhysPositionP property.

Single Relationship Traversal Function
Single Relationship Traversal Function
VHPI provides the vhpi_handle() function to traverse one-to-one relationships between
objects. The one-to-one relationships are defined by the information model. A one-to-one
relationship exists between a reference (source) class and a target (destination) class if
there is at most one handle of the target class type that can be obtained by traversing this
relationship. Given a reference handle of a VHPI kind (refHdl), and given the relationship,
the interface returns a handle of that destination VHPI class reflecting the traversal of the
relation.
For example in the diagram below, from a vhpiCompInstStmtK reference handle, it is
possible to access the design unit that is bound to the component instance by following
the relationship between a vhpiCompInstStmt and the vhpiDesignUnit class.

vhpiHandleT duHdl;
char duName[MAXSTR];
char libName[MAXSTR];

switch (vhpi_get(vhpiKindP, instHdl)) {
case vhpiCompInstStmtK:
case vhpiRootInstK:
case vhpiPackInstK:
duHdl = vhpi_handle(vhpiDesignUnit, instHdl);
sprintf (duName, "%s", vhpi_get_str(vhpiUnitNameP, duHdl));
sprintf(libName, "%s", vhpi_get_str(vhpiLibLogicalNameP, duHdl));
vhpi_printf(design unit name %s in library %s\n,

Access by Name Lookup
VHPI provides a function for access by name, which given a reference scope handle and
an instantiated hierarchical name identifying a given VHDL item, returns a handle to the
designated item if an item of that name exists in that scope.
You can use the vhpi_handle_by_name()function only for VHPI classes that possess the
vhpiFullNameP property. A scope reference handle of NULL denotes the top level of the
design. The scope of search can be any of the packages instances or root instance of the
design hierarchy or an entire model. vhpi_handle_by_name()does not accept names of
type declarations, subtype declarations or anonymous types.
A string returned by vhpiFullNameP consists of the concatenation of every simple name
string returned by the vhpiNameP property.

A string returned by vhpiFullNameP consists of the concatenation of every simple name
string returned by the vhpiNameP property. The separator between names of hierarchy
instances or declarative items is the ‘:‘ character. The ‘.’ character is only used within a
selected name (object of a record field type). The string is always predefined with the top-
level entity name for objects in the design hierarchy.
Unlabeled processes are assigned a name that starts by “_P” or “_p” and ends by an
integer denoting the sequence of appearance of the equivalent process in the VHDL
source text of the current entity/architecture pair, block or generate statements. Numbering
starts at 0 and increments by 1. For example, the first unlabeled process will have a
vhpiNameP of “_p0”.

For example, to get a handle for a variable named var1 that is declared in the package
pkg1, which in turn was analyzed into the logical library lib1, write your C code as the
following fragment:
handle = vhpi_handle_by_name("@lib1:pkg1:var1", NULL);
VHPI lets you traverse one-to-many relationships. These relationships are defined by the
information model. This is a two phase mechanism.
First, an iterator handle for the collection of objects you want to iterate over is created
and initialized using the vhpi_iterator() function. Second, a function, vhpi_scan(),
is provided to scan the list of handles designated by this iterator. The vhpi_scan()
function returns a handle for each of the objects of the requested iteration type in the
iteration list. The function vhpi_iterator() returns NULL if there is no element in the iteration
list. The iteration list can be a dynamic list, as in the case of callbacks. The iteration
reflects the current simulation state. Therefore handles to dynamic data returned by
vhpi_scan() might become invalid as simulation progresses. Callbacks can be added or
removed during simulation by either the VHDL simulator or by the VHPI functions such as
vhpi_register_cb(), or vhpi_remove_cb().
Unless specified by the information model, an iteration does not define an order.
Therefore your code cannot be dependent upon the order the handles are
returned to be portable across VHPI implementations.
Examples
Using VHPI functions, you can access the following static information of a VHDL design:
• Hierarchy
• Declarations
• Types
The following VHDL code is referenced in the examples shown in the next two sections:
library IEEE;
use IEEE.std_logic_1164.all;

Objects With Value
The first parameter to VHPI value functions is a handle to an object of the following kind:
• Declarations: vhpiConstDeclK, vhpiVarDeclK, vhpiSigDeclK, vhpiGenericDeclK,
or vhpiPortDeclK
• Expressions: vhpiIndexedNameK or vhpiSelectedNameK
• Drivers: vhpiDriverK
• Transactions: vhpiTransactionK
Value Data Structure
The second parameter to VHPI value access functions is a pointer to the following
data structure that you allocated before the call (to vhpi_get_value() and
vhpi_put_value()):
typedef struct
{
vhpiValueFormatT format; /* value format */
int bufSize; /* allocated buffer size */
/* the number of scalars in the value. filled in by VHPI */
vhpiIntT numscalars;
vhpiIntT unit; /* physical unit. filled by VHPI */

Vector Handling
union
{
vhpiEnumT enumval, *enums; /* enumeration */
vhpiIntT intg, *intgs; /* integer */
vhpiRealT real, *reals; /* real */
vhpiPhysT phys, *physs; /* physical */
char ch, *str; /* formatting */
/* a raw data format to return internal storage and
to get values of access types */
void *ptr, **ptrs;
} value;
} vhpiValueT;
This data structure provides value support for all scalar objects and one dimensional
arrays (vectors) of scalars.
format: Specifies the format of the value. This is an enumerated type.
bufSize: Specifies a placeholder for the number of bytes that you allocated in the buffer.
The standard requires that the interface checks the size you provide against the size in
bytes required to copy the value. Further, the standard requires VHPI to return the right
size in case of a discrepancy. VCS VHDL does not support this for performance reasons.
You must use the vhpi_value_size() function to query the size in bytes required to store
the value in the specified format.
numscalars: Specifies the number of elements in the enums, intgs, reals, physs, or str
vectors. This corresponds to the number of scalars in the composite typed object and is
updated in by VHPI.
The actual value is copied into one of the fields of the union in the above structure, where
there are fields for each basic type of VHDL scalars or vectors of scalars.
ch: Specifies character literals and you can get character literals by using vhpiCharVal as
the value format.
str: Specifies string formatting and is NULL terminated. You can get string format values by
using vhpiStrVal for the format field.
Vector Handling
You must provide memory for both the value data structure and the buffers to hold vector
values. The memory you allocate does not need to be persistent, it can be released after
the call.
The VHPI model or application uses vhpi_value_size() to query the size-in-
bytes required for a buffer to store the handle's value in the specified format. You
allocate the buffer appropriately and set the appropriate field in the value union in the
vhpiValueT structure to the allocated buffer. This value-structure is then passed to the
vhpi_put_value() or vhpi_get_value() functions.

Value Access Function
For example, to get the value of the signal t in the following VHDL fragment
type real_vector_10 is array(1 to 10) of real;
signal t : real_vector_10;
the C code is
void value_test(vhpiHandleT h)
{
/* h is a handle to signal t */

double *r;
vhpiValueT v;
unsigned size_of_vec;

size_of_vec = vhpi_value_size(h, vhpiRealVecVal);
r = (vhpiRealT *) malloc(size_of_vec);

v.value.reals = r;
v.format = vhpiRealVecVal;

vhpi_get_value(h, &v);

/* r contains the 10 reals of signal t */
Value Access Function
VHPI provides the vhpi_get_value() function to get the value of an object. Only certain
classes of objects have a value that you can access with this function. Valid classes
include VHPI handle types denoting VHDL objects or VHDL expressions. Note that it is not
possible to get the value of any complex expression directly.
The function gets the current value of the designated object. Therefore, default or initial
values of VHDL objects can be fetched at the beginning of simulation, thereafter the value
of the object is the simulation value at the current time. The vhpi_get_value() function
takes a handle to a VHPI object, and a pointer to a value structure that you allocated and
fills up the value field in the requested format.
For example, to get the value of an input port of an instance in your VHDL design, you
first get a handle for it, allocate the value data structure, then use the vhpi_get_value()
function.
The vhpi_handle_by_index() function uses index value 0 to index the first
port of the port declaration returned by applying it on vhpiPortDecls and
compInst.
vhpiHandleT port1;
vhpiValueT* value1;

port1 = vhpi_handle_by_index(vhpiPortDecls, compInst, 0);
if (vhpi_get(vhpiModeP, port1) != vhpiIn) {
vhpi_get_str(vhpiFullNameP, port1));
}

/* Allocate value-structures for the port */
value1 = (vhpiValueT*) malloc(sizeof(vhpiValueT));
value1->format = vhpiEnumVal;

vhpi_get_value(port1, value1);
VHPI provides functions to update the value on a VHPI object by either performing an
immediate update with vhpi_put_value() function or by scheduling a transaction on a
driver of the VHPI object with the vhpi_schedule_transaction() function.

• Scheduling a Transaction
Immediate Update
VHPI provides the vhpi_put_value() function to perform an immediate update on the
value of a VHPI object. You can modify only certain classes of objects with this function,
such as signals, variables, or ports. VHPI classes of objects that are valid for this function
are marked in the information by having the vhpi_put_value method.
Synopsys provides an additional function called vhpi_put_value_delayed

h this function,
such as signals, variables, or ports. VHPI classes of objects that are valid for this function
are marked in the information by having the vhpi_put_value method.
Synopsys provides an additional function called vhpi_put_value_delayed
(this function is not part of the VHPI standard) which is similar to
vhpi_put_value but the updates take effect after a specified delay.
vhpi_put_value_delayed is defined in $SYNOPSYS_SIM/$ARCH/sim/include/
vhpi_snps.h. See vhpi_put_value_delayed().
You can use the following immediate update flag values:
• vhpiForce - Deposits a value without propagation. The object value is not placed on
hold. Subsequent writes overwrite this value.
• vhpiForcePropagate - Writes value with propagation. The object is again not placed
on hold. If this form of immediate update is used after network propagation, VCS VHDL
introduces a new delta cycle on the event side.

• vhpiForceHold - Writes value in this cycle without propagation and place the value on
hold it until released by the vhpi_release_hold() function.
• vhpiForceHoldPropagate - Writes value with propagation and place the value on
hold. After network propagation, this introduces a new delta cycle on the event side.
The hold remains until released by the vhpi_release_hold() function.
For example, to put a value on an output port of type std_logic of an instance in your
VHDL design, you must get a handle to it and allocate the value data structure. Then you
use the vhpi_put_value() function to write the value using the appropriate flag, in this
example vhpiForcePropagate.
The vhpi_handle_by_index() function uses index value 1 to index the second
port of the port declaration returned by applying it on vhpiPortDecls and
compInst.
vhpiHandleT port2;
vhpiValueT* value2;

port2 = vhpi_handle_by_index(vhpiPortDecls, compInst, 1);
if (vhpi_get(vhpiModeP, port2) != vhpiOut) {
vhpi_printf("Error: Port '%s' is not of mode out\n",
vhpi_get_str(vhpiFullNameP, port2));
}

To schedule a value on a driver of a signal/port, you need to have
• a handle to the driver, hdl
• allocate a value data structure (or array of value data structures), valuep
• the number of values, numValues
• a delay value, delayp
• a delay mode, delayMode
• pulse rejection limit, pulsRejp
The drivers returned by the interface will always be drivers to basic signals. A basic signal
is either a scalar for unresolved signal/port types or resolved composite signal/port types.
The delay modes that are supported are vhpiInertial and vhpiTransport. In the case
of inertial delays, you could specify non-zero pointer to pulse rejection limit data structure,
that should be passed in pulse rejection limit argument.
Current version does not support pulse rejection limit.
For a driver to a scalar signal/port, a single value structure should be passed with format
set to indicate a scalar value.
Scheduling transaction for drivers of composite types not resolved at the
composite level, such as bit vectors, standard logic vectors, record types must
be done by scheduling individual transactions on each scalar driver.
Transaction for driver of signals resolved at the composite level must be
scheduled at once.
When the type of a signal is a resolved array of scalars, a single data value structure
should be passed with format being a vector format, with allocated value buffer having as
many scalar values as the number of scalars. The numValues parameter should be always
be 1.
When the type of a signal is either an array of composites or a record, an array of values
structures should be passed. The value data structure should be passed at the coarsest
granularity possible. This implies that for all subsignals/subports of the composite signal/
port, which are arrays of scalars, the value has to be passed as a vector for all the
scalars. For all other subsignals, the same rule should be used recursively, down the type
hierarchy. All value data structures passed can only be either values to scalars or array of
scalars.
NULL transaction can be posted by setting valuep to NULL pointer.

The specified delay is a relative delay and is specified by using the time structure
vhpiTimeT by providing a 64 bits value.
The delay value is truncated if it is smaller than the VHDL simulator resolution limit. The
delay value must be legal as if it were the delay value of a VHDL signal assignment. Zero
delay transactions are specified by setting the delay value to 0. Scheduling a zero delay
transaction is only allowed during process execution (vhpiCbEndOfProcesses) and at last
known delta cycle (vhpiCbLastDeltaCycle). It will cause a new delta cycle to be created
if the transaction generates an event. Non-zero delay transaction can be scheduled at
any time before the end of the time step (vhpiCbEndOfTimeStep), effectively before the
next time is computed. Scheduling a transaction at any other phase has no effect and
generates an error. All zero delay transactions will be scheduled for the next delta cycle
and all other delay transactions will be scheduled for the time that corresponds to the
current simulation time added to the specified relative delay.
The following example shows how use the function to schedule a transaction on a bit
driver.
Example
In this example, iteration is done on vhpiIndexedNames to get a handle to each bit
element of the signal, then use of driver iteration methods to get the drivers of each bit
element. Then schedule a bit value transaction on each driver.
int schedule_bitvector_value (vhpiHandleT sigHdl)
{
int ret = 1;
vhpiHandleT baseTypeHdl, biyItr, bitHdl, driverItr,
driverHdl;
vhpiHandleT eltSubtypeHdl;
char* name;
vhpiValueT value;
vhpiTimeT delay;
delay = 0;
baseTypeHdl = vhpi_handle(vhpiBaseType, sigHdl);
if (vhpi_get(vhpiIsCompositeP, baseTypeHdl))
{
if(!vhpi_get (vhpiIsResolved, sigHdl))
{
if (vhpi_get (vhpiKindP, baseTypeHdl) ==
vhpiArrayTypeDeclK)
elemSubtypeHdl =
vhpi_handle (vhpiElemSubtype, baseTypeHdl);
baseTypeHdl =
vhpi_handle (vhpiBaseType, elemSubtypeHdl);
name = vhpi_get_str (vhpiNameP, baseTypeHdl);
if (!strcmp (name, "BIT"))
{
value.format = vhpiLogicVal;
value.value.enumval = vhpiBit0;
bitItr =

vhpi_iterator (vhpiIndexedNames, sigHdl);
while (bitHdl=vhpi_scan (bitItr))
{
driverItr =
vhpi_iterator (vhpiDrivers, bitHdl);
while (driverHdl=vhpi_scan (driverItr))
{
ret=vhpi_schedule_transaction (driverHdl,
&value,
1,
&delay,
vhpiInertial,
0);
}
}
}
}
}
}
return ret;
}

VHPI Callbacks
callbacks
Callbacks allow for communication between the C code and the simulator. Typically
callbacks are registered to trigger on specific conditions. The VHPI interface defines a set
of reasons for the callbacks. Depending on the reason, the callbacks can be repetitive
or non-repetitive (one-shot). A non-repetitive callback can be re-enabled in order for it to
occur again once it matures.
This section consists of the following topics:
• Callback Data Structure
• Registering Callbacks
• Removing Callbacks
• Disabling and Enabling Callbacks
• Getting Callback Information
• CallBack Reasons
• Callback Properties
• Callback Methods
• Callback Execution
• Example
Callback Data Structure
You pass the information to set up a callback through a data structure of type
vhpiCbDataT, defined as follows:
typedef struct vhpiCbDataS
{
vhpiCbReasonT reason; /* callback reason */
void (*cbf)(struct vhpiCbDataS*);/* callback function */
vhpiHandleT obj; /* trigger object */
vhpiTimeT* time; /* callback time */
vhpiValueT* value; /* trigger object value */
void* user_data; /* to be passed to the callback function */
} vhpiCbDataT;

Registering Callbacks
The callback data information is passed by the caller and provides at least the following
information:
• Callback reason for all callbacks
• Callback function C pointer for all callbacks
• Object field for value change callbacks
All other fields are optional. For more information about the optional and required fields,
see VHPI Callbacks.
Registering Callbacks

reason for all callbacks
• Callback function C pointer for all callbacks
• Object field for value change callbacks
All other fields are optional. For more information about the optional and required fields,
see VHPI Callbacks.
Registering Callbacks
The registration of callbacks can happen at the end of elaboration, during initialization or
during simulation run-time execution. The callback registration is immediate upon a call to
vhpi_register_cb().
vhpiHandleT vhpi_register_cb(vhpiCbDataT*);
With vhpiStateP property, you can request a callback handle returned by the
vhpi_register_cb() function to check the state of the callback whether the callback
occurred (vhpiCbStateMatured), is disabled (vhpiCbStateDisabled), or is active
(vhpiCbStateEnabled).
Removing Callbacks
Given a callback handle, the vhpi_remove_cb() function removes the callback. The
callback does not occur anymore.
int vhpi_remove_cb(vhpiHandleT);
The function returns 0 on success and 1 on failure. It will also free the callback handle and
any internal references to that callback.
Disabling and Enabling Callbacks
Any callback can be disabled and enabled respectively with vhpi_disable_cb() and
vhpi_enable_cb().
int vhpi_disable_cb(vhpiHandleT);

int vhpi_enable_cb(vhpiHandleT);
The functions return 0 on success and 1 on failure.

Getting Callback Information
Matured callbacks can be re-enabled by calling vhpi_enable_cb() with the handle for the
matured callback. In that case, the effect is same as registering a callback with the same
reason at that instant. This is recommended as an alternative to re-registering the one-
shot callbacks.
Getting Callback Information
Given a callback handle, fills a vhpiCbDataT structure that you allocate with information
that was passed during registration.
int vhpi_get_cb_info (vhpiHandleT, vhpiCbDataT*);
The function returns 0 on success and 1 on failure.
CallBack Reasons
To describe various callback reasons, the different phases that VHPI recognizes in a
simulation cycle are first described. There are no restrictions on callback registrations
based on simulation phase.
• Simulation Cycle in VHDL
• Object Callbacks
• Time Callbacks
• Checkpoint/restart Callbacks
Simulation Cycle in VHDL
The various phases of a simulation cycle are
1. New time step
This marks the beginning of a time step. The current time (Tc) has just advanced to the
next time (Tn) where events or actions are scheduled to occur. Signal effective values
are not changed yet.
2. Signal update, resolution, and propagation
The driving values of the signal drivers are computed from the transactions that
mature. Resolution functions are executed to compute resolved signal values.
The effective values are propagated through any port connections and conversion
functions.

CallBack Reasons
3. Process execution
The events determined at the signal update cause the execution of all sensitive
processes. Further, processes that were suspended and were scheduled to continue at
this time resume execution during this delta cycle. These processes execute and can
cause new transactions on the signal drivers. The next phase to execute is determined
by finding the next time Tn of execution. If Tn = Tc, this is a new simulation delta cycle
for the same time step and the simulation algorithm goes back to phase 2 (signal
update, resolution and propagation). If Tn is different from Tc, phase 4 is executed
(postponed processes execution).
4. Postponed process execution
The postponed processes are executed if this is the last delta simulation cycle for
the time Tc. Postponed processes are executed until they suspend. The execution of
postponed processes must not cause any new delta cycle.
5. End of time step
This phase marks the end of the current time Tc. The next step to be executed is step 1
at a new time if there are scheduled transactions, otherwise the simulation has reached
a quiescent state.
The callback reason specifies when during a simulation cycle the callback happens. In the
following section, when describing a callback reason, the callback function triggers is also
described. For all callback registrations, you must set the fields relevant for that callback
reason. For all callbacks, you must set the reason and the cbf fields (callback function
pointer). If the time and value fields are not null, they must point to valid, allocated time
and value objects. Further, for value change callbacks, the value structure must have the
right format and must have an allocated buffer for vectors of scalars. Additional settings
are described for each callback reason.
There are three main categories of callbacks that are supported: object, time, and action
callbacks.
Object Callbacks
Object callbacks are repetitive callbacks. They remain in effect until they are removed by
calling vhpi_remove_cb(). The registration of an object callback consists of setting the
obj field to a handle to the object of interest. If the time or value fields are set to NULL, the
caller is not interested in this information and the VHPI does not provide them when the
callback fires.
You can request that the value of the object resulting from the value change and the
time of the value change be returned in the callback data structure. If so, memory for the
value and time structures needs to be allocated and the value and time fields set to these
structures. The value structure must specify the format in which the object value is to be

returned (see vhpi_get_value()). These fields are updated in by VHPI when the callback
function is called.
The vhpiValueT data structure supports only scalars and vectors of scalars,
and hence callbacks can be registered only for such objects.
vhpiCbValueChange
The vhpiCbValueChange callback reason tracks value changes for object declarations,
indexed names, or selected names. The object kind can be vhpiSigDeclK,
vhpiPortDeclK, vhpiVarDeclK, vhpiIndexedNameK (subelements of signals, ports and
variables only), and vhpiSelectedNameK (subelements of signals, ports and variables
only) and vhpiDriverK.
For signals, the callback tracks signal effective value change and callback functions
are executed after phase 2 (signal update and propagation), before phase 3 (process
execution). For ports of mode out, or the out-side of inout ports, this callback tracks
changes in the driving value. Value change callbacks on objects in the cycle side fire
during phase 3 (process execution).
A callback on a composite signal triggers only once, even when several of its scalar
elements are modified. For variables, the callback triggers during process execution.
Variable callbacks are not supported when the simulation is running in optimized mode.
Variable callbacks trigger immediately when a process changes the value. A callback
on a variable of composite type triggers multiple times during a process execution if that
process modifies any of its scalars multiple times. Subprogram variables callbacks are not
supported.
For vhpiCbValueChange reason, in the callback data structure, if the value or
the time fields are not required in the callback, they must be set to 0 before
registering the callback with the vhpi_cb_register() function.
vhpiCbTransaction
The vhpiCbTransaction callback reason tracks the activity and value updates for
object declarations, indexed names, or selected names. The object can be a signal, port,
variable, or subelements (of signals, ports, or variables).
For signals, the callback tracks signal effective value update and callback functions are
executed after signal update and propagation phase, before process execution phase.
For ports of mode out, or the out-side of inout ports, the callback tracks updates in the
driving value.

CallBack Reasons
vhpiCbActive
The vhpiCbActive callback reason is similar to vhpiCbTransaction callback reason.
vhpiCbActive callback reason is not part of the standard.
Time Callbacks
Time callbacks are all one-time occurrence callbacks. The obj field is ignored by the
interface for time callbacks. The simulator does not fill any field of the vhpiCbDataS
structure when the time callback occurs.
vhpiCbNextTimeStep
A callback registered for the vhpiCbNextTimeStep reason triggers at the beginning of
the next time slice that has driver transactions or processes waking up, and where Tn
(next time) is different from Tc (current time). The callback triggers before phase 2 of the
simulation cycle starts, that is, the simulation time has advanced, and no signal values
have been updated yet.
vhpiCbAfterDelay
A callback registered for the vhpiCbAfterDelay reason, triggers at the time determined
by the current simulation time plus the delay that is indicated by the time structure even
if there is no transaction scheduled at this time.

vhpiCbAfterDelay
A callback registered for the vhpiCbAfterDelay reason, triggers at the time determined
by the current simulation time plus the delay that is indicated by the time structure even
if there is no transaction scheduled at this time. The callback function is executed before
phase 2.
vhpiCbStartOfNextCycle
A callback registered for the vhpiCbStartOfNextCycle reason, triggers at the beginning
of the next simulation delta cycle either for the present time step or for the next time step
if there are no more delta cycles in the current simulation cycle. The callback function
executes before phase 2.
vhpiCbEndOfPropagation
A callback registered for the vhpiCbEndOfPropagation reason, triggers after phase 2
(signals values have been updated), before phase 3 (process execution).
vhpiCbStartOfProcesses
Similar to vhpiCbEndOFPropagation, but is provided for standard compatibility and logical
separation.
vhpiCbEndOfProcesses
A callback registered for the vhpiCbEndOfProcesses reason, triggers after phase 3
(process execution).

CallBack Reasons
vhpiCbLastDeltaCycle
A callback registered for the vhpiCbLastDeltaCycle reason, triggers at the end of the
last delta cycle in a simulation cycle after phase 3 (process execution) and before phase 4
(postponed process execution). If there are no postponed processes, the callback triggers
after the last delta before time advance.
vhpiCbStartOfPostponed
A callback registered for the vhpiCbStartOfPostponed reason, triggers at the beginning
of phase 4 just before the postponed processes execute. No zero delay transactions can
be done by the callback function because this marks the last delta cycle.
vhpiCbEndOfTimeStep
A callback registered for the vhpiCbEndOfTimeStep reason, triggers at the end of the time
step (phase 5), the current time Tc has not advanced yet to next computed time Tn. No
zero delay transaction can be done by the callback function because this marks the end of
a time step. No other field settings are necessary for this type of callback.
Action Callbacks
The obj field is ignored for these callbacks. The simulator does not update any field of the
vhpiCbDataS structure when the callback occurs.
vhpiCbEndOfSimulation
A callback registered for the vhpiCbEndOfSimulation reason, triggers when a simulation
session is about to stop and exit. This cannot be re-enabled.
vhpiCbPLIError
A callback registered for the vhpiCbPLIError reason, triggers when a VHPI error
occurs. The callback function can then check the error using the VHPI function
vhpi_chk_error(). This is a repetitive callback.

Checkpoint/restart Callbacks
The obj field is ignored for these callbacks. The simulator does not update any field of the
vhpiCbDataS structure when the callback occurs.
vhpiCbStartOfSave
A callback registered for the vhpiCbStartOfSave reason, triggers when a simulation
session is about to checkpoint current simulation state into a file before the memory image
is saved.
vhpiCbEndOfSave
A callback registered for the vhpiCbEndOfSave reason, triggers when a simulation session
is about to checkpoint current simulation state into a file after the memory image is saved.
vhpiCbStartOfRestart
A callback registered for the vhpiCbStartOfRestart reason, triggers when a simulation
session is restored from a checkpoint file.
vhpiCbEndOfRestart
A callback registered for the vhpiCbEndOfRestart reason, triggers when a simulation
session is restored from a checkpoint file and after vhpiCbStartOfRestart callbacks are
fired.
Callback Properties
There are three integer type callback properties that can be queried given a callback
handle.
• vhpiKindP - Gets the callback kind
• vhpiReasonP - Gets the callback reason

Callback Methods
• vhpiStateP - Returns the callback state, which is one of the following:
◦ vhpiCbStateDisabled - The callback was disabled using vhpi_disable_cb().
◦ vhpiCbStateEnabled - The callback is ready to fire when the reason holds.
◦ vhpiCbStateMatured - The callback is one-shot and has fired. Repetitive callbacks
have vhpiCbStateEnabled status after each fire. A fired one-shot callback can be
re-enabled using vhpi_enable_cb().
Callback Methods
Iteration from an object declaration with the vhpiCallbacks one-to-many relationship
returns handles to all value change callbacks (vhpiCbValueChange reason) that are
registered on that object.
Iteration over the vhpiCallbacks relationship with NULL, returns all the
callbacks currently registered (enabled, disabled, matured). This can be used to
query all the callbacks when the foreign model or application want to remove all
of its callbacks and quit.
Callback Execution
The callback function is called when the condition indicated by the reason becomes true.
The callback function is called with a single argument that is a pointer to a vhpiCbDataS
structure. This argument contains information about the callback that caused the routine to
be invoked.
During the callback routine execution all access to the information model is allowed. The
callback routine is of type void. You can use the user_data field to store private data,
handles, and so on. The user_data is preserved from call to call, unless you change them
within an invoked callback function. This is the only field that you can legitimately change.
Changing any of the other fields can have unpredictable consequences.
