Foreign Models and Applications
There are two kinds of
foreign models
foreign models: architectures and subprograms which can
themselves be either functions or procedures. VHPI foreign models have a VHDL shell
declaration and a C language behavior implementation that uses VHPI functions. The
VHDL shell specifies the interface of the foreign model to the simulator.
A foreign application is an autonomous C program that uses VHPI functions. The simulator
loads the shared object of the foreign application and the application runs concurrently
with the simulation in the same address space. Hierarchy browsers and VHDL code
profilers are examples of such an application.
• Foreign Architectures
• Foreign Subprograms
• Foreign Applications
Foreign Architectures
VHPI enables you to use foreign architecture based models written in C language in the
VCS VHDL runtime environment. The C behavior implementation of the model uses VHPI
functions to interact with the simulator and the simulation environment.
A complete foreign model consists of two major parts. A collection of C entry points
(functions) that you compile into a shared object library and a VHDL shell for the model.
Creating a foreign architecture based model involves the following steps:
1. Writing the VHDL shell
2. Writing the C code
3. Compiling the C code into a shared object library
To use the foreign model in a design, you must first analyze the design VHDL source files
including the VHDL shell for the model and then simulate the design.

Foreign Architectures
Writing the VHDL Shell
The VHDL shell of a foreign architecture includes the entity declaration and architecture
declarative parts. In the VHDL design code, you must create an entity-architecture pair to
interface the VHDL design with the C language implementation of the foreign model.
Writing the entity Declaration
In the entity declaration, add the generics and ports for the foreign model. The following
example shows the VHDL entity declaration of a COUNTER model example.
Example 1 Entity Declaration for COUNTER Example
Entity Counter is
Port ( clk : in std_ulogic;
reset : in std_ulogic;
count : out std_ulogic_vector(0 to 7));
End entity;
Writing the architecture Declaration
The architecture declaration must include
• A foreign attribute specification for the architecture that specifies the model's principal
C entry point functions, namely an elaboration function and an initialization function.
• An empty architecture body
The syntax for the FOREIGN attribute statement is
attribute FOREIGN of <architecture_name> : architecture is
"vhpi:<library_name>:<elaboration_function_name>:<initialization_functio
n_name>:<model_name>";
<architecture_name>: Is the VHDL architecture name.
<library_name>: Specifies the platform independent name of the foreign model library
you want to be loaded. It gets translated into a platform-specific name by the simulator
when it loads the model. For example, on Solaris the string "LibName" is translated to
"libLibName.so".
<elaboration_function_name>: Specifies the name of the C elaboration function in the
user-created shared object library that is called by simv during elaboration.
<initialization_function_name>: Specifies the name of the C initialization function in the
user-created shared object library that is called by simv after elaboration and before
simulation.
<model_name>: Specifies a unique name associated with the model that is used by simv
for printing out informative and error messages during elaboration and simulation.

Foreign Architectures
The following example shows the VHDL architecture declaration for the COUNTER model
example.
Example 2 Architecture Declaration for COUNTER Example
Architecture C of Counter is
Attribute FOREIGN of C: architecture is "vhpi:counter_lib:counter_elab:counte
r_init:c_Counter";
Begin
End architecture;
In the example, the foreign attribute in the architecture specifies that libcounter_lib.so
is the name of the shared object library of the counter C model on Solaris. It also
specifies that counter_elab() and counter_init() are the elaboration and initialization
functions, respectively, for the model. The VHDL shell calls the initialization function during
simulation startup for each instance of the entity counter with architecture C and passes
the function a VHPI handle of that specific component instance.
Writing the C Code for a Foreign Architecture
You must use ANSI C to implement foreign architecture-based models. The C program
must include the vhpi_user.h header file.
Only use standard malloc() and free() for memory management. A memory
corruption can occur if you use functions other than free().
Writing the Elaboration Function
The simulator calls the elaboration function for elaboration of the foreign architecture-
based model. It calls the elaboration function once for each instance of the foreign model.
You write the function to allocate memory and initialize variables for simulating the foreign
model.
Writing the Initialization Function
The simulator executes the initialization function just before simulation starts. It calls the
initialization function once for each instance of the foreign model.
You write the function to traverse the design hierarchy, read and write values, and setup
appropriate callbacks for the correct functionality. See Static Design Access, Dynamic
Value Access, and VHPI Callbacks for more information about using the VHPI functions.
Compiling the C Code
After writing the C code for the model, you must compile the code into a shared object
library. This library must either reside in the directory from which you invoke the simulator

or in one of the directories covered by the OS specific dynamic library path variable, for
example, the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable on Solaris platforms.

compiler documentation for details. For example, to compile the C code for the counter

See Foreign Models Example and Tutorial for a complete example on the foreign
architecture based models.
Similar to foreign architectures, foreign subprograms require a VHDL shell that specifies
the interface of the foreign subprogram to the simulator.
This section consists of the following topics:
• Elaboration of Foreign Subprograms
• Execution of Foreign Subprograms
• Creating a Foreign Subprogram
Elaboration of Foreign Subprograms
The subprogram formal parameters as well as the subprogram declarative part are
elaborated when the subprogram call statement is encountered during simulation
execution.
No special elaboration C function entry point is needed unlike in the case of
foreign architectures.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Execution of Foreign Subprograms
Foreign subprograms are executed in the same way as VHDL subprograms, that is, when
they are encountered as a sequential call within a process or another subprogram or when
they are concurrent procedure calls.
The foreign subprograms are called under one of the following conditions:
• The execution flow in a sequential region encounters the subprogram call
• A concurrent procedural call is triggered in the initialization phase and then afterward,
when any of its inputs change
• A function call is used to initialize a signal, variable, constant, or generic in a
declarative region
• A port initialization is performed using a function call
• A type conversion function is applied within a port map
• A resolution function is applied to determine signal effective values
Creating a Foreign Subprogram
Creating a foreign subprogram involves the following steps:
1. Writing the VHDL shell
2. Writing the C code
3. Compiling the C code into a shared object library
Writing the VHDL Shell
The VHDL shell for a foreign subprogram contains the subprogram declaration with an
empty subprogram body. As in the case of foreign architectures, foreign subprograms are
identified through a foreign attribute specification.
The syntax for the FOREIGN attribute statement is
attribute FOREIGN of <subprogram_name[signature]>: procedure | function
is "vhpi: <library_name>:<simulation_function_name>:<model_name>"
The vhpi identifier indicates that this subprogram has a VHPI based implementation.
<library_name>: Specifies the platform independent name of the foreign subprogram
library. The library can either be in the directory from which the simulator is invoked or
in one of the directories covered by the operating system specific dynamic library path
variable.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
<simulation_function_name>: Specifies the name of the C function in the previously stated
C library. The C function is the runtime function to be called when the subprogram is
encountered as a sequential statement or as a concurrent procedure call.
<model_name>: Specifies a unique name associated with the VHPI based model.
Example 3 VHDL Shell Example for a Foreign Procedure
procedure myproc(signal f1: OUT bit; constant f2: IN integer);
attribute foreign of myproc: procedure is "vhpi:
myLibrary:myRuntimeProcedure:myModel";
Example 4 VHDL Shell Example for a Foreign Function
function myfunc(signal f1: IN bit) return integer;
attribute foreign of myfunc: function is "vhpi:
myLibrary:myRuntimeFunction:myModel";
Writing the C Code for a Foreign Subprogram
You must use ANSI C to implement foreign subprograms. The C program must include the
vhpi_user.h header file.
Only use standard malloc() and free() for memory management. A memory
corruption can occur if you use functions other than free().
The C function that is the implementation of the foreign subprogram must have the
following signature:
void myFunction(vhpiCbDataT* pCbData)
where pCbData is a callback data structure that is created and managed by the simulator
and passed to the C implementation at the point of call.
The obj field in the callback data structure is a handle to the subprogram call. The kind of
the subprogram call handle is either a vhpiFuncCallK or vhpiProcCallStmtK depending
on whether the foreign subprogram is a function or a procedure.
The reason field in the callback structure is updated with one of the following values:
• vhpiCbElaboration - If the foreign subprogram is called during elaboration
• vhpiCbInitialization - If the subprogram is called during initialization
• vhpiCbStartOfSubpCall - If the subprogram is called at runtime
From a handle to the subprogram call, you can access all formal parameters, access or
modify their values, or set the return values of foreign functions. The values of the formals
have the same interpretation as outlined in the LRM for VHDL subprograms.

• Other relationships from a subprogram call handle such as the stack
information in case of nested subprogram calls and access to actual
associations are not supported.
• Getting handles for VHDL subprograms that do not have VHPI foreign
attribute specification is not supported.
You can obtain the parameters to the subprogram by using the vhpiParamDecls one-
to-many ordered relationship from the subprogram call handle. For efficiency, once you
obtain these parameter handles, you can reused them in subsequent invocations of the
same subprogram. The interpretation of the parameters is as follows:
• Constants are passed as vhpiConstParamDeclK type of handles. By default the mode
is in. The values can be read within the subprogram, but not written.
• Variables are passed as vhpiVariableParamDeclK type of handles.
• Signals are passed as vhpiSigParamDeclK type of handles.
The semantics associated with accessing the values of formal parameters are specified in
the LRM and are outlined below for convenience:
• For variables of mode in, the value can be read within the subprogram but not assigned
to.
• For variables of mode inout, the value can be read or changed within the subprogram.
The simulator copies the assigned value to the actual.
• For variables of mode out, the value can only be written but not read.
• For signals of mode in, the value can be read but not assigned to within the
subprogram.
• For signals of mode inout or out, the following semantics apply:
◦ Values of signals of mode inout can be read or changed.
◦ Values of signals of mode out can only be written.
◦ As the association of actuals to formals for subprogram calls is by reference,
accessing the formal is equivalent to accessing the actual. If the value of the formal
is read within the subprogram, it is equivalent to reading the value of the actual.
◦ Assigning values to formal signal parameters follow the immediate signal update
semantics defined in Dynamic Value Access. As all subprograms that have signal
parameters of mode inout or out must be procedures, they can only execute
during process execution. Therefore, assigning values to these parameters with a
request for propagation (flags vhpiForcePropagate or vhpiForceHoldPropagate)
results in the change being seen only in the next delta cycle. If there is no delta

cycle through normal VHDL execution, the interface creates a new delta cycle
within which the actual is updated and propagated. The use of vhpiForce or
vhpiForceHold results in the value being immediately updated and seen by
subsequent readers of the actual.
Foreign Functions Return Value
For foreign functions, the return value can be set using a vhpi_put_value call on the
subprogram call handle. The semantics associated with this call are exactly the same as
setting values of variables. See Static Design Access for related information.
The following points also apply to writing the C code of foreign functions:
• You must set the function return value. The simulator generates an error if the return
value is not set.
• For functions returning arrays, the return value must match the expected constraints in
length. If there is a mismatch, a runtime constraints error is generated.
• For functions returning constrained arrays, the vhpi_value_size VHPI function
can be used to get the size in bytes for the return value. You do not need to set the
numscalars field in the value structure.
• For functions returning unconstrained arrays, you cannot use vhpi_value_size to
get the size of the expected return value. In these cases you must specify the number
of scalars in the numscalars field of the value structure. You also must determine the
buffer size based on the number of scalars that you need to set.
• If a function returns a constrained array, you can iterate over the indexed names of
the function call.

• If a function returns a constrained array, you can iterate over the indexed names of

• The functions vhpi_put_value and vhpi_get_value work only with scalars or arrays

Simulation Control
The vhpi_sim_control() function provides control capabilities over the simulator. The
argument specifies the command request.
(int) vhpi_sim_control(vhpiControlFlagsT controlFlag);
VCS VHDL supports a command request to finish the simulation, specified by setting the
value of the controlFlag to vhpiFinish. Also, VCS VHDL supports a command to stop
the simulation, specified by setting the value of the controlFlag to vhpiStop.
Error Checking and Handling
You can call the
vhpi_chk_error() function
vhpi_chk_error() function to determine if the last vhpi function call had
or caused an error.
(int) vhpi_chk_error(vhpiErrorInfoT *errorp);
The function checks whether an error occurred and retrieves detailed error information.
vhpi_chk_error() takes an argument (a pointer to error structure) and returns 0 if no
error occurred, or a pointer integer indicating the number of errors queued.
If the parameter errorp is non-NULL and if the previous VHPI call generated an error, the
error information structure pointed out by errorp is updated on return with the last error
information. You must allocate the error information structure.
If 0 is returned, the error information structure fields are meaningless. The message string
is a static string buffer which contains the formatted error message. The error message is
only valid until the the next VHPI function call.
The error information is not persistent. The internal error information structure is static.
Filtering of some errors can be performed via the registration of an error handler callback
function. Such a callback must be registered using the vhpiCbPLIError reason. (See
VHPI Callbacks).

Foreign Models Example and Tutorial
The example in this section helps you learn how to use the VHPI functions and data
structures to develop foreign architecture based models and how to integrate these
models into your design. Specifically, the example shows how to use VHPI functions to do
the following tasks:
• Writing the entity declaration of a foreign model
• Writing the architecture declaration of a foreign model
• Writing the C behavior for a foreign model, which includes
◦ Getting static information about ports of a model
◦ Registering value change callbacks on ports of a model
◦ Reading and writing values to ports of a model
The example uses a one-bit multiplexer design (MUX) that instantiates three two-input
nand gates (NAND2) and one invertor gate (INV). Both the nand gate and the invertor gate
are foreign architecture based models. The MUX block diagram is shown in the following
figure.

The entity-architecture definitions the C behavior for the invertor gate are described here.

Invertor Gate (INV)
VHDL Entity-Architecture Declarations
The entity-architecture definitions for the gate behavior are shown below. Note that the
architecture body is empty of simulation code and uses the FOREIGN attribute to flag the
simulator that the actual behavior is defined in a C foreign model.
The VHDL shell for the invertor gate is
library Synopsys, IEEE;
use IEEE.std_logic_1164.all;
use Synopsys.attributes.all;

entity inv is
port (a : in std_logic; y : out std_logic);
end inv;

architecture A of inv is
attribute FOREIGN of A : architecture is
"vhpi:inv-O:inv_elab:inv_init:inverter";
end A;

configuration cfg_inv of inv is
for a
end cfg_inv;
The FOREIGN attribute in the architecture body tells the simulator that the C behavior of
the invertor gate is compiled into the libinv-O.so shared library, the elaboration function
name is inv_elab(), and the initialization function name is inv_init().

Executing the MUX Example
The instructions in this section help you learn how to analyze the VHDL source files,
compile the C files, and simulate the MUX design.
Example Files
The source code files are in the $VCS_HOME/doc/examples/programming_interfaces/
vhpi/ directory. The files are:
Makefile: Contains the make commands to analyze, compile, and simulate the entire
example.
README: Contains brief instructions for using the Makefile to run the example. A more
complete instruction is provided in this section.
expected.output: Contains a listing of the simulator output for the example.
sim.inc: Contains the commands to simulate the example. You can invoke the simulator to
read the file and execute the commands.

Executing the MUX Example
inv.c: Contains the C code for the INV routines: elaboration, initialization, evaluation, value-
change callback, and error handling.
inv.vhd: Contains the VHDL code for the INV component definition.
mux.vhd: Contains the VHDL entity-architecture-configuration for the MUX.
nand2.c: Contains the C code for the NAND2 routines: elaboration, initialization,
evaluation, value-change callback, and error handling.
nand2.vhd: Contains the VHDL code for the NAND2 component definition.
part.cy: Contains the cycle partition information.
testmux.vhd: Contains the VHDL testbench for the example.
If you have not done so already, copy files for the example from the installation
examples directory ($VCS_HOME/doc/examples/programming_interfaces/vhpi/
examples) to a local examples directory.

Perform the following steps to prepare for analysis.
1. Move to your home directory, then move to the vhpi subdirectory of your local
examples directory. Type
% cd
% cd examples/vhpi
2. Clean the example directory in case another user has run the example. Type
% make clean
3. List the vhpi directory to confirm that files have been copied. Type
% ls

Analyzing the VHDL Files
Before you can run the simulation, you must analyze your VHDL design files. To analyze
the VHDL files, type
% make analyze
The make command creates a directory called WORK, analyzes the VHDL files, and
places them in WORK. You must see the following output:
mkdir WORK
chmod 777 WORK
vhdlan -nc -event inv.vhd
vhdlan -nc -event nand2.vhd
vhdlan -nc -event mux.vhd
vhdlan -nc -event testmux.vhd
Compiling and Linking the C Files
Execute the following steps to compile and generate the shared library objects for the INV
and NAND2 foreign models.
1. To generate the shared library object of the INV foreign model, type
% source ./setup
The command compiles inv.c and generates the shared library object libinv-O.so for
Solaris platform.
2. To generate the shared library object of the NAND2 foreign model, type
% source ./setup
The command compiles nand2.c and generates the shared library object libnand2-O.so
for Solaris platform.

vhpi_assert()
Synopsis: Raise an assertion
Syntax: vhpi_assert(msg, severity)
Arguments: char * msg assertion message
vhpiSeverityT severity severity level of the assertion
The vhpi_assert() function is equivalent to the execution of a VHDL report assertion
statement. The function returns 0 on success and 1 on failure. The first argument,
message, is the assertion string that gets printed. The second argument, severity, is
a value corresponding to one of the VHDL severity levels: vhpiNote, vhpiMessage,
vhpiWarning, vhpiError, vhpiException, vhpiFailure, vhpiFatal, or vhpiInternal.

title: 1 for true and 0 for false. Some properties such as vhpiSizeP can return any integer
text:
while other properties return a defined value. For such properties (for example
vhpiPrecisionP), the vhpi header file predefines the integer value to be returned.
vhpi_get_cb_info
vhpi_get_cb_info()
Synopsis: Retrieve information about a callback registered with vhpi_register_cb()
Syntax: vhpi_get_cb_info(hdl, cbDatap)
Returns: Int 0 on success, 1 on failure
Arguments: VhpiHandleT hdl Handle to the callback
VhpiCbDataT cbDatap Pointer to a structure containing callback
information
Use vhpi_register_cb() to register a callback
The vhpi_get_cb_info() function retrieves callback information for a registered callback.
The information is returned in a data structure that you specify.
The cbDatap argument points to a vhpiCbDataT structure defined by the VHPI standard
header file. The memory for cbData parameter must be allocated by you. The first
argument is a handle to the callback of kind vhpiCallbackK. The callback information

vhpi_get_real
returned is equivalent to the callback data information that was passed at the registration
of the callback.
typedef struct vhpiCbDataT
{
int reason; /* the reason of the callback */
(void) (*cbf)(); /* the callback function pointer */
vhpiHandleT obj; /* a handle to an object */
vhpiTimeT *time; /* a time */
vhpiValueT *value; /* a value */
char *user_data; /* user data information */
} vhpiCbDataT, *vhpiCbDatap;
vhpi_get_real
vhpi_get_real()
Synopsis: Get the value of a real property of an object.
Syntax: vhpi_get_real(prop, hdl)
Returns: vhpiRealT Value of a real property
Arguments: vhpiRealPropertyT prop An enumerated real property constant
representing the property of an object for
which to obtain the value.
vhpiHandleT hdl Handle to an object
Use vhpi_get() to get integer valued properties
Use vhpi_get_str to get string valued properties
The vhpi_get_real() function returns the value of an object property of type
vhpiRealPropertyT. The value is returned as a double.
vhpi_get_phys
vhpi_get_phys()
Synopsis: Get the value of a real property of an object.
Syntax: vhpi_get_phys(prop, hdl)

vhpi_get_str
Returns: vhpiPhysT Value of a physical property
Arguments: vhpiPhysPropertyT prop An enumerated physical property constant
representing the property of an object for
which to obtain the value.
vhpiHandleT hdl Handle to an object
Use vhpi_get() to get integer valued properties
Use vhpi_get_str to get string valued properties
The vhpi_get_phys function returns a physical value. Use this property to get
vhpiPhysLeftBoundP and vhpiPhysRightBoundP for physical ranges. You can also use it
for the vhpiPhysPositionP property.
vhpiHandleT type; /* a float type declaration */;
vhpiHandleT range = vhpi_handle(vhpiFloatRange, type);
vhpi_printf(" right bound of floating type is %f\n",
vhpi_get_real(vhpiFloatRightBoundP, range));
vhpi_release_handle(type);
vhpi_release_handle(range);
vhpi_get_str
vhpi_get_str()
Synopsis: Get the value of a string property of an object
Syntax: vhpi_get_str(prop, hdl)
Returns: char * Pointer to a character string that represents the
property value
Arguments: VhpiStrPropertyT prop An enumerated string property constant
representing the property of an object for
which to obtain the value
VhpiHandleT hdl Handle to an object

vhpi_get_time
Use vhpi_get() to get integer valued properties
Use vhpi_get_real to get real valued properties
The vhpi_get_str() function returns the value of an object property of type
vhpiStrPropertyT. A temporary string buffer is used by vhpi_get_str() to return string
properties. If you want to use the string after this call, you must copy the string to another
location, because subsequent calls to vhpi_get_str() overwrites the internal string
buffer. The string buffer used by vhpi_get_str() is different from the string buffer used
by vhpi_get_value().
char name[MAX_LENGTH];
vhpiHandleT inst = vhpi_handle_by_name(":u1", NULL);
strcpy(name, vhpi_get_str(vhpiKindStrP, inst) );
vhpi_printf("instance u1 is a %s\n", name);
vhpi_release_handle(inst);

vhpi_get_time
vhpi_get_time()
Synopsis: Retrieve the current simulation time
Syntax: vhpi_get_time(time_p, cycles_p)
Arguments: vhpiTimeT * time_p A pointer to a time structure containing time
information
long * cycles_p The number of relative or absolute delta cycles
Use vhpi_get(vhpiPrecisionP, NULL) to get the simulator precision
The vhpi_get_time() function returns the current simulation time. You must allocate the
time parameter before calling the function. The second parameter (cycles_p) is a pointer
to long. If cycles_p is not NULL, the number of delta cycles is returned. The number of

vhpi_get_next_time
delta cycles is relative to the current time if the time_p pointer is not null or the absolute
number of delta cycles if time_p is NULL.
vhpiTimeT time;
vhpi_get_time(&time, NULL);
vhpi_printf("time = %lld \n", time);

vhpi_get_next_time
vhpi_get_next_ time()
Synopsis: Retrieve the next simulation time when some activity is scheduled
Syntax: vhpi_get_next_time(time_p)
Returns: int 0 on success, vhpiNoActivity if nothing is scheduled, non
zero on other errors
Arguments: vhpiTimeT * time_p A pointer to a time structure containing time
information
Use vhpi_get_time () to get current simulation time
The vhpi_get_next_time() function returns the next active time when called during
postponded process or end of time phase, and returns current time when called in any
other phase. If no activity is scheduled, the time low and high fields are both set to
represent the value of Time’HIGH and the function returns vhpiNoActivity. This function
can be called at the end of time step or at end of initialization.
vhpiTimeT time;
vhpi_get_next_time(&time);
vhpi_printf("time = %lld \n", time);

vhpi_get_transaction_time
vhpi_get_transaction_time
vhpi_get_transaction_time()
Synopsis: Retrieve the scheduled transaction time
Syntax: vhpi_get_transaction_time(time_p, objHdl)
Arguments: vhpiTimeT * time_p A pointer to a time structure containing time
information
vhpiHandleT objHdl Transaction’s VHPI handle
Use vhpi_get_time (), vhpi_get_next_time ()
The vhpi_get_transaction_time() function returns the scheduled transaction time. You
must allocate the time parameter before calling the function. The second parameter objHdl
is the transaction’s object handle.
vhpiTimeT time;
vhpi_get_transaction_time(&time, objHdl);
vhpi_printf("time = %lld \n", time);

{

value.format = vhpiIntVal;

vhpi_schedule_transaction()
Synopsis: Schedule a transaction to signal driver.
Syntax: vhpi_schedule_transaction(hdl, valuep, numValues, delayp, delayMode,
pulseRejP)
Arguments: vhpiHandleT hdl Handle to an object which has a value
vhpiValueT** valuep Array of pointers to values for the driver
transaction
int numValues Number of values in valuep
vhpiTimeT* delayp Relative time delay for the transaction
int delayMode Delay mode to apply
vhpiTimeT* pulseRejp Pulse rejection limit for inertial mode
Use vhpi_put_value() to change the effective value of a signal
The vhpi_schedule_transaction() function is used to schedule a transaction on a
VHPI object’s driver. The transaction can be scheduled with zero or non-zero delay and
with inertial or transport mode.
To schedule a value on a driver of a signal/port, you need to have
• a handle to the driver, hdl
• allocate a value data structure (or array of value data structures), valuep
• the number of values, numValues
• a delay value, delayp
• a delay mode, delayMode
• pulse rejection limit, pulsRejp

vhpi_schedule_transaction
The drivers returned by the interface will always be drivers to basic signals. A basic signal
is either a scalar for unresolved signal/port types or resolved composite signal/port types.
The delay modes that are supported are vhpiInertial and vhpiTransport. In the case
of inertial delays, you could specify non-zero pointer to pulse rejection limit data structure,
that should be passed in pulse rejection limit argument.
Current version does not support pulse rejection limit.
For a driver to a scalar signal/port, a single value structure should be passed with format
set to indicate a scalar value.
Scheduling transaction for drivers of composite types not resolved at the
composite level, such as bit vectors, standard logic vectors, record types must
be done by scheduling individual transactions on each scalar driver.
Transaction for driver of signals resolved at the composite level must be
scheduled at once.
When the type of a signal is a resolved array of scalars, a single data value structure
should be passed with format being a vector format, with allocated value buffer having as
many scalar values as the number of scalars. The numValues parameter should be always
be 1.
When the type of a signal is either an array of composites or a record, an array of values
structures should be passed. The value data structure should be passed at the coarsest
granularity possible. This implies that for all subsignals/subports of the composite signal/
port, which are arrays of scalars, the value has to be passed as a vector for all the
scalars. For all other subsignals, the same rule should be used recursively, down the type
hierarchy. All value data structures passed can only be either values to scalars or array of
scalars.
NULL transaction can be posted by setting valuep to NULL pointer.
The specified delay is a relative delay and is specified by using the time structure
vhpiTimeT by providing a 64 bits value.
The delay value is truncated if it is smaller than the VHDL simulator resolution limit. The
delay value must be legal as if it were the delay value of a VHDL signal assignment. Zero
delay transactions are specified by setting the delay value to 0. Scheduling a zero delay
transaction is only allowed during process execution (vhpiCbEndOfProcesses) and at last
known delta cycle (vhpiCbLastDeltaCycle). It will cause a new delta cycle to be created
if the transaction generates an event. Non-zero delay transaction can be scheduled at
any time before the end of the time step (vhpiCbEndOfTimeStep), effectively before the
next time is computed. Scheduling a transaction at any other phase has no effect and

vhpi_schedule_transaction
generates an error. All zero delay transactions will be scheduled for the next delta cycle
and all other delay transactions will be scheduled for the time that corresponds to the
current simulation time added to the specified relative delay.
The following example shows how use the function to schedule a transaction on a bit
driver.

element of the signal, then use of driver iteration methods to get the drivers of each bit

VHPI Information Model
This
information model
section describes the following five classes of objects:
• Regions
• Types
• Declarations
• Expressions
• Drivers
The first class of objects are regions. Regions can be one of the following:
• CompInstStmt - component instantiation concurrent statement class
• RootInst - design root class
• PackInst - package instance class, each package is instantiated once
• IfGenerate - if generate concurrent statements class
• ForGenerate - for generate concurrent statement class
• BlockStmt - block statement concurrent statement class
• ProcessStmt - process statement class
• ArchBody - architecture design unit class
• CompConfig - component configuration specification class
• ConfigDecl - configuration design unit class
• EntityDecl - entity design unit class
• PackBody - package body design unit class
• PackDecl - package design unit class

CompInstStmt
• vhpiInternalRegions - Returns all the regions instantiated within this component
instance. Use this mechanism to traverse the design hierarchy.
• vhpiStmts - Returns the statements within this component instance. These statements
are concurrent statements which can be process statements, block statements,
component instance statements, if or for generate statements.
• vhpiCompInstStmts - Returns the list of the component instances within this component
• vhpiBlockStmts - Returns the list of block statements within this component instance.
• vhpiDecls - Returns all the declarations within this component instance.
• vhpiGenericDecls - Specialized form of vhpiDecls, returns only the generic
declarations.
• vhpiSigDecls - Returns the set of all signal declarations within this component instance.
• vhpiConstDecls - Returns the set of all constant declarations within this component
• vhpiPortDecls - Returns the set of all port declarations within this component instance.
• vhpiAttrDecls - Returns the set of all attribute declarations within this component
• vhpiAttrSpecs - Returns the set of all attribute specifications within this component
• vhpiConfigSpec - Returns the configuration specification corresponding to this
component instance.
• vhpiUpperRegion - Returns the upper region within which this component instance is
instantiated. This coupled with the one-to-many relation vhpiInternalRegions can be
used to traverse the design hierarchy.
• vhpiDesignUnit - Returns the secondary design unit that this component instance is
bound to, that is, the architecture.

The declarations are the second class of objects after regions, with the classes being,
• AttrDecl - Attribute declaration class
• AttrSpec - Attribute specification class
• CompDecl - Component declaration
• ConstDecl - Constant declaration
• GenericDecl - Generic declaration
• PortDecl - Port declaration
• SigDecl - Signal declaration
• VarDecl - Variable declaration
Other classes of objects, including constant, variable or signal parameters to
subprograms are not supported.

The following are the declarations:
• AttrDecl
• AttrSpec
• CompDecl
• ConstDecl
• GenericDecl
• PortDecl
• SigDecl
• VarDecl
AttrDecl
• vhpiSubtype - Use this relationship to get the subtype of this attribute declaration. The
handle returned is of type subtype indication. Given a subtype indication, you can get
either the base type (which can be unconstrained) or a typemark (which can either be
the basetype or a subtype declaration).
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiAttrDeclK
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns "vhpiAttrDeclK"
• vhpiFullCaseNameP - same as vhpiFullNameP
• vhpiCaseNameP - same as above

string.
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiAttrSpecK
• vhpiLineNoP - Returns the line number of the statement in the VHDL source file.
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiAttrSpecK”

• vhpiIndexedNames - This relationship applies only to constant declarations that are
array types. It can be used to iterate over the sequence of indexed names, which are
expressions and necessarily sub-elements of the constant declaration.
• vhpiSelectedNames - This relationship is similar to the one above, but applies only to
constants that are record types. Use this relationship to create an iterate over all of the
fields of the record. The type of the handles returned by scanning through the iteration
list is element declarations.
• vhpiImmScope - Enclosing region for this constant declaration
• vhpiSubtype - Constant subtype
• vhpiBaseType - This is a short cut that returns the base type of this constant
declaration without going through its subtype indication using the relationship
vhpiSubtype.
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiConstDeclK
• vhpiIsScalarP - Use this property to check whether the constant is a scalar or a
composite typed object. Returns 1 if the constant is a scalar, otherwise returns 0.
• vhpiIsCompositeP - Use this property to check whether the constant is a scalar or a
composite typed object, similar to the one above, with the values reversed. Returns 1 if
the constant is a composite, otherwise returns 0.
• vhpiSizeP - Returns the number of scalars in this constant declaration. Returns 1 for
scalars and the number of scalars for composites.
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiConstDeclK”

• vhpiContributors - Returns the list of all contributors that contribute value to the

• vhpiBaseType - Returns the base type of the port declaration

• vhpiIsBasicP - Use this property to test if the port is a basic signal. A basic signal is a

• vhpiIsCompositeP - Returns 1 if the port is a composite
• vhpiModeP - Use this property to get the mode of the port, which is one of in, out, inout,

• vhpiPositionP - Returns the position of the port in the port declarations list

• vhpiFullNameP - Returns the VHDL pathname of the port

ArrayTypeDecl
• vhpiIndexConstraints - Returns the array index constraints, one for each dimension.
This includes only integer range handles.
The return handle type changes when you perform vhpi_scan. They are
integer range type of handles.
• vhpiIndexedNames - Returns the indexed names for this array type declaration. As
these are indexed names of a type declaration, operations such as put or get value do
not apply.

• vhpiBaseType - Returns the base type of a type, subtype, subtype indication or object
declaration. For type declarations, returns a copy of the reference handle. This is
because every type is a base type of itself according to the LRM.
• vhpiElemSubtype - Use this relationship to get the array element subtype, which is a
subtype indication type of handle.
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiArrayTypeDeclK
• vhpiIsScalarP - Returns 0, as there is an array type declaration as a reference
handle
• vhpiIsCompositeP - Returns 1, as there is an array type declaration as a reference
handle
• vhpiNumDimensionsP - Use this property to get the number of dimensions of the array
type declaration
• vhpiIsAnonymousP - A type declaration cannot be anonymous, always returns 0
• vhpiSizeP - Returns the number of scalars in the array
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiArrayTypeDeclK”
ElemDecl
• vhpiIndexedNames - If the element decl is an array, returns the index subelements as
indexed names. With these indexed names you cannot get or set values, as they are
not instances.
• vhpiSelectedNames - If the element decl is a record, returns the fields of that record,
which is again a list of element decls.

• vhpiElemSubtype - Returns the subtype of the record field. This relationship is a
subtype indication type of handle.
• vhpiImmScope - Returns the region scope for this declaration
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiElemDeclK
• vhpiPositionP - The field number of this element declaration, zero based. The
selected names of a record is an ordered relationship. Hence there is a zero based
field number corresponding to every field.
• vhpiIsScalarP - Returns 1 if the element is a scalar, otherwise returns 0
• vhpiIsCompositeP - Returns 1 if the element is a composite, otherwise returns 0
• vhpiSizeP - Returns the number of scalars in the array
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiElemDeclK”
EnumLiteral
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiEnumLiteralK
• vhpiPositionP - Returns the enumeration literal positional value, which is an integer
• vhpiSizeP - The size property always stands for the number of scalars and in this
case is 1 and returns 1.
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiEnumLiteralK”
• vhpiStrValP - Returns the string value of the literal

EnumTypeDecl
• vhpiEnumLiterals - Use this relationship to get the enumeration literals of this
enumeration type declaration. On scanning through the list, you get vhpiEnumLiteralK
type of handles.
• vhpiBaseType - Returns the base type for this enum type declaration, which is a copy
of itself.
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiEnumTypeDeclK
• vhpiIsScalarP - Returns 1
• vhpiIsCompositeP - Returns 0
• vhpiNumLiteralsP - Use this property to get the number of enumeration literals in the
enum type declaration.
• vhpiIsAnonymousP - Always Returns 0
• vhpiSizeP - Returns 1
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiEnumTypeDeclK”
FloatRange
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiFloatRangeK
• vhpiIsDiscreteP - Enumeration types and integer types are discrete types. Float type
is not discrete type. Always returns 0.

• vhpiIsUp - Use this property to determine if the direction of the range is TO rather
than DOWNTO. Returns 1 if the direction is TO (up) and 0 if the direction is DOWNTO
(down).
• vhpiIsNullP - Use this property to check if the range is a NULL range. The return
value is 1 if the range is a NULL range.
• vhpiIsUnconstrainedP - Returns 1 if the range is unconstrained
• vhpiFloatLeftBoundP - Returns the real number corresponding to the left bound of
the range. Use the vhpi_get_real function and the return type is vhpiRealT.
• vhpiFloatRightBoundP - Returns the right bound of this floating range
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiFloatRangeK”
FloatTypeDecl
• vhpiBaseType - Returns the base type for this type declaration, which is a copy of
itself.
• vhpiRange - Returns the range of this type declaration. The returned handle type is
vhpiFloatRangeK.
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiFloatTypeDeclK
• vhpiIsScalarP - Returns 1
• vhpiIsCompositeP - Returns 0
• vhpiIsAnonymousP - Always returns 0
• vhpiSizeP - Returns 1
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns "vhpiFloatTypeDeclK"
• vhpiCaseNameP - same as vhpiNameP
• vhpiFileNameP - Returns the VHDL file in which the float declaration appears

IntRange
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiIntRangeK
• vhpiIsDiscreteP - Returns 0
• vhpiIsUp - Returns the direction of the range
• vhpiIsNullP - Returns 1 if the range is a NULL range
• vhpiIsUnconstrainedP - Returns 1 if the range is unconstrained
• vhpiLeftBoundP - Returns the integer corresponding to the left bound of the range.
Returns vhpiIntT.
• vhpiRightBoundP - Returns the right bound of this integer range
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiIntRangeK”
IntTypeDecl
• vhpiBaseType - Returns the base type for this type declaration, which is a copy of
itself.
• vhpiRange - Returns the integer range of this type declaration. Is a vhpiIntRangeK type

• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiIntTypeDeclK
• vhpiIsScalarP - Returns 1
• vhpiIsCompositeP - Returns 0
• vhpiIsAnonymousP - Always returns 0
• vhpiSizeP - Returns 1
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiIntTypeDeclK”

declarations of this physical type declaration. The type of the handle returned on

• vhpiBaseType - Returns the base type for this type declaration, which is a copy of
itself.
• vhpiRange - Use this relationship to get the integer range of this type declaration. This

• vhpiBaseUnit - Returns the base unit for this physical type declaration. This relation is
a vhpiUnitDeclK type of handle.
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiPhysTypeDeclK
• vhpiIsScalarP - Returns 1
• vhpiIsCompositeP - Returns 0
• vhpiIsAnonymousP - Always Returns 0
• vhpiSizeP - Returns 1
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiPhysTypeDeclK”
• vhpiCaseNameP - Same as vhpiNameP

RecordTypeDecl
• vhpiRecordElems - Use this relationship to get the record element declarations. These
declarations correspond to the fields of the record and the type of the handles returned
through vhpi_scan is vhpiElemDeclK.
• vhpiBaseType - Returns the base type for this type declaration, which is a copy of
itself.
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiRecordTypeDeclK
• vhpiNumFieldsP - Returns the number of fields in the record
• vhpiIsScalarP - Returns 0
• vhpiIsCompositeP - Returns 1
• vhpiIsAnonymousP - Always returns 0
• vhpiSizeP - Returns the number of scalars in the record type
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiRecordTypeDeclK”
• vhpiCaseNameP - Same as vhpiNameP
SubtypeDecl
• vhpiConstraints - Returns the constraints for this subtype declaration and is an
iterator over range type of handles.

• vhpiBaseType - Returns the base type for this subtype declaration
• vhpiTypeMark - Returns the typemark corresponding to this subtype declaration. The
returned handle can be a subtype or a type declaration. Use this relation to traverse a
type hierarchy.
• vhpiKindP - Returns vhpiSubtypeDeclK
• vhpiIsResolvedP - Returns 1 if the subtype declaration provides a resolution function
to resolve the typemark
• vhpiIsAnonymousP - Always returns 0 as the handle corresponds to a subtype
declaration
• vhpiSizeP - Returns the size in terms of number of scalars for this subtype declaration
• vhpiKindStrP - Returns “vhpiSubtypeDeclK”
SubtypeIndic
• vhpiConstraints - Returns the index constraints for array, float, and discrete types.
Returns NULL for all other cases.
• vhpiBaseType - Returns the base type of the subtype indication
• vhpiTypeMark - Returns either a subtype declaration or a type declaration, which is the
typemark of the subtype indication. Use this relation to traverse the type hierarchy for

Using the PLI
PLI is the programming language interface (PLI) between C/C++ functions and VCS.
It helps to link applications containing C/C++ functions with VCS so that they execute
concurrently mixed HDL designs. The C/C++ functions in the application use the PLI to
read and write delay and simulation values in the VCS executable, and VCS can call these
functions during simulation.
VCS has implemented the TF and ACC routines for the PLI. It has also implemented the
VPI procedural interface routine to some extent.
VCS also supports a number of ACC routines that are not part of the IEEE Verilog
language reference manual. These routines access:
• Reading and writing to memories
• Multi-dimensional arrays
• Probabilistic distribution
• Returning a string pointer to a parameter value
• Extended VCD files
• Line callbacks
• Source protection
• Signal in a generate block
ACC routines, which access the values in a design, changing, for example, the delay
values of module paths or the simulation values of individual signals, are more powerful
that the TF routines which operate only on data passed to them. However, the ACC
routines also have a greater performance cost. The ability of ACC routines to traverse
the entire design and make extensive value changes requires VCS to omit powerful
performance optimizations so that it is possible for the ACC routines to make these
changes.
This performance cost of the ACC routines is a major consideration in VCS performance.
There are ways to limit this performance cost and doing so is an important step in
developing a PLI application that uses ACC routines.

Writing a PLI Application
This chapter covers the following topics:
• Writing a PLI Application
• Functions in a PLI Application
• Header Files for PLI Applications
• The PLI Table File
• Using VPI Routines
• Writing Your Own main() Routine
Writing a PLI Application
When writing a PLI application, you need to do the following:
1. Write the C/C++ functions of the application calling the TF and ACC routines that
Synopsys has implemented to access data inside VCS.
2. Associate user-defined system tasks and system functions with the C/C++ functions
in your application. VCS will call these functions when it compiles or executes these
system tasks or system functions in the Verilog source code. In VCS, associate the
user-defined system tasks and system functions with the C/C++ functions in your
application using a PLI table file (see The PLI Table File). In this file, you can also limit
the scope and operations of the ACC routines for faster performance.
3. Enter the user-defined system tasks and functions in the Verilog source code.
4. Compile and simulate your design, specifying the table file and including the C/C++
source files (or compiled object files or libraries) so that the application is linked with
VCS in the simv executable. If you include object files, use the -cc and -ld options to
specify the compiler and linker that generated them. Linker errors occur if you include a
C/C++ function in the PLI table file but omit the source code for this function at compile-
time.
To use the debugging features, do the following:
1. Write a PLI table file, limiting the scope and operations of the ACC routines used by the
debugging features.
2. Compile and simulate your design, specifying the table file.

Functions in a PLI Application
These procedures are not mutually exclusive. It is, for example, quite possible that you
have a PLI application that you write and use during the debugging phase of your design.
If so you can write a PLI table file that both:
• Associates user-defined system tasks or system functions with the functions in your
application and limits the scope and operations of the ACC routines called by your
functions for faster performance.
• Limits scope and operations of the ACC routines called by the debugging features in
VCS.
Functions in a PLI Application
When you write a PLI application you typically write a number of functions. The following
are PLI functions that VCS expects with a user-defined system task or system function:
• The function that VCS calls when it executes the user-defined system task. Other
functions are not necessary but this call function must be present. It’s not unusual for
there to be more than one call function. You’ll need a separate user-defined system
task for each call function. If the function returns a value then you must write a user-
defined system function for it instead of a user-defined system task.
• The function that VCS calls during compilation to check if the user-defined system task
has the correct syntax. You can omit this check function.
• The function that VCS calls for miscellaneous reasons such as the execution of $stop,
or $finish, or other reasons such a value change. When VCS calls this function it
passes a reason argument to it that explains why VCS is calling it. You can omit this
miscellaneous function.
These functions are the ones you tell VCS about in the PLI table file; apart from these PLI
applications can have several more functions that are called by other functions.
You do not specify a function to determine the return value size of a user-
defined system function; instead you specify the size directly in the PLI table
file.
Header Files for PLI Applications
For PLI applications, you need to include one or more of the following header files:
acc_user.h: For PLI Applications whose functions call IEEE Standard ACC routines as
documented in the IEEE Verilog language reference manual.

vcsuser.h: For PLI applications whose functions call IEEE Standard TF routines as
documented in the IEEE Verilog language reference manual.
vcs_acc_user.h: For PLI applications whose functions call the special ACC routines
implemented exclusively for VCS.
You will find these header files at $VCS_HOME/platform/lib, where platform is the platform
you are using, such as sun_sparc_solaris_5.7.
The header file for the VPI routines is $VCS_HOME/include/vpi_user.h. See Using VPI
Routines.
The PLI table file (commonly called the pli.tab file) has two purposes:
• To associate user-defined system tasks and system functions with functions in a PLI
application, so VCS calls these functions when it compiles or executes the system task
or function.
• To limit the scope and operation of the ACC routines called by the debugging features.
If this is all that you need to do in the PLI table file, see Specifying ACC Capabilities for
PLI Functions and Specifying ACC Capabilities for VCS Debugging Features.
When writing a PLI application, after you write the functions for the application, you need
to write a PLI table file. This file contains a line for each user-defined system task or
system function your application needs. Each line should contain the following information:
• The name of the user-defined system task or system function. This name begins with
the dollar sign $.
• The PLI specifications for the user-defined system task or system function. These
specifications must include the call function. For user-defined system functions, they
must also include the size of the return value.
These specifications can also include the check and miscellaneous functions. There
are a number of other PLI specifications, such as the one that allows the entering of the
user-defined system task on the command line. You can also enter these specifications
on a line in the PLI table file.
• The ACC capabilities that you want to enable for the functions, particularly the call
function, for the user-defined system task or system function. When you specify ACC
capabilities you specify the types of ACC operations that the ACC routines will perform
and where in the design they can perform these operations. Entering ACC capabilities
to limit ACC routine scope and operations is optional but recommended to enhance
performance.

The syntax for a line in a PLI table file is as follows:
$name PLI_specifications [ACC_capabilities]
Here:
$name: The name of the user-defined system task or system function
PLI_specifications: One or more specifications such as the name of the C function
VCS calls when it executes the user-defined system task or system function. For a list of
valid PLI specifications, see PLI Specifications.
ACC_capabilities: Specifications for ACC capabilities to be added, removed, or
changed in various parts of the design hierarchy. For details on ACC capabilities, see ACC
Capabilities.
PLI Specifications
The valid PLI specifications are as follows:call PLI specificationPLI specificationscall
call=function: Specifies the name of call function. This specification is required.
check PLI specificationPLI specificationscheck
check=function: Specifies the name of check function.
misc PLI specificationPLI specificationsmisc
misc=function: Specifies the name of misc function.
data PLI specificationPLI specificationsdata
data=integer: Specifies the data value passed as first argument to call, check, and misc
routines. The default is 0. Use this argument if you want more than one user-defined
system task or system function to use the same call, check, or misc function. Specify a
different integer for each user-defined system task or system function in the PLI table file
that uses the same call, check, or misc function.size PLI specificationPLI specificationssize
size=number: Specifies the size of returned value in bits. This specification is required
for user-defined system functions. You can omit this specification or specify 0 in the PLI
specifications for a user-defined system function. For user-defined system functions,
specify a decimal value for the number or bits. For example: size=64. If the user-defined
system function returns a real value, specify r. For example: size=r
args PLI SpecificactionPLI specificationsargs

system function.minargs PLI specificationPLI specificationsminargs

The following are example lines in PLI table files that contain PLI specifications (the ACC
capabilities parts are omitted):
Example 1
$val_proc call=val_proc check=check_proc misc=misc_proc
In this line, VCS calls the function named val_proc when it executes the associated user-
defined system task named $val_proc. It calls the check_proc function at compile-time
to see if the user-defined system task has the correct syntax, and calls the misc_proc
function in special circumstances like interrupts.
Example 2
$value_passer size=0 args=2 call=value_passer persistent
In this line, there is an associated user-defined system task (because it has a return size
of 0). The system task takes two arguments. When VCS executes the $value_passer
system task it calls the function named value_passer, and you can enter the system task
on the UCLI command line without including the debug compile-time options.
Example 3
$set_true size=16 call=set_true
In this line, there is an associated user-defined system function that returns a 15 bit return
value. VCS calls the function named set_true when it executes this system function.
Do not enter blank spaces inside a PLI specification. The following copy of the
last example of PLI specifications does not work:
$set_true size = 16 call = set_true
ACC Capabilities
You can specify ACC capabilities in a PLI table file for the following reasons:
• To specify the ACC capabilities for the PLI functions associated with your user-defined
system task or system function. To do this, specify the ACC capabilities on a line in a
PLI table file after the name of the user-defined system task or system function and its
PLI specifications. See Specifying ACC Capabilities for PLI Functions for more details.

• To specify the ACC capabilities that the debugging features of VCS can use. To do
this, specify ACC capabilities alone on a line in a PLI table file, without an associated
user-defined system task or system function. See Specifying ACC Capabilities for VCS
Debugging Features for more details.
When you specify ACC capabilities, you specify both of the following:
• The ACC capabilities you want to enable or disable.
• The part or parts of the design that you want this enabling or disabling to occur.
In many ways, specifying ACC capabilities for your PLI functions, and specifying them for
VCS debugging features, is the same, but the capabilities that you enable, and the parts of
the design to which you can apply them are different.
Specifying ACC Capabilities for PLI Functions
The format for specifying ACC capabilities is as follows:
acc=|+=|-=|:=capabilities:module_names[+]|%CELL|%TASK|*
Here:
acc: Keyword that begins a line for specifying ACC capabilities.
=|+=|-=|:=: Operators for adding, removing, or changing ACC capabilities. The operators
in this syntax are as follows:
=: A shorthand for +=.
+=: Specifies adding the ACC capabilities that follow to the parts of the design that follow,
as specified by module name, %CELL,%TASK, or * wildcard character.
-=: Specifies removing the ACC capabilities that follow from the parts of the design that
follow, as specified by module name, %CELL,%TASK, or * wildcard character.
:=: Specifies changing the ACC capabilities of the parts of the design that follow, as
specified by module name, %CELL,%TASK, or * wildcard character, to only those in the
list of capabilities on this specification. A specification with this operator can change the
capabilities specified in a previous specification.
capabilities: Comma-separated list of ACC capabilities. The ACC capabilities that you
can specify for the functions in your PLI specifications are as follows:
r ACC capability
r orread: Reads the values of nets and registers in your design.
rw ACC capability
rw or read_write: Both reads from and writes to the values of registers or variables (but
not nets) in your design.wn ACC capability
wn: Enables writing values to nets.
cbk ACC capability
cbk or callback: To be called when named objects (nets registers, ports) change value.

cbka ACC capability
cbka or callback_all: To be called when named and unnamed objects (such as primitive
terminals) change value.frc ACC capability
frc or force: Forces values on nets and registers.
prx ACC capability
prx or pulserx_backannotation: Sets pulse error and pulse rejection percentages for
module path delays.s ACC capability
s or static_info: Enables access to static information, such as instance or signal names
and connectivity information. Signal values are not static information.tchk ACC capability
tchk or timing_check_backannotation: Back annotates timing check delay values.
gate ACC capability
gate or gate_backannotation: Back annotates delay values on gates.
mp ACC capability
mp or module_path_backannotation: Back annotates module path delays.
mip ACC capability
mip or module_input_port_backannotation: Back annotates delays on module input
ports.mipb ACC capability
mipb or module_input_port_bit_backannotation: Back annotates delays on individual
bits of module input ports.
module_names: Comma-separated list of module identifiers. Specifying modules enables,
disables, or changes (depending on the operator) the ability of the PLI function to use the
ACC capability in all instances of the specified module.
+: Specifies adding, removing, or changing the ACC capabilities for not only the instances
of the specified modules but also the instances hierarchically under the instances of the
specified modules.%CELL
%CELL: Enables, disables, or changes (depending on the operator) the ability of the PLI
function to use the ACC capability in all instances of module definitions compiled under the
'celldefine compiler directive and all module definitions in Verilog library directories and
library files (as specified with the -y and -v compile-time options).
%TASK
%TASK: Enables, disables, or changes (depending on the operator) the ability of the PLI
function to use the ACC capability in all instances of module definitions that contain the
user-defined system task or system function associated with the PLI function.
%TFARGS: Same as %TASK, but also enables debug capability on any arguments to the TF
call.
*: Enables, disables, or changes (depending on the operator) the ability of the PLI function
to use the ACC capability throughout the entire design. Using wildcard characters will
impact the performance of VCS.
There are no blank spaces when specifying ACC capabilities.

The following examples are the PLI specification examples from the previous section with
ACC capabilities added to them. The examples wrap to more than one line, but when you
edit your PLI table file, be sure there are no line breaks in these lines.
Example 1
$val_proc call=val_proc check=check_proc misc=misc_proc acc+=
rw,tchk:top,bot acc-=tchk:top
This example adds the ACC capabilities for reading and writing to nets and registers, and
for back annotating timing check delays, to these PLI functions, and enables them to do
these things in all instances of modules top and bot. It then removes the ACC capability
for back annotating timing check delay values from these PLI functions in all instances of
module top.
Example 2
$value_passer size=0 args=2 call=value_passer persistent acc+=rw:%TASK
acc-=rw:%CELL
This example adds the ACC capability to read from and write to the values of nets and
registers to these PLI functions. It enables them to do these things in all instances of
modules declared in module definitions that contain the $value_passer user-defined
system task. The example then removes the ACC capability to read from and write to
the values of nets and registers, from these PLI functions, in module definitions compiled
under the 'celldefine compiler directive and all module definitions in Verilog library
directories and library files.
Example 3
$set_true size=16 call=set_true acc+=rw:*
This example adds the ACC capability to read from and write to the values of nets and
registers to the PLI functions. It enables them to do this throughout the entire design.
Specifying ACC Capabilities for VCS Debugging Features
The format for specifying ACC capabilities for VCS debugging features is as follows:
acc=|+=|-=|:=capabilities:module_names[+]|%CELL|*
Here:
acc: Keyword that begins a line for specifying ACC capabilities.
=|+=|-=|:=: Operators for adding, removing, or changing ACC capabilities.
The removal of capability is done after all additions/changes are performed.
capabilities: Comma separated list of ACC capabilities.

module_names: Comma-separated list of module identifiers. The specified ACC
capabilities will be added, removed, or changed for all instances of these modules.
+: Specifies adding, removing, or changing the ACC capabilities for not only the instances
of the specified modules but also the instances hierarchically under the instances of the
specified modules.%CELL
%CELL: Specifies all modules compiled under the ‘celldefine compiler directive and all
modules in Verilog library directories and library files (as specified with the -y and -v
compile-time options.)
*: Specifies that the debug capability is applied to all modules in the design.

Using VPI Routines
Using the PLI Table File
You specify the PLI table file with the
-P pli.tab-P pli.tab[P pli.tab]
-P compile-time option, followed by the name of the
PLI table file (by convention, the PLI table file has a .tab extension). For example:
-P pli.tab
When you enter this option on the vcs command line, you can also enter C source files,
or compiled .o object files or .a libraries on the vcs command line, to specify the PLI
application that you want to link with VCS. For example:
vcs -P pli.tab pli.c my_design.v
One advantage to entering .o object files and .a libraries is that you do not have to
recompile the PLI application every time you compile your design.
Using VPI Routines
To enable VPI capabilities in VCS, you must include the +vpi compile-time option. For
example:
vcs +vpi test.v -P test.tab test.c
The header file for the VPI routines is $VCS_HOME/include/vpi_user.h.
You can also use a PLI .tab file to associate your user defined system tasks with your VPI
routines, see PLI Table File for VPI Routines.
VCS has not implemented everything specified for VPI routines in the IEEE Verilog
language reference manual because some routines would be rarely used and some of
the data access operations of other routines would be rarely used. The unimplemented
routines are as follows:
• vpi_get_data
• vpi_put_data
• vpi_sim_control
Object data model diagrams in the IEEE Verilog language reference manual specify that
some VPI routines should be able to access data that is rarely needed. These routines
and the data they can’t access are as follows:
vpi_get_value

Using VPI Routines
• Cannot retrieve the value of var select objects (diagram 26.6.8 Variables) and func call
objects (diagram 26.6.18 Task, function declaration).
• Cannot retrieve the value of VPI operators (expressions) unless they are arguments to
system tasks or system functions.
• Cannot retrieve the value of UDP table entries (vpiVectorVal not implemented).
vpi_put_value: Cannot set the value of var select objects (diagram 26.6.8 Variables) and
primitive objects (diagram 26.6.13 Primitive, prim term).
vpi_get_delays: Cannot retrieve the values of continuous assign objects (diagram
26.6.24 Continuous assignment) or procedurally assigned objects.
vpi_put_delays: Cannot put values on continuous assign objects (diagram 26.6.24
Continuous assignment) or procedurally assigned objects.
vpi_register_cb: Cannot register the following types of callbacks that are defined for this
routine:
cbEndOfSimulation cbError cbPliError
cbTchkViolation cbSignal cbForce
cbRelease cbAssign cbDeassign
Also, the cbValueChange callback is not supported for the following objects:
• A memory or a memory word (index or element)
• VarArray or VarSelect
PLI Table File for VPI Routines
The PLI table file for VPI routines works the same way, and with the same syntax as a
PLI table file for user-defined system tasks that execute C functions, which call PLI ACC
routines. The following is an example of such a PLI table file:
$set_mipd_delays call=PLIbook_SetMipd_calltf
check=PLIbook_SetMipd_compiletf acc=mip,mp,gate,tchk,rw:test+
Note that this entry includes acc= even though the C functions in the PLI specification call
VPI routines instead of ACC routines. The syntax has not changed; you use the same
syntax for enabling ACC and VPI routines.
This PLI table file is for an example file named set_mipd_delays_vpi.c that is available
with The Verilog PLI Handbook by Stuart Sutherland.

Writing Your Own main() Routine
Integrating a VPI Application With VCS
If you create one or more shared libraries for a VPI application, the application should not
contain the array named vlog_startup_routines.
Instead you enter the
-load-load[-]
-load compile-time option to specify the registration routine. The
syntax is as follows:
-load shared_library:registration_routine
You do not have to specify the pathname of the shared library if that path is part of your
LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable.
The following are some examples of using this option:
• -load lib1:my_register : The my_register() routine is in lib1.so. The location of
lib1.so is in the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable.
• -load lib1:my_register,new_register : The registration routines my_register()
and new_register() are in lib1.so.The location of lib1.so is in the LD_LIBRARY_PATH
environment variable.
• -load lib1:my_register -load lib2:new_register : The registration routine
my_register() is in lib1.so and the second registration routine new_register() is in
lib2.so. The path to both of these libraries are in the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment
variable. You can enter more than one -load option to specify multiple shared libraries
and their registration routines.
• -load lib1.so:my_register : The registration routine my_register() is in lib1.so. The
location of lib1.so is in the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable.
• -load /usr/lib/mylib.so:my_register : The registration routine my_register() is
in lib1.so, which is in /usr/lib/mylib.so, and not in the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment
variable.
Writing Your Own main() Routine
You write your own main() routine if you wrote your PLI application in C++ code or if your
standard C code application does some processing before starting the simv executable.
When you write your own main() routine you must include the -e compile-time option
-e name_for_main-e name_for_main [-]
on
the vcs command line. The syntax is as follows:
-e new_name_for_main
For example:
vcs -P my_main.tab my_main.cc -e SimvMain source.v

Writing Your Own main() Routine
The contents of my_main.cc is as follows:
#if defined(__cplusplus)
extern "C" {
#endif

extern int SimvMain(int argc, char *argv[]);
extern void vcs_atexit (void(*pfun)(int code));

#if defined(__cplusplus)
}
#endif

static void do_cleanup(int code)
{
/* do simv post-processing work */
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
/* Startup code (if any) goes here. */

vcs_atexit(do_cleanup); /* Register callback */

SimvMain(argc, argv); /* Run simv */

return 0; /* Never gets here */
}
Note that SimvMain does not return, it calls exit() directly. If you need to do any post-
processing, you can register at-exit functions using vcs_atexit().
The function you pass to vcs_atexit() is called with the exit status. If you make multiple
calls to vcs_atexit(), your functions are called in the reverse order of registration.
You cannot use this feature when using the VCS SystemC cosimulation
interface.

Example 7 C Source Code for Functions Calling acc_getmem_int, acc_setmem_int, and

void error_handle(char *msg)
{
printf("%s",msg);
fflush(stdout);
exit(1);
}

void set_mem()
{
handle memhand = NULL;
int value = -1;
int row = -1;
int start_bit = -1;
int len = -1;

memhand = acc_handle_tfarg(1);
if(!memhand) error_handle("NULL MEM HANDLE\n");
value = acc_fetch_tfarg_int(2);
row = acc_fetch_tfarg_int(3);
start_bit = acc_fetch_tfarg_int(4);
len = acc_fetch_tfarg_int(5);

acc_setmem_int(memhand, value, row, start_bit, len);
}

void get_mem()
{
handle memhand = NULL;
int row = -1;
int start_bit = -1;

int len = -1;
int value = -1;

memhand = acc_handle_tfarg(1);
if(!memhand) error_handle("NULL MEM HANDLE\n");
row = acc_fetch_tfarg_int(2);
start_bit = acc_fetch_tfarg_int(3);
len = acc_fetch_tfarg_int(4);
value = acc_getmem_int(memhand, row, start_bit, len);
printf("getmem: value of word %d is : %d\n",row,value);
fflush(stdout);
}

void clear_mem()
{
handle memhand = NULL;

memhand = acc_handle_tfarg(1);
if(!memhand) error_handle("NULL MEM HANDLE\n");

acc_clearmem_int(memhand);
}
The function with the set_mem identifier calls the IEEE standard acc_fetch_tfarg_int
routine to get the handles for arguments to the user-defined system task that you
associate with this function in the PLI table file. It then assigns the handles to local
variables and calls acc_setmem_int to write to the specified memory in the specified
word, start bit, for the specified length.
Similarly, the function with the get_mem identifier calls the acc_fetch_tfarg_int routine
to get the handles for arguments to a user-defined system task and assign them to
local variables. It then calls acc_gtetmem_int to read from the specified memory in the
specified word, starting with the specified start bit for the specified length. It then displays
the word index of the memory and its value.
The function with the clear_mem identifier likewise calls the acc_fetch_tfarg_int
routine to get a handle and then calls acc_clear_mem_int with that handle.
Example 8 PLI Table File
$set_mem call=set_mem acc+=rw:*
$get_mem call=get_mem acc+=r:*
$clear_mem call=clear_mem acc+=rw:*
Here, the $set_mem user-defined system task is associated with the set_mem function in
the C code, as are the $get_mem and $clear_mem with their corresponding get_mem and
clear_mem function identifiers.

Example 9 Verilog Source Code Using These System Tasks
// read and print out data of memory
parameter start = 0;
parameter finish =9 ;
parameter bstart =1 ;
parameter bfinish =8 ;
parameter size = finish - start + 1;
reg [bfinish:bstart] mymem[start:finish];
integer i;
integer len;
integer value;

// $set_mem(mem_name, value, row, start_bit, len)
$clear_mem(mymem);

// set values
#1 $set_mem(mymem, 8, 2, 1, 5);
#1 $set_mem(mymem, 32, 3, 1, 6);
#1 $set_mem(mymem, 144, 4, 1, 8);
#1 $set_mem(mymem,29,5,1,8);

// print values through acc_getmem_int
#1 len = bfinish - bstart + 1;
$display();
$display("Begin Memory Values");
for (i=start;i<=finish;i=i+1)
$get_mem(mymem,i,bstart,len);
end
$display("End Memory Values");
$display();

// display values
#1 $display();
$display("Begin Memory Display");
for (i=start;i<=finish;i=i+1)
$display("mymem word %d is %b",i,mymem[i]);
end
$display("End Memory Display");
$display();
end

In this Verilog code, in the initial block, the following events occur:
1. The $clear_mem system task clears the memory.
2. Then the $set_mem system task deposits values in specified words, and in specified
bits in the memory named mymem.
3. In a for loop, the $get_mem system task reads values from the memory and displays
those values.

Example 10 C Source Code For an Application Calling acc_setmem_hexstr
#include "vcsuser.h"
#define NAME_SIZE 256
#define len 100
pli()
{
FILE *infile;
char memory_name[NAME_SIZE] ;
char value[len];
handle memory_handle;
int row,start;

infile = fopen("initfile","r");
while ( fscanf(infile,"%s %s %d %d ",
memory_name,value,&row,&start) != EOF )
{
printf("The mem= %s \n value= %s \n row= %d \n start= %d \n ",
memory_name,value,row,start);
memory_handle=acc_handle_object(memory_name);
acc_setmem_hexstr(memory_handle,value,row,start);
}
}

The above example shows the source code for a PLI application that:
1. Reads a data file named initfile to find the memory identifiers of the memories it
writes to, the hexadecimal string to be converted to its bit representation when written
to the memory, the index of the memory where it writes this value, and the starting bit
for writing the binary value.
2. Displays where in the memory it is writing these values
3. Calls the access routine to write the values in the initfile.

acc_mod_lcb_add
void acc_mod_lcb_add(handle handleModule,
void (*consumer)(), char *user_data)
Registers a line callback routine with a module so that VCS calls the routine whenever
VCS executes the specified module.
The prototype for the callback routine is:
void consumer(char *filename, int lineno, char *user_data,
int tag)
The tag field is a unique identifier that you use to distinguish between multiple 'include
files.
Protected modules cannot be registered for callback. This routine will just ignore the
request.
Example 17 Example of acc_mod_lcb_add

/* VCS callback rtn */
void line_call_back(filename, lineno, userdata, tag)
char *filename;
int lineno;
char *userdata;
int tag;
{
handle handle_mod = (handle)userdata;

io_printf("Tag %2d, file %s, line %2d, module %s\n",
tag, filename, lineno,
acc_fetch_fullname(handle_mod));
}

/* register all modules for line callback (recursive) */
void register_lcb (parent_mod)

handle parent_mod;
{
handle child = NULL;

if (! acc_object_of_type(parent_mod, accModule)) return;

io_printf("Registering %s\n",
acc_fetch_fullname (parent_mod));

acc_mod_lcb_add (parent_mod, line_call_back, parent_mod);

while ((child = acc_next_child (parent_mod, child))) {
register_lcb (child);
}
}
acc_mod_lcb_del
void acc_mod_lcb_del(handle handleModule,
void (*consumer)(), char *user_data)
Unregisters a line callback routine previously registered with the acc_mod_lcb_add()
routine.
Example 18 Example of acc_mod_lcb_del

/* VCS 4.x callback rtn */
void line_call_back(filename, lineno, userdata, tag)
char *filename;
int lineno;
char *userdata;
int tag;
{
handle handle_mod = (handle)userdata;

io_printf("Tag %2d, file %s, line %2d, module %s\n",
tag, filename, lineno,
acc_fetch_fullname(handle_mod));
}

/* unregister all line callbacks (recursive) */
void unregister_lcb (parent_mod)
handle parent_mod;
{
handle child = NULL;

if (! acc_object_of_type(parent_mod, accModule)) return;

io_printf("Unregistering %s\n",
acc_fetch_fullname (parent_mod));

acc_mod_lcb_del (parent_mod, line_call_back, parent_mod);

while ((child = acc_next_child (parent_mod, child))) {
register_lcb (child);
}
}
The module handle, consumer routine and user data arguments must match those
supplied to the acc_mod_lcb_add() routine for a successful delete.
For example, using the result of a call such as acc_fetch_name() as the user data will
fail, because that routine returns a different pointer each time it is called.

p_location acc_mod_lcb_fetch(handle handleModule)
Returns an array of breakable lines.
This routine returns all the lines in a module that you can set breakpoints on.
The return value is an array of line number, file name pairs. Termination of the array is

void ShowLines(handleModule)
handle handleModule;
{

io_printf(" [%s:%d]\n",

plocation[i].line_no);
