Using VCS SmartSearch
SmartSearch is an advanced search solution integrated with the HTML documentation.
VCS SmartSearch is an application of Artificial Intelligence and uses Natural Language
Processing techniques to provide you an efficient search experience. VCS SmartSearch is
customized to provide most relevant results for your queries. It also enables you to specify
the documents where you can search. You can either search the entire documentation
set or search in the selected documents by using the Settings -> Documentation
Paneloption.
Prerequisites for Using VCS SmartSearch
If you are using SmartSearch for the first time, you must download the Python package
from SolvNetPlus and install it on your system. For subsequent releases, you do not need
to download the python package again unless communicated otherwise.
SmartSearch works only with the python package available on SolvNetPlus
because it uses a customized python files package.
To install Python, perform the following steps:
1. Download the Python package (vcs_smartseacrh_python3.6.1.tar.gz) file from the
Files/Related Files section of the How to Use VCS SmartSearch article.
2. Extract the python package to any directory.
tar -zxvf vcs_smartseacrh_python3.6.1.tar.gz
3. Provide read and execute permissions recursively to the extracted directory
(python3.6.1_smartsearch) by using the following command:
chmod -R 755 python3.6.1_smartsearch
4. Go to the $VCS_HOME/doc/UserGuide/smartsearch/ directory.
5. Provide read and execute permissions to $VCS_HOME/doc/UserGuide/smartsearch/
by using the following command:
chmod -R 755 $VCS_HOME/doc/UserGuide/smartsearch

Setting Up the User Environment
6. Create a link to Python by using the following command:
ln -s $python_extraxted_directory/python3.6.1_smartsearch python
For example, ln -s $VCS_HOME/python3.6.1_smartsearch python
Python is now installed.
To use VCS SmartSearch, perform the following steps:
1. Set the VCS_HOME environment variable as follows:
% setenv VCS_HOME <VCS_ installation_directory>
2. Set the path variable as follows:
% set path=($VCS_HOME/bin $path)
3. Use the following command to invoke SmartSearch:
% vcs -doc (for 32-bit)
% vcs -doc -full64 (for 64-bit)
Setting Up the User Environment

1. Set the license file environment variable.
% setenv SNPSLMD_LICENSE_FILE <port_number@server>:\
<path_to_license.dat>
OR
% setenv LM_LICENSE_FILE <port_number@server>:\
<path_to_license.dat>
If both SNPSLMD_LICENSE_FILE and LM_LICENSE_FILE variables are set,
SNPSLMD_LICENSE_FILE takes precedence while LM_LICENSE_FILE is

2. Set the VCS_HOME environment variable.

Verifying the VCS Installation
To verify the VCS installation, execute the following steps:
1. Change to a directory where you have read/write privileges.
% cd $HOME
2. Invoke the tool by entering the following command on a licensed machine:
32-bit installation:
% vcs -id
64-bit installation:
% vcs -id -full64
If you see information about the product version, production date, and operating system,
the installation was successful.

Enhancements to the Result Metric
The enum-type result metric is enhanced to support the following features:
• Derived Percent
• Goal Expressions
• Metric Expressions
Derived Percent
When an enum-type result metric is created, a derived percent metric is created
automatically for each enum value.
For example, if you want to define a metric to track the status of features in a plan, you
could create a result metric definition feat_status with enum values fail and pass as
shown below:
result enum {fail, pass} feat_status;
value.pass = default;
value.fail = (test > 0) && (test.pass < test);

Enhancements to the Result Metric
aggregator = sum;
As this is an enum-type metric, Planner automatically counts the number of features
with status fail and status pass. The Derived Percent enhancement also causes a
percentage to be computed for each legal value of the enum. So in this example, Planner
automatically computes the percentage of features that have feat_status equal to pass,
and the percentage of features that have feat_status equal to fail.
These derived metrics are given the following names:
• feat_status.percent.pass
• feat_status.percent.fail
The scores of these percent metrics are calculated as follows:
• feat_status.percent.pass = feat_status.pass/feat_status*100%
• feat_status.percent.fail = feat_status.pass/feat_status*100%
When a new result metric is added in an HVP plan, one new column is added for the
metric and one column is added for each of its enum values in the following reports:
• XML Plan
• URG
• Verdi

Goal Expressions
The enum-type result metric supports goal expressions. The goal expression evaluates
the goal status for each score in the current plan/feature scope. The final evaluation of a
goal expression is a boolean value: either true or false, as shown here:

Enhancements to the Result Metric
Consider the following example that evaluates the goal expression in the current feature; if
all goal meets, the expression (goal == MET) is true and the result value is true:
result bool summary_result;
value.fail = default;
value.pass = (goal == MET);
aggregator = and;
end metric
Consider a feature, f_sub, which has two goals , Line>0.5 and FSM>0.6:
When one goal is met, one goal is not met, and one does not have any goal, then the final
expression result is 0 and summary_result for the feature fails.
A built-in result metric, GoalStatus is created that can be directly used in any plan. Th
built-in GoalStatus metric is automatically defined as shown below.
result bool GoalStatus;
value.fail = default;
value.pass = (goal != NOTMET);
aggregator = and;
endmetric

Metric Expressions
When a metric has no score in a feature, the metric is set to NULL. If a NULL metric is
used in an expression, that expression is evaluated to true.
Planner supports <metric> ==/!= NULL expressions to set the expected behavior of the
NULL metric. For example, if a Line metric has no score in a feature, then Line == NULL
can be used and it is evaluated to true. However, if you want to specify that all features
should have a Line score, use Line != NULL.
Consider a plan top that contains multiple features as shown in the following figure:

Supporting enum Values for the Result Metric

In the example, a feature is “complete” if it meets the following conditions:
• A test is not NULL.
• All tests must be passed.
• Line and Group must not be NULL.
• Coverage scores must be greater than or equal to 90%.
Note that if a feature does not have test score or all its tests are unknown, then the feature
is not started.
In the figure, the completionSummary column is calculated as follows:
result completionSummary;
value.in_progress = default;
value.not_started = ((test == NULL) || (test == test.unknown));
value.complete = (((test != NULL) && (test == test.pass)) && (((Line !=
NULL) && (Line >= 90%)) || ((Group != NULL) && (Group >= 90%))));
In the top plan, f_complete, f_complete_line, and f_complete_group are complete
features, as their tests are not NULL, all tests are passed, Line and Group are not NULL,
and their coverage scores are 100%. However, the following features are not started:
• f_not_started as its tests are NULL.
• f_empty as its tests are unknown.
Note that the value in_progress is the default value.
Supporting enum Values for the Result Metric
The result metric is enhanced to support enum-type values. The result metric already
supports string-type values; this is explained in the "Defining Result Value for a Plan"
section in the Verdi and Siloti LCA Features Guide.

Supporting enum Values for the Result Metric
The syntax of the enum-type result metric is as follows:
result enum-type identifier;
{value-specification}
Consider a plan, myplan, with five features as F_1, F_2, F_3, F_4, and F_5. To track the
verification results of these features, consider the following result metric definition of a
metric status with enum values unknown, fail, and pass:
result enum {unknown, fail(default), pass} status;
value.unknown = default;
value.fail = (((Line < 0.8 || (cond < 0.5)) &&
(test.percent.pass < 0.7));
value.pass = (((Line >= 0.8 || (cond >= 0.5)) &&
(test.percent.pass >= 0.7));
aggregator = sum;
In this example, expressions are used to determine the status of a feature based on its
line and condition coverage and on the percentage of tests linked to that feature that are
passing. If line coverage is less than 80% or condition coverage is less than 50% and
test.percent.pass is less than 70%, then the value of the status metric is value.fail.
Alternatively, if line coverage is more than or equal to 80% or condition coverage is
more than or equal to 50% and test.percent.pass is more than or equal to 70%, then
the value of the status metric is value.pass. Note that test.percent.pass is the
percent metric that reports the total number of passed tests in a feature. For details on
test.percent.pass, see "Percent Metric for Test Metric" in the Verification Planner User

The set Type Attribute
Verification Planner provides a new attribute type named set. The set type enables you
to specify multiple values for an attribute. To declare an attribute of the set type, use the
following syntax:
attribute set{<element_list>} identifier = <default_set_value>;
identifier = <set_value>;
where <set_value> is an identifier. Identifiers in <set_value> must start with an
alphabetic character, but otherwise can use alphanumeric or the underscore character in
their names.
For example, the following code shows the definition of the my_set attribute of type set
with values as S0, S1, S2, and S_other:
attribute set{S0, S1, S2, S_other} my_set = {};
my_set = {S0, S2};
Attributes of type set in a plan can be propagated to sub-plans by setting their
propagation value to Yes. The attributes propagated from a parent plan cannot be
modified in a sub-plan. The attributes defined in a sub-plan can be used within the sub-
plan but are not visible in the parent plan.
The set attribute type allows you to perform filtering. The set type can be filtered using
the == and != operators. Operators such as >, <, >=, <=, +, -, * and / are not supported.
For example, consider the following filter that shows the usage of == and != operators:
filter eg_filter;

the == and != operators. Operators such as >, <, >=, <=, +, -, * and / are not supported.
For example, consider the following filter that shows the usage of == and != operators:
filter eg_filter;
//# == and != is an exact match,

//# {S0} == {S1,S2} returns false
//# {S0,S1,S2} != {S0,S1} returns true
remove feature where my_set == {S0,S1};
keep feature where my_set != {};
endfilter
In the example above, the my_set == {S0,S1} filter removes the features where my_set
is exactly {S0,S1}. However, the my_set != {} filter restores any feature that has a null
my_set.
Verification Planner also provides the contains function for filtering with the set type
attribute:
contains(<set_attribute_identifier>, <set_val>)
The contains function returns true when <set_val> is equal to or a subset of the value
of the set type attribute specified by <set_attribute_identifier>. Also, consider the
following contains statement that always returns true because the null set is a subset of
every set:
contains(any_attribute, {})
Consider the following filter:
filter eg_filter;
//# returns true when my_set contains both S0 and S1
//# {S0,S1,S2} != {S0,S1} returns true
remove feature where contains (my_set, {S0,S1});
keep feature where my_set == {S0, S1};
remove feature where contains (my_set,{S0})&&(contains(my_set,{S1}));
endfilter
In this example, the filter removes all features that contain S0, S1, and some other set
member. It does not remove any feature that has my_set defined exactly as {S0, S1}.
The contains(my_set, {S0, S1})criteria is exactly the same as
contains(my_set, {S0}) && contains(my_set, {S1}) .

attribute, my_set and six features (f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, and f6) that contains different values
of the attribute:
plan top;
attribute set{S0,S1,S2,S_other} my_set = {s0};
feature f1;
my_set = {};
feature f2;
my_set = {S0};
feature f3;
my_set = {S0,S0};
feature f4;
my_set = {S1,S2};
feature f5;
my_set = {S2,S1};
feature f6;
my_set = {S0,S1,S2,S_other};

URG
To view the details of an attribute in a URG report, use the following command:
urg -plan <HVP_file> -attribute
For example, to view the details of the attributes of spec.hvp in the URG report, use the
following command:
urg -plan spec.hvp -attribute

Measure Concealment in Reports
HVP provides you the flexibility to create multiple measures and metric sources within
features. Though this flexibility is useful for many HVP use models, it may produce
complex reports for simple models. HVP is enhanced to simplify usage and reporting for
portions of the plan that follow a simplified pattern of a single source for each feature.
This is referred to as a 1:1:1 feature because one feature contains one measure and one
source.
This section consists of the following topics:
• Inferencing of the 1:1:1 Compression
Consider a feature add with a measure m1 and a source /dut/block/add. To conceal the
details of measure m1 and to generate a compact and simple report, provide the -show
hvpcompfeat switch with URG as follows:
urg -plan spec.hvp -userdata spec.data -show hvpcompfeat

Inferencing of the 1:1:1 Compression
You can conceal a measure in a report if a feature qualifies for the 1:1:1 compression.
VCS can infer from the structure of the feature whether it is qualified for the compression.
To qualify for the compression, the feature should meet the following criteria:
1. The feature is a leaf feature, that is, it does not contain any subfeature.
2. The feature contains exactly one measure.
3. The measure contains exactly one source.
4. The source name should not contain wildcard and regular expressions.
For example, the following feature is qualified for the 1:1:1 compression:
feature add;
owner = "a";
measure test m1;
source = "/dut/block/add";
The Verification Planner Doc annotator enables creation of verification plans using
Microsoft Office (.doc) documents, and back-annotation of coverage and other scores into
the .doc plan. You must properly format the .doc verification plan with predefined styles
and keywords built into the Verification Planner Doc annotator.
You can use MS-Word 2003 or later to create the .doc verification plan.
Unlike the Verification Planner Spreadsheet annotator flow, the Word Doc flow
does not currently support OpenOffice input.
Back-annotation is an extension of the existing Verification Planner Spreadsheet annotator
flow. The hvp annotate command and most of its switches are used for back-annotation
in the same way that they are used with the spreadsheet annotator.
This section contains the following topics:
• Introduction
• hvp annotate Command Arguments
• Capturing a Verification Plan in the Doc XML Format

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
• Debugging the Doc Plan
• Getting Scores Back-Annotated in the Doc
The Verification Planner Doc annotator provides the following features:
• Simple hooks in MS Word-compliant documents to interface with Verification Planner-
enabled applications.
• Flexibility in formatting verification plan doc XML for nicely formatted coverage reports.
The same doc XML file is used by Verification Planner as a verification plan and as an
annotated report. Formatting features such as selectable fonts, text alignment, graphics,
charts, tables, and descriptions are applied in both the plan and the annotated output
report.
The following figure shows Word Doc annotator use model.
Figure 1 Word Doc annotator Use Model
This section contains the following topics:
• Doc Annotator Usage
• Supported Platforms
• Compatibility With the Verification Planner Spreadsheet Annotation Flow

Doc Annotator Usage
MS Word has many auto-correction options that might cause problems in your Doc
verification plan. Before you start editing a Doc verification plan, it is recommended to turn
off auto-correction options as described below:
1. Click the Office button at the left-top corner, and then click Word Options in the pop-
up menu.
2. Select Proofing in the left menu and then click AutoCorrect Options in the right pane.
3. Select the AutoCorrect tab, and uncheck each of the Capitalize options.
4. Select the AutoFormat tab, and uncheck "Straight quotes" with "smart quotes".
5. Select the AutoFormat As You Type tab, and uncheck "Straight quotes" with
"smart quotes".
6. Turn off any other unnecessary options.
These instructions are for MS Word 2003. For other versions of MS Word, turn off the
equivalent options.
Process Flow
1. Capture your verification plan in the Doc XML format. This is typically done by starting
with a Synopsys-provided template file and marking-key paragraphs in the created doc
with Synopsys-defined styles, and copying and pasting Synopsys-defined tables.
You can access the template file from the following location:
$VCS_HOME/doc/examples/coverage/Verification_Planner/VerificationPlann
er_template/DocPlanTemplate.xml
2. Prepare Synopsys coverage database and HVP user data files.
3. Run hvp annotate with XML plan , covdb, userdata, and other required switches.
4. Fix any errors you see. You can find more error information in filename.dbg.xml.
Even if you do not see any errors, open the filename.dbg.xml file, and check to make
sure that Verification Planner processed your verification plan hierarchy and contents
as you intended. This debug check process only needs to be done on newly-created
or recently-edited plans. Once the plan becomes stable, you can skip this debug check
step when annotating with new coverage databases.
5. If there are no errors, open filename.ann.xml to see the annotated scores.

text:
Supported Platforms
Following is the list of supported platforms:
• RHEL32
• RHEL64
• suse32

• sparcOS5
Compatibility With the Verification Planner Spreadsheet
Annotation Flow
The Verification Planner Spreadsheet annotator flow and Doc annotator flow share the hvp
annotate command and most of its switches. When an XML plan file is specified in -plan
xml-in-file, Verification Planner automatically detects the XML file format and invokes
the proper process depending on the format of the XML.
hvp annotate Command Arguments
hvp annotate -plan xml-in-file
[-h]
[-mod hvpfiles]
[-plan_out annfile]
[-feature " hierarchies"|-featurefile txtfile]
[-dir covdbpath|-f txtfile]
[-userdata vedata|-userdatafile txtfile]
[-userdata_out outvedata]
[-metric_prefix prefix]
[-group ratio|merge_across_scopes]
[-show_ratio]
[-show_incomplete]
[-v]
[-q]
Options
-plan xml-in-file: Specifies a Spreadsheet XML file or Word XML file containing your
verification plan. This option is mandatory.
For example: -plan myplan.xml

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
-h: Shows the help message.
-mod hvpfiles: Filters or overrides files in the HVP language format. You can specify
multiple files. They are applied in the order in which they are specified.
For example: -mod override.hvp filter.hvp
-plan_out annfile: Specifies the name for the output annotated spreadsheet or doc
XML file. If -plan_out is not entered, a file with the original filename and .ann.xml
extension is generated.
-feature " hierarchy [ hierarchy]": Specifies HVP scopes, which you want
to annotate with the covdb or HVP userdata database. You can use multiple scopes
and wildcards (*, **, ?), but you should enclose the string with the double quotes. Sub-
hierarchies of matched scope are automatically annotated. If the -feature option is not
given, covdb and HVP userdata are annotated to the entire plan.
Example 1:
% hvp annotate -feature "myplan.feat1.play*" -dir \
cov1.vdb -feature "myplan.feat1.rec*" cov2.vdb -plan \
<myplan.xml>
where, myplan.feat1.play* expands to the following:
myplan.feat1.play1
myplan.feat1.play2
myplan.feat1.play3
The score of myplan.feat1.play1, mplan.feat1.play2, and myplan.feat1.play3 is
annotated with cov1.vdb.
Similarly, myplan.feat1.rec* expands to the following:
myplan.feat1.rec1
myplan.feat1.rec2
myplan.feat1.rec3
The score of myplan.feat1.rec, mplan.feat1.rec2,and myplan.feat1.rec3 is
annotated with cov2.vdb.
Example 2:
% hvp annotate -dir global.vdb -feature \
"myplan.feat1.play*" -dir cov1.vdb -feature \
"myplan.feat1.rec*" cov2.vdb -plan <myplan.xml>
The scores of the matching regions of the play feature is the average aggregator of
cov1.vdb and global.vdb. Similarly, scores of the matching regions of the rec feature is
the average aggregator of cov2.vdb and global.vdb.

-featurefile feature-database mapping file : Specifies a text file that contains a
list of hierarchy feature paths. Verification Planner puts a feature path on separate lines of
feature-database mapping file . This file is used in conjunction with the -dir switch to
provide a list of feature paths inline without required to specify each feature.
For example, a feature-database mapping file with three feature paths is arranged as
shown in the following examples:
Example 1:
% hvp annotate -featurefile map1 -dir cov1.vdb -plan \
<myplan.xml>
where, map1 is the text feature database mapping file that contains previous feature
hierarchies. Following is the content of the text feature file with three feature hierarchies:
a.b.c
a.b.d
a.b.e
When you invoke the above hvp annotate command, it effectively expands to the
following:
% hvp annotate -feature "a.b.c a.b.d a.b.e" -dir \ cov1.vdb -plan
<myplan.xml>
Here, the scores of a.b.c, a.b.d, and a.b.e are annotated with cov1.vdb.
Example 2:
% hvp annotate -dir global.vdb -featurefile map1 -dir \
cov1.vdb -dir cov2.vdb -plan <myplan.xml>
This command effectively expands to the following:
% hvp annotate -dir global.vdb -feature "a.b.c a.b.d \
a.b.e" -dir cov1.vdb -dir cov2.vdb -plan <myplan.xml>
Example 3:
% hvp annotate -userdatda myfile1 -feature a.b.c -dir cov3.vdb -userdata
myfile2 -plan <myplan.xml>
The annotated score of the a.b.c feature for userdata is the aggregator of myfile1 and
myfile2.
To make -feature and -featurefile options work effectively, always specify -feature
and -featurefile options followed by the -dir switch and the coverage database.
-dir covdbpath: Specifies the path to a Synopsys coverage database (cm, vdb). You can
specify multiple paths separated by commas.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
For example: -dir wishbone.cm wishbone.vdb
-f txtfile: Specifies a text file that contains a list of covdb coverage database paths.
-userdata vedata: Specifies the ve.data file path. You can specify multiple paths
separated by commas.
For example: -userdata result.txt bugcount.txt
-userdatafile txtfile: Specifies a text file that contains a list of user database file
paths.
-userdata_out outvedata: Dumps an annotated score of all measures into the specified
outvedata userdata file.
-metric_prefix prefix: Changes a metric name in the output user database file used
by -userdata_out.
-group ratio | merge_across_scopes :
-group ratio : Aggregates the group metric score as a ratio type (covered/coverable)
instead of as a percent.
-group merge_across_scopes : Merges the group score across scopes.
-show_ratio: Displays ratio type scores in a ratio form instead of a percent.
-show_incomplete: Indicates incomplete scores with [inc].
-v: Activates the Verbose mode, which shows progress status messages.
-q: Activates the Quiet mode, which turns off all warning messages.
Capturing a Verification Plan in the Doc XML Format
This section contains the following topics:
• Built-In Styles
• Table Keyword
• Other Contents
Built-In Styles
In the Doc XML plan template, there are predefined styles that are prefixed with HVP.
Verification Planner extracts contents and their styles to establish the HVP hierarchy. A
template document containing predefined styles is provided with the Verification Planner
Doc annotator. Make a copy of that template and then use your copy as a basis to create a
new plan.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
• HVP Plan Style
• HVP Feature 1 to HVP Feature 9
• HVP Description
• HVP Assignment
• HVP Measure name
• HVP Metric name
• HVP Attribute name, HVP Annotation name
• HVP Include File
HVP Plan Style
Content with the HVP Plan style (see the figures below) is assigned as the name of the
HVP Plan. Use this style only once in the plan, typically at the very top of the document.

HVP Feature 1 to HVP Feature 9
There are nine levels of "HVP Feature" styles, which are used to represent the HVP
feature hierarchy. The index is seamless in terms of hierarchy, which means that HVP
Feature 1 is either followed by another HVP Feature 1 or by HVP Feature 2 , but not by
HVP Feature 3 or HVP Feature 4 , for example. If HVP Feature 2 is found, the feature
becomes a subfeature of the previous HVP Feature 1 . If HVP Feature 1 is found, the
feature becomes a sibling of the previous HVP Feature 1 , if one exists.
This limited number of styles also limits the number of levels of hierarchical depth in a
verification plan. You cannot create a plan with more than nine levels of features.

You can also use HVP Feature number for subplan declaration. To instantiate a subplan,
place the subplan keyword as the first word on the HVP Feature number line followed by
the name of the subplan. For example, subplan name-of-subplan.
You can also pass attributes to the subplan. Annotation value overrides using the #()
syntax, which is the same syntax as in the HVP language. For more information about
syntax for instantiating a parameterized subplan in the HVP language, see the Verification
Planner User Guide.
Since Verification Planner does not allow duplicate identifiers under the same parent
feature you must add one more feature level to instantiate multiple instances of subplans
with the same name as shown in the following example:

HVP Description
The paragraph with the HVP description style is extracted as the built-in description
attribute in the HVP feature. You can also use an HVP Assignment table to override
description values.
Table Keyword
When a table is found, Verification Planner looks at the contents in the first cell of the
table, and determines whether the table needs to be interpreted as part of the HVP
hierarchy. The following keywords are reserved:
• HVP Assignment
• HVP Measure name
• HVP Metric name
• HVP Attribute name, HVP Annotation name
• HVP Include File
HVP Assignment
A table with an HVP Assignment style is used to override attributes, annotations, and
goals for metrics. The keyword cell is followed by two-column rows. The left cell must have
the name of an attribute or annotation to override the value of the name or annotation, or
the name of a metric to override a goal expression. All names of attributes, annotations, or
metrics in this table must be defined in the plan. Otherwise, Verification Planner generates
warnings and ignores the undefined names.
HVP Assignment
phase 2
owner Snps

Although the HVP language is case-sensitive, Verification Planner searches
for the names of attributes, annotations, and metrics in its definition tables
with case-insensitive matching, as MS Word sometimes capitalizes the first
character of a word.
HVP Measure name
The table with the HVP Measure name keyword in the first cell is used to declare HVP
measure statements. You can specify a unique measure name or leave it blank. If no
measure name is entered, then Verification Planner automatically generates a measure
name.
The keyword cell is followed by two-column rows. You specify at least one source string.
To specify multiple sources, you can list multiple source strings in the same cell separated
by commas, or add multiple rows with the source keyword in the left cell of each row.
After the source row, append one or more two-column rows, with a metric name in the left
cell of each of those rows. Leave the right cell empty. The annotation process fills each
empty cell with its score.
HVP Measure m1
source group instance:
memsys_test_top.testbench::cpu::cpu_cov.my_cpu0
Group
HVP Measure
source group: memsys_test_top
source group: memsys_test_top2
Group
HVP Measure
source group: memsys_test_top, group: memsys_test_top2
Group
Assert

HVP Metric name
A table with an HVP Metric name keyword in the first cell is used to define an HVP metric.
In the keyword cell, a unique metric name is specified after HVP Metric (bugs in the
example table below).
The following are the rules for creating an HVP metric table:
• One table per one metric definition.
• Following the first row, use two-column rows with predefined keywords in the left cell.
Rows for type and aggregator are mandatory. A row for goal is optional.
type is one of the following: integer, ratio, real, percent, enum {entry1,
entry2, }
Not all entries are available for all types. For more information, see "Using the HVP
Language".
aggregator is one of the following:
sum, average, max, min
goal is an expression for the coverage goal.
HVP Metric bugs
type Integer
aggregator Sum
goal bugs < 3
HVP Attribute name, HVP Annotation name
A table with an HVP Attribute name or HVP Annotation name keyword in the first cell is
used to define an HVP attribute or annotation, respectively. In the keyword cell, a unique
name is specified after the HVP Attribute or HVP Annotation keyword. For example,
phase in the first example table below and spec in the second example table below.
Following are the rules for creating an HVP metric table:
• One table per one definition.
• Following the first row, use two, two-column rows with predefined keywords type and
default in the left cells.
type is one of the following:
integer, ratio, real, percent, enum {entry1, entry2, }

default is the default value of the attribute or annotation.
HVP Attribute phase
type Integer
default 1
HVP Annotation spec
type String
default
HVP Include File
A table with the HVP Include file keyword in the first cell is used to declare other XML
plans to be included as subplans.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
he attribute or annotation.
HVP Attribute phase
type Integer
default 1
HVP Annotation spec
type String
default
HVP Include File
A table with the HVP Include file keyword in the first cell is used to declare other XML
plans to be included as subplans. The XML plans that are included in this table are used
as subplans. Add as many one-column rows containing XML filenames as you need.
HVP Include file
sram_wordplan.xml
dram_wordplan.xml
Other Contents
Other content is text, images, and charts, which are neither in a predefined HVP style nor
in a table with a predefined keyword. All such content is ignored during the annotation
process and appears in the annotated plan exactly as it appears in the original plan
document. Formatting is limited to the formatting features that are allowed in Microsoft
Word 2003 XML .doc format.
Debugging the Doc Plan
When an error is detected in a .doc verification plan, it is difficult to find where the error
occurred. In addition, Verification Planner might interpret your verification plan in a different
way than what you intended or expected due to reasons such as typographic errors,
incorrect styles, and so on. This is because the paragraph styles are essentially invisible
in the normal WYSIWYG view of the document. You might, for example, select the wrong
style, not knowing that Verification Planner may not recognize the paragraph properly.

When you run hvp annotate , a filename.dbg.xml is created for each plan file, which
provides detailed debugging information.
This section contains the following topics:
• [Style|Table] Keyword Indicator
• Unique Error Code in Error Messages
[Style|Table] Keyword Indicator
In filename.dbg.xml, a blue term enclosed in square brackets, [Style|Table],
indicates that the section is either a predefined HVP style or a predefined HVP table.
Several examples are shown below. If you do not see [Style|Table] where you expect
to see it, there is an error in your HVP file such as a wrongly used style or a typographic
error.

Unique Error Code in Error Messages
The following error while running hvp annotate indicates that an invalid metric, Group 1 ,
is found at the location of ERR001:
Error:[DOC_060] memsys_wordplan.xml:ERR001: Invalid metric name(Group1)
was used in Measure(_m1) in Feature(1.2. cpu1)
To find where Group1 is used, you can open the file named memsys_wordplan.dbg.xml
and search for the ERR001 string. ERR001 is a unique string in the filename.dbg.xml file,
so you can easily find the location of the error. Then, you can open the original plan and
edit it to fix the error.
Getting Scores Back-Annotated in the Doc
Running hvp annotate , creates one or more filename.ann.xml files. Verification
Planner produces one filename.ann.xml file per plan or subplan instance in the HVP

hierarchy. If your plan does not include any subplans, then only one filename.ann.xml is
produced.
If a plan is used as a subplan multiple times, then Verification Planner produces
filename.ann.1.xml, filename.ann.2.xml, and so on.
It is not necessary to open the *ann.*.xml file to view a subplan. You can open only the
top-level plan .ann.xml file and navigate to any subplan .ann.xml from there.
This section contains the following topics:
• Plan/Feature Score Summary
• Measure Score Table
• Navigating Down to a Subplan
Plan/Feature Score Summary
The hvp annotate command generates a score summary table for each plan or feature.
Each score cell in the score summary table is filled in with a color determined by the score
and the goal. The meanings of the colors are as follows:
• If a goal is specified:
◦ Green indicates that the goal is met.
◦ Red indicates that the goal is not met.
• If no goal is specified:
For Synopsys coverage,
◦ Green indicates 100% coverage.
◦ Red indicates 0% coverage.
◦ A coverage score between 0 and 100% is indicated by one of six different colors.
For information about setting the colors, see the Unified Coverage Reporting User
For a test metric,
◦ Green indicates a pass/total ratio of 1 (100%).
◦ Red indicates a pass/total ratio of 0 (0%).
◦ A coverage score between 0 and 100% is indicated by one of six different colors.
For information about setting the colors, see the Unified Coverage Reporting User
The following figure shows a score summary table:

Measure Score Table
In the measure score table, the score cell is colored using the same scheme as the Plan/
Feature Score Summary. If no score is available, then the cell contains N/A.
If the -show_incomplete switch is used, [incomplete] appears in front of any source
string that does not match any of the regions in the coverage database or userdata.
Navigating Down to a Subplan
In a filename.ann.xml file, click a subplan name that uses the HVP Feature style to
open the ann.xml file for the subplan instance. Press Ctrl and click the subplan name (for

Defining Conditional Results in Verification Planner
Defining Conditional Results in Verification Planner
VCS Coverage provides a new block named result in the HVP language that defines
the overall status of a feature. The value of the result field is derived from various metric
scores present in an annotated plan. This helps you perform further analysis on the plan/
feature and improve on it, if required.
result overall;
value.In_Progress = default;
value.Not_Started = ((SnpsAvg <= 0)&&(test == 0));
value.Done = ((SnpsAvg >= 100%) && (test>0)) &&
(test.fail == 0));
Conditional results are useful for combining score information from multiple metrics and
translating them into a more meaningful summarized status. In the example, these status
values are as follows:
• In_Progress: The verification effort has started, but is not yet complete.
• Not_Started: The verification effort has not yet started.
• Done: The verification effort is complete.

Support for Low Power Subplans in HVP
You can add the low power subplan snps_LP to any HVP plan without including the
definition plan file in your normal HVP plan, as shown in the following example:
plan top;
feature feat_line;
measure Line Measure_1;
source = "tree: tb.i_top.level_1_test_a_dut";
feature feat_lp_plan;
subplan snps_LP;
Verification Planner automatically finds the plan definition for the snps_LP plan from
simv.vdb when it needs to be annotated. If simv.vdb does not contain the plan definition,
an empty plan node is used, as shown in the following example:
urg -dir simv.vdb -plan plan_w_lp_subplan.hvp
plan top;
feature feat_line;
measure Line Measure_1;
source = "tree: tb.i_top.level_1_test_a_dut";
feature feat_lp_plan;
subplan snps_LP;
If you provide only the -metric option and do not specify the group, the
annotated report does not capture low power objects.

VCS Mixed-HDL Features
This chapter includes the following VCS mixed-HDL features:
• Accessing VHDL Signals From Verilog Using Language XMRs
• Binding SVA to a Design in VCS to Include Hierarchies

Accessing VHDL Signals From Verilog Using Language XMRs
VCS enables you to access VHDL signals from Verilog using language cross module
references (XMR, also called as “hierarchical named references” in the LRM). When
the target of an XMR is a VHDL signal, the value of the VHDL signal is converted to its
equivalent Verilog value before it is used in Verilog. This conversion follows the mixed-
HDL boundary port value conversion mechanism.
These are the supported XMR to VHDL signal types:
• std_logic, std_logic_vector, bit, bit_vector
• integer, real
These are the supported types of XMRs:
• Absolute XMRs (top-down XMRs).
For example, top.m.vh.in1 in module top in Example 2.
• Downward relative XMRs.
For example: vh.in1 in module mid in Example 2.
• Upward XMRs.
For example: vh.in1 in module bot in Example 2.

Enabling Language Force Across VCS Mixed-HDL Boundary
In a Verilog design, if force is applied on a wire port, it is visible in the entire hierarchy
to which the port is connected. As a result, no other module can override the forced
value. VCS is enhanced to support the Verilog language force applied on a Verilog inout
port across the mixed-HDL instance hierarchy. This enables you to preserve the force
semantics across the mixed-HDL boundary. With this enhancement:
• The force value is available in all language layers.
• The force value does not change in case of other drivers.
• Multiple language forces are supported at different time lines.
The -mx_force runtime option enables Verilog language force on Verilog inout port
scalar or vector (including bit-/part- select) connected to VHDL. With this, force value and

force semantic is visible on port in all VHDL and Verilog layers where the port is present.
Perform these steps to enable force across mixed-HDL boundaries:
1. Analyze VHDL and Verilog design source code using these commands:
% vlogan -sverilog <test.v>
% vhdlan <test.vhd>
2. Elaborate or compile the design using the command:
% vcs -sverilog top
3. Simulate the design using the -mx_force option in the command line:
% simv -mx_force
Impact of UCLI Force or hdl_xmr_force
You can force a signal or port from UCLI or use the hdl_xmr_force system task. Both
UCLI and hdl_xmr_force support force with deposit or freeze. This section describes
the behavior when UCLI or hdl_xmr_force is used in conjunction with Verilog language
force.
• Force-deposit: This option assigns the value on to the signal. Any other writes to this
signal can override the deposited value.
• Force-freeze: This option assigns the force value (with force semantic) on to the signal/
port. Signal/port retains this value until it is explicitly released or another force (freeze)
is applied to same.
Verilog language force is same as that of force-freeze. The UCLI and hdl_xmr_force
deposit have no impact when a net has a Verilog language force applied. When UCLI
freeze, hdl_xmr_force freeze, and Verilog language force are applied, the last applied
takes effect for the value and the force semantics.
If the config automxforce off UCLI command is specified in presence of
-mx_force, VCS displays the following warning message:

automxforce off

UCLI config flag 'automxforce off' and runtime switch
-mx_force are mutually exclusive. Ignoring config flag
'automxforce off'.

Sequential Distance Coverage for Assertions
This feature provides coverage of sequential elements for assertions by measuring the
sequential distance between an assertion and a sequential element (a latch, a register, or
a primary input).
This feature is supported for designs written in
• Verilog
• SystemVerilog
• OVA using bind statements to bind OVA units to the design. An OVA unit shall be
considered as an assertion, and the inputs of the OVA unit shall be considered the
inputs of that assertion.
This capability is part of VCS Design Checker, provided as a rule to be
checked during compile-time static checking. Other rules provided by
VCS Design Checker can also be invoked during this analysis. For more
information about how to use VCS Design Checker, see the VCS Design
Checker User Guide.
When you write assertions to check the behavior of a design, it is equally important to
know what portion of the logic is being tested by the assertions as it is to know what
behavior is being captured by those assertions.
For any complex design, it is not practical to write assertions such that all signals are
included in one or more assertions. The number of assertions required for such inclusion
of all signals is neither productive nor provides effective use of resources to test a design.
Given these consideration, an effective measure is needed that can be an indicator of how
well logic is being addressed by the assertions.
One such measure is the notion of sequential distance between an assertion and a
sequential element. You can call this sequential distance coverage of sequential elements
by assertions. A sequential element is a latch, a register or a primary input.

Sequential Distance Analysis
Sequential Distance Analysis
Consider the case of typical logic as conceptualized by a series of sequential elements
with combinational logic between the sequential elements. This is shown in the following
figure.
Figure 9 Structural view of a digital circuit
An input to an assertion is a signal included in any expression that is evaluated to
determine the truth of the assertion. This excludes clocking event expressions and
expressions used in task/function calls of sequence match items.
Sequential distance from a sequential element to an assertion is the minimum number of
sequential elements in any path from an input of the assertion to that sequential element,
excluding the assertion input. The sequential element itself is counted in the distance.
For example, if there is no sequential element between the input and the sequential
element, then the distance is 1. If there is one sequential element between the input and
the sequential element, then the distance is 2.
If the sequential element is an input to the assertion, then the sequential distance is said
to be 0. The sequential distance of a sequential element from an assertion is calculated as
follows.
If a sequential element is part of an expression of the assertion, then the distance is 0.
Otherwise, all signals in the expressions of the assertion are examined to determine if
the fanin logic cone of any signal includes the sequential element. If so, the distance is

Sequential Distance Analysis
considered to be 1. If no such signal is found, then the sequential elements included in
these fanin cones of all signals are examined. These sequential elements have a distance
of 1. Once again, if a sequential element is found in any fanin logic cone of the sequential
elements with distance 1, then the distance of that element is considered to be 2. In
this manner, the distance of all sequential elements is measured with respect to each
assertion.
Figure 10 Sequential Distance
From this analysis, following information is of prime interest:
• List of sequential elements that are not within a specified sequential distance from
any assertion.
• Sequential distance of a sequential element from any assertion.
• Number of assertions from which a sequential element is found with a specified
sequential distance.
• Sequential elements with a specified sequential distance from an assertion.
• Assertions with identical inputs.

The above measures indicates how encompassing an assertion is to include logic that is
observed by that assertion and whether any sequential logic is being left out of assertions.
Based on these measures, you can write additional assertions, so that full logic of the
design is effectively monitored by the assertions. As it is with coverage functionality, an
important trade-off in these measures is the amount of information vs. the time needed
to analyze the provided information. To assist in this trade-off, following capabilities are
provided:
• An option to exclude portions of hierarchy from the analysis.
• An option to exclude assertions from the analysis.
• A parameter to select the maximum sequential distance to be considered. Above the
maximum distance, an element is considered not monitored by the assertion.
• An option to count the number of assertions that cover a sequential element with a
specific distance. This distance you can select.
• An option to select a cover, assume, or assert directive.

Force/Release Functionality for Cross-Module
References
This chapter describes the following features:
• Force/Release Functionality for Mixed HDL Cross-Module References
• Using hdl_xmr Through SPICE Designs in VCS-PrimeSim XA Cosimulation
Force/Release Functionality for Mixed HDL Cross-Module
References
VCS allows you to force or release any VHDL signal, or a Verilog wire/reg in a mixed
HDL design. You can use the following VHDL procedures or Verilog system tasks to
achieve the same:
• hdl_xmr_force() and hdl_xmr_release()
• $hdl_xmr_force() and $hdl_xmr_release()
Synopsys recommends to call these procedures and system tasks from the
testbench.
Important:
With hdl_xmr_force for mixed language design, force (freeze) value
propagates across the language boundary, however, force property does not
propagate.
Instead, you can use the UCLI force to propagate both force freeze and
force property values across the language boundary.

Data Types Supported
hdl_xmr_force(), hdl_xmr_release(), $hdl_xmr_force() and $hdl_xmr_release
supports the following data types:
• The following data types of VHDL signals are supported:
◦ Integer
◦ Bit
◦ Boolean
◦ UX01, UX01, X01, X01Z
◦ std_logic/std_ulogic/std_logic_vector/std_ulogic_vector
• On the Verilog side, the following data types are supported:
◦ Scalars and Vectors
◦ Signed and Unsigned
hdl_xmr_force() Procedure and $hdl_xmr_force System Task
Using the hdl_xmr_force() procedure or the $hdl_xmr_force system task you can force
a value on any existing VHDL or Verilog node at any level of the design hierarchy. You
can also invoke hdl_xmr_force() from a VHDL procedure to control force enabling by an
event.
All these following delimiters are supported - /, ., : except for a pure VHDL
design where you cannot use . as a delimiter.
Using the hdl_xmr_force() Procedure
To use the hdl_xmr_force procedure in your VHDL code, include the following library
declarations along with other required library declarations:
use work.sigdecl.all;
library synopsys;
use synopsys.hdl_xmr_pkg.all;
hdl_xmr_force("destination_object", " value",
" rel_time"|open, "force_type"|open, " cancel_time"|open[,
verbose|open]);

destination_object: destination_object could be a VHDL signal or a Verilog register.
Specify an absolute path or a relative path to the object. VCS issues a warning message if
the destination_object does not exist or is not specified.
By default, Verilog nets are read-only, therefore, they cannot be used as
destination objects. To specify Verilog nets as destination objects, you should
turn on the write capability on these nets using a tab file.
value: Specify the value to which the destination_object is to be forced. The specified
value must be appropriate for the type and can be specified in any valid syntax for any
radix as supported by the language.
rel_time: Specify a time relative to the current simulation time. VCS forces the specified
value on the specified destination object at the specified time plus the current time.
Specify the relative time in the format shown below:
rel_time [fs | ps | ns | us | ms ]
hdl_xmr_force("top.dut.reset", "0", "4 ns",
open, "5 ns");
If the specified time is less than the simulation precision, then the force happens at the
end of the current time step.
force_type: force_type must be one of the following:
• freeze - forces the specified value on the specified destination_object at the
specified time. Any drivers later in time have no impact on the destination_object.
• deposit - forces the specified value on the specified destination_object at the
specified time. Any driver later in time can override the forced value.
• default - is freeze.
cancel_time: Specify a time relative to the current simulation time. VCS cancels the
forced value on the specified destination object at the specified time plus the current time.
Specify the relative time in the format as follows:
cancel_time [fs | ps | ns | us | ms ]
hdl_xmr_force("top.dut.reset","0", "4 ns","freeze","5 ns");
If the specified time is less than the simulation precision, then the forced value is canceled
at the end of the current time step.

The default behavior is to never cancel the forced value and is specified by the open
keyword instead of leaving it blank.
hdl_xmr_force("top.dut.reset", "0", "4 ns","freeze", open);
cancel_time is irrelevant to the ‘deposit’ force_type. If specified, the cancel
time is ignored.
verbose: If the argument is not specified then the default value is 0, otherwise, possible
integer values are 0 or 1. Value 0 indicates no verbosity and value 1 enables verbosity.
Set the environment variable LD_LIBRARY_PATH to include the libhdlxmr.so file as
% setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VCS_HOME/{ARCH}/ \
lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

Example 3
In this example, the first initial block has $hdl_xmr call to bind top.dut1.pin1
and top.dut2.pin2. The second initial block has $hdl_xmr_force call to force
top.dut2.pin2 to the value 1. In this case, the order of execution is indeterministic, and is
one of the two following scenarios:
Scenario 1:
If $hdl_xmr_force is executed first, the destination node is forced to the value 1. Later,
when the $hdl_xmr () task is called, VCS binds the source and destination nodes.
However, it generates a warning message stating that an existing force of 1 continues to
override the connection until the $hdl_xmr_force is released or canceled.
Scenario 2:
If the $hdl_xmr() task is executed first, then the source and the destination nodes are
bound together and the source continually drives the destination node. However, when
$hdl_xmr_force() is executed, a warning message is generated stating that the force
overrides the $hdl_xmr() connection and the forced value drives the destination node.
Therefore, the source node have no effect on the destination node.

Multiple $hdl_xmr_force() or hdl_xmr_force() calls
You can have multiple $hdl_xmr_force system tasks or hdl_xmr_force procedure
calls in your code. In such cases, if multiple calls are executed at the same time step,
but if each call has different relative time, then each force command executes at the
corresponding future time. However, at the same time-step, if there are more than one call
to the same node and have the same relative time, then the force command executed last
prevails. Note that VCS does not generate warning message in such situations.
The last force command can be UCLI force,
$hdl_xmr_force/hdl_xmr_force() or the force command in your code.
Example 1 - Multiple force calls from the same scope

wire [15:00] tmp_sig, tmp_node;
src_module src (
.pin(tmp_node),
.node(tmp_sig));
src_module src2 (

$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", ,"deposit","3 ns",1); // 2
#100; // 3
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0", , "freeze","5 ns",1); // 4
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", ,"deposit", ,1); // 5;
#50; // 6
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0", , "freeze","5 ns",1); // 7
#10; // 8
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", ,"deposit","3 ns",1); // 9
#10; // 10
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0", "5 ns", "deposit", "8 ns"
,1); // 11
#2; // 12
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1","2 ns","freeze",
"3 ns", );// 13
#10; // 14

$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0","2 ns","deposit",
"3 ns",); // 15

Line1 and line2 force the same dest_node with two repeated calls at the same time to
occur at the same time. Here, line2 prevails and dest_node is forced with a value of 1 at
the end of current simulation time step and is scheduled to be canceled in 3ns after the
current time-step.
Line4 and line5 force the same dest_node with two repeated calls at the same time to
occur at the same time. Here line5 prevails and dest_node is forced with a value of 1 at
the end of the current simulation time-step and is never canceled unless a future release
or a new force happens.
Line7 is a force by itself and hence happens and forces a new value of 0 on dest_node at
the end of current time step to be canceled in 5ns.
Line9 is a force by itself and hence happens and forces a value of 1 on to the dest_node
at the end of current time step to be canceled in 3ns.
Line11 schedules to force a value of 0 on to the dest_node to occur 5ns from the current
simulation time and to cancel it 3ns after that. But 2ns later line13 schedules a new force
of 0 on the same node in 2ns, which conflicts with the previously scheduled and yet to
happen events. This is a typical scheduler conflict that a scheduler is able to handle like
any other set of conflicting events.
Line15 schedules a force a value of 0 on dest_node to occur 2ns after current time and
to cancel it 3ns after current time (1ns after force happens). But 2ns later (the previous
scheduled cancel occurs 3ns from this point in time) line17 schedules a new force of 1 on
the same dest_node to happen 1ns later that happens before the previous cancellation
event. Again this should be up to the scheduler to handle these conflicting events just like
any other conflicting events.

Line3 and line17 force the same dest_node with two force calls at the same time of
100ns to occur at the same time from two different scopes. Here, the order of execution is
indeterministic and hence the prevailing force is unpredictable.
Line5 and line19 force the same dest_node with two force calls at the same time of

The hdl_xmr_release() Procedure and the $hdl_xmr_release
System Task
Use the hdl_xmr_release() procedure or $hdl_xmr_release() system task
to release the force applied to an existing VHDL or Verilog destination. You can
use hdl_xmr_release() or $hdl_xmr_release() to any objects forced using
hdl_xmr_force() or $hdl_xmr_release(), UI or the force commands in the design.
hdl_xmr_release works the same as the Verilog release command. These signal release
functions can be called concurrently or sequentially from a VHDL architecture (For
example: a testbench), a process or from any Verilog scope where a system call can be
made. Once the signal is released using hdl_xmr_release, the expected behavior of the
released node is as follows:
• If the destination node is of type VHDL signal and if there is no driver on the destination
node, then the node is forced to U.
• If the destination node is of type Verilog wire and if there is no driver on the destination
node, then the node is forced to Z.
• If the destination node is of type Verilog reg and if there is no driver on the destination
node, then the node retains the current value until future evaluations.

• If there is a $hdl_xmr connection or any other drivers on the node, then future
evaluations causes the corresponding driver or drivers to drive this released node with
a resolved value.
• If there is no force and also a direct connection, then hdl_xmr_release removes any
hdl_xmr_force on that node and the node is scheduled for a re-evaluation, so that the
driver’s value may get resolved to drive this destination node.
Using the hdl_xmr_release() Procedure
To use the hdl_xmr_force procedure in your VHDL code, include the following library
declarations along with other required library declarations:
use work.sigdecl.all;
library synopsys;
use synopsys.hdl_xmr_pkg.all;
hdl_xmr_release (" destination_object", [ verbose]);
destination_object: destination_object could be a VHDL signal or a Verilog register.
Specify an absolute path or a relative path to the object. VCS issues a warning message if
the destination_object does not exist or not specified.
Verilog nets are read-only by default. Therefore Verilog nets cannot be used as
destination objects. To specify Verilog nets as destination objects, you should
turn on the write capability on these nets using a tab file.
verbose: If the argument is not specified then the default value is 0, otherwise possible
integer values are 0 or 1. Value 0 indicates no verbosity, and value 1 enables verbosity.

below:
% setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VCS_HOME/{ARCH}/ \
lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

Using hdl_xmr Through SPICE Designs in VCS-PrimeSim XA
Cosimulation
The
hdl_xmr callsSPICE designs
hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force and hdl_xmr_release functionalities support SPICE
designs. The path to source object or destination object can go through the SPICE
hierarchy.
This feature is supported in SystemVerilog-SPICE, Mixed HDL-SPICE flow and SV-Mixed
HDL-SPICE flows
For SPICE designs, the value is treated as voltage.
Supported Data Types
The following are the data types that are supported:
• Nettype scalars
• Nettype vectors
• Index of SV nettype arrays
• Array of nettypes
In Verilog or VHDL, the $hdl_xmr/hdl_xmr calls can be specified in the following format:
Verilog Scope:
$hdl_xmr(source_object, destination_object, verbose);

$hdl_xmr_force(destination_object, valueOrNode, rel_time,
force_type, cancel_time, verbose);

$hdl_xmr_release(destination_object, verbose);
VHDL Scope:
hdl_xmr(source_object, destination_object, verbose);

hdl_xmr_force(destination_object, valueOrNode, rel_time,
force_type, cancel_time, verbose);

hdl_xmr_release(destination_object, verbose);
Specifying the Hierarchy

The path to source object and destination object can go through SPICE hierarchy. The
hierarchy path specification when denoting the source and/or destination nodes must
always consist of / or . or : separating the modules of the hierarchy and should not have
a combination of these formats.
$hdl_xmr from Verilog hdl_xmr from VHDL
Using absolute paths
$hdl_xmr("/top/i1/reset", "/top/h1");

$hdl_xmr_force(":top:i1:reset","1","10
ns","freeze","20 ns",0);

$hdl_xmr_release("top.i1.reset");
hdl_xmr("/top/i1/reset",
"/top/i1/h1");

hdl_xmr_force(":top:i1:reset","1","10
ns","freeze","20 ns",0);

hdl_xmr_release("top.i1.reset");
Using relative paths
$hdl_xmr("i1/reset", "h1");

$hdl_xmr_force("i1:reset","1","10
ns","freeze","20 ns",0);

$hdl_xmr_release("i1.reset");
hdl_xmr("i1/reset", "h1");

hdl_xmr_force("i1:reset","1","10
ns","freeze","20 ns",0);

hdl_xmr_release("i1.reset");
Using hdl_xmr and $hdl_xmr
The $hdl_xmr() (or hdl_xmr() in VHDL scope) connects two signals specified in the
argument list. With each value change the value of the source_object gets deposited on
the destination_object.
$hdl_xmr(source_object, destination_object, verbose);
hdl_xmr(source_object, destination_object, verbose);
The following table provides the description of these arguments.
Argument Details
source_object The source_object is a hierarchical path specified as a string.
A full hierarchical path (or relative path with reference to the
calling block) to an existing VHDL signal or Verilog register/net
or a SPICE node can be specified. The path can contain any
hierarchy including SPICE hierarchy.

Argument Details
destination_object The destination_object is a hierarchical path specified as
a string. The destination_object can include the SPICE
hierarchy. The destination_object cannot be a SPICE
node. This is because PrimeSim XA does not support deposit.
A full hierarchical path (or relative path with reference to
the calling block) to an existing VHDL signal or Verilog
register or SystemVerilog (SV) register can be specified. The
destination_object cannot be a SV nettype as deposit is not
supported on SV nettype.
verbose The verbose is an optional argument to the hdl_xmr call.The
possible integer values are 0 or 1. If the argument is not
specified, the default value 0 is used. Value 0 indicates no
verbosity, and value 1 enables verbosity. When verbosity is
1, every time a value of the source object is copied onto the
destination object, a message is displayed.
Using $hdl_xmr_force (Verilog) and hdl_xmr_force (VHDL)
The $hdl_xmr_force() or hdl_xmr_force() calls can be used to force a value on an
existing Verilog or SPICE or VHDL node. It allows you to force signals, from and at any
level of the design hierarchy from within the VHDL architecture or the Verilog module and
from any scope from where the standard defined system functions can be called. The
hdl_xmr_force() procedure works similar to the Verilog force command. A status is
returned from this function, which can be used to control the flow of the code.
$hdl_xmr_force(destination_object, value, rel_time,
force_type, cancel_period, verbose);
The following table provides the description of these arguments
Argument Details
destination_object The destination_object is a hierarchical path specified as
a string. A full hierarchical path (or relative path with reference
to the calling block) to an existing VHDL signal or Verilog
register/net or SV nettype or a SPICE node can be specified.
The path can contain any hierarchy including SPICE hierarchy.
value The actual value is the value to which the destination_object
is to be forced. The value should be specified within quotes.
The specified value must be appropriate for the type and can be
specified in any valid syntax for any radix as supported by the
language.

Argument Details
rel_time The rel_time argument can of type string and must be
specified using the following format:
"<time><space><unit>".
Where, <time> is an integer and <unit> is a supported unit
type.Specify a time relative to the current simulation time for the
force to occur. The actual time when the force gets applied is
equal to Current Time + Rel Time.Time should be specified in
units such as 3ps or 5ns with a space between the integer and
the unit. If the time specified is less than simulation precision,
the force happens at the end of current time step.If the time is
specified without a unit, an error message is displayed and 0 is
returned as status.
force_type The force_type argument can be of type string. It is used to
specify the type of force that will be applied. The value can be
"default", "deposit", "drive" or "freeze".For a SPICE target, only
"freeze" is supported.
cancel_period The cancel_period argument can be of type string and must be
specified using the following format:
"<time><space> <unit>"
Where, <time> is an integer and <unit> is a supported unit
type.
Specify a time relative to the current simulation time for the force
to cancel. Cancellation occurs at the last simulation delta cycle
of a time unit.
The actual time when force gets canceled is equal to Current
Time + Cancel Time.Time should be specified in units, such as
"3 ps" or "5 ns" with a space between the integer and the unit.
If the time specified is less than simulation precision, the forced
cancelation occurs at the end of current time step.Cancel Time
is irrelevant to the 'deposit' type of forces and if specified, the
cancel time is ignored.
If the cancel time specified is less than the rel-time for applying
the force, then the cancel time is ignored and the force is never
canceled.
verbose The “verbose” is an optional argument to the hdl_xmr call.The
possible integer values are 0 or 1. If the argument is not
specified, the default value 0 is used. Value 0 indicates no
verbosity, and value 1 enables verbosity. When verbosity is
1, every time a value of the source object is copied onto the
destination object, a message is displayed.
Repeated calls to $hdl_xmr_force or hdl_xmr_force are allowed and the last call
prevails. If force calls at the same time has different relative times, then each force
executes at the corresponding future time. If more than one call to the same node gets
called at the same time and set to force at the same future time, the last call prevails. Note

that no warnings are issued about force calls that are overridden by subsequent force
calls.
The last force always prevails and this is applied to force through the code, through UCLI
or through $hdl_xmr_force()/hdl_xmr_force() interface.
Using $hdl_xmr_release (Verilog) and hdl_xmr_release (VHDL)
The $hdl_xmr_release() or hdl_xmr_release() calls release any force that is applied
to an existing VHDL or Verilog destination objects through hdl_xmr_force or all forces
from the designs or from the user interface.
The hdl_xmr_release call works similar to the Verilog release command. These signal
release functions can be called concurrently or sequentially in a process.
$hdl_xmr_release (destination_object, verbose);
The following table provides the description of these arguments.
Argument Details
destination_object The destination_object is a hierarchical path specified as a
string. A full hierarchical path (or relative path with reference to
the calling block) to an existing VHDL signal or Verilog register
or SV register or a SPICE node can be specified. The path can
contain any hierarchy including SPICE hierarchy. Target node
can be SPICE node.
If the destination object does not exist or if it is not specified, VCS
generates a warning message and returns value 0.
verbose The verbose is an optional argument to the hdl_xmr call.
The possible integer values are 0 or 1. If the argument is not
specified, the default value 0 is used. Value 0 indicates no
verbosity, and value 1 enables verbosity. When verbosity is
1, every time a value of the source object is copied onto the
destination object, a message is displayed.
hdl_xmr_release does not require hdl_xmr_force to have been called. However, it
affects only if the node or the object is forced through hdl_xmr_force. At the end of
hdl_xmr_release, the behavior of the released node is as follows:
• If there is no other driver on the destination node, the node becomes Z if it is of type
wire in the Verilog scope.
• If there is no other driver on the destination node, the node retains its current value
until future evaluations if it is of type reg in the Verilog scope.

• If there is no other driver on the destination node, the node becomes U if it is of type
signal in the VHDL scope.
• If there is a UCLI force or a $hdl_xmr_force or a code force on the destination node,
hdl_xmr_release removes any force attached to that node and the behavior is as
mentioned previously.
• If there is no force and if there is a direct connection, hdl_xmr_release removes any
hdl_xmr_force on that node and the node is scheduled for a re-evaluation, so that the
driver's value may get resolved to drive this destination node.
A2D or D2A Fidelity and Delta
In an HDL testbench and UCLI run scripts, hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force and UCLI force are
required on an analog target.
When a cell view is switched from a digital HDL view to an analog view the same hdl_xmr,
hdl_xmr_force or UCLI force must be applied to the analog target.
Correct digital to analog conversion must take place for a digital 0,1,X,Z force on what was
a digital target that has now changed to an analog target.
An auto vdd detection mechanism similar to that used for traditional interface element
thresholds and voltage swings must be used to automatically select voltage thresholds
and voltage swings for analog2digital conversions and digital2analog conversions required
for the hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force or UCLI force.
If the auto vdd methodology breaks down or fails, the voltage thresholds and swings
can be manually changed with the mixed signal control commands and the vcsAD.init
A new report file named runtime_interface_element.rpt is generated in the simv.msv
directory. The report file is generated and dynamically updated at runtime for any hdl_xmr,
hdl_xmr_force/release or UCLI force/release on an analog target. The applicable auto-
generated voltage swings, thresholds and options are recorded in the report file.
Commands and options generated in the runtime_interface_element.rpt file can be
used, copied and pasted to use in the mixed signal control file (vcsAD.init) to change or
modify any auto-generated voltage swings or thresholds or options.
When a hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force/release or UCLI force/release is used on an analog
target, a runtime notice message is issued with information on the options that are used
for any analog2digital or digital2analog conversion, electrical2real or real2electrical
conversion.
This feature is enabled by the default mixed-signal commands. For information about
these analog mixed-signal commands, see the Discovery AMS: Mixed-Signal Simulation
User Guide.

ucli> force top.g1.g2.y 1

runtime_interface_element.rpt:
rt_d2a hiv=1.8v lov=0.0v node=top.g1.g2.y;
Example 2 - hdl_xmr_force on an analog target
Verilog testbench: $hdl_xmr_force("top.g1.g2.Y","1'b1","50 ns");
output on screen @ 50ns:

Notice [MSV-RT-D2A] - runtime d2a conversion:

runtime_interface_element.rpt:
rt_d2a hiv=1.8v lov=0.0v node=top.g1.g2.y;
Following are the limitations with this feature:
• For the hdl_xmr() procedure calls, the target cannot be a SPICE node. (This is
because of the limitation in PrimeSim XA).
• For targets of hdl_xmr or hdl_xmr_force, only SPICE ports that are visible in shadow
module are supported. Internal SPICE nodes or primitives are not supported.
• The feature is not supported in the Verilog-AMS flow.
• PrimeSim XA is the only analog solver that is supported. Other analog solvers, such as
HSIM and FineSim are not supported.
• Multidimensional Array (MDA) inside the SPICE hierarchy are not supported.

Fast Compilation
The VCS compile-time performance optimizations called
compilationfastfast compilation
fast compilation that you can use
to reduce compile-time for your design (and therefore overall turnaround time). You can
enable fast compilation using the -fastcomp compile-time option.
There are two levels of fast compilation, specified by the -fastcomp=0 and -fastcomp=1
compile-time options.
• -fastcomp=0 is same as the -fastcomp option (without the argument). This is the
recommended fast compilation mode. This option accelerates the compile time by
suppressing internal optimizations in VCS front end with moderate simulation time
degradation.
• -fastcomp=1 is same as the -fastcomp=all option. This option applies more
aggressive compile-time performance than the default mode. However, the simulation
time degradation is high compared to the default mode.
The above options are a trade-off between the compile time and the simulation time. You
can choose the option based on which performance is more important to you.

Guard Check Utility
Guard Check Utility
The Guard Check utility checks all source files parsed by VCS (design files, header files,
testbench files, library files, and so on.) for the presence of Guard statements and the
characteristics of the guard directives. It reports the characteristics of the guards in the
parsed file.
A guard directive is a combination of an `ifndef compiler directive and a `define
compiler directive with the same guard name.
`ifndef <guard_name>
`define <guard_name> <optional_value>
This is the recommended option for the Guard Check utility.
It is also defined by a combination of an `ifdef, `else compiler directive, and a `define
compiler directive with the same guard name.
`ifdef <guard_name>
`else
`define <guard_name> <optional_value>
Duplicate guard directives exclude processing of the other guard. For example, a
duplicated file guard directive which has the same guard name _VH_GUARD_1_ is shared
by two different files File_1.v and File_2.v. The shared guard name creates a condition
where inclusion of one of the files excludes processing of the other file. The file is
processed based on the other factors such as, file order of compilation, which may make
the process non-predictable across different tools.
To generate the data for the Guard Check utility, use the -gather_guard compile-time
option as follows:
% vcs <vcs options> <source.v> -gather_guard<dir> /

guardCheck [-all-guards]
-sources <source_files>
-includes <include_files>
-defines <cmd_defines>
Each of these files contain one item (filename or macro name) per line.

Guard Check Utility
The output of the utility is a set of errors or warnings and the error count. In the case of a
non-unique guard, the utility lists all the files that share the same guard name, if not, only
the corresponding erroneous file name is listed.
When the -gather_guard compile-time option is specified, the following three files are
generated in a directory called Guards:
• source_files: The name of each file processed during compilation (one per line).
• include_files: The name of each file read by a `include directive.
• cmd_defines: The name of all +define command line directives specified.
% cmd_defines include_files source_files
For example, the above three files can be directly included in the Guard Check utility as
guardCheck -sources ./Guards/source_files -includes ./Guards/
include_files -defines ./Guards/cmd_defines
The name of the Guards directory can be changed by specifying the option as
-gather_guard=<dir>, where <dir> is the name of the directory. If the directory name is
not specified, the default directory name Guards is used. This option allows different sets
of files to be gathered separately in the same directory. Note that in order to perform the
global checks (for example, unique guard names), all the files must be collected together
prior to running the guard utility.
Example 3 source.v
`include "include.v"
`ifndef SOURCE_1
`define SOURCE_1
module s1();

`undef SOURCE_1
module s2();
Example 4 include.v
`ifdef MACRO
`ifndef GUARD `define GUARD 100
`else
`ifndef GUARD `define GUARD 100

Enhancing Vlogan Command to Compile Files into Multiple
Libraries
Invoking many vlogan commands (about hundreds to thousands) to analyze different files
takes a long time because of UNIX process invocation, command line processing, vlogan
initialization, license checkout, and so on.
To resolve this issue, VCS supports a job manifest file to specify libraries and option
files for each compilation job. Therefore, you can run many jobs by running fewer vlogan
commands.

Enhancing Vlogan Command to Compile Files into Multiple Libraries
The use model to specify libraries and option files for each compilation job is as follows:
% vlogan -jm job_manifest_file [other_vlogan_option …]
The -jm option specifies a job manifest file. Jobs are run with the options on the command
line plus the ones in the job manifest file. The job manifest file has the following clauses:
1. Global options clause
global_options: <global_options_file> [global_options_file …]
global_options specifies the option files that applies to all the jobs with -file option.
Here, you can specify multiple files separated with space.
2. Library clause
library <library_name>: <library_options_file> [library_options_file
…]
library specifies the option files for a library which are applied to a job with -f option.
Here, you can specify multiple files separated with space.
3. Number of parallel jobs clause
parallel_jobs: <positive_integer>
parallel_jobs specifies the number of jobs to run simultaneously.
The following example shows how the jobs runs in parallel.
Execute the following command:
% vlogan -jm job-manifest -full64
The content of the job_manifest_file is as follows:
parallel_jobs:2 // the number specifies the number of jobs to run
simultaneously
global_options: global.f global2.f
library LIB2: filelists/file_2 filelists/file_4
library LIB1: filelists/file_3

Support Multi-Dimensional Array of Interface/Module Instances and Interface ports
The contents of global.f and global2.f file is as follows:
-kdb +v2k +libverbose -sverilog -V -incr_vlogan
The contents of file_2, file_3 and file_4 file are as follows:
+incdir+test +define+A +define+B -assert svaext -kdb -timescale=1ns/1ps
+libext+*.v+*.sv+*.vs +librescan +v2k
test/Test.v
test/new_top.v
The options available in file_2 is applicable only to the sources available in
file_2. Similarly, the options available in file_3 and file_4 is applicable only
to sources available in file_3 and file_4 respectively.
You cannot specify the compilation order in job-manifest file.

and Interface ports
VCS supports multi-dimensional array of interfaces/module instances and interface ports
using the -mda_inst option.

The limitations of this feature are as follows:

and multi-dimensional arrays.

Relaxed Time Scale and Time Precision
You can use the -xlrm timescale_relaxed compile option to enable relaxed (or flexible)
delay adjustments for delays and time literals for the entire module. If a timeunit or
timeprecision keyword is specified, this feature is applied consistently to the entire
module. This option also provides relaxed constraint on time scopes like modules,
programs, packages, or interfaces.
This feature is enabled using -xlrm timescale_relaxed compile-time option as follows:
%vcs -xlrm timescale_relaxed -full64 -sverilog <filename>

Relaxed Time Scale and Time Precision
The following are the examples of this feature.
Example 7 test1.sv

Example 8 test2.sv
#100 $display("%t", $time());
end

% vcs -xlrm timescale_relaxed -full64 -sverilog test2.sv

If the above examples are run without -xlrm timescale_relaxed option, then the
following errors are displayed:
Error-[SV-MTP] Misplaced timeprecision
test1.v, 7

time scope. This is illegal.

VCS does not support this feature at scopes such as class, task/function, process, and
