Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
VCS allows you to set black box by module-based and instance-based with value of the
output ports of black boxes.
VCS ignores and removes the following contexts:
• Bind directive failed to apply
• Assertions crossing black box boundary
This feature is supported using +optconfigfile option.
The following are the use models of this feature:
• Module-level black-box:
module {comma_separated_module_list} {blackbox} [{0|1}];
comma_separated_module_list ::=
[library_name.]module_name {,[library_name.]module_name }
◦ library_name is case-insensitive
◦ When library_name is omitted, and VCS bricks the module once the module_name
is matched.
◦ Both library_name and module_name can use wildcard, ‘*’ and ‘?’, and can use
Verilog escaped identifier.
◦ [{0|1}] specifies the value to tie on the output port(s).
module {middle2, sub*} {blackbox} {1};

module {MYLIB.modB, MY*.modC} {blackbox};
• Instance-level black box:
instance {comma_separated_instance_list} {blackbox} [{0|1}];
comma_separated_instance_list::=
hieracrchical_identifier{, hieracrchical_identifier}

Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
hierarchical_identifier specifies the Verilog hierarchical identifier, each identifier
can use wildcard, ‘*’ and ‘?’.
instance {top.m1.sub1, top.*.sub2} {blackbox};

instance {top.m*.sub1, top.\spe*s .sub2} {blackbox} {0};

instance {top.m*.sub3} {blackbox} {0};
When a module or instance matched any one of the rules, VCS black box this
module or instance. This feature cannot be used with -bboxModule and VCS
reports error message.
Following are the list of scenarios or usecases supported by this feature:
• Black box module replacement.
• Tie value to the output port.
• Remove assertions with hierarchical references crossing boundary.
• VCS suppresses and ignores all bind failures if any module or instance is bricked.
• VCS shows the following diagnostic messages on compilation log:
◦ Module/instances replaced by the black box and its tied value of output ports.
◦ Assertions being removed due to having unresolved hierarchical references.
◦ Bind statement being ignored.
These messages are note messages([Note]).
Following are the examples of this feature:
Example 1: Hierarchical Identifier Crossing Black Box Boundary
Example 9 test1.sv
mid m1();
assign w1 = m1.o1; // OK, if o1 is output port of mid

Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
assign w2 = m1.local_w1; // Error due to unable to resolved.
assign w3 = m1.s1.o1; // Error due to unable to resolve.

module mid(o1, in1, in2);

Use the following command to run the above example:
vcs -sverilog test1.sv +optconfigfile+bb1.cfg
bb1.cfg configuration file specifies the following:
module {mid} {blackbox};
Example 2: Tie Value To Output Ports
Example 10 test2.sv
mid m1();

module mid(o1, in1, in2);
modC c1_inst(); // tie 0 to the output port
modC c1_dummy(); // tie 1 to the output port
modC c2_inst(); // leave undriven

module modC(o1, in1, in2);

Use the following command to run the above example:
vcs -sverilog test2.sv +optconfigfile+bb2.cfg
bb2.cfg configuration file specifies the following:
module {modC} {blackbox};
instance {top.m1.c1_*} {blackbox} {1};
instance {top.m1.c1_inst} {blackbox} {0};
Example 3: Remove Assertions Crossing Black Box Boundary
Example 11 test3.sv
wire mclk, data_phase;

sub s1();
assert(s1.r1); // this assertion will be removed
end
module sub;
reg r1;
Use the following command to run the above example:
vcs -sverilog test3.sv +optconfigfile+bb3.cfg
bb3.cfg configuration file specifies the following:
instance {top.s1} {blackbox};
• This feature cannot be used at the same time with -Xpartialdesign or -bboxModule
options.
The target module and instance can only be Verilog. This feature can use when design
have other languages but if target is not Verilog, the black box does not happen and
does not apply to the black box module.
• This feature does not support the following and VCS displays NYI error:
◦ Native Low Power (NLP) ( -upf)
◦ Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) ( -sdc)
◦ Analog Mixed-Signal Simulation (AMS) ( -coerce, -ad, -ams )
◦ Parallel Compile ( -parallelcomp)
◦ Partition Compile ( -partcomp)
Enabling and Using SystemVerilog 2023 Method Specifiers in
VCS
Starting with this release, SystemVerilog 2023 (SV'23) introduces the following new
method specifiers such as :initial, :extends, and :final. These specifiers give you
more control over class method declarations, helping you define how methods can be
overridden in class hierarchies. VCS now supports these specifiers when you enable the

SystemVerilog 2023 standard. This feature helps you write clearer, more robust object-
oriented code and catch errors related to method overriding at compile time.
Usage
To use the new method specifiers, you must enable the SystemVerilog 2023 standard
in VCS. Use -std=1800-2023 VCS compile-time option to enable SystemVerilog 2023
standard in VCS.
To write class methods with specifiers, you can use the following method specifiers:
• :initial
Marks a method as the initial implementation in the class hierarchy.
• :extends
Marks a method as an extension (override) of a virtual method in a base class.
• :final
Prevents further overriding of the method in derived classes.
The LRM does not allow the following:
• Using both :initial and :extends on the same method.
• Marking a pure virtual method as :final.
The SV'23 LRM supports the following syntax for the method specifiers:
function_declaration ::=
function [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 [ lifetime ]
function_body_declaration

function_prototype ::=
function [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 data_type_or_void
function_identifier [ ( [ tf_port_list ] ) ]

task_declaration ::=
task [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 [ lifetime ]
task_body_declaration

task_prototype ::=
task [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 task_identifier
[ ( [ tf_port_list ] ) ]

dynamic_override_specifiers ::= [ initial_or_extends_specifier ]
[ final_specifier ]
initial_or_extends_specifier ::= : initial | : extends

final_specifier ::= : final
According to SV'23 LRM, the dynamic_override_specifiers is applicable on
method declarations inside a non-interface class scope.
The extends specifier imply that the method is virtual. therefore, virtual
keyword is optional when using the extends specifier.
Example 12 Normal Usage
//normal_usage.v

virtual function :initial void func;

function :extends void func;

class sub_class2 extends sub_class1;
function :extends void func;
$display("Sub class 2 function called");

class sub_class3 extends sub_class2;
function void func;
$display("Sub class 3 function called");

class sub_class4 extends sub_class3;
$display("Sub class 4 function called");

sub_class2 sc2;
sub_class3 sc3;
sub_class4 sc4;

sc2 = new();
sc3 = new();
sc4 = new();
end
vcs -full64 -sverilog normal_usage.v -std=1800-2023
No error is displayed in the output.
Example 13 Initial Override Virtual Function in Base Class
//initial_overrides_virtual_func.v

virtual function void func;

function :initial void func;

end
vcs -full64 -sverilog -std=1800-2023 initial_overrides_virtual_func.v
The following error message is displayed:
Error-[CMOI] Initial method overriding a virtual method
initial_overrides_virtual_func.v, 8
Initial method 'sub_class1::func' overrides virtual method

'base_class::func' (initial_overrides_virtual_func.v, line 2.)
A method with an initial specifier should not override any virtual
method in base classes.
Example 14 Initial Override Non-Virtual Function in Base Class
//initial_overrides_nonVirtual_func.v

function void func;

function :initial void func;

end
vcs -full64 -sverilog -std=1800-2023 initial_overrides_nonVirtual_func.v
No error is displayed in the output.
Example 15 Extends Override Non-Virtual Function in Base Class

end

A method with an extends specifier should override a virtual method in
base classes.

end
vcs -full64 -sverilog -std=1800-2023 extends_overrides_virtual_func.v

end

Example 19 Without Extends Override Final Method

$display("Sub class 2 function called");

sc2 = new();
end

The following error message is displayed:
Error-[CMOF] Final method overridden
override_final.v, 14

Method 'sub_class2::func' overrides final method 'sub_class1::func'
(override_final.v, line 8.)
A method with a final specifier should not be overriden in derived
classes.

sc2 = new();

override_final_withExtend.v, 14

(override_final_withExtend.v, line 8.)

sc2 = new();

(override_final_withInitial.v, line 8.)

Enabling SystemVerilog 2023 Static type(this) Support in VCS
Starting with this release, VCS allows you to use the type(this) operator inside class
static functions in SystemVerilog, as defined by the SystemVerilog 2023 (SV'23) standard.
Previously, type(this) was only available in non-static functions. With this enhancement,
VCS now parses and displays error if type(this) is used incorrectly in static functions.
Usage
Use the following option to enable SV'23 static type(this) support:
-std=1800-2023
The type(this) points to the type of the enclosing class of the static method.
Example 22 Usage of type(this) in Functions
//lrm.v

class registry #(type T=int);
static function type(this) get(); // calls to get() return a
registry #(T)
static type(this) m_inst;
if (m_inst == null) m_inst = new();
return m_inst;

registry #(int) obj = new();

$display("return type of function get is: %p",
$typename(obj.get()));
end
Behavior With SV'23 Standard

Enabling SystemVerilog 2023 Static type(this) Support in VCS

No error message is displayed during compilation.
Run the following simulation command:
%simv
The following is the output:
return type of function get is: "class top.registry#(int)"

or
class-member

top

of the
class handle will be null.
The above warning message is displayed if type(this) used as node type,
and error message is displayed if type(this) is used as static class method
return type.

$display("tb: %s", $typename(arg));

module tb;

Force/Release Functionality for Cross-Module
References
This chapter describes the following features:
• Force/Release Functionality for Mixed HDL Cross-Module References
• Using hdl_xmr Through SPICE Designs in VCS-PrimeSim XA Cosimulation
Force/Release Functionality for Mixed HDL Cross-Module
References
VCS allows you to force or release any VHDL signal, or a Verilog wire/reg in a mixed
HDL design. You can use the following VHDL procedures or Verilog system tasks to
achieve the same:
• hdl_xmr_force() and hdl_xmr_release()
• $hdl_xmr_force() and $hdl_xmr_release()
Synopsys recommends to call these procedures and system tasks from the
testbench.
Important:
With hdl_xmr_force for mixed language design, force (freeze) value
propagates across the language boundary, however, force property does not
propagate.
Instead, you can use the UCLI force to propagate both force freeze and
force property values across the language boundary.

Data Types Supported
hdl_xmr_force(), hdl_xmr_release(), $hdl_xmr_force() and $hdl_xmr_release
supports the following data types:
• The following data types of VHDL signals are supported:
◦ Integer
◦ Bit
◦ Boolean
◦ UX01, UX01, X01, X01Z
◦ std_logic/std_ulogic/std_logic_vector/std_ulogic_vector
• On the Verilog side, the following data types are supported:
◦ Scalars and Vectors
◦ Signed and Unsigned
hdl_xmr_force() Procedure and $hdl_xmr_force System Task
Using the hdl_xmr_force() procedure or the $hdl_xmr_force system task you can force
a value on any existing VHDL or Verilog node at any level of the design hierarchy. You
can also invoke hdl_xmr_force() from a VHDL procedure to control force enabling by an
event.
All these following delimiters are supported - /, ., : except for a pure VHDL
design where you cannot use . as a delimiter.
Using the hdl_xmr_force() Procedure
To use the hdl_xmr_force procedure in your VHDL code, include the following library
declarations along with other required library declarations:
use work.sigdecl.all;
library synopsys;
use synopsys.hdl_xmr_pkg.all;
hdl_xmr_force("destination_object", " value",
" rel_time"|open, "force_type"|open, " cancel_time"|open[,
verbose|open]);

destination_object: destination_object could be a VHDL signal or a Verilog register.
Specify an absolute path or a relative path to the object. VCS issues a warning message if
the destination_object does not exist or is not specified.
By default, Verilog nets are read-only, therefore, they cannot be used as
destination objects. To specify Verilog nets as destination objects, you should
turn on the write capability on these nets using a tab file.
value: Specify the value to which the destination_object is to be forced. The specified
value must be appropriate for the type and can be specified in any valid syntax for any
radix as supported by the language.
rel_time: Specify a time relative to the current simulation time. VCS forces the specified
value on the specified destination object at the specified time plus the current time.
Specify the relative time in the format shown below:
rel_time [fs | ps | ns | us | ms ]
hdl_xmr_force("top.dut.reset", "0", "4 ns",
open, "5 ns");
If the specified time is less than the simulation precision, then the force happens at the
end of the current time step.
force_type: force_type must be one of the following:
• freeze - forces the specified value on the specified destination_object at the
specified time. Any drivers later in time have no impact on the destination_object.
• deposit - forces the specified value on the specified destination_object at the
specified time. Any driver later in time can override the forced value.
• default - is freeze.
cancel_time: Specify a time relative to the current simulation time. VCS cancels the
forced value on the specified destination object at the specified time plus the current time.
Specify the relative time in the format as follows:
cancel_time [fs | ps | ns | us | ms ]
hdl_xmr_force("top.dut.reset","0", "4 ns","freeze","5 ns");
If the specified time is less than the simulation precision, then the forced value is canceled
at the end of the current time step.

The default behavior is to never cancel the forced value and is specified by the open
keyword instead of leaving it blank.
hdl_xmr_force("top.dut.reset", "0", "4 ns","freeze", open);
cancel_time is irrelevant to the ‘deposit’ force_type. If specified, the cancel
time is ignored.
verbose: If the argument is not specified then the default value is 0, otherwise, possible
integer values are 0 or 1. Value 0 indicates no verbosity and value 1 enables verbosity.
Set the environment variable LD_LIBRARY_PATH to include the libhdlxmr.so file as
% setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VCS_HOME/{ARCH}/ \
lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
Analysis
% vlogan [vlogan_options] file2.v file3.v file4.v
(Analyze all Verilog files except the top-level Verilog file)
% vhdlan [vhdlan_options] file5.vhd file6.vhd
(The VHDL bottom-most entity first, then move up in order)
Elaboration
% vcs -debug_access+all +vpi [ vcs_options] entity
Simulation
% simv [ simv_options]
In this example, the top.dut.reset destination node is forced to 1 after 0ns. The cancel
time is specified as open, so that the forced value is never canceled.

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
library synopsys;
use synopsys.hdl_xmr_pkg.all;

entity testbench is

architecture only of testbench is
force_process : process
hdl_xmr_force("/top/dut/reset", "1", "0 ns", "freeze",
open, 1);
wait;

Example 3
In this example, the first initial block has $hdl_xmr call to bind top.dut1.pin1
and top.dut2.pin2. The second initial block has $hdl_xmr_force call to force
top.dut2.pin2 to the value 1. In this case, the order of execution is indeterministic, and is
one of the two following scenarios:
Scenario 1:
If $hdl_xmr_force is executed first, the destination node is forced to the value 1. Later,
when the $hdl_xmr () task is called, VCS binds the source and destination nodes.
However, it generates a warning message stating that an existing force of 1 continues to
override the connection until the $hdl_xmr_force is released or canceled.
Scenario 2:
If the $hdl_xmr() task is executed first, then the source and the destination nodes are
bound together and the source continually drives the destination node. However, when
$hdl_xmr_force() is executed, a warning message is generated stating that the force
overrides the $hdl_xmr() connection and the forced value drives the destination node.
Therefore, the source node have no effect on the destination node.

Multiple $hdl_xmr_force() or hdl_xmr_force() calls
You can have multiple $hdl_xmr_force system tasks or hdl_xmr_force procedure
calls in your code. In such cases, if multiple calls are executed at the same time step,
but if each call has different relative time, then each force command executes at the
corresponding future time. However, at the same time-step, if there are more than one call
to the same node and have the same relative time, then the force command executed last
prevails. Note that VCS does not generate warning message in such situations.
The last force command can be UCLI force,
$hdl_xmr_force/hdl_xmr_force() or the force command in your code.
Example 1 - Multiple force calls from the same scope
module tmp;
wire [15:00] tmp_sig, tmp_node;
src_module src (
.pin(tmp_node),
.node(tmp_sig));
src_module src2 (
.pin(tmp_node),
.
.
.node(tmp_sig));

dest_module dest (
.pin(tmp_sig),
.
.
.node());

$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0", ,"freeze", "5 ns", 1); // 1
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", ,"deposit","3 ns",1); // 2
#100; // 3
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0", , "freeze","5 ns",1); // 4
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", ,"deposit", ,1); // 5;
#50; // 6
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0", , "freeze","5 ns",1); // 7
#10; // 8
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", ,"deposit","3 ns",1); // 9
#10; // 10
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0", "5 ns", "deposit", "8 ns"
,1); // 11
#2; // 12
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1","2 ns","freeze",
"3 ns", );// 13
#10; // 14

$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0","2 ns","deposit",
"3 ns",); // 15
#2; // 16
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1","1 ns", "freeze",
"5 ns",1); // 17
end
Line1 and line2 force the same dest_node with two repeated calls at the same time to
occur at the same time. Here, line2 prevails and dest_node is forced with a value of 1 at
the end of current simulation time step and is scheduled to be canceled in 3ns after the
current time-step.
Line4 and line5 force the same dest_node with two repeated calls at the same time to
occur at the same time. Here line5 prevails and dest_node is forced with a value of 1 at
the end of the current simulation time-step and is never canceled unless a future release
or a new force happens.
Line7 is a force by itself and hence happens and forces a new value of 0 on dest_node at
the end of current time step to be canceled in 5ns.
Line9 is a force by itself and hence happens and forces a value of 1 on to the dest_node
at the end of current time step to be canceled in 3ns.
Line11 schedules to force a value of 0 on to the dest_node to occur 5ns from the current
simulation time and to cancel it 3ns after that. But 2ns later line13 schedules a new force
of 0 on the same node in 2ns, which conflicts with the previously scheduled and yet to
happen events. This is a typical scheduler conflict that a scheduler is able to handle like
any other set of conflicting events.
Line15 schedules a force a value of 0 on dest_node to occur 2ns after current time and
to cancel it 3ns after current time (1ns after force happens). But 2ns later (the previous
scheduled cancel occurs 3ns from this point in time) line17 schedules a new force of 1 on
the same dest_node to happen 1ns later that happens before the previous cancellation
event. Again this should be up to the scheduler to handle these conflicting events just like
any other conflicting events.
Example 2 - Multiple force calls from different scopes
module tmp1;
wire [15:00] tmp_sig, tmp_node;

src_module src(
.pin(tmp_node),
.
.
.node(tmp_sig));

dest_module dest(
.pin(tmp_sig),
.
.
.node());

$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0", , "freeze", "5 ns", 1); // 1
#100; // 2
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", , "deposit", , 1); // 3
#50; // 4
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", , "freeze", "5 ns", 1); // 5
#10; // 6
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0, , "freeze", "3 ns", 1); // 7
#10; // 8
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", "5 ns", "deposit",
"8 ns", 1);// 9
#2; // 10
#10; // 182ns // 11
#2; // 184ns // 12
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0","1 ns", "freeze",
"5 ns",1); // 13
end

$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", , "deposit", "3 ns", 1); // 14
#100; // 100ns // 15
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "0x0", , "freeze", , 1); // 17
#50; // 150ns // 18
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node", "1", , "freeze","5 ns", 1); // 19
#10; // 160ns // 2
#10; // 170ns // 21
#2; // 172ns // 22
$hdl_xmr_force("<hier>.dest.node","0","2 ns","deposit",
"3 ns",1); // 23
#10; // 182ns // 24

Line1 and line14 force the same dest_node with two force calls at the same time to occur
at the same time from two different scopes. Here, the order of execution is indeterministic
and hence the prevailing force is unpredictable.

Line3 and line17 force the same dest_node with two force calls at the same time of
100ns to occur at the same time from two different scopes. Here, the order of execution is
indeterministic and hence the prevailing force is unpredictable.
Line5 and line19 force the same dest_node with two force calls at the same time of
150ns to occur at the same time from two different scopes. Here, the order of execution
is indeterministic but it does not matter as both scopes are forcing the same value of 1 on
dest_node.
Line7 is a call from one scope to force src.pin on dest.node at 160ns and there is
no force from the second scope at that time. Hence, no conflicts and dest.node get
scheduled to get forced with the current value of the node src.pin at the end of current
time step to be canceled in 3ns.
Line9 is a call from one scope to force 1 on dest.node at 170ns and there is no force from
the second scope at that time. Hence, no conflicts and dest.node get scheduled to get
forced with 1 at the end of 175ns to be canceled at 178ns.
At 172ns, the second scope makes a force call for dest.node to occur at 174ns that
is prior to the previous scheduled force to occur at 175ns. This is a scheduler issue to
resolve these conflicting events that has nothing to do with different scopes.
Remaining force calls for both scopes are handled by the scheduler.
The hdl_xmr_release() Procedure and the $hdl_xmr_release
System Task
Use the hdl_xmr_release() procedure or $hdl_xmr_release() system task
to release the force applied to an existing VHDL or Verilog destination. You can
use hdl_xmr_release() or $hdl_xmr_release() to any objects forced using
hdl_xmr_force() or $hdl_xmr_release(), UI or the force commands in the design.
hdl_xmr_release works the same as the Verilog release command. These signal release
functions can be called concurrently or sequentially from a VHDL architecture (For
example: a testbench), a process or from any Verilog scope where a system call can be
made. Once the signal is released using hdl_xmr_release, the expected behavior of the
released node is as follows:
• If the destination node is of type VHDL signal and if there is no driver on the destination
node, then the node is forced to U.
• If the destination node is of type Verilog wire and if there is no driver on the destination
node, then the node is forced to Z.
• If the destination node is of type Verilog reg and if there is no driver on the destination
node, then the node retains the current value until future evaluations.

• If there is a $hdl_xmr connection or any other drivers on the node, then future
evaluations causes the corresponding driver or drivers to drive this released node with
a resolved value.
• If there is no force and also a direct connection, then hdl_xmr_release removes any
hdl_xmr_force on that node and the node is scheduled for a re-evaluation, so that the
driver’s value may get resolved to drive this destination node.
Using the hdl_xmr_release() Procedure
To use the hdl_xmr_force procedure in your VHDL code, include the following library
declarations along with other required library declarations:
use work.sigdecl.all;
library synopsys;
use synopsys.hdl_xmr_pkg.all;
hdl_xmr_release (" destination_object", [ verbose]);
destination_object: destination_object could be a VHDL signal or a Verilog register.
Specify an absolute path or a relative path to the object. VCS issues a warning message if
the destination_object does not exist or not specified.
Verilog nets are read-only by default. Therefore Verilog nets cannot be used as
destination objects. To specify Verilog nets as destination objects, you should
turn on the write capability on these nets using a tab file.
verbose: If the argument is not specified then the default value is 0, otherwise possible
integer values are 0 or 1. Value 0 indicates no verbosity, and value 1 enables verbosity.
Set the environment variable LD_LIBRARY_PATH to include libhdlxmr.so file as shown
below:
% setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VCS_HOME/{ARCH}/ \
lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
Analysis
% vlogan [ vlogan_options] file2.v file3.v file4.v
( Analyze all Verilog files except the top-level Verilog file)
% vhdlan [ vhdlan_options] file5.vhd file6.vhd
(The VHDL bottom-most entity first, then move up in order)

Elaboration
% vcs -debug_access+all +vpi [ vcs_options] entity
Simulation
% simv [ simv_options]
In this example, the hdl_xmr_release() procedure calls are used to release the forced
signals data and reset when the release_flag signal is set to 1. Since the verbose option
is turned on, by specifying 1, both calls send a message to the transcript stating signal
name and the time it was released.
use work.sigdecl.all;
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
library synopsys;
use synopsys.hdl_xmr_pkg.all;

entity testbench is

architecture only of testbench is
signal release_flag : std_logic;
stim_design : process

wait until release_flag = '1';
hdl_xmr_release("top/dut/data", 1);
hdl_xmr_release("top/dut/reset", 1);

end process stim_design;

signals data and reset when the release_flag signal is set to 1.

Using the $hdl_xmr_release() System Task
$hdl_xmr_release ( destination_object, [ verbose]);
destination_object: destination_object could be a VHDL signal or a Verilog register.
Specify an absolute path or a relative path to the object. VCS generates a warning
message if the destination_object does not exist or is not specified.
Verilog nets are read-only by default. Therefore, Verilog nets cannot be used as
destination objects. To specify Verilog nets as destination objects, you should
turn on write capability on these nets using a tab file.
verbose: If the argument is not specified then the default value is 0, otherwise, possible
integer values are 0 or 1. The value 0 indicates no verbosity and value 1 enables
verbosity.

Using hdl_xmr Through SPICE Designs in VCS-PrimeSim XA
Cosimulation
The
hdl_xmr callsSPICE designs
hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force and hdl_xmr_release functionalities support SPICE
designs. The path to source object or destination object can go through the SPICE
hierarchy.
This feature is supported in SystemVerilog-SPICE, Mixed HDL-SPICE flow and SV-Mixed
HDL-SPICE flows
For SPICE designs, the value is treated as voltage.
Supported Data Types
The following are the data types that are supported:
• Nettype scalars
• Nettype vectors
• Index of SV nettype arrays
• Array of nettypes
In Verilog or VHDL, the $hdl_xmr/hdl_xmr calls can be specified in the following format:
Verilog Scope:
$hdl_xmr(source_object, destination_object, verbose);

$hdl_xmr_force(destination_object, valueOrNode, rel_time,
force_type, cancel_time, verbose);

$hdl_xmr_release(destination_object, verbose);
VHDL Scope:
hdl_xmr(source_object, destination_object, verbose);

hdl_xmr_force(destination_object, valueOrNode, rel_time,
force_type, cancel_time, verbose);

hdl_xmr_release(destination_object, verbose);
Specifying the Hierarchy

The path to source object and destination object can go through SPICE hierarchy. The
hierarchy path specification when denoting the source and/or destination nodes must
always consist of / or . or : separating the modules of the hierarchy and should not have
a combination of these formats.
$hdl_xmr from Verilog hdl_xmr from VHDL
Using absolute paths
$hdl_xmr("/top/i1/reset", "/top/h1");

$hdl_xmr_force(":top:i1:reset","1","10
ns","freeze","20 ns",0);

$hdl_xmr_release("top.i1.reset");
hdl_xmr("/top/i1/reset",
"/top/i1/h1");

hdl_xmr_force(":top:i1:reset","1","10
ns","freeze","20 ns",0);

hdl_xmr_release("top.i1.reset");
Using relative paths
$hdl_xmr("i1/reset", "h1");

$hdl_xmr_force("i1:reset","1","10
ns","freeze","20 ns",0);

$hdl_xmr_release("i1.reset");
hdl_xmr("i1/reset", "h1");

hdl_xmr_force("i1:reset","1","10
ns","freeze","20 ns",0);

hdl_xmr_release("i1.reset");
Using hdl_xmr and $hdl_xmr
The $hdl_xmr() (or hdl_xmr() in VHDL scope) connects two signals specified in the
argument list. With each value change the value of the source_object gets deposited on
the destination_object.
$hdl_xmr(source_object, destination_object, verbose);
hdl_xmr(source_object, destination_object, verbose);
The following table provides the description of these arguments.
Argument Details
source_object The source_object is a hierarchical path specified as a string.
A full hierarchical path (or relative path with reference to the
calling block) to an existing VHDL signal or Verilog register/net
or a SPICE node can be specified. The path can contain any
hierarchy including SPICE hierarchy.

Argument Details
destination_object The destination_object is a hierarchical path specified as
a string. The destination_object can include the SPICE
hierarchy. The destination_object cannot be a SPICE
node. This is because PrimeSim XA does not support deposit.
A full hierarchical path (or relative path with reference to
the calling block) to an existing VHDL signal or Verilog
register or SystemVerilog (SV) register can be specified. The
destination_object cannot be a SV nettype as deposit is not
supported on SV nettype.
verbose The verbose is an optional argument to the hdl_xmr call.The
possible integer values are 0 or 1.

register or SystemVerilog (SV) register can be specified. The
destination_object cannot be a SV nettype as deposit is not
supported on SV nettype.
verbose The verbose is an optional argument to the hdl_xmr call.The
possible integer values are 0 or 1. If the argument is not
specified, the default value 0 is used. Value 0 indicates no
verbosity, and value 1 enables verbosity. When verbosity is
1, every time a value of the source object is copied onto the
destination object, a message is displayed.
Using $hdl_xmr_force (Verilog) and hdl_xmr_force (VHDL)
The $hdl_xmr_force() or hdl_xmr_force() calls can be used to force a value on an
existing Verilog or SPICE or VHDL node. It allows you to force signals, from and at any
level of the design hierarchy from within the VHDL architecture or the Verilog module and
from any scope from where the standard defined system functions can be called. The
hdl_xmr_force() procedure works similar to the Verilog force command. A status is
returned from this function, which can be used to control the flow of the code.
$hdl_xmr_force(destination_object, value, rel_time,
force_type, cancel_period, verbose);
The following table provides the description of these arguments
Argument Details
destination_object The destination_object is a hierarchical path specified as
a string. A full hierarchical path (or relative path with reference
to the calling block) to an existing VHDL signal or Verilog
register/net or SV nettype or a SPICE node can be specified.
The path can contain any hierarchy including SPICE hierarchy.
value The actual value is the value to which the destination_object
is to be forced. The value should be specified within quotes.
The specified value must be appropriate for the type and can be
specified in any valid syntax for any radix as supported by the
language.

Argument Details
rel_time The rel_time argument can of type string and must be
specified using the following format:
"<time><space><unit>".
Where, <time> is an integer and <unit> is a supported unit
type.Specify a time relative to the current simulation time for the
force to occur. The actual time when the force gets applied is
equal to Current Time + Rel Time.Time should be specified in
units such as 3ps or 5ns with a space between the integer and
the unit. If the time specified is less than simulation precision,
the force happens at the end of current time step.If the time is
specified without a unit, an error message is displayed and 0 is
returned as status.
force_type The force_type argument can be of type string. It is used to
specify the type of force that will be applied. The value can be
"default", "deposit", "drive" or "freeze".For a SPICE target, only
"freeze" is supported.
cancel_period The cancel_period argument can be of type string and must be
specified using the following format:
"<time><space> <unit>"
Where, <time> is an integer and <unit> is a supported unit
type.
Specify a time relative to the current simulation time for the force
to cancel. Cancellation occurs at the last simulation delta cycle
of a time unit.
The actual time when force gets canceled is equal to Current
Time + Cancel Time.Time should be specified in units, such as
"3 ps" or "5 ns" with a space between the integer and the unit.
If the time specified is less than simulation precision, the forced
cancelation occurs at the end of current time step.Cancel Time
is irrelevant to the 'deposit' type of forces and if specified, the
cancel time is ignored.
If the cancel time specified is less than the rel-time for applying
the force, then the cancel time is ignored and the force is never
canceled.
verbose The “verbose” is an optional argument to the hdl_xmr call.The
possible integer values are 0 or 1. If the argument is not
specified, the default value 0 is used. Value 0 indicates no
verbosity, and value 1 enables verbosity. When verbosity is
1, every time a value of the source object is copied onto the
destination object, a message is displayed.
Repeated calls to $hdl_xmr_force or hdl_xmr_force are allowed and the last call
prevails. If force calls at the same time has different relative times, then each force
executes at the corresponding future time. If more than one call to the same node gets
called at the same time and set to force at the same future time, the last call prevails. Note

that no warnings are issued about force calls that are overridden by subsequent force
calls.
The last force always prevails and this is applied to force through the code, through UCLI
or through $hdl_xmr_force()/hdl_xmr_force() interface.
Using $hdl_xmr_release (Verilog) and hdl_xmr_release (VHDL)
The $hdl_xmr_release() or hdl_xmr_release() calls release any force that is applied
to an existing VHDL or Verilog destination objects through hdl_xmr_force or all forces
from the designs or from the user interface.
The hdl_xmr_release call works similar to the Verilog release command. These signal
release functions can be called concurrently or sequentially in a process.
$hdl_xmr_release (destination_object, verbose);
The following table provides the description of these arguments.
Argument Details
destination_object The destination_object is a hierarchical path specified as a
string. A full hierarchical path (or relative path with reference to
the calling block) to an existing VHDL signal or Verilog register
or SV register or a SPICE node can be specified. The path can
contain any hierarchy including SPICE hierarchy. Target node
can be SPICE node.
If the destination object does not exist or if it is not specified, VCS
generates a warning message and returns value 0.
verbose The verbose is an optional argument to the hdl_xmr call.
The possible integer values are 0 or 1. If the argument is not
specified, the default value 0 is used. Value 0 indicates no
verbosity, and value 1 enables verbosity. When verbosity is
1, every time a value of the source object is copied onto the
destination object, a message is displayed.

title: 3 /top/dut/fifo/iptr[4] <fifo.v, 3>
text:
If the argument is not
specified, the default value 0 is used. Value 0 indicates no
verbosity, and value 1 enables verbosity. When verbosity is
1, every time a value of the source object is copied onto the
destination object, a message is displayed.
hdl_xmr_release does not require hdl_xmr_force to have been called. However, it
affects only if the node or the object is forced through hdl_xmr_force. At the end of
hdl_xmr_release, the behavior of the released node is as follows:
• If there is no other driver on the destination node, the node becomes Z if it is of type
wire in the Verilog scope.
• If there is no other driver on the destination node, the node retains its current value
until future evaluations if it is of type reg in the Verilog scope.

• If there is no other driver on the destination node, the node becomes U if it is of type
signal in the VHDL scope.
• If there is a UCLI force or a $hdl_xmr_force or a code force on the destination node,
hdl_xmr_release removes any force attached to that node and the behavior is as
mentioned previously.
• If there is no force and if there is a direct connection, hdl_xmr_release removes any
hdl_xmr_force on that node and the node is scheduled for a re-evaluation, so that the
driver's value may get resolved to drive this destination node.
A2D or D2A Fidelity and Delta
In an HDL testbench and UCLI run scripts, hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force and UCLI force are
required on an analog target.
When a cell view is switched from a digital HDL view to an analog view the same hdl_xmr,
hdl_xmr_force or UCLI force must be applied to the analog target.
Correct digital to analog conversion must take place for a digital 0,1,X,Z force on what was
a digital target that has now changed to an analog target.
An auto vdd detection mechanism similar to that used for traditional interface element
thresholds and voltage swings must be used to automatically select voltage thresholds
and voltage swings for analog2digital conversions and digital2analog conversions required
for the hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force or UCLI force.
If the auto vdd methodology breaks down or fails, the voltage thresholds and swings
can be manually changed with the mixed signal control commands and the vcsAD.init
A new report file named runtime_interface_element.rpt is generated in the simv.msv
directory. The report file is generated and dynamically updated at runtime for any hdl_xmr,
hdl_xmr_force/release or UCLI force/release on an analog target. The applicable auto-
generated voltage swings, thresholds and options are recorded in the report file.
Commands and options generated in the runtime_interface_element.rpt file can be
used, copied and pasted to use in the mixed signal control file (vcsAD.init) to change or
modify any auto-generated voltage swings or thresholds or options.
When a hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force/release or UCLI force/release is used on an analog
target, a runtime notice message is issued with information on the options that are used
for any analog2digital or digital2analog conversion, electrical2real or real2electrical
conversion.
This feature is enabled by the default mixed-signal commands. For information about
these analog mixed-signal commands, see the Discovery AMS: Mixed-Signal Simulation
User Guide.

Fast Compilation
The VCS compile-time performance optimizations called
compilationfastfast compilation
fast compilation that you can use
to reduce compile-time for your design (and therefore overall turnaround time). You can
enable fast compilation using the -fastcomp compile-time option.
There are two levels of fast compilation, specified by the -fastcomp=0 and -fastcomp=1
compile-time options.
• -fastcomp=0 is same as the -fastcomp option (without the argument). This is the
recommended fast compilation mode. This option accelerates the compile time by
suppressing internal optimizations in VCS front end with moderate simulation time
degradation.
• -fastcomp=1 is same as the -fastcomp=all option. This option applies more
aggressive compile-time performance than the default mode. However, the simulation
time degradation is high compared to the default mode.
The above options are a trade-off between the compile time and the simulation time. You
can choose the option based on which performance is more important to you.

Guard Check Utility
Guard Check Utility
The Guard Check utility checks all source files parsed by VCS (design files, header files,
testbench files, library files, and so on.) for the presence of Guard statements and the
characteristics of the guard directives. It reports the characteristics of the guards in the
parsed file.
A guard directive is a combination of an `ifndef compiler directive and a `define
compiler directive with the same guard name.
`ifndef <guard_name>
`define <guard_name> <optional_value>
This is the recommended option for the Guard Check utility.
It is also defined by a combination of an `ifdef, `else compiler directive, and a `define
compiler directive with the same guard name.
`ifdef <guard_name>
`else
`define <guard_name> <optional_value>
Duplicate guard directives exclude processing of the other guard. For example, a
duplicated file guard directive which has the same guard name _VH_GUARD_1_ is shared
by two different files File_1.v and File_2.v. The shared guard name creates a condition
where inclusion of one of the files excludes processing of the other file. The file is
processed based on the other factors such as, file order of compilation, which may make
the process non-predictable across different tools.
To generate the data for the Guard Check utility, use the -gather_guard compile-time
option as follows:
% vcs <vcs options> <source.v> -gather_guard<dir> /

When the -gather_guard compile-time option is specified, the following three files are

• source_files: The name of each file processed during compilation (one per line).
• include_files: The name of each file read by a `include directive.
• cmd_defines: The name of all +define command line directives specified.

-gather_guard=<dir>, where <dir> is the name of the directory. If the directory name is
not specified, the default directory name Guards is used. This option allows different sets

Enhancing Vlogan Command to Compile Files into Multiple
Libraries
Invoking many vlogan commands (about hundreds to thousands) to analyze different files
takes a long time because of UNIX process invocation, command line processing, vlogan
initialization, license checkout, and so on.
To resolve this issue, VCS supports a job manifest file to specify libraries and option
files for each compilation job. Therefore, you can run many jobs by running fewer vlogan
commands.

Enhancing Vlogan Command to Compile Files into Multiple Libraries
The use model to specify libraries and option files for each compilation job is as follows:
% vlogan -jm job_manifest_file [other_vlogan_option …]
The -jm option specifies a job manifest file. Jobs are run with the options on the command
line plus the ones in the job manifest file. The job manifest file has the following clauses:
1. Global options clause
global_options: <global_options_file> [global_options_file …]
global_options specifies the option files that applies to all the jobs with -file option.
Here, you can specify multiple files separated with space.
2. Library clause
library <library_name>: <library_options_file> [library_options_file
…]
library specifies the option files for a library which are applied to a job with -f option.
Here, you can specify multiple files separated with space.
3. Number of parallel jobs clause
parallel_jobs: <positive_integer>
parallel_jobs specifies the number of jobs to run simultaneously.
The following example shows how the jobs runs in parallel.
Execute the following command:
% vlogan -jm job-manifest -full64
The content of the job_manifest_file is as follows:
parallel_jobs:2 // the number specifies the number of jobs to run
simultaneously
global_options: global.f global2.f
library LIB2: filelists/file_2 filelists/file_4
library LIB1: filelists/file_3

Support Multi-Dimensional Array of Interface/Module Instances and Interface ports
The contents of global.f and global2.f file is as follows:
-kdb +v2k +libverbose -sverilog -V -incr_vlogan
The contents of file_2, file_3 and file_4 file are as follows:
+incdir+test +define+A +define+B -assert svaext -kdb -timescale=1ns/1ps
+libext+*.v+*.sv+*.vs +librescan +v2k
test/Test.v
test/new_top.v
The options available in file_2 is applicable only to the sources available in
file_2. Similarly, the options available in file_3 and file_4 is applicable only
to sources available in file_3 and file_4 respectively.
You cannot specify the compilation order in job-manifest file.

Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
VCS allows you to set black box by module-based and instance-based with value of the
output ports of black boxes.
VCS ignores and removes the following contexts:
• Bind directive failed to apply
• Assertions crossing black box boundary
This feature is supported using +optconfigfile option.
The following are the use models of this feature:
• Module-level black-box:
module {comma_separated_module_list} {blackbox} [{0|1}];
comma_separated_module_list ::=
[library_name.]module_name {,[library_name.]module_name }
◦ library_name is case-insensitive
◦ When library_name is omitted, and VCS bricks the module once the module_name
is matched.
◦ Both library_name and module_name can use wildcard, ‘*’ and ‘?’, and can use
Verilog escaped identifier.
◦ [{0|1}] specifies the value to tie on the output port(s).
module {middle2, sub*} {blackbox} {1};

module {MYLIB.modB, MY*.modC} {blackbox};
• Instance-level black box:
instance {comma_separated_instance_list} {blackbox} [{0|1}];
comma_separated_instance_list::=
hieracrchical_identifier{, hieracrchical_identifier}

Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
hierarchical_identifier specifies the Verilog hierarchical identifier, each identifier
can use wildcard, ‘*’ and ‘?’.
instance {top.m1.sub1, top.*.sub2} {blackbox};

instance {top.m*.sub1, top.\spe*s .sub2} {blackbox} {0};

instance {top.m*.sub3} {blackbox} {0};
When a module or instance matched any one of the rules, VCS black box this
module or instance. This feature cannot be used with -bboxModule and VCS
reports error message.
Following are the list of scenarios or usecases supported by this feature:
• Black box module replacement.
• Tie value to the output port.
• Remove assertions with hierarchical references crossing boundary.
• VCS suppresses and ignores all bind failures if any module or instance is bricked.
• VCS shows the following diagnostic messages on compilation log:
◦ Module/instances replaced by the black box and its tied value of output ports.
◦ Assertions being removed due to having unresolved hierarchical references.
◦ Bind statement being ignored.
These messages are note messages([Note]).

Enabling and Using SystemVerilog 2023 Method Specifiers in
VCS
Starting with this release, SystemVerilog 2023 (SV'23) introduces the following new
method specifiers such as :initial, :extends, and :final. These specifiers give you
more control over class method declarations, helping you define how methods can be
overridden in class hierarchies. VCS now supports these specifiers when you enable the

SystemVerilog 2023 standard. This feature helps you write clearer, more robust object-
oriented code and catch errors related to method overriding at compile time.
Usage
To use the new method specifiers, you must enable the SystemVerilog 2023 standard
in VCS. Use -std=1800-2023 VCS compile-time option to enable SystemVerilog 2023
standard in VCS.
To write class methods with specifiers, you can use the following method specifiers:
• :initial
Marks a method as the initial implementation in the class hierarchy.
• :extends
Marks a method as an extension (override) of a virtual method in a base class.
• :final
Prevents further overriding of the method in derived classes.
The LRM does not allow the following:
• Using both :initial and :extends on the same method.
• Marking a pure virtual method as :final.
The SV'23 LRM supports the following syntax for the method specifiers:
function_declaration ::=
function [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 [ lifetime ]
function_body_declaration

function_prototype ::=
function [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 data_type_or_void
function_identifier [ ( [ tf_port_list ] ) ]

task_declaration ::=
task [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 [ lifetime ]
task_body_declaration

task_prototype ::=
task [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 task_identifier
[ ( [ tf_port_list ] ) ]

dynamic_override_specifiers ::= [ initial_or_extends_specifier ]
[ final_specifier ]
initial_or_extends_specifier ::= : initial | : extends

final_specifier ::= : final
According to SV'23 LRM, the dynamic_override_specifiers is applicable on
method declarations inside a non-interface class scope.
The extends specifier imply that the method is virtual. therefore, virtual
keyword is optional when using the extends specifier.
Example 12 Normal Usage
//normal_usage.v

virtual function :initial void func;

Enabling SystemVerilog 2023 Static type(this) Support in VCS
Starting with this release, VCS allows you to use the type(this) operator inside class
static functions in SystemVerilog, as defined by the SystemVerilog 2023 (SV'23) standard.
Previously, type(this) was only available in non-static functions. With this enhancement,
VCS now parses and displays error if type(this) is used incorrectly in static functions.
Usage
Use the following option to enable SV'23 static type(this) support:
-std=1800-2023
The type(this) points to the type of the enclosing class of the static method.

class registry #(type T=int);
static function type(this) get(); // calls to get() return a
registry #(T)
static type(this) m_inst;
if (m_inst == null) m_inst = new();
return m_inst;

registry #(int) obj = new();

$display("return type of function get is: %p",
$typename(obj.get()));
end

Static Bug Finding in VCS
Static defects like the following can be functional hazards:
• Glitches: glitches on asynchronous paths, Multicycle Paths (MCP), and DFT Logic and
P2P.
• Reset Domain Crossing (RDC): metastability caused by asynchronous reset assertions
VCS leverages the results of the structural analysis from VC SpyGlass to perform dynamic
SDC verification. Using this feature, you can inject Delay/X at RTL to improve confidence
for RDC/Glitch sign off and verify the correctness of RTL level by providing SDC dumped
by VC Spyglass to VCS.
VCS uses the database generated by VC SpyGlass and determines whether a glitch or
RDC property can fail. The database is in the SDC format that contains both user written
constraints for example, MCP/FP/GC, and so on. and the property data.
This feature helps you with the following:
• Identify unsafe RDC using dynamic simulation.
• Report simulation failure in the downstream circuit caused by an RDC.
• Accurate classification of rising and falling glitches (010, 101 type).
• Checking RDC, Flop-to-Flop glitches, and Point-to-Point glitches.
The following diagram gives a high level overview of the Static Bug Finding flow

How Glitch Detection Works
Figure 11 Static Bug Finding Flow
How Glitch Detection Works
• First, VC SpyGlass structurally verifies point-to-point glitches and reset path glitches
as defined. The tool outputs a Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) file with the
verified paths, which can be used by VCS. To specify glitches for verification, use the
set_point2point_glitch command in the input SDC file provided to VC SpyGlass as
shown in the following example.
set_point2point_glitch -from [get_ports in1] -to [get_pins FF1/D] =>
P2P glitch path

How Glitch Detection Works
set_point2point_glitch -from [get_ports in1] -to [get_pins FF1/RST] =>
reset path glitch
For clock-domain crossing(CDC) glitch verification, it is sufficient to provide
set_clock_groups command in the input SDC as the following:
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clk1} -group {clk2}
Glitch verification is also supported on false paths and multicycle paths as specified.
To perform structural verification of glitches, VC SpyGlass uses the check_glitch
command. For CDC glitches, the check_cdc command is required. If the include_sdc
option is specified, the write_property command generates a glitch SDC file for
dynamic verification in VCS.
For Glitch Verification:
write_property -app glitch -type <p2p/mcp/fp/all> -file <output SDC>
-include_sdc
For CDC Glitch Verification:
write_property -app cdc -type glitch -file <output SDC> -include_sdc
Output SDC is generated for VCS consumption in SBF flow. VCS uses X-injection in
this flow to check if the glitch is detectable.
The following is an example VC SpyGlass script for running the static analysis phase of
the SBF flow:
set_app_var enable_glitch true --> Enables glitch checks
set_app_var enable_dc_naming_style true

<analyze design>
elaborate <top>

read_sdc <input sdc> --> Read input SDC with
set_point2point_glitch/set_clock_groups/FP/MCP commands

report_glitch

write_property -app glitch -type p2p -file <output SDC> -include_sdc

For more information about the set_point2point_glitch, check_glitch, and
write_property commands, refer the VC SpyGlass User Guide VC SpyGlass Clock
Domain Crossing User Guide.
• In VCS, for a n-source glitch path, an X value is injected at all the sources and the
destination is observed. If this X value reaches the destination, it implies that X is
observable, and the glitch can reach the destination. If it is not, it implies that the glitch

How Glitch Detection Works
is blocked and, therefore, the circuit is not prone to glitches. The glitch 101 or 010
determines the propagation of the X value.
• Additionally, you need to check if the current value at the output is the same as the
previous value.
The circuit is considered prone to glitches when both the above specified
conditions are met.
Figure 12 Example Circuit with Possible Glitches
Here, X is injected at A, B and C. X is observable as the outcome of the logic. The
simulation values are, thereafter, computing the previous cycle values, where p is the
previous cycle value. The AND gate output is 0, as Ap=0. When Cp=1, the output is 1.
Upon computing the current cycle values, it is observed that the AND gate output is 1, as
A=1, B=1. When C=0, the output is 1.
This case results in a glitch as the conditions are met. X is observable at the output and
the simulation value also does not change.
Figure 13 Example Circuit with no Glitches

How RDC Checking Works
Here, X is injected at A. X is observable as the outcome of the logic. The simulation value
changes because the previous cycle value at output is 0, where, Ap=0 and B=1. The value
of the output at the current cycle is 1, where Ap=1 and B=1. Therefore, this case does not
result in a glitch.
.
Figure 14 Example Circuit with no Glitches
Here, X is injected at A. However as B is at 0, X is not observable at the output. Therefore,
this case does not result in a glitch.
How RDC Checking Works
VC Spyglass performs structural Reset Domain Crossing (RDC) verification. Any RDC
violations are reported as source-destination pairs in the output Synopsys Design
Constraints (SDC) file. These SDC files can then be used for further verification in VCS.
Provide the Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) file to VC SpyGlass with the reset
defined using the create_reset command as shown in the following example:
create_reset rst1 -async -sense low
Use the check_rdc command to perform Reset Domain Crossing (RDC) checks. To
generate an SDC file containing RDC paths, use the write_property command as you
would use for glitch verification.
write_property -app rdc -type rdc -file <output SDC> -include_sdc
The Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) output is used by VCS in the SBF flow. In this
flow, VCS applies X-injection to determine whether a Reset Domain Crossing (RDC)
violation is observable during simulation.
The following is an example VC SpyGlass script used to perform Reset Domain Crossing
(RDC) checks as part of the Static Bug Finding (SBF) flow.
set_app_var enable_rdc true --> Enables RDC checks

<analyze design>

How to Enable Glitch and RDC Verification in VCS SDC
elaborate <top>

<configure_rdc_corrupt> --> To configure RDC corruption checks s
read_sdc <input SDC> --> Read input SDC with create_reset commands

check_rdc
report_rdc

write_property -app rdc -type rdc -file <output SDC> -include_sdc -- >
Dump output SDC with set_rdc_path commands for VCS consumption
For more information about the create_reset, check_rdc, configure_rdc_corrupt
and write_property commands, refer VC SpyGlass user guide VC SpyGlass® Reset
Domain Crossing User Guide.
How to Enable Glitch and RDC Verification in VCS SDC
VCS provides the following compile-time option to enable the static bug finding flow:
% vcs -sdc=static_bug_finding
• When you use the -sdc=static_bug_finding compile option, all other
SDC verifications (MCP, False Path, Asynchronous Path, and Max delay)
are turned off.
• VCS injects uncertainty (X or retain previous value) during RDC violation.
You can use the -sdc=verify_rdc_path:bool|x runtime option to control
uncertainty value.
• The -sdc=max_destination_violation:<N> runtime option is applicable
for RDC and glitch violations.
Usage Information for Glitch and RDC Verification in VCS SDC
The following is the usage information for glitch in VCS SDC:

-sdc=<file_name>
%simv -l sim.log

Usage Information for Glitch and RDC Verification in VCS SDC

Calculation of Glitch Delay and Pulse Width:
By default, the glitch delay and pulse width are supported as a fraction of the clock cycle.
VCS-SBF Glitch Delay and Pulse Width by Clock Period
The following switch defines the fraction of clock cycle after which a glitch check should be
performed:
-sdc= glcapdel:<N(in float)>
-sdc=glcapdel:.3
clk_period = 10 ns
The glitch check is performed at the destination after 3 ns of the source change.

The following switch defines the fraction of clock period for which a glitch is inserted in the
destination:
-sdc= glxdelta:<N(in float)>
Ex: -sdc=glxdelta:.3
Clk_period = 10ns
Glitch is inserted for 3ns.
Virtual clocks are also supported in VCS-SBF, Glitch violation is as per the time
period of a virtual clock.
The VCS-SBF Clock Glitch identifies all potential post-simulation clock glitches during
the RTL-level phase. The goal is to inject glitches in RTL simulation to cause simulation
failures, enabling designers to detect and address clock glitch circuits earlier in the design
process.
• Detects all possible post-simulation clock glitches during RTL simulation.
• Ensures glitches are injected and cause simulation failures, so issues are not missed.
• Avoids injecting false glitches that could cause incorrect simulation failures.
Clock glitch check in VC Static
The following scenario explains how to detect glitches in a clock path when the select pin
of a multiplexer (MUX) changes, such as during clock mode selection.

Figure 15 Example 1
VC Static generates the following glitch command for all clock merging cases:
SETUP_SYNC_CLOCK_OVERLAP*,
SETUP_ASYNC_CLOCK_OVERLAP*
set_glitch_path -from <sig_list> -to <gate_output> -type clock
Here,
sig_list: All first-level RTL signals in the fan-in of the MUX select pin.
gate_output: Output of the MUX. If the MUX output is an internal net, the first RTL net in
the fanout is reported.
• If async or sync clock overlap occurs on a combinational gate other than a
MUX, VC Static does not generate a set_glitch_path command for that
overlap.
Generated SDC Example:
Glitch paths are generated at the VC Static stage, and the SDC includes an
extra field to mark it as a clock path glitch:
set_glitch_path -from {d} -to {clk_mux1/O} -to_clock {clk} -type
clock

Glitch Identification in VCS SBF
When the select pin toggles, X propagates to the MUX output following the X-propagation
mechanism. A glitch violation is reported at the MUX output. The glitch remains until the
glclkdel time elapses.
Figure 16 Glitch Detection at Clock MUX Output
At the VC static stage, the tool dumps {mux_out} as the -to pin in the set_glitch_path
command. The glitch is detected by VCS SBF at the output of the clock MUX (mux_out).
For Figure 16, the following set_glitch_path command is dumped by VC Static:
create_clock -name CLK1 -period 10 [get_ports {clk1}]
create_clock -name CLK2 -period 10 [get_ports {clk2}]
set_clock_groups -name CLK1_1 -asynchronous -group {CLK1 } -group
{CLK2 }
set_glitch_path -from { En } -to { mux_out } -type clock
Pulse insertion:
When the select pin En toggles, a glitch pulse is injected at the output of the clock MUX
mux_out. The corruption is done for the glclkdel duration, and it gets cleared after this
time.

Case 1: If MUX input(s) changes during the corruption time glclkdel such that
both MUX inputs have opposite values, then X remains at mux_out.
Case 2: If MUX input(s) changes such that both inputs have the same value,
then mux_out gets the input value and the corruption stops.
For case 2, use the runtime switch -sdc=glxprop for uniform X injection on the mux output
throughout the entire glclkdel duration. This switch enables Xprop (xmerge) for the
entire duration of glclkdel, starting from the time of select line change. If this switch is
not used, then Xprop (xmerge) is enabled only at the time of select line change and
mux_out follows the vmerge behavior after this time instance. This switch might have
impact on the design simulation behavior and should be used accordingly.
In both Case 1 and Case 2, Verdi marking is visible for complete duration of glclkdel.
The following Glitch violation messages are reported for mux_out at runtime:
[1] GLITCH-VIOLATION @Time: 21, @Type: clock. TO testbench.dut.mux_out
|--> FROM:: testbench.dut.En changed @ Time: 21(set_glitch_path,
report_glitch.sdc:6)
Output:
Figure 17 Glitch Injection at MUX Output
• The select line signals are dumped at the register level, not at the
expression level.
For a clock multiplexer such as clk_mux = (A & B) ? clk1 : clk2 , the
source signals are {A, B} and not the expression (A & B) .
• There is no Boolean corruption for clock glitch cases.
• The option -sdc=glcapdel is not supported for set_glitch_path
commands with -type clock .

• A new runtime switch -sdc=glclkdel:<N> is added, where N is the fraction
of the clock period for which the glitch needs to be injected at mux output.
• The use of -sdc=glxdelta:<N> for clock glitches has been eliminated, as
long-duration delay injection is not needed for propagation to flops.
• X propagation from select to mux output and from mux output to downward
hierarchy follows the Xprop mechanism.
• Verdi marking on mux output is done for the entire -sdc=glclkdel:<N>
duration, regardless of input changes to the mux.
• Clock mux output should not be given as a P2P glitch destination; an error is
reported if the input clocks to this mux, are defined in SDC.
• Only Boolean changes ( 0→1, 1→0) in mux select line are considered for clock
glitch.
• If select changes while mux output is already X, no violation or glitch
injection is reported.
• For UDPs, penultimate module pins going into the UDP instance are
dumped from VC Static.
• Multiplexer outputs have multiple drivers.
• The -sdc=no_x runtime option has no impact on clock glitch paths.
• MDANETs and MDAs as select or mux output are not currently supported.
• For UDP muxes, the X injection time at mux output is for -sdc=glclkdel
value, regardless of any input/select changes.
• Both destination and source of set_glitch_path command should be
present in the same module.

Limiting Glitch Checks on Specific Clock Paths
Figure 18 Limiting Glitch Checks on Specific Clock Paths
To limit glitch detection to specific clock paths going to a particular clock pin, use the
following command in SDC file given as input to VC Static:
set_point2point_glitch -to [get_pins <flop_name>/CP] -type clock
set_point2point_glitch -to [get_pins q_reg/CP] -type clock
The above command limits the glitch checks on clock paths ending at the destination
q_reg/CP.
• With -type clock , only CP pin of the endpoint is supported in
set_point2point_glitch command.
• Other options, except -through <cells> are not supported and are
reported for sanity.
You can also limit glitch checks on clock paths when clock merging happens inside a
specific cell or module. Use the following command in SDC file given as input to VC Static
to specify the cell or module where the clock merging occurs. The -through objects refers
to the muxes involved in the violation
set_point2point_glitch -through [get_cells -hier Module|LibCell] -type
clock

If you give following input to VC Static:
set_point2point_glitch -through [get_cells clk_mux1] -type clock
Then VC Static tool generates the following command:
set_glitch_path -from d2 -to clk_mux1/O -type clock
• When using -type clock with set_point2point_glitch command, only
cells are allowed with the -throughoption. Other values with -through are
not supported.
• If you use both -toand -through options in set_point2point_glitch
command, the tool checks only the paths that satisfy both conditions.
To exclude certain cells from clock glitch checking, use the following command:
configure_glitch_free_cells –path_type CLOCK –ignore_instances
<cell_name>
You must exclude the cell cell_name from clock glitch checking.
If you provide the following input to VC Static:
configure_glitch_free_cells –path_type CLOCK –ignore_instances
<clk_gfree_mux >
VC Static tool generates the following commands:
set_glitch_path -from d2 -to clk_mux1/O -type clock
set_glitch_path -from d3 -to clk_rtlc/O -type clock

Reporting Signals Subjected to Glitches in the Clock Path
Figure 19 Reporting Signals with Glitches in the Clock Path
For verifying glitches in the clock select path, VC Static tool generates the following glitch
command for every INTEGRITY_CLOCK_ENABLE_GLITCH violation:
set_glitch_path -from <source> -to <reconv_gate_output> -to_clock
<destination clock name>
If reconv_gate_output is an internal net, then VC Static tool dumps the first RTL net in
the fanout.
Such set_glitch_path commands having -to_clock are supported by VCS SBF as
normal P2P commands.

The SDC file dumped from VC Static needs to be passed to VCS SBF in compile time
options. You must provide the -sdc=static_bug_finding option .
The runtime switch -sdc=glclkdel:<N> is used to control the duration of X-injection at

For Example:

tb.v -sdc=report_glitch.sdc,current_design:top,print_violation,

run.log -sdc=glclkdel:.3
Support for -sdc=glmaxdel Option in P2P Glitch Multi-Clock
Scenarios
In VCS, when a point-to-point (p2p) glitch command references multiple clocks, the tool
must select a clock period to compute the glitch delay for checking and injection. By
default, VCS selects the smallest-period (fastest) clock, ensuring conservative glitch
detection. However, for certain validation scenarios—such as worst-case or maximum-
delay analysis—it is desirable to use the largest-period (slowest) clock instead.
The -sdc=glmaxdel simulation-time option changes the clock selection rule for p2p
glitch commands referencing multiple clocks.
When a p2p glitch command uses more than one clock, the tool must choose one clock
period to calculate the glitch delay for checking and injection.
Clock Selection Behavior
• Default Behavior:
◦ The tool selects the smallest-period (fastest) clock among those specified.
◦ Glitch delay is computed using this period.
◦ No user action required.
• Behavior with -sdc=glmaxdel option:
◦ The tool selects the largest-period clock among those specified.
◦ Glitch delay is computed using this maximum period.
◦ Enable this behavior by passing -sdc=glmaxdel at simulation time.

Support for -sdc=glmaxdel Option in P2P Glitch Multi-Clock Scenarios
Usage Example:
Suppose a p2p glitch command references three clocks: clk1 (10ns) , clk2 (20ns) ,
clk3 (30ns) .
p2p glitch command:
Figure 20 Clock periods
Default behavior (No Override):
Selected clock: clk1
- Period used: 10 ns
- Glitch delay: 10 ns
No special action is needed. The tool uses the fastest clock by default.
To enable Maximum-Period Selection, use -sdc=glmaxdel at simulation time to use the
maximum clock period for glitch delay calculation in p2p glitch scenarios.
With -sdc=glmaxdel option:
- Selected clock: clk3
- Period used: 30 ns
- Glitch delay: 30 ns

text:
Static Bug Finding in VCS
Static defects like the following can be functional hazards:
• Glitches: glitches on asynchronous paths, Multicycle Paths (MCP), and DFT Logic and
P2P.
• Reset Domain Crossing (RDC): metastability caused by asynchronous reset assertions
VCS leverages the results of the structural analysis from VC SpyGlass to perform dynamic
SDC verification. Using this feature, you can inject Delay/X at RTL to improve confidence
for RDC/Glitch sign off and verify the correctness of RTL level by providing SDC dumped
by VC Spyglass to VCS.
VCS uses the database generated by VC SpyGlass and determines whether a glitch or
RDC property can fail. The database is in the SDC format that contains both user written
constraints for example, MCP/FP/GC, and so on. and the property data.
This feature helps you with the following:
• Identify unsafe RDC using dynamic simulation.
• Report simulation failure in the downstream circuit caused by an RDC.
• Accurate classification of rising and falling glitches (010, 101 type).
• Checking RDC, Flop-to-Flop glitches, and Point-to-Point glitches.
The following diagram gives a high level overview of the Static Bug Finding flow

How Glitch Detection Works
Figure 11 Static Bug Finding Flow
How Glitch Detection Works
• First, VC SpyGlass structurally verifies point-to-point glitches and reset path glitches
as defined. The tool outputs a Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) file with the
verified paths, which can be used by VCS. To specify glitches for verification, use the
set_point2point_glitch command in the input SDC file provided to VC SpyGlass as
shown in the following example.
set_point2point_glitch -from [get_ports in1] -to [get_pins FF1/D] =>
P2P glitch path

reset path glitch
For clock-domain crossing(CDC) glitch verification, it is sufficient to provide
set_clock_groups command in the input SDC as the following:
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clk1} -group {clk2}
Glitch verification is also supported on false paths and multicycle paths as specified.
To perform structural verification of glitches, VC SpyGlass uses the check_glitch
command. For CDC glitches, the check_cdc command is required. If the include_sdc
option is specified, the write_property command generates a glitch SDC file for
dynamic verification in VCS.
For Glitch Verification:
write_property -app glitch -type <p2p/mcp/fp/all> -file <output SDC>
-include_sdc
For CDC Glitch Verification:
write_property -app cdc -type glitch -file <output SDC> -include_sdc
Output SDC is generated for VCS consumption in SBF flow. VCS uses X-injection in
this flow to check if the glitch is detectable.

the SBF flow:

How RDC Checking Works
VC Spyglass performs structural Reset Domain Crossing (RDC) verification. Any RDC
violations are reported as source-destination pairs in the output Synopsys Design
Constraints (SDC) file. These SDC files can then be used for further verification in VCS.
Provide the Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) file to VC SpyGlass with the reset
defined using the create_reset command as shown in the following example:
create_reset rst1 -async -sense low
Use the check_rdc command to perform Reset Domain Crossing (RDC) checks. To
generate an SDC file containing RDC paths, use the write_property command as you
would use for glitch verification.
write_property -app rdc -type rdc -file <output SDC> -include_sdc
The Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) output is used by VCS in the SBF flow. In this
flow, VCS applies X-injection to determine whether a Reset Domain Crossing (RDC)
violation is observable during simulation.

(RDC) checks as part of the Static Bug Finding (SBF) flow.

Calculation of Glitch Delay and Pulse Width:
By default, the glitch delay and pulse width are supported as a fraction of the clock cycle.
VCS-SBF Glitch Delay and Pulse Width by Clock Period
The following switch defines the fraction of clock cycle after which a glitch check should be
performed:
-sdc= glcapdel:<N(in float)>
-sdc=glcapdel:.3
clk_period = 10 ns
The glitch check is performed at the destination after 3 ns of the source change.

The following switch defines the fraction of clock period for which a glitch is inserted in the
destination:
-sdc= glxdelta:<N(in float)>
Ex: -sdc=glxdelta:.3
Clk_period = 10ns
Glitch is inserted for 3ns.
Virtual clocks are also supported in VCS-SBF, Glitch violation is as per the time
period of a virtual clock.
The VCS-SBF Clock Glitch identifies all potential post-simulation clock glitches during
the RTL-level phase. The goal is to inject glitches in RTL simulation to cause simulation
failures, enabling designers to detect and address clock glitch circuits earlier in the design
process.
• Detects all possible post-simulation clock glitches during RTL simulation.
• Ensures glitches are injected and cause simulation failures, so issues are not missed.
• Avoids injecting false glitches that could cause incorrect simulation failures.
Clock glitch check in VC Static
The following scenario explains how to detect glitches in a clock path when the select pin
of a multiplexer (MUX) changes, such as during clock mode selection.

Figure 15 Example 1
VC Static generates the following glitch command for all clock merging cases:
SETUP_SYNC_CLOCK_OVERLAP*,
SETUP_ASYNC_CLOCK_OVERLAP*
set_glitch_path -from <sig_list> -to <gate_output> -type clock
Here,
sig_list: All first-level RTL signals in the fan-in of the MUX select pin.
gate_output: Output of the MUX. If the MUX output is an internal net, the first RTL net in
the fanout is reported.
• If async or sync clock overlap occurs on a combinational gate other than a
MUX, VC Static does not generate a set_glitch_path command for that
overlap.
Generated SDC Example:
Glitch paths are generated at the VC Static stage, and the SDC includes an
extra field to mark it as a clock path glitch:
set_glitch_path -from {d} -to {clk_mux1/O} -to_clock {clk} -type
clock

Glitch Identification in VCS SBF
When the select pin toggles, X propagates to the MUX output following the X-propagation
mechanism. A glitch violation is reported at the MUX output. The glitch remains until the
glclkdel time elapses.
Figure 16 Glitch Detection at Clock MUX Output
At the VC static stage, the tool dumps {mux_out} as the -to pin in the set_glitch_path
command. The glitch is detected by VCS SBF at the output of the clock MUX (mux_out).
For Figure 16, the following set_glitch_path command is dumped by VC Static:
create_clock -name CLK1 -period 10 [get_ports {clk1}]
create_clock -name CLK2 -period 10 [get_ports {clk2}]
set_clock_groups -name CLK1_1 -asynchronous -group {CLK1 } -group
{CLK2 }
set_glitch_path -from { En } -to { mux_out } -type clock
Pulse insertion:
When the select pin En toggles, a glitch pulse is injected at the output of the clock MUX
mux_out. The corruption is done for the glclkdel duration, and it gets cleared after this
time.

Case 1: If MUX input(s) changes during the corruption time glclkdel such that
both MUX inputs have opposite values, then X remains at mux_out.
Case 2: If MUX input(s) changes such that both inputs have the same value,
then mux_out gets the input value and the corruption stops.
For case 2, use the runtime switch -sdc=glxprop for uniform X injection on the mux output
throughout the entire glclkdel duration. This switch enables Xprop (xmerge) for the
entire duration of glclkdel, starting from the time of select line change. If this switch is
not used, then Xprop (xmerge) is enabled only at the time of select line change and
mux_out follows the vmerge behavior after this time instance. This switch might have
impact on the design simulation behavior and should be used accordingly.
In both Case 1 and Case 2, Verdi marking is visible for complete duration of glclkdel.
The following Glitch violation messages are reported for mux_out at runtime:
[1] GLITCH-VIOLATION @Time: 21, @Type: clock. TO testbench.dut.mux_out
|--> FROM:: testbench.dut.En changed @ Time: 21(set_glitch_path,
report_glitch.sdc:6)
Output:
Figure 17 Glitch Injection at MUX Output
• The select line signals are dumped at the register level, not at the
expression level.
For a clock multiplexer such as clk_mux = (A & B) ? clk1 : clk2 , the
source signals are {A, B} and not the expression (A & B) .
• There is no Boolean corruption for clock glitch cases.
• The option -sdc=glcapdel is not supported for set_glitch_path
commands with -type clock .

title: 1 error
text:
• A new runtime switch -sdc=glclkdel:<N> is added, where N is the fraction
of the clock period for which the glitch needs to be injected at mux output.
• The use of -sdc=glxdelta:<N> for clock glitches has been eliminated, as
long-duration delay injection is not needed for propagation to flops.
• X propagation from select to mux output and from mux output to downward
hierarchy follows the Xprop mechanism.
• Verdi marking on mux output is done for the entire -sdc=glclkdel:<N>
duration, regardless of input changes to the mux.
• Clock mux output should not be given as a P2P glitch destination; an error is
reported if the input clocks to this mux, are defined in SDC.
• Only Boolean changes ( 0→1, 1→0) in mux select line are considered for clock
glitch.
• If select changes while mux output is already X, no violation or glitch
injection is reported.
• For UDPs, penultimate module pins going into the UDP instance are
dumped from VC Static.
• Multiplexer outputs have multiple drivers.
• The -sdc=no_x runtime option has no impact on clock glitch paths.
• MDANETs and MDAs as select or mux output are not currently supported.
• For UDP muxes, the X injection time at mux output is for -sdc=glclkdel
value, regardless of any input/select changes.
• Both destination and source of set_glitch_path command should be
present in the same module.
