starts with the next integer value after the one that (n-1)st bin ended with. For example,
consider the declaration of the following integral coverpoints:

bins b2 = {[2:3]};
bins b3 = {[4:5]};

In fact, there is no way with real numbers to specify an upper bound value for a bin that
is the "last number" before the left bound in the next bin. VCS allows specification of

If the bin boundaries are specified, then there is no loss of values between the bins. For
example, consider a value that is close to the boundary of b[0] and b[1]. If a value is less
than 0.000000003, it matches b[0]. If a value is greater than or equal to 0.000000003, it
matches b[1]. Also, a value cannot be monitored twice as each value in the range maps
to exactly one bin. For example, 0.000000003 is counted only in b[0] and not in b[1].
In these examples and in the creation of your own coverage models, it is important
to remember that with any comparisons of real values, the approximation due to the
floating point representation might result in unexpected coverage results. The intention
in the above example is that the value 0.0000000040 would be included in bin a[3], for
example. However, when that value is converted to a double float representation, its value
is rounded down to just under the value 0.0000000040. Therefore, if this value were seen
during simulation, bin a[2] would count the hit and not bin a[3].

Echo Features
The following are the Echo features:
• Support for Procedural Sampling
• Crosses With Non-Random Coverpoints

Support for Procedural Sampling
Echo analyzes procedural context to find targetable coverpoints. Echo supports the
following two aspects of procedural sampling:
• Sampling a non-random variable that is assigned with a targetable random variable.
Echo targets a non-random coverpoint when the non-random variable is assigned with
an expression of random variables.
• Randomizing a sibling class of sampled variables. At runtime, Echo collects targetable
holes from the sibling classes. Echo currently supports only one level of inheritance.
Note that all the variables involved in the expression of a coverpoint must be inherited
from the targeted base class.
Crosses With Non-Random Coverpoints
You can target a cross with non-random coverpoints using Echo. The cross must contain
at least one random coverpoint.
While collecting Echo targetable cross holes for non-random coverpoints, VCS ignores
cross-bin combinations with bins that are not sampled. However, if the non-random
coverpoint is properly sampled during the first few cycles, it is collected as a targetable
hole at the next collection.
If transition bins are involved in coverpoints that contribute crosses, VCS ignores the cross
bins (including transition bins) when collecting the holes.
For more information about Echo, see the Echo chapter under the LCA category in the
VCS Online Documentation.

The procedural context considered by Echo includes three new coding styles:

Sampling a Non-Random Coverpoint Variable Assigned With a
Random Variable of Another Class
The following examples show how you can sample a non-random coverpoint variable
assigned with a targetable random member variable of another class.
In Example 35, a non-random coverpoint variable, i1 (MyClass), of the obj1 object is
assigned by the targetable rand variable ri1 (OtherClass) of the oo object.
Example 35
class OtherClass;
rand int ri1;
program test;
int i1;
cp1 : coverpoint (i1);
task my_sample();
enclass
MyClass obj1 = new;
OtherClass oo = new;
repeat(5)
oo.randomize;
obj1.i1 = oo.ri1;
obj1.my_sample();
end
end

Merging of Identical VDBs
When you specify the flex_merge code_union option, VCS Coverage detects the VDBs
that have identical structural constructs and automatically merges them using the basic
merge algorithm. The VDBs with different structural constructs are merged using the
flex_merge code_union option.

Precomputed Scores Mode
The feature is currently under the switch -smart_merge.
The following example has VDBs with identical structural constructs and a different
structural construct.
urg -dir base.vdb/ input0.vdb/ input1.vdb/ input2.vdb/ -format text
-flex_merge code_union -lca
The base, input0, and input2 are identical structural constructs and are merged using
the basic merge algorithm. The input1 is a different structural construct and is merged
using the flex_merge code_union with the default merged VDBs.
The following is the limitation of smart merging of identical VDBs:
• Intermediate VDB names are visible in the reports and warning messages for some of
the usages
Precomputed Scores Mode
When creating a merged coverage database (VDB), you can direct URG to precompute
scores at the region level. This can significantly speed up Verdi startup time for larger
designs.
URG Use Model
To use the precomputed scores mode, add the -dbname_opt precomputescores option
to your URG command line when creating a merged VDB, as shown below:
$VCS_HOME/bin/urg -dbname_opt precomputescores -dbname
<new_database_path> -dir <old_database_path>
$VCS_HOME/bin/urg -dbname_opt precomputescores -dbname simv_lazy.vdb -dir
simv.vdb
This option precomputes the region scores and saves them in the VDB so they can be
quickly loaded later.

UCAPI Use Model
To save the precomputed scores into the merged VDB, use the covdbPrecomputeScores
UCAPI configuration before calling covdb_save from your application, as shown below:
covdb_qualified_configure(designHdl, covdbPrecomputeScores, "true");
covdb_save(designHdl,db_name);
After the merged VDB is generated, the precomputed scores can be used to generate
results with the covdbLazyLoading UCAPI configuration, as shown below:
covdb_qualified_configure(designHdl, covdbLazyLoading, "true");
The following example shows how to load a merged VDB with UCAPI in the precomputed
scores mode:
covdb_qualified_configure(designHdl, covdbLazyLoading, "true");
covdb_save(designHdl,db_name);
covdbHandle designH = covdb_load(covdbDesign, NULL,"merged.vdb");
covdbHandle testH = covdb_load(covdbTest, design,"simv/test");
If the precomputed scores mode is disabled, the normal loading behavior persists.
Updates in Verdi
To use the precomputed scores mode in Verdi after creating a merged VDB with
precomputed scores, use the following command:
verdi –cov –covdir merge.vdb -lazy_load
When you use the -lazy_load option, Verdi starts up faster and allows you to browse top-
level scores without the overhead of loading and computing all of the detailed scores.
SystemVerilog's functional coverage covergroups are used to measure how well an RTL
design has been tested by recording the values or transitions of signals during simulation.
Until now, this measurement has been limited to only integral expressions. In many
designs, especially in analog or mixed-signal designs, real-valued signals are used to
represent physical quantities such as voltage, current, or time.
Coverpoint on Real Expression
A covergroup can contain one or more coverage points. A coverage point specifies an
integral or real expression that is to be covered. Each coverage point includes a set of
bins associated with the sampled values or value transitions of the covered expression.
SystemVerilog allows coverpoints to be defined on real expressions.

Differences Between Real and Integral Ranges
• Integral Ranges: [1:4] covers discrete values: 1, 2, 3, 4.
• Real Ranges: [1.0:4.0] covers all real values between 1.0 and 4.0, not just discrete
points.
When partitioning real ranges into bins, each bin represents an interval. The last bin is
inclusive of its high value.
Fixed Array Bin
For a fixed number of bins, declared as binname[N], bin names range from binname[0]
through binname[N-1]. The number of items to be distributed is the sum of the number
of intervals of the specified ranges and the number of individual values. If the number of
bins is smaller than the specified number of items, then the items are uniformly distributed
among the specified bins.
If the number of items is not evenly divisible by the number of bins, then the last bin
includes the remaining items. Duplicate items are retained; thus, the same value or
interval can be assigned to multiple bins. Consider the following code, using the default
real interval of 1.0:
bins fixed[4] = {[1.0:4.0], [2.0:5.0], 1.0, 4.0, 7.0};
This example has six intervals: [1.0:2.0), [2.0:3.0), [3.0:4.0], [2.0:3.0), [3.0:4.0), [4.0:5.0],
and three values.
Number of items = 9, number of bins = 4; therefore, number of items per bin = 9/4 = 2.
The items are distributed as follows: <[1.0:2.0), [2.0:3.0)>, <[3.0:4.0], [2.0:3.0)>, <[3.0:4.0),
[4.0:5.0]>, <1.0, 4.0, 7.0>.
If the number of bins exceeds the number of items, then some of the bins are empty. For
example:
bins fixed[5] = {[1.0:3.0], 7.0};

Backward Compatibility
Support for the real datatype in covergroup is already present in VCS to some extent,
under the compile option -xlrm real_cg . However, there is a difference between the
support VCS has and what the LRM mandates.
• VCS provides option.real_array_bin_max to control the number of bins created
from an open array bin (bins b[] = ). This option must be set at the covergroup
definition level. It cannot be set at the coverpoint or cross level. VCS does not have any
option to control the interval size of range distribution.
• Open array bin names are reported differently in VCS.
For an open array bin, bins b_open[] = {[1.001:1.201]};
Following are the bin names reported by VCS/URG/Verdi:
b_open_1.001:
b_open_1.041:
b_open_1.081:

Accelerating Coverage Database Merging
b_open_1.121:
b_open_1.161:1.201
Whereas bin names for a fixed array bin like bins b_fix[5] = {[1.001:1.201]}; are
as following:
b_fix[0]
b_fix[1]
b_fix[2]
b_fix[3]
b_fix[4]
As seen above, as per LRM, the reporting of open array bin uses close “[” and open “)”
interval range syntaxes. However, the fixed array naming mechanism is the same.
To maintain backward compatibility, if option.real_array_bin_max is found in any
covergroup, then VCS uses the current format (not LRM compliant) to report bin names for
this covergroup. If both option.real_array_bin_max and type_option.real_interval
are set in a covergroup, then a warning is issued, and VCS follows LRM compliant
behavior.
The real expression in covergroup with VCS does not support the following:
• Tolerance taken (+/- and +%-) is not yet supported in VCS. Therefore, it is not
supported in covergroup as well.
• Cross coverage of hierarchical real coverpoints, that is, cross of real coverpoints from
different covergroups.
• Cross coverage user bins.
• User-defined cross coverage bin and select expression.
• CrossQueue type bin in cross of real-valued coverpoints.
• Showing bin values in report.
Accelerating Coverage Database Merging
To improve the performance of coverage database merging, you can use the -cm_instr
load_ids switch at compile time. This switch instructs VCS to create VDBs in a format
that enables faster merging operations.
vcs -f tr690.vc -cm line+tgl+fsm+cond+branch+assert -sverilog
-cm_instr load_ids

The optimized versions of UVM Direct Programming Interface (DPI) routines are available
for mixed Verilog and VHDL designs. These routines execute faster than the default
routines. These routines should not be used with pure Verilog designs. For pure Verilog
designs, the default routines run faster.
Optimized UVM DPI routines are linked when compiling UVM and the user-defined *.c

VCS provides a callback mechanism to call the API functions before or after each
randomize call to the constraint solver. These API functions influence the constraint solver
(without modifying the SV code) before each randomize call and get feedback after the
randomize task is done.
You must provide SystemVerilog design and C++ files. At compile stage, VCS compiles
the SystemVerilog design to generate simv and compiles the user-provided C++ files to
the shared library.
At runtime, simv imports the generated shared library and triggers callbacks in the shared
library. In your application, constraints and the values of variables can be observed
or modified through the ML C++ Interface topic. This feature allows you to control the
constraint solver through APIs without modifying the SystemVerilog code.

solver is completed, see the highlighted section in Figure 52.
Return Values:
• Retry is true, when the return value is: cumlCBRetryC or cumlCBRetryAndTraceOnC.
• Retry is false, when the return value is: cumlCBFailC or cumlCBSucceedC.

Options to Compile User-Defined C++ Code
Following is the use model to compile user-defined C++ files:
vcs <other_options> [ -cumlf=<cpp filelist> |
-cumlc=<c1.cpp>,<c2.cpp>,] [ -cumlr=rulefile ]
-cumlf/-cumlc
Allows you to specify .cpp files.
• User-defined C++ codes are compiled as a shared library.
• Shared library is created as libcumluser.so in the simv.daidir directory.
-cumlr=rulefile
Allows you to apply filter rule at compile time.
Following is the format of rulefile:
class=<class name pattern>
Each class name should be specified in a new line. Glob-wildcards are supported. A glob
wildcard is opposite to regex pattern.
If rulefile is not specified, callbacks are registered on pre_randomize/post_randomize
for all SystemVerilog (SV) classes. If rulefile is specified, callbacks are registered only
for the matched SV classes.
Run Simulation
./simv [other simulation options]
Simv automatically loads the generated shared library.

Compile-Only User-Defined C++ Codes
Following is the command to compile only user-defined C++ code:
vcs [-cumlf=<cpp filelist> | -cumlc=<c1.cpp>,<c2.cpp>, ]
[-cumlr=rulefile] -Mdir=<existing csrc>
If you change C++ code without modifying the SV design, this command allows you to
compile only C++ codes, rebuild the shared library, and avoid recompiling the SV design.
Pre-Compiled Shared Library
You can generate the pre-compiled shared library file using the following command:
vcs [-cumlf=<cpp filelist> | -cumlc=<c1.cpp>,<c2.cpp>, ] -
cuml_gen_lib=<shared library file>
• The -cuml_gen_lib compile option allows you to specify the .so file name, for
example, output/mysolverlib.so.
• Specified C++ input files are compiled to the object files *.o in csrc/cuml.
◦ No SV input codes are required.
◦ You must have a dedicated machine in which the C++ compiler version and related
standard C++ library packages are installed to make sure that the shared library
can be built correctly.
◦ Verbose messages are reported to show how to build the shared library with a C+
+ compiler. You can also directly use C++ compiler commands to compile the C++
files from those messages.
◦ No license check is required.
You can load the pre-compiled shared library file using the following command:
vcs [vcs opts] -cuml_load_lib=<shared library file>

• The -cuml_load_lib compile option specifies the shared library that is dynamically
linked to simv.
◦ The specified shared library is generated in the first command line.
◦ SV input codes are required, but the C++ input codes are not specified for solver
API.
• Requires normal VCS compilation and simulation. No dedicated machine is required.
Supported Data Types
The following data types are supported:
• Basic types (int, bit, longint, and so on)
• Enum
• Single-dimension array (fixed-size, queue, and dynamic array)
• Struct (packed and unpacked)
• Constant part-select and bit-select
SystemVerilog type API svType::get_name() Attributes
int int 2-state, 32-bit, signed
integer integer 4-state, 32-bit, signed
bit bit or bit [msb:lsb] 2-state, user-defined vector size,
unsigned
reg, logic reg or reg [msb:lsb] 4-state, user-defined vector size,
unsigned
enum enum <enum type>
string string Variables used in constraints
Function call in constraints function call Variables used in constraints

• The following constraint types are not supported:
◦ Foreach constraint
◦ If-else/implication constraint
◦ inside {array}
• The following data types in new_constraint() are not supported:
◦ Associative array
◦ Variable-size MDA
◦ Function calls in constraints (including array reduction methods, array sum, and so
on)
◦ Non-constant part-select/bit-select
◦ XMR
◦ Type-casting operators
◦ Non-constant array index
• Limited support for the query functions on dynamic arrays, aggregate type of variables
or MDA.
• NYI items listed in the cuml_solver_api.hh file.
Using Constraints Debug Option for Detecting Conflict Error
Caused by Hard Partitioning
VCS provides run-time option +ntb_solver_debug=<value> to detect the conflict error
that occur due to hard partitioning. Following are the reasons for the hard partitioning:
• Solve before hard
• Array.size()
• Function call
The following is the use model of this feature:
% simv +ntb_solver_debug=<value>

%simv +ntb_solver_debug=cif_rca

RCA Report for Constraint Inconsistency
The following figure describes the RCA report.

Figure 53 RCA Report for Constraint Inconsistency
RCA report has the following sections:
• Randomize Section
This section describes VCS version, date, solver runtime switches and randomize.
Some runtime switches may affect hard partitioning. Information about runtime
switches help root cause the issue.
• Variable Table Section
This section describes VCS version, date, solver runtime switches and randomize.
Some runtime switches may affect hard partitioning. Information about runtime
switches help root cause the issue.
◦ variable: Indicates the variable name.
◦ value(s): Indicates the solved values. Variable that has no solution is marked in red
for emphasizing.
◦ rand mode/type: Indicates the rand mode or type. When ‘rand mode’ is off, it
means rand_mode is off. when ‘partition(s)' is not blank, it means that the random
variable is solved in the given partition and then turn the rand mode off.

◦ partition(s): Specifies the partition number. The partition number is a hyper-link
which you can access to know how the variable is solved by clicking it. For more
information, see Hard Partition Report.
◦ notes: Specifies the comments. For example, whenever variable’s rand_mode is
turned to OFF or STATE by solver, add the comments in ‘notes’ column.
• Inconsistent Constraints Section
This section describes the minimal set of conflicting/inconsistent constraints.
• Reason Table Section
This section describes the random variables that caused hard partitioning, order type,
and constraint information as follows: random minimal set of conflicting/inconsistent
constraints.
◦ variable@partition: Indicates the random variables caused hard partitioning, and
earlier partition number or later partition which have dependency on the current
partition. Click partition number to cross-probe the corresponding partition.
◦ ordering type: Indicates the ordering types as follows:
▪ solve-before hard
▪ function call
▪ size () constraint size solve-before hard
. The following are the ordering types: are solved values. Variable that has no
solution is marked in red for emphasizing.
◦ rand mode/type: Indicates the rand mode or type. When ‘rand mode’ is off
indicates that rand_mode is off. If the ‘partition(s)' is not blank, it indicates that the
random variable is solved in the given partition and then turn the rand_mode to off.

Applying Module, Instance, and Hierarchical Tree
Level Delays for Sequential UDPs
You can use the
-add_seq_delay
-add_seq_delay option to set the delays of the sequential User-Defined
Primitives (UDPs) that are without delays. This is a global option and it applies the same
delays to all the UDPs. However, the -add_seq_delay option is enhanced to add delays in
module, instance, hierarchical tree level using a configuration file. For example, consider
the following modules:
module top; module A; module B;
A a1(); B b1(); udp u();
A a2(); B b2(); endmodule
endmodule endmodule
You can apply the following type of delays:
• defaultvalue n ns : Applies a delay of n ns in all UDP instances in the design.
• instance top.a1.b1.u n ns : Applies a delay of n ns to only one UDP instance.
• module top n ns : Applies a delay of n ns to all UDP instances in that module.
• tree top.a1 d n ns : Applies a delay of n ns to all UDP instances below top.a1 and
depth up to d.
• modtree A d n ns : Applies a delay of n ns to all UDP instances below A and depth up
to d
The use model is as follows:
% vcs test.v +optconfigfile+config_file_name
The following rules apply to the use model:
• Rules having higher line number in the configuration file is given higher priority and can
overwrite previously written rules.
• Whitespace is mandatory between delay value and the time unit.

Chapter 11: Applying Module, Instance, and Hierarchical Tree Level Delays for Sequential
UDPs
• Delay values cannot be negative.
• Depth can be -1, 0 or any positive integer. A depth of -1 indicates that all depths are
below the target module/instance.
Example 43 test.v
module test ();
reg A,B;
wire Y;
u_and uut(Y, A,B);

A=0; B=0; #10
A=0; B=1; #10
A=1; B=1; #10
A=1; B=0; #10
$finish;
end
always @(Y)
$monitor($time ,," A=%b, B=%b\t Y=%b", A, B, Y);
primitive u_and(y, a, b);
output y;
input a,b;
reg y;
initial y=1'b0;
table
//a b _y y
? 0 : ? : 0;
0 ? : ? : 0;
1 1 : ? : 1;
endtable
endprimitive

The following options describe the debug support:

+asd_debug=printfinaldelay

+asd_debug=printunresolved

Echo
This chapter describes the Echo technology available with VCS. This chapter contains the
following sections:
• Introduction to Echo and Bias Files
• Automatic Generation of a Coverage Model From Constraints
• Diagnostic Mode
• Echo Targeted Status in the URG Report
• Support of Crosses With Non-Random Coverage Points
• Procedural Sampling
• Stimulus Coverage
• Usage Scenarios
• Methodology and Flow Issues
• Echo Command Reference
Introduction to Echo and Bias Files
Echo is a technology that automatically analyzes the testbench constraint space and
generates stimuli that significantly reduces the manual effort required to verify a large
number of functional scenarios. In addition, it allows auto-generation of a stimulus
coverage model and uses the bias files to guide the convergence process of either auto-
generated or user-developed stimulus coverage.
In addition, if you have developed your stimulus cover model, then Echo can identify holes
in the stimulus cover model and similarly direct the constraint solver to generate stimulus
such that these cover holes are hit. Echo works at the test level, that is, Echo tries to hit
coverage holes within a test.
Verification tests are mostly run on a regression farm, where multiple copies of the tests
are being executed in parallel on different machines in the farm, with each simulation
being assigned a different random seed. It is desirable that with Echo enabled, each test

be able to target different portions of the coverage space in order to meet coverage goals
in the shortest possible clock time.
What is a “Test”?
A test in the context of Echo is an executable that can be simulated (for example, simv
generated by VCS). The source files, such as testbench files, design files and so on are
compiled by VCS and linked with the simulation engine to create the executable. The
executable can then be invoked multiple times with different runtime options, such as
different random seeds or configuration files and the simulation results can be observed.
Note that the executable is created once, that is, the source files (constraint, coverage
models, transactors, modules and so on) do not change with every execution. The
different options passed with every execution lead to different behavior of the simulation.
From the Echo point of view, a “test” should consist of a testbench with an “open” set of
constraints: the constraints should represent the entire legal stimulus space. Note that in
many existing methodologies, the constraints in a “test” consist of the legal constraints
as well as a set of test constraints that limit the solution space of the legal stimulus. This
is typically done to focus the test towards some verification targets such as coverage or
specific features.
The goal of Echo is to generate stimuli that efficiently cover the testbench constraint
space. To achieve this, Echo extracts a functional coverage model from the constraint
expressions, and automatically covers it. The intuition is that a better sampling of the
stimulus space exercises the design behaviors more exhaustively, and therefore verify a
large number of functional scenarios more efficiently.
The following topics describe this section in detail:
• Coverage Groups
• Contribution to Coverage Scoring
• Coverage Model Inference for In-line Constraints
Coverage Groups
A covergroup is generated for each class by default.

A covergroup is generated for each class to contain the coverage model derived from
variable declarations in the class. The covergroup for the class that contains the coverage
model for variables is called covg_<class_name>.
The members of the covergroup (coverpoints, crosses) are annotated with comment
attributes in a manner that allows tracking back to the original constraint expressions.
The following sections provide details about the types of coverpoints and crosses that are
inferred.
the covergroups contains the following items:
Coverpoints
Variable Coverage
Each rand variable has a coverpoint associated with it, except for variables that have an
unguarded set membership constraint at the top-level, in any of the constraint blocks of
the class. For example:
enum PktType = {Type1, Type2};
rand bit[7:0] x;
rand PktType p;
PktType prevp;
constraint c1 {
x in {0:1, 5};
}
Here, a coverpoint is inferred for p, but not for x or prevp. Note that a set membership
coverpoint is inferred for x.
The coverpoint expression is just the variable. The following rules apply to the creation of
bins:
• Autobinning for enum type variables.
• Equal volume autobinning, with a maximum of 64 bins, for variables with precision 8
bits or less.
rand bit[7:0] x;
rand PktType p;
rand bit[31:0] y;
In the above example, autobinned coverpoints are created for x and p, with the bins for x
having the ranges 0-3, 4-7, , 252-255, and the bins for p having the values Type1 and
Type2.
The built-in function rand_mode can be used to turn off the randomness of a rand variable.
But the collection of coverage for such variables continues irrespective of the mode
change.

The coverpoints for variables are called covp_<cover_point_id>. Here,
<cover_point_id> is a unique integer identifier for every coverpoint. The autobins for the
coverpoints are named by the usual naming convention for autobins. The comment for the
cover point indicates details about the variable.
Branch Coverage
Each conditional block has an associated Boolean coverpoint. The coverpoint expression
is the conjunction of all the enclosing conditional guards. For example:
if (p) {
if (q) {
x == y;
}
}
In the above example, there is a coverpoint with the expression p&&q.
The comment for the cover point has the expression string.
Condition Coverage (Sensitized)
Each sensitizing guard condition has a Boolean cover bin associated with it. For example:
if (p || (q && r)) {

}
In the above example, there is a coverpoint with expressions p || (q && r) with one bin
corresponding to the case when expression p is ON (or true) and one bin corresponding
to the case when expression q&&r is true. The idea is to make sure that the conditional
expression becomes true at least once for every implicant in the expression being true.
The coverpoints are guarded by the conjunction of all the enclosing conditional guards.
The subexpressions of the guard expression involving operators other than &&,
||, ! are considered as atomic, and the sensitizing conditions are defined over
these atomic subexpressions.
When the condition expression is a set expression, the condition coverage model is
generated like the set membership coverage model. For example:
if (p in {0:4, 7}) {

}
Here the coverpoint expression is p, and the bins 0, 1-3, 4, 7 are created.
The comment for the coverpoint has the expression string.

Set Membership Coverage
Echo infers a coverpoint for constraints coded using in and dist operations. Equivalent
ways of writing the same constraints using other operators might not result in an inferred
coverage model. For example:
x in {0:5};
results in an inferred cover point, whereas
x >= 0 && x <= 5;
does not result in an inferred cover point. Also, use of set membership in complex
constraints does not result in an inferred cover point.
For membership in sets with constant members:
• A single coverpoint is created. The sample expression is the same as the LHS.
• Value in the set membership constraint.
• A bin is created for the low value of each range.
• A bin is created for the high value of each range, for non-singleton ranges.
• A bin is created for the range excluding low and high values of each range, if the
resulting range is non-empty.
x in {0:5, 7};
In the above example, a cover point with expression x and four bins, 0, 1-4, 5, 7 is
created.
The functional coverage language does not allow dynamic variables (those that are not
parameters to the coverage groups) to describe bin ranges. Hence, for membership in
sets with non-constant members:
• A coverpoint with three Boolean cover bins is created for each of the ranges as follows:
◦ A bin with the expression (range_low_expression).
◦ A bin with the expression (range_low_expression + 1 : range_high_expression -1).
◦ A bin with the expression (range_high_expression).
x in {a:5, b};

In the above example, a coverpoint is created for variable x with the following bins:
• One bin with value a;
• One bin with value range (a+1:4);
• One bin with value 5;
• One bin with value b;
◦ If the set membership range expressions use random variables, then no coverage
bin is inferred for that range. For example, if a in the above example is specified as
rand, then the first two bins are not inferred.
◦ All the coverpoints above are guarded by the conjunction of all the enclosing
conditional guards.
Crosses
Combinations of control variables in the class are used to generate crosses.
Control variables are defined as variables that are of enumerated types or bit-vectors that
are 8 bits wide or less, for which a variable coverage coverpoint is generated.
Cross on Variables Within a Class
If a class contains control variables x, y, then a cross x, y is generated. The cross is
autobinned. The coverpoints and bins for x, y are as described in the section on variable
coverage.
The set of variables that participate in one cross is determined as follows:
Control variables are added to a cross until the total number of expected bins (product of
underlying cover point bins) of the cross does not exceed 64000.
If more control variables still remain after previous step, then a new cross is created.
The crosses are called covc_<cross_id>. Here, <cross_id> is a unique integer identifier
for the cross. The comment for the cross indicates details about the crossed variables
(class name, file, line, and so on).
Cross of Condition and Constraint Expressions
The sections on condition coverage and set membership described two kinds of
coverpoints. In the case of set membership constraints inside conditionals, a cross of

the coverpoints is generated for coverage of the condition (sensitizing). This cross is
autobinned. For example,
if (p || (q && r)) {
x in {0:5, 7};
}
In the above example, coverpoints for x are generated from the set membership
constraint. Coverpoints for the condition expression are generated. A cross for the two
coverpoints are generated.
Sampling Event
A special built-in sample event called @(randomize) is used to determine the sampling for
the generated coverage groups.
This event can be used in user-defined covergroups that are embedded in classes.
The event is triggered when an instance of this class is randomized, either directly or
through containment in an instance of another class being randomized. When the event
is triggered, coverage is tracked for the instance and/or the cover group definition (that is,
cumulative).
The @(randomize) event is triggered on all rand objects in the context being randomized,
after the solver is done, and values have been populated in the objects. If objects are
being allocated by randomize, then the allocation of the objects is done before the values
are populated back, hence before @(randomize) is triggered.
Contribution to Coverage Scoring
The automatically generated coverage model contributes to the coverage score by default
with a weight of 1.0.
Coverage Model Inference for In-line Constraints
As in-line constraints (randomize with {..}) are recommended for use in the
specification of test constraints, a coverage model from such constraints is not inferred. In
fact, the use of test constraints is expected to be minimized after coverage driven stimulus
generation is implemented.
Autogeneration of coverage model is done as part of the VCS compile step. The switch
to enable coverage model generation is -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen . All the coverage
models are written out as text files in the echo_cov_gen directory. The echo_cov_gen
directory is present wherever simv.daidir and simv files are generated by VCS compiler.

Diagnostic Mode
The language in which the coverage model is generated is the same as the syntax of the
testbench.
Example command line for a SystemVerilog testbench.
vcs -sverilog -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen foo.sv
It is expected that the user firstly creates a coverage model using the auto_gen option.
Then, the user includes the coverage model into their testbench (using `include or
#include directives) and then makes sure the coverage model is instantiated in the new
task for the enclosing class (that is, the class where constraints and random variables are
specified). The user is encouraged to view the autogenerated coverage model and make
changes if required.
The VCS compiler does not compile the design when echo_cov_gen is specified (that is,
no simv is created).
Diagnostic Mode
To enable diagnostic mode at compile-time, you need to provide the -ntb_opts
echo_diagnostics switch with -ntb_opts echo+echo_new_flow .
Targetable and untargetable covergroups, samples, and crosses are displayed when
compile time diagnostic mode is enabled.
At the end of the compilation, Echo status summary is provided. The number of targetable
objects may not be exact, as the result is based on the compile-time analysis. The actual
status and the number is referred in runtime diagnostic messages.
Echo Targeted Status in the URG Report
Every coverage bin (coverpoint and cross) that is targeted by Echo has an additional
annotation called Echo Targeted. This annotation is displayed for both covered and
uncovered objects and is shown in a separate column. For covered bins, it means that the
bins are targeted by Echo and got hit (and covered). For uncovered bins, it means that
Echo did target the bin but the bin was not hit. In URG Report group information page,
Echo Targeted annotation is visible in the Status column.

Support of Crosses With Non-Random Coverage Points
You can target a cross with non-random cover points using Echo. The cross must contain
at least one random cover point.
While collecting Echo targetable cross holes for non-random cover points, cross bin
combinations with bins that are not sampled, are ignored. However, if the non-random
coverpoint is properly sampled during the first few cycles, it is collected as targetable hole
at the next collection.
If transition bins are involved in cover points that contribute crosses, the cross bins
including transition bins are ignored when collecting the holes.
Following example of three coverpoints explains how Echo targets crosses with non-
random coverpoints:
rand integer i1, i2;
integer i3;

cp1 : coverpoint i1 {
bin s0 = {0};
bin s1 = {1};
}
cp2 : coverpoint i2 {
bin s2 = {2};
bin s3 = {3};

Support of Crosses With Non-Random Coverage Points
}
cp3 : coverpoint i3 {
bin s4 = {4};
bin s5 = {5};
}
cc : cross cp1, cp2, cp3;
There are 8 possible combinations of cross bins in the cross 'cc', but Echo does not collect
all the 8 cross bin combinations for targeting.
If 'cp3' is sampled with bin 's4', when Echo collects holes in cross 'cc', it only collects holes
from all possible cross bins with 'cp3.s4'.
If the value of 'cp3' changes in the middle of simulation, for instance in the collected
holes, there are still two cross bins (s1-s2-s4 and s1-s3-s4) to be targeted at the next two
randomizations. However, if cp3 is sampled with 's5', targeting 's1-s2-s4' and 's1-s3-s4'
actually hits 's1-s2-s5' and 's1-s3-s5', respectively.
After running out of holes to target, at the next round of hole collection, 's0-s2-s5' and 's0-
s3-s5' are collected as hole, because cp3 is sampled with 's5'.
As you see, 's1-s2-s4' and 's1-s3-s4' will never have a chance to be hit, unless 'cp3' is
sampled with 's4' back again. Hence, Echo gives a notification message as follows to let
you know the non-random bin changes.

Note-[CCT_NRBIN_CHG] Non-random sample bin changed.
The sampled bin of the non random coverpoint 'cp3' in covergroup 'MyClass::MyCov',
which is part of cross, has changed from 's4' to 's5'.
At the very first hit of collecting the target holes during simulation, if the non-random cover
point is not sampled, none of the cross bins is collected as the target holes. However, if
the non-random cover point 'cp3' is properly sampled during the first few cycles, the cross
bins are collected as the target hole at the next collection.
Considering simulation with bias files, cross bins in bias file are targeted regardless of any
of the above conditions. However, the targeted cross bin may cause some other cross
bin to be hit depending on the actual value of non-random sample as described in the
previous example.
Echo analyzes procedural context to find targetable cover points. The support for
procedural sampling by Echo contains the following two aspects:
• Sampling a non-random variable that is assigned with targetable random variable.
• Randomizing a sibling class of sampled variables.
Targeting a Non-Random Cover Point Assigned With Random
Variables
Echo targets a non-random coverpoint when the non-random variable is assigned with an
expression of random variables.
Case 1: Non-random variable is assigned with an expression of random variables.
Consider the following example, a non-random variable i3 is procedurally assigned
'i1+i2', where i1 and i2 are both random variables. In such case, Echo is able to target
i3 due to the procedural relationship.

rand integer i1, i2;
integer i3;

cp1 : coverpoint (i3) {
bins s0 = {0};
bins s1 = {1};

bins s2 = {2};
bins s3 = {3};
}

end

task my_sample();
i3 = i1+i2;
end

MyClass obj1 = new;
repeat(4)
obj1.randomize();
obj1.my_sample();
end
end

Case 2: Similar to Case 1, except expression, contains variables inherited via class
extension.

class Base;
rand integer i1, i2;

class Derived extends Base;
integer i3;

cp1 : coverpoint (i3);

end

task my_sample();
i3 = i1+i2;
end

Derived obj1 = new;
repeat(4)
obj1.randomize();
obj1.my_sample();
end
end

Case3: Similar to Case 1, random variables are within scope, but not part of the class
inheritance model.
The procedural assignment can be resolved when a VMM style random variable is used.
(Random variables in another class object.)

class OtherClass;
rand integer ri1;

OtherClass objo;
integer i1;

cp1 : coverpoint (i1) {
bins s0 = {0};
bins s1 = {1};
bins s2 = {2};
bins s3 = {3};
}

objo = new;

end

task my_sample();
i1 = objo.ri1;
end

MyClass obj1 = new;
repeat(4)
obj1.objo.randomize();
obj1.my_sample();
end
end

Case4: Echo resolves and targets when the ternary expression is assigned to the sampled
variable.

rand integer i1,i2;
integer i3;
bit cond;

cp1 : coverpoint (i3) {
bins s0 = {0};
bins s1 = {1};
bins s2 = {2};
bins s3 = {3};
}

end

task my_sample();

i3 = (cond ? i1 : i2);
end

MyClass obj1 = new;
integer cnt;
cnt = 0;
repeat (4)
obj1.cond = (cnt++)%2;
obj1.randomize();
obj1.my_sample();
end
end

Coverage Model and Randomization in Sibling Classes
Assume that the two sibling classes (class D1, D2) are derived from the same base
class (class B) that contains some random variables. The class D1 has a covergroup
that samples the random variables defined in the base class. In the simulation, the
randomization takes place in the class D2 which has no coverage model (see the following
example).
At runtime, Echo collects targetable holes from the sibling classes to target. Echo
currently supports only one level of inheritance. Note that all the variables involved in the
expression of coverpoint must be inherited from the base class to be targeted.
class B;
rand integer i1;

class D1 extends B;
covergroup MyGrp@(cov_event);
cp1 : coverpoint (i1);

class D2 extends B;

D1 objd1 = new;
D2 objd2 = new;

->objd1.cov_event;
objd2.randomize();
end
An extended scenario is as follows.
The classes D1 and D2 are derived from the base class B, and the actual covergroup
is defined in another class E. A coverpoint in E is sampling d2.i1, but randomization
happens on D1 object.
class B;
rand integer i1;

class D1 extends B;

class D2 extends B;

class E;
D2 d2;
covergroup MyGrp@(cov_event);
cp1 : coverpoint (d2.i1);

D1 objd1 = new;
D2 objd2 = new;
E obje = new;
obj1.randomize();
->obje.cov_event;
end

Term Description

Compile-time Options
To enable Echo flow, use the -ntb_opts echo_new_flow compile-time option along with
the existing compile-time option -ntp_opts echo :
% vcs -ntb_opts echo -ntb_opts echo_new_flow
For procedural sampling where the cover point variable is not directly driven by a rand
variable, Echo attempts to capture the logic using the config-file approach. The compile-
time use model is as follows:
-ntb_opts config-file=<fname>
The config file format is as follows:
<CONS PROP START>
<file> <cls_inheritence.sv:40> //where <filename:line_info> points to the
assignment.
<CONS PROP END>
You can specify a maximum of 10 statements in the configuration file.
Support for Existing Compile-time Options
This use model supports all compile-time options (including compile-time diagnostic
options) except the echo_gen_exclusion_file option. During compile-time, this option
generates an exclusion file for the coverage points (CPs) which cannot be targeted by
Echo. This was primarily supported in Echo to avoid dumping of untargetable CPs in
the generated bias files. In this flow, this is not required since the new engine treats the
untargetable CPs as constants.
Runtime Options
Following are the runtime options:
-echo_hints
Generates positive and negative hints for the CPs targeted by Echo.
-echo_dir
This flow supports only -echo_dir=<>. This option specifies the coverage convergence
database directory.
Example: -echo_dir=<>

The default coverage convergence database directory where reports are generated is
simv.ccdb.
• Conflicting constraint detection is disabled in this flow.
• Targeting transition bins is not supported.
-echo_filter_cov_include
Echo targets all functional coverage points, by default. The -echo_filter_cov_include
switch enables you to limit the functional coverage points by using the following command:
-echo_filter_cov_include=<filter_string>
Here, filter_string may be a bin name or a file name.
-echo_filter_cov_file_include
Enables you to specify multiple filter strings in a single file and pass the file to Echo. The
syntax of this switch is as follows:
-echo_filter_cov_file_include=<filter_file_name>

Following are the replay options:
Argument Description
-echo_replay Specifies the test to replay. Each test targets one or more CPs. All
the tests must be replayed to hit all the targeted CPs.
-echo_dir Specifies the coverage convergence database directory (where
the data was dumped during -echo_hints run). Default is
simv.ccdb dir
-echo_replay_dir Specifies the database directory where replay run data is dumped.
Default is simv.ccdb.replay.
-echo_replay_sym Enables the mode for replaying positive hints for the CPs.

(case where the test file is present in non-coverage convergence

Bias Files
Options to Generate Bias Files
Following are the options to generate bias files. You can provide these options during

-echo_select_cps
Divides the targeted coverage space into multiple ranges, or sets it similar to the Echo

-echo_vdb_dir
Specifies the coverage database used to generate the targeted holes.
Examples:

Where, x and y are start and end numbers for the range.

Usage Scenarios
This section discusses Echo usage in various common verification scenarios. In all the
scenarios in this section, it is assumed that the guidelines mentioned in the previous
section are being followed (for example, coverage and constraints are on the same
variables, and so on).
You can load a pre-existing coverage database in every scenario to screen out already-
covered coverage bins. By doing so, the current run can focus only on uncovered bins.
The coverage database must be loaded after all the testbench components have been
instantiated, so that the coverage data from the database can be loaded in the proper (in-
memory) runtime database.

Usage Scenarios
Running a Single Test with Randomized Configurations
This scenario generally applies to multimedia devices, in which the device has many
interfaces and many modes and the device can be configured to select some interfaces
and some modes.
The object of verification is to exercise all the interesting configurations of the device. In
the testbench, configurations are selected, and then data (possibly random) is passed
through the device.
Configurations for a device are typically chosen (through randomize) a few times per
test run. In the extreme case, only one configuration might be selected (for example,
config.randomize is performed only once).
In this scenario, it is important to pre-load the coverage database to ensure that already-
selected configurations are not chosen.
Running a Single Test With Randomized Transactions
This scenario applies to transaction-based verification environments. This scenario is
required for packet-processing devices or instruction-based processor verification.
The device is set in some mode, and then multiple transactions are generated and
passed through the device. You use constraints to generate the transaction objects. In this
scenario, you can use the default arguments for Echo.
If you assume that many transactions are generated (randomized), then it is appropriate
for the convergence heuristics to take over and apply reactive calls as needed.
status = transObj.randomize();
or
repeat (1000) {
transObj = new;
status = transObj.randomize();
}
Autogenerating a Coverage Model
Echo can generate a coverage model from the constraints specification. However, you
must instantiate the coverage model that you intend to use in the simulation.
1. Autogenerate the coverage model:
% vcs -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen foo.vr
Echo generates the model in the file ./echo_cov_gen/MyClass.vr.

3. Add the declaration for the generated covergroup as part of the class member
declarations.
For example, if the name of the covergroup is MyCov and it is of the class MyClass,
then you must add to the other member declarations for the class MyClass:
coverage_group MyCov;
4. The autogenerated coverage group must be instantiated in the constructor of the
enclosing class. Perform the instantiation with the following statement:
5. Make the cover group instantiation the last statement of the constructor. If the
constructor does not exist, then you must add the method to the covergroup
instantiation.
6. Since the name of the autogenerated cover group is deterministic, the declaration and
the instantiation can be done once during testbench development phase.
Methodology and Flow Issues
This section addresses methodology and regression execution issues.
Scenario: All Tests have the Same Constraints and Coverage
Space (Recommended)
When all the tests being executed in parallel have exactly the same coverage space and
the same legal stimulus space (that is, the constraints are exactly the same for all the
tests), then the Echo bias file approach can be used to achieve high efficiency test runs.
Each test should have its own bias file. The input database for the URG utility can be
obtained by running any test and using the output coverage database. The number of test
runs should be used as the value for the echo_gen_bias argument for URG. Once the
bias files are generated, they can be used again and again for repeated regression runs.
It is desirable that the number of times the stimulus objects are randomized in a test be
at least equal to the average number of coverage bins in the bias files. After all the tests
are done running, the coverage database from all the tests can be merged to get the final
coverage number. It is possible but not efficient to use both the random seed and the bias
file for every test.

Methodology and Flow Issues
Scenario: Tests are Grouped into Categories With Each Category
having Specific Test Constraints
In this scenario, tests have test specific test constraints which further constrain the legal
stimulus space and thus also reduce the hittable coverage bins. (Coverage bins whose
value ranges lie outside the space of the test constraints cannot be hit). A bias file can
be created for every category of tests. The bias file should be such that all the coverage
bins in the file are hittable given the test constraints for that category. Each test within
this category can use the same bias file but with a different random seed. The URG bias
generation utility can be used to generate a bias file template. (Note that the URG does
not look at test constraints when generating the bias files). The test writer can then modify
this template to include the hittable coverage bins. As in the previous scenario, assuming
test constraints remain constant across regression runs, then the bias files have to be
generated once and can be used for multiple regression runs. Even if all the bins in a
bias file are not hittable, all it causes is less efficient utilization of resources. Echo may
use some cycles in the test run to try to target unhittable bins, but remaining cycles still
target hittable coverage bins. In this scenario too, the coverage data from all the tests
can be collected and merged. Then a sequential run can be used to target any remaining
coverage holes. For this final sequential run, the merged coverage database can be used
as an input along with the fully open constraints.
Scenario: Coverage Database Being Loaded in the Beginning of a
Test Run
If a coverage database is being loaded as part of the configuration for a test, then there
is no need to use an Echo bias file. Echo only targets coverage bins that are not covered
in the loaded database, so it is already biased in some sense. If the same database
is loaded in multiple tests, then a random seed can be used so that each test targets
different holes. This is useful in a batch mode type of regression environment. Here all
tests have the same constraints and coverage space, but one batch of tests is run at one
time. After the batch is complete, the coverage databases are merged and the merged
database is used as input for the next batch of tests. Note that for repeatability purposes,
the input database associated with a test needs to be preserved in case the test needs to
be run in a stand alone mode. If an Echo bias file is used, then it overrides the bias from
the loaded coverage database, that is, holes in the bias file are targeted even if they are
marked as covered in the loaded coverage database. Hence it does not make sense to
use both coverage database load and Echo bias file approaches for a test.

Echo Command Reference
Echo Command Reference
The following table describes all the compile-time switches available with Echo:
Table 7 Compile-time switches
Switch Name Description

Compile-Time Options
This section describes the options you use to enable the Echo technology when using the
VCS compiler.
You also need to specify the options described in this chapter (as appropriate) when you
execute simulation (that is, when you run simv).
Echo Option
-ntb_opts echo+echo_new_flow
Ensures that the required Echo-related processing is done for all relevant coverage points.
Example for OpenVera testbench:
vcs -ntb_opts echo+echo_new_flow foo.vr
Example for SystemVerilog testbench:
vcs -sverilog -ntb_opts echo+echo_new_flow foo.sv
Coverage Model Autogeneration Options
-ntb_opts echo_cov_gen
Generates a coverage model for a stimulus object—that is, for a class that contains
random variables and/or constraints.
See Support of Crosses With Non-Random Coverage Points for details on how a
coverage model is inferred from constraints.

Echo Command Reference
When you specify this option, Echo writes automatically inferred cover groups (if any) to
the directory ${SIMV_DIR}/echo_cov_gen. You can specify a different directory with the
-ntb_opts echo_cov_gen_dir option.
Note that if the echo_cov_gen directory already exists, any files in that directory are
overwritten when you rerun Echo with the -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen option.
The names of the files created (and the names of the coverage groups themselves)
depend on the names of classes and constraints blocks in the source file.
Example for SystemVerilog testbench:
vcs -sverilog -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen foo.sv
-ntb_opts echo_cov_gen_dir <directory_name>
Overrides the default directory (./echo_cov_gen) into which Echo writes automatically
inferred covergroups.

Methodology Features
This chapter describes the following UVM/OVM/VMM Methodology LCA features:
• Ralgen Support for IEEE Standard 2014 for IP-XACT
• Support for UVM Profiler
Ralgen supports the following features to comply with the IEEE Standard 2014 for IP-
XACT:
• Support elements relevant to register model, which are listed in Annexure C and
Annexure E sections of IEEE Standard for IP-XACT, 1685-2014.
• Specify backdoor paths using accessHandles and the elements contained inside it.
• Support expressions involving arithmetic operators.
To convert IP-XACT to RALF, use the following command:
ralgen -ipxact2014 -ipxact2ralf
To generate the SV model directly from IP-XACT, use the following command:
ralgen -ipxact2014 -ipxact <other options for model generation>
Apart from -ipxact or -ipxact2ralf, additionally -ipxact2014 is required to
parse the XML as per IEEE Standard for IP-XACT, 1685-2014.
Following is the list of the IP-XACT elements that are relevant to the register model:
• C.1 accessHandles
• C.3 complexBaseExpressions
• C.5 configurableElementValues

• C.6 configurableLibraryRefType
• C.9 indices
• C.10 isPresent
• C.11 libraryRefType
• C.12 nameGroup
• C.13 nameGroupTOKEN
• C.16 nameGroupString
• C.18 parameters
• C.19 attributes
• C.21 pathSegments
• C.22 range
• C.23 vectors
• C.24 vendorExtensions
• C.25 versionIdentifier
• C.26 viewRef
• Annexure E
The sections below provide details regarding the correlation between input IP-XACT and
expected output XML.
Support for Backdoor Path
You can specify backdoor paths using accessHandles and the elements contained inside
it.
Note that,
• Each index entry in the indices element corresponds to the select element in one
dimension each. Multiple index entries model a select into a multidimensional array.
• When the indices element is specified inside pathSegment, it corresponds to the
select being applied on the RTL. However, when the indices element is specified
directly inside accessHandle, it indicates the IP-XACT array element to which the
corresponding pathSegement is paired, such as, register array.

◦ The latter case of specifying unique path for each array element is not supported
in this release. You can specify the pathSegmentName using %d to denote the index
being used in the RTL path. The final RAL model substitutes the index accordingly.
• For modeling RTL paths involving concatenation or part-selects, slices must be used
to specify the path.

Support for Expressions
Ralgen supports expressions involving arithmetic operators; however, other operators
are not supported. Ralgen supports the type of expressions that are defined in C.3
complexBaseExpression section of IEEE Standard for IP-XACT, 1685-2014.
These type of expressions are as follows:
realExpression, signedLongintExpression, stringExpression,
unsignedBitExpression, unsignedBitVectorExpression,
unsignedIntExpression, unsignedLongintExpression,
unsignedPositiveIntExpression, unsignedPositiveLongintExpression
Support for Constants

Support for UVM Profiler
IP-XACT has the concept of parameters which can hold the literal value and these
parameters can then be used in the context of expressions in ralgen. For example,
<ipxact:paramters>
<ipxact:parameter parameterId="addrBits" choiceRef="bitsize"
prompt="Address Bits" type="shortint" resolve="user">
<ipxact:name>addrBits</ipxact:name>
<ipxact:value>32</ipxact:value>
</ipxact:parameter>
</ipxact:parameters>
Only arithmetic operators are supported in expressions.
Support for UVM Profiler
VCS offers simprofile using which you can identify the functions in the design where
most of the time is spent, their call count, and the memory used by various parts of the
design. However, this information is not always usable because it does not point to the
exact object in your design or object based call chain information.
VCS provides UVM profiler that allows you to have a comprehensive view of the profile
information. The UVM profiler can provide object level details for each call to the UVM
class methods and also assists in narrowing down to the sub-optimal code in the UVM
testbench faster. Hence, the UVM profiler helps you to resolve the bottlenecks in the UVM
based testbench.
At compile time:
Pass the -simprofile=uvm option during elaboration.
If you want to dump only specific data, you can use the following options:
• -simprofile=uvm:user- This option allows you to dump data on user classes only.
The option does not dump data on UVM base classes.
• -simprofile=uvm:component - This option allows you to dump data on UVM
component and its derived classes (same as the -simprofile=uvm). This is the default
behavior starting from O-2018.09-SP2 release.
• -simprofile=uvm:all - This option allows you to dump data for all the classes. This
was the default behavior of the -simprofile=uvm option till O-2018.09-SP1-1 release.

Support for UVM Profiler
At Runtime:
No option is required at runtime. Once the simulation is completed, uvm_profiler.db is
generated. This contains the information that can be post-processed to create HTML files.
Post-Processing Utility
uvmprofrpt is the post processing utility that generates the HTML files.
Syntax:
uvmprofrpt -uvm_profiler=db:uvm_profiler.db
When you run this utility, it generates a directory called uvm_profiler. This directory
contains two types of HTML reports, which are hierarchical report and flat report. The
following figures show the sample reports:
Figure 55 UVM Profiler Hierarchical Report
In the above figure, rows with brown background refer to the UVM base class functions
and the rows with purple background refer to the user class functions.

Support for UVM Profiler
Figure 56 UVM Profiler Flat Report
The UVM Profiler Flat report provides the function definition based count and the
respective time consumption. This does not have object based association. The function
calls made from different objects are counted cumulatively based on the definition.
In both the hierarchical view and flat view, when you click on the method name, it shows
the caller-callee list related to that function and the corresponding statistics as shown in
the Caller-Callee report.
Additional Options on UVM Profiler
The following are some of the additional options that can be used to customize the reports:
% simv -uvm_profiler[= num_entries:{value} | ignoreUVMCalls]
% simv -uvm_profiler=num_entries:200
% simv -uvm_profiler=num_entries:200+ignoreUVMCalls
These are the descriptions of arguments used in the example:
• num_entries=value - Indicates the number of entries that you need. In the above
example, the top 200 entries that are sorted by Exclusive Wall Time are reported. The
default is 500.
• ignoreUVMCalls - When you specify this option, all UVM functions and tasks called
internally within UVM methods are not reported in detail. Their time consumption is
reported in the first UVM method directly called by user function/task. By default it
includes UVM calls.

Support for UVM Profiler
These options can also be passed to the uvmprofrpt utility.
The feature has the following limitation:
• UVM phase based reporting is currently not supported.
• UVM profiler is applicable only to SystemVerilog.

Gate-Level Simulation
This chapter contains the following sections:
• Delay in RETAIN Calculation for Accurate Simulation Behavior
• Using Module Path Delay Feature to Reduce Pulses
Delay in RETAIN Calculation for Accurate Simulation Behavior
VCS considers delayed versions of clock and data signals when you use +neg_tchk
for negative timing checks. The IOPATH calculation is not affected by the +neg_tchk
option. However, you can consider delayed signals in RETAIN calculations when you use
(-sdfretain) with negative timing check (+neg_tchk).
Consider the following SDF example:
(DELAY
(ABSOLUTE
(COND (COND) (IOPATH CLK O (RETAIN (5) (10)) (7) (14) ))
)
)
In this example, RETAIN is applied only when the condition COND is true. By default, VCS
samples COND at the edge of the original CLK signal. However, when negative timing
checks are involved, sampling the condition value on the original clock edge is not correct.
This is because data might not be valid at this time. This version of VCS enables you
to sample the RETAIN condition on the delayed clock edge. This results in accurate
calculation.
To enable this feature, use the option
-xlrm retain_with_delayed_sig
-xlrm retain_with_delayed_sig along with
-sdfretain and +neg_tchk option.
The following is the use model:
%vcs -xlrm retain_with_delayed_sig -sdfretain +neg_tchk <>

Chapter 14: Gate-Level Simulation
Delay in RETAIN Calculation for Accurate Simulation Behavior
The following example illustrates a delay calculation. It includes the outputs that are
generated with delay and without delay in the RETAIN calculation. To run this example,
use the file general.sdf. The following is an example general.sdf file:

(DELAYFILE
(SDFVERSION "OVI 3.0")
(DIVIDER /)
(TIMESCALE 1ns)
(CELL
(CELLTYPE "dut")
(INSTANCE top/I1)
(DELAY
(ABSOLUTE
(COND (COND) (IOPATH CLK O (RETAIN (5) (10)) (7) (14) ))
)
)
)
(CELL
(CELLTYPE "dut")
(INSTANCE top/I1)
(TIMINGCHECK
(SETUPHOLD (posedge D) (negedge CLK) (-8) (20))
(SETUPHOLD (negedge D) (posedge CLK) (-8) (20))
)
)
)

Echo
This chapter describes the Echo technology available with VCS. This chapter contains the
following sections:
• Introduction to Echo and Bias Files
• Automatic Generation of a Coverage Model From Constraints
• Diagnostic Mode
• Echo Targeted Status in the URG Report
• Support of Crosses With Non-Random Coverage Points
• Procedural Sampling
• Stimulus Coverage
• Usage Scenarios
• Methodology and Flow Issues
• Echo Command Reference
Introduction to Echo and Bias Files
Echo is a technology that automatically analyzes the testbench constraint space and
generates stimuli that significantly reduces the manual effort required to verify a large
number of functional scenarios. In addition, it allows auto-generation of a stimulus
coverage model and uses the bias files to guide the convergence process of either auto-
generated or user-developed stimulus coverage.
In addition, if you have developed your stimulus cover model, then Echo can identify holes
in the stimulus cover model and similarly direct the constraint solver to generate stimulus
such that these cover holes are hit. Echo works at the test level, that is, Echo tries to hit
coverage holes within a test.
Verification tests are mostly run on a regression farm, where multiple copies of the tests
are being executed in parallel on different machines in the farm, with each simulation
being assigned a different random seed. It is desirable that with Echo enabled, each test

be able to target different portions of the coverage space in order to meet coverage goals
in the shortest possible clock time.
What is a “Test”?
A test in the context of Echo is an executable that can be simulated (for example, simv
generated by VCS). The source files, such as testbench files, design files and so on are
compiled by VCS and linked with the simulation engine to create the executable. The
executable can then be invoked multiple times with different runtime options, such as
different random seeds or configuration files and the simulation results can be observed.
Note that the executable is created once, that is, the source files (constraint, coverage
models, transactors, modules and so on) do not change with every execution. The
different options passed with every execution lead to different behavior of the simulation.
From the Echo point of view, a “test” should consist of a testbench with an “open” set of
constraints: the constraints should represent the entire legal stimulus space. Note that in
many existing methodologies, the constraints in a “test” consist of the legal constraints
as well as a set of test constraints that limit the solution space of the legal stimulus. This
is typically done to focus the test towards some verification targets such as coverage or
specific features.
The goal of Echo is to generate stimuli that efficiently cover the testbench constraint
space. To achieve this, Echo extracts a functional coverage model from the constraint
expressions, and automatically covers it. The intuition is that a better sampling of the
stimulus space exercises the design behaviors more exhaustively, and therefore verify a
large number of functional scenarios more efficiently.
The following topics describe this section in detail:
• Coverage Groups
• Contribution to Coverage Scoring
• Coverage Model Inference for In-line Constraints
Coverage Groups
A covergroup is generated for each class by default.

A covergroup is generated for each class to contain the coverage model derived from
variable declarations in the class. The covergroup for the class that contains the coverage
model for variables is called covg_<class_name>.
The members of the covergroup (coverpoints, crosses) are annotated with comment
attributes in a manner that allows tracking back to the original constraint expressions.
The following sections provide details about the types of coverpoints and crosses that are
inferred.
the covergroups contains the following items:
Coverpoints
Variable Coverage
Each rand variable has a coverpoint associated with it, except for variables that have an
unguarded set membership constraint at the top-level, in any of the constraint blocks of
the class. For example:
enum PktType = {Type1, Type2};
rand bit[7:0] x;
rand PktType p;
PktType prevp;
constraint c1 {
x in {0:1, 5};
}
Here, a coverpoint is inferred for p, but not for x or prevp. Note that a set membership
coverpoint is inferred for x.
The coverpoint expression is just the variable. The following rules apply to the creation of
bins:
• Autobinning for enum type variables.
• Equal volume autobinning, with a maximum of 64 bins, for variables with precision 8
bits or less.
rand bit[7:0] x;
rand PktType p;
rand bit[31:0] y;
In the above example, autobinned coverpoints are created for x and p, with the bins for x
having the ranges 0-3, 4-7, , 252-255, and the bins for p having the values Type1 and
Type2.
The built-in function rand_mode can be used to turn off the randomness of a rand variable.
But the collection of coverage for such variables continues irrespective of the mode
change.

, 252-255, and the bins for p having the values Type1 and
Type2.
The built-in function rand_mode can be used to turn off the randomness of a rand variable.
But the collection of coverage for such variables continues irrespective of the mode
change.

The coverpoints for variables are called covp_<cover_point_id>. Here,
<cover_point_id> is a unique integer identifier for every coverpoint. The autobins for the
coverpoints are named by the usual naming convention for autobins. The comment for the
cover point indicates details about the variable.
Branch Coverage
Each conditional block has an associated Boolean coverpoint. The coverpoint expression
is the conjunction of all the enclosing conditional guards. For example:
if (p) {
if (q) {
x == y;
}
}
In the above example, there is a coverpoint with the expression p&&q.
The comment for the cover point has the expression string.
Condition Coverage (Sensitized)
Each sensitizing guard condition has a Boolean cover bin associated with it. For example:
if (p || (q && r)) {

}
In the above example, there is a coverpoint with expressions p || (q && r) with one bin
corresponding to the case when expression p is ON (or true) and one bin corresponding
to the case when expression q&&r is true. The idea is to make sure that the conditional
expression becomes true at least once for every implicant in the expression being true.
The coverpoints are guarded by the conjunction of all the enclosing conditional guards.
The subexpressions of the guard expression involving operators other than &&,
||, ! are considered as atomic, and the sensitizing conditions are defined over
these atomic subexpressions.
When the condition expression is a set expression, the condition coverage model is
generated like the set membership coverage model. For example:
if (p in {0:4, 7}) {

}
Here the coverpoint expression is p, and the bins 0, 1-3, 4, 7 are created.
The comment for the coverpoint has the expression string.

Set Membership Coverage
Echo infers a coverpoint for constraints coded using in and dist operations. Equivalent
ways of writing the same constraints using other operators might not result in an inferred
coverage model. For example:
x in {0:5};
results in an inferred cover point, whereas
x >= 0 && x <= 5;
does not result in an inferred cover point. Also, use of set membership in complex
constraints does not result in an inferred cover point.
For membership in sets with constant members:
• A single coverpoint is created. The sample expression is the same as the LHS.
• Value in the set membership constraint.
• A bin is created for the low value of each range.
• A bin is created for the high value of each range, for non-singleton ranges.
• A bin is created for the range excluding low and high values of each range, if the
resulting range is non-empty.
x in {0:5, 7};
In the above example, a cover point with expression x and four bins, 0, 1-4, 5, 7 is
created.
The functional coverage language does not allow dynamic variables (those that are not
parameters to the coverage groups) to describe bin ranges. Hence, for membership in
sets with non-constant members:
• A coverpoint with three Boolean cover bins is created for each of the ranges as follows:
◦ A bin with the expression (range_low_expression).
◦ A bin with the expression (range_low_expression + 1 : range_high_expression -1).
◦ A bin with the expression (range_high_expression).
x in {a:5, b};

In the above example, a coverpoint is created for variable x with the following bins:
• One bin with value a;
• One bin with value range (a+1:4);
• One bin with value 5;
• One bin with value b;
◦ If the set membership range expressions use random variables, then no coverage
bin is inferred for that range. For example, if a in the above example is specified as
rand, then the first two bins are not inferred.
◦ All the coverpoints above are guarded by the conjunction of all the enclosing
conditional guards.
Crosses
Combinations of control variables in the class are used to generate crosses.
Control variables are defined as variables that are of enumerated types or bit-vectors that
are 8 bits wide or less, for which a variable coverage coverpoint is generated.
Cross on Variables Within a Class
If a class contains control variables x, y, then a cross x, y is generated. The cross is
autobinned. The coverpoints and bins for x, y are as described in the section on variable
coverage.
The set of variables that participate in one cross is determined as follows:
Control variables are added to a cross until the total number of expected bins (product of
underlying cover point bins) of the cross does not exceed 64000.
If more control variables still remain after previous step, then a new cross is created.
The crosses are called covc_<cross_id>. Here, <cross_id> is a unique integer identifier
for the cross. The comment for the cross indicates details about the crossed variables
(class name, file, line, and so on).
Cross of Condition and Constraint Expressions
The sections on condition coverage and set membership described two kinds of
coverpoints. In the case of set membership constraints inside conditionals, a cross of

the coverpoints is generated for coverage of the condition (sensitizing). This cross is
autobinned. For example,
if (p || (q && r)) {
x in {0:5, 7};
}
In the above example, coverpoints for x are generated from the set membership
constraint. Coverpoints for the condition expression are generated. A cross for the two
coverpoints are generated.
Sampling Event
A special built-in sample event called @(randomize) is used to determine the sampling for
the generated coverage groups.
This event can be used in user-defined covergroups that are embedded in classes.
The event is triggered when an instance of this class is randomized, either directly or
through containment in an instance of another class being randomized. When the event

The @(randomize) event is triggered on all rand objects in the context being randomized,
after the solver is done, and values have been populated in the objects. If objects are
being allocated by randomize, then the allocation of the objects is done before the values
are populated back, hence before @(randomize) is triggered.
Contribution to Coverage Scoring
The automatically generated coverage model contributes to the coverage score by default
with a weight of 1.0.
Coverage Model Inference for In-line Constraints
As in-line constraints (randomize with {..}) are recommended for use in the
specification of test constraints, a coverage model from such constraints is not inferred. In
fact, the use of test constraints is expected to be minimized after coverage driven stimulus
generation is implemented.
Autogeneration of coverage model is done as part of the VCS compile step. The switch
to enable coverage model generation is -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen . All the coverage
models are written out as text files in the echo_cov_gen directory. The echo_cov_gen
directory is present wherever simv.daidir and simv files are generated by VCS compiler.

Diagnostic Mode
The language in which the coverage model is generated is the same as the syntax of the
testbench.
Example command line for a SystemVerilog testbench.
vcs -sverilog -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen foo.sv
It is expected that the user firstly creates a coverage model using the auto_gen option.
Then, the user includes the coverage model into their testbench (using `include or
#include directives) and then makes sure the coverage model is instantiated in the new
task for the enclosing class (that is, the class where constraints and random variables are
specified). The user is encouraged to view the autogenerated coverage model and make
changes if required.
The VCS compiler does not compile the design when echo_cov_gen is specified (that is,
no simv is created).
Diagnostic Mode
To enable diagnostic mode at compile-time, you need to provide the -ntb_opts
echo_diagnostics switch with -ntb_opts echo+echo_new_flow .
Targetable and untargetable covergroups, samples, and crosses are displayed when
compile time diagnostic mode is enabled.
At the end of the compilation, Echo status summary is provided. The number of targetable
objects may not be exact, as the result is based on the compile-time analysis. The actual
status and the number is referred in runtime diagnostic messages.
Echo Targeted Status in the URG Report
Every coverage bin (coverpoint and cross) that is targeted by Echo has an additional
annotation called Echo Targeted. This annotation is displayed for both covered and
uncovered objects and is shown in a separate column. For covered bins, it means that the
bins are targeted by Echo and got hit (and covered). For uncovered bins, it means that
Echo did target the bin but the bin was not hit. In URG Report group information page,
Echo Targeted annotation is visible in the Status column.

Support of Crosses With Non-Random Coverage Points
You can target a cross with non-random cover points using Echo. The cross must contain
at least one random cover point.
While collecting Echo targetable cross holes for non-random cover points, cross bin
combinations with bins that are not sampled, are ignored. However, if the non-random
coverpoint is properly sampled during the first few cycles, it is collected as targetable hole
at the next collection.
If transition bins are involved in cover points that contribute crosses, the cross bins
including transition bins are ignored when collecting the holes.
Following example of three coverpoints explains how Echo targets crosses with non-
random coverpoints:
rand integer i1, i2;
integer i3;

cp1 : coverpoint i1 {
bin s0 = {0};
bin s1 = {1};
}
cp2 : coverpoint i2 {
bin s2 = {2};
bin s3 = {3};

Support of Crosses With Non-Random Coverage Points
}
cp3 : coverpoint i3 {
bin s4 = {4};
bin s5 = {5};
}
cc : cross cp1, cp2, cp3;
There are 8 possible combinations of cross bins in the cross 'cc', but Echo does not collect
all the 8 cross bin combinations for targeting.
If 'cp3' is sampled with bin 's4', when Echo collects holes in cross 'cc', it only collects holes
from all possible cross bins with 'cp3.s4'.
If the value of 'cp3' changes in the middle of simulation, for instance in the collected
holes, there are still two cross bins (s1-s2-s4 and s1-s3-s4) to be targeted at the next two
randomizations. However, if cp3 is sampled with 's5', targeting 's1-s2-s4' and 's1-s3-s4'
actually hits 's1-s2-s5' and 's1-s3-s5', respectively.
After running out of holes to target, at the next round of hole collection, 's0-s2-s5' and 's0-
s3-s5' are collected as hole, because cp3 is sampled with 's5'.
As you see, 's1-s2-s4' and 's1-s3-s4' will never have a chance to be hit, unless 'cp3' is
sampled with 's4' back again. Hence, Echo gives a notification message as follows to let
you know the non-random bin changes.

Note-[CCT_NRBIN_CHG] Non-random sample bin changed.
The sampled bin of the non random coverpoint 'cp3' in covergroup 'MyClass::MyCov',
which is part of cross, has changed from 's4' to 's5'.
