Compile-time Options
To enable Echo flow, use the -ntb_opts echo_new_flow compile-time option along with
the existing compile-time option -ntp_opts echo :
% vcs -ntb_opts echo -ntb_opts echo_new_flow
For procedural sampling where the cover point variable is not directly driven by a rand
variable, Echo attempts to capture the logic using the config-file approach. The compile-
time use model is as follows:
-ntb_opts config-file=<fname>
The config file format is as follows:
<CONS PROP START>
<file> <cls_inheritence.sv:40> //where <filename:line_info> points to the
assignment.
<CONS PROP END>
You can specify a maximum of 10 statements in the configuration file.
Support for Existing Compile-time Options
This use model supports all compile-time options (including compile-time diagnostic
options) except the echo_gen_exclusion_file option. During compile-time, this option
generates an exclusion file for the coverage points (CPs) which cannot be targeted by
Echo. This was primarily supported in Echo to avoid dumping of untargetable CPs in
the generated bias files. In this flow, this is not required since the new engine treats the
untargetable CPs as constants.
Runtime Options
Following are the runtime options:
-echo_hints
Generates positive and negative hints for the CPs targeted by Echo.
-echo_dir
This flow supports only -echo_dir=<>. This option specifies the coverage convergence
database directory.
Example: -echo_dir=<>

text:
The default coverage convergence database directory where reports are generated is
simv.ccdb.
• Conflicting constraint detection is disabled in this flow.
• Targeting transition bins is not supported.
-echo_filter_cov_include
Echo targets all functional coverage points, by default. The -echo_filter_cov_include
switch enables you to limit the functional coverage points by using the following command:
-echo_filter_cov_include=<filter_string>
Here, filter_string may be a bin name or a file name.
-echo_filter_cov_file_include
Enables you to specify multiple filter strings in a single file and pass the file to Echo. The
syntax of this switch is as follows:
-echo_filter_cov_file_include=<filter_file_name>
Replay Options
Following are the replay options:
Argument Description
-echo_replay Specifies the test to replay. Each test targets one or more CPs. All
the tests must be replayed to hit all the targeted CPs.
-echo_dir Specifies the coverage convergence database directory (where
the data was dumped during -echo_hints run). Default is
simv.ccdb dir
-echo_replay_dir Specifies the database directory where replay run data is dumped.
Default is simv.ccdb.replay.
-echo_replay_sym Enables the mode for replaying positive hints for the CPs.
-echo_replay_tests File having information to replay the tests to hit targeted CPs
(case where the test file is present in non-coverage convergence
database directory).
Example,
% ./simv -echo_replay_sym -echo_replay=1 \
-echo_replay_tests=<echo_dir>/cc.tests

Bias Files
Options to Generate Bias Files
Following are the options to generate bias files. You can provide these options during
simulation as well as replay.
-echo_select_cps
Divides the targeted coverage space into multiple ranges, or sets it similar to the Echo
bias file. Each selected range or set can be targeted and replayed separately or in parallel.
-echo_vdb_dir
Specifies the coverage database used to generate the targeted holes.
Examples:
• % ./simv -echo_hints -echo_select_cps=range,<x>,<y>
-echo_vdb_dir=<coverage_database>
Where, x and y are start and end numbers for the range.
• % ./simv -echo_hints -echo_select_cps=set,<x>,<y>
-echo_vdb_dir=<coverage_database>
Where, x is the number of sets into which the targeted coverage space is to be divided,
and y is the number set to the target.
Files Generated During Simulation
During the simulation, VCS generates the following files (see Table 6) in the <echo_dir>
directory or simv.ccdb. The default coverage convergence database directory where
reports are generated is simv.ccdb.
Table 6 Files Generated During Simulation
File Name Description
report_init.txt VCS generates this file at the end of the simulation. This file
contains the following information for the targeted CPs:
NOT TRIGGERED: CPs not triggered during simulation
UNCONTROLLABLE: CPs which are not controllable
Positive const branches: uncontrollable CPs which got
hit during simulation
Negative const branches: uncontrollable CPs which did
not get hit during simulation
CONTROLLABLE: CPs which are controllable

Table 6 Files Generated During Simulation (Continued)
File Name Description
report_solving.txt This file contains solving or coverage analysis related information.
This file provides information for periodic dump on the number of
solved CPs, remaining CPs, and SAT for coverable and UNSAT
for uncoverable CPs.
hint_report.txt This file contains the final hint report after solving or coverage
analysis is complete. This file provides information on positive and
negative hints. It reports SAT for coverable objects and UNSAT
for uncoverable objects.
cc.tests This file contains tests (in internal format) to replay all the CPs for
which positive hints are generated. This file is used in the third

Usage Scenarios
This section discusses Echo usage in various common verification scenarios. In all the
scenarios in this section, it is assumed that the guidelines mentioned in the previous
section are being followed (for example, coverage and constraints are on the same
variables, and so on).
You can load a pre-existing coverage database in every scenario to screen out already-
covered coverage bins. By doing so, the current run can focus only on uncovered bins.
The coverage database must be loaded after all the testbench components have been
instantiated, so that the coverage data from the database can be loaded in the proper (in-
memory) runtime database.

title: 33 A=1, B=0 Y=0
text:
Usage Scenarios
Running a Single Test with Randomized Configurations
This scenario generally applies to multimedia devices, in which the device has many
interfaces and many modes and the device can be configured to select some interfaces
and some modes.
The object of verification is to exercise all the interesting configurations of the device. In
the testbench, configurations are selected, and then data (possibly random) is passed
through the device.
Configurations for a device are typically chosen (through randomize) a few times per
test run. In the extreme case, only one configuration might be selected (for example,
config.randomize is performed only once).
In this scenario, it is important to pre-load the coverage database to ensure that already-
selected configurations are not chosen.
Running a Single Test With Randomized Transactions
This scenario applies to transaction-based verification environments. This scenario is
required for packet-processing devices or instruction-based processor verification.
The device is set in some mode, and then multiple transactions are generated and
passed through the device. You use constraints to generate the transaction objects. In this
scenario, you can use the default arguments for Echo.
If you assume that many transactions are generated (randomized), then it is appropriate
for the convergence heuristics to take over and apply reactive calls as needed.
status = transObj.randomize();
or
repeat (1000) {
transObj = new;
status = transObj.randomize();
}
Autogenerating a Coverage Model
Echo can generate a coverage model from the constraints specification. However, you
must instantiate the coverage model that you intend to use in the simulation.
1. Autogenerate the coverage model:
% vcs -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen foo.vr
Echo generates the model in the file ./echo_cov_gen/MyClass.vr.

Methodology and Flow Issues
This section addresses methodology and regression execution issues.
Scenario: All Tests have the Same Constraints and Coverage
Space (Recommended)
When all the tests being executed in parallel have exactly the same coverage space and
the same legal stimulus space (that is, the constraints are exactly the same for all the
tests), then the Echo bias file approach can be used to achieve high efficiency test runs.
Each test should have its own bias file. The input database for the URG utility can be
obtained by running any test and using the output coverage database. The number of test
runs should be used as the value for the echo_gen_bias argument for URG. Once the
bias files are generated, they can be used again and again for repeated regression runs.
It is desirable that the number of times the stimulus objects are randomized in a test be
at least equal to the average number of coverage bins in the bias files. After all the tests
are done running, the coverage database from all the tests can be merged to get the final
coverage number. It is possible but not efficient to use both the random seed and the bias
file for every test.

Methodology and Flow Issues
Scenario: Tests are Grouped into Categories With Each Category
having Specific Test Constraints
In this scenario, tests have test specific test constraints which further constrain the legal
stimulus space and thus also reduce the hittable coverage bins. (Coverage bins whose
value ranges lie outside the space of the test constraints cannot be hit). A bias file can
be created for every category of tests. The bias file should be such that all the coverage
bins in the file are hittable given the test constraints for that category. Each test within
this category can use the same bias file but with a different random seed. The URG bias
generation utility can be used to generate a bias file template. (Note that the URG does
not look at test constraints when generating the bias files). The test writer can then modify
this template to include the hittable coverage bins. As in the previous scenario, assuming
test constraints remain constant across regression runs, then the bias files have to be
generated once and can be used for multiple regression runs. Even if all the bins in a
bias file are not hittable, all it causes is less efficient utilization of resources. Echo may
use some cycles in the test run to try to target unhittable bins, but remaining cycles still
target hittable coverage bins. In this scenario too, the coverage data from all the tests
can be collected and merged. Then a sequential run can be used to target any remaining
coverage holes. For this final sequential run, the merged coverage database can be used
as an input along with the fully open constraints.
Scenario: Coverage Database Being Loaded in the Beginning of a
Test Run
If a coverage database is being loaded as part of the configuration for a test, then there
is no need to use an Echo bias file. Echo only targets coverage bins that are not covered
in the loaded database, so it is already biased in some sense. If the same database
is loaded in multiple tests, then a random seed can be used so that each test targets
different holes. This is useful in a batch mode type of regression environment. Here all
tests have the same constraints and coverage space, but one batch of tests is run at one
time. After the batch is complete, the coverage databases are merged and the merged
database is used as input for the next batch of tests. Note that for repeatability purposes,
the input database associated with a test needs to be preserved in case the test needs to
be run in a stand alone mode. If an Echo bias file is used, then it overrides the bias from
the loaded coverage database, that is, holes in the bias file are targeted even if they are
marked as covered in the loaded coverage database. Hence it does not make sense to
use both coverage database load and Echo bias file approaches for a test.

Compile-Time Options
This section describes the options you use to enable the Echo technology when using the
VCS compiler.
You also need to specify the options described in this chapter (as appropriate) when you
execute simulation (that is, when you run simv).
Echo Option
-ntb_opts echo+echo_new_flow
Ensures that the required Echo-related processing is done for all relevant coverage points.
Example for OpenVera testbench:
vcs -ntb_opts echo+echo_new_flow foo.vr
Example for SystemVerilog testbench:
vcs -sverilog -ntb_opts echo+echo_new_flow foo.sv
Coverage Model Autogeneration Options
-ntb_opts echo_cov_gen
Generates a coverage model for a stimulus object—that is, for a class that contains
random variables and/or constraints.
See Support of Crosses With Non-Random Coverage Points for details on how a
coverage model is inferred from constraints.

Echo Command Reference
When you specify this option, Echo writes automatically inferred cover groups (if any) to
the directory ${SIMV_DIR}/echo_cov_gen. You can specify a different directory with the
-ntb_opts echo_cov_gen_dir option.
Note that if the echo_cov_gen directory already exists, any files in that directory are
overwritten when you rerun Echo with the -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen option.
The names of the files created (and the names of the coverage groups themselves)
depend on the names of classes and constraints blocks in the source file.
Example for SystemVerilog testbench:
vcs -sverilog -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen foo.sv
-ntb_opts echo_cov_gen_dir <directory_name>
Overrides the default directory (./echo_cov_gen) into which Echo writes automatically
inferred covergroups.

Methodology Features
This chapter describes the following UVM/OVM/VMM Methodology LCA features:
• Ralgen Support for IEEE Standard 2014 for IP-XACT
• Support for UVM Profiler
Ralgen supports the following features to comply with the IEEE Standard 2014 for IP-
XACT:
• Support elements relevant to register model, which are listed in Annexure C and
Annexure E sections of IEEE Standard for IP-XACT, 1685-2014.
• Specify backdoor paths using accessHandles and the elements contained inside it.
• Support expressions involving arithmetic operators.
To convert IP-XACT to RALF, use the following command:
ralgen -ipxact2014 -ipxact2ralf
To generate the SV model directly from IP-XACT, use the following command:
ralgen -ipxact2014 -ipxact <other options for model generation>
Apart from -ipxact or -ipxact2ralf, additionally -ipxact2014 is required to
parse the XML as per IEEE Standard for IP-XACT, 1685-2014.
Following is the list of the IP-XACT elements that are relevant to the register model:
• C.1 accessHandles
• C.3 complexBaseExpressions
• C.5 configurableElementValues

• C.6 configurableLibraryRefType

Support for Backdoor Path
You can specify backdoor paths using accessHandles and the elements contained inside
it.
Note that,
• Each index entry in the indices element corresponds to the select element in one
dimension each. Multiple index entries model a select into a multidimensional array.
• When the indices element is specified inside pathSegment, it corresponds to the
select being applied on the RTL. However, when the indices element is specified
directly inside accessHandle, it indicates the IP-XACT array element to which the
corresponding pathSegement is paired, such as, register array.

◦ The latter case of specifying unique path for each array element is not supported
in this release. You can specify the pathSegmentName using %d to denote the index
being used in the RTL path. The final RAL model substitutes the index accordingly.
• For modeling RTL paths involving concatenation or part-selects, slices must be used
to specify the path.

Support for Expressions
Ralgen supports expressions involving arithmetic operators; however, other operators
are not supported. Ralgen supports the type of expressions that are defined in C.3
complexBaseExpression section of IEEE Standard for IP-XACT, 1685-2014.
These type of expressions are as follows:
realExpression, signedLongintExpression, stringExpression,
unsignedBitExpression, unsignedBitVectorExpression,
unsignedIntExpression, unsignedLongintExpression,
unsignedPositiveIntExpression, unsignedPositiveLongintExpression
Support for Constants

Support for UVM Profiler
IP-XACT has the concept of parameters which can hold the literal value and these
parameters can then be used in the context of expressions in ralgen. For example,
<ipxact:paramters>
<ipxact:parameter parameterId="addrBits" choiceRef="bitsize"
prompt="Address Bits" type="shortint" resolve="user">
<ipxact:name>addrBits</ipxact:name>
<ipxact:value>32</ipxact:value>
</ipxact:parameter>
</ipxact:parameters>
Only arithmetic operators are supported in expressions.
Support for UVM Profiler
VCS offers simprofile using which you can identify the functions in the design where
most of the time is spent, their call count, and the memory used by various parts of the
design. However, this information is not always usable because it does not point to the
exact object in your design or object based call chain information.
VCS provides UVM profiler that allows you to have a comprehensive view of the profile
information. The UVM profiler can provide object level details for each call to the UVM
class methods and also assists in narrowing down to the sub-optimal code in the UVM
testbench faster. Hence, the UVM profiler helps you to resolve the bottlenecks in the UVM
based testbench.
At compile time:
Pass the -simprofile=uvm option during elaboration.
If you want to dump only specific data, you can use the following options:
• -simprofile=uvm:user- This option allows you to dump data on user classes only.
The option does not dump data on UVM base classes.

Support for UVM Profiler
At Runtime:
No option is required at runtime. Once the simulation is completed, uvm_profiler.db is
generated. This contains the information that can be post-processed to create HTML files.
Post-Processing Utility
uvmprofrpt is the post processing utility that generates the HTML files.
Syntax:
uvmprofrpt -uvm_profiler=db:uvm_profiler.db
When you run this utility, it generates a directory called uvm_profiler. This directory
contains two types of HTML reports, which are hierarchical report and flat report. The
following figures show the sample reports:
Figure 55 UVM Profiler Hierarchical Report
In the above figure, rows with brown background refer to the UVM base class functions
and the rows with purple background refer to the user class functions.

Support for UVM Profiler
Figure 56 UVM Profiler Flat Report
The UVM Profiler Flat report provides the function definition based count and the
respective time consumption. This does not have object based association. The function
calls made from different objects are counted cumulatively based on the definition.
In both the hierarchical view and flat view, when you click on the method name, it shows
the caller-callee list related to that function and the corresponding statistics as shown in
the Caller-Callee report.
Additional Options on UVM Profiler
The following are some of the additional options that can be used to customize the reports:
% simv -uvm_profiler[= num_entries:{value} | ignoreUVMCalls]
% simv -uvm_profiler=num_entries:200
% simv -uvm_profiler=num_entries:200+ignoreUVMCalls
These are the descriptions of arguments used in the example:
• num_entries=value - Indicates the number of entries that you need. In the above
example, the top 200 entries that are sorted by Exclusive Wall Time are reported. The
default is 500.
• ignoreUVMCalls - When you specify this option, all UVM functions and tasks called
internally within UVM methods are not reported in detail. Their time consumption is
reported in the first UVM method directly called by user function/task. By default it
includes UVM calls.

Support for UVM Profiler
These options can also be passed to the uvmprofrpt utility.
The feature has the following limitation:
• UVM phase based reporting is currently not supported.
• UVM profiler is applicable only to SystemVerilog.

• Delay in RETAIN Calculation for Accurate Simulation Behavior
• Using Module Path Delay Feature to Reduce Pulses
Delay in RETAIN Calculation for Accurate Simulation Behavior
VCS considers delayed versions of clock and data signals when you use +neg_tchk
for negative timing checks. The IOPATH calculation is not affected by the +neg_tchk
option. However, you can consider delayed signals in RETAIN calculations when you use
(-sdfretain) with negative timing check (+neg_tchk).
Consider the following SDF example:
(DELAY
(ABSOLUTE
(COND (COND) (IOPATH CLK O (RETAIN (5) (10)) (7) (14) ))
)
)
In this example, RETAIN is applied only when the condition COND is true. By default, VCS
samples COND at the edge of the original CLK signal. However, when negative timing
checks are involved, sampling the condition value on the original clock edge is not correct.
This is because data might not be valid at this time. This version of VCS enables you
to sample the RETAIN condition on the delayed clock edge. This results in accurate
calculation.
To enable this feature, use the option
-xlrm retain_with_delayed_sig
-xlrm retain_with_delayed_sig along with
-sdfretain and +neg_tchk option.
The following is the use model:
%vcs -xlrm retain_with_delayed_sig -sdfretain +neg_tchk <>

Chapter 14: Gate-Level Simulation
Delay in RETAIN Calculation for Accurate Simulation Behavior
The following example illustrates a delay calculation. It includes the outputs that are
generated with delay and without delay in the RETAIN calculation. To run this example,
use the file general.sdf. The following is an example general.sdf file:
Example 45 general.sdf
(DELAYFILE
(SDFVERSION "OVI 3.0")
(DIVIDER /)
(TIMESCALE 1ns)
(CELL
(CELLTYPE "dut")
(INSTANCE top/I1)
(DELAY
(ABSOLUTE
(COND (COND) (IOPATH CLK O (RETAIN (5) (10)) (7) (14) ))
)
)
)
(CELL
(CELLTYPE "dut")
(INSTANCE top/I1)
(TIMINGCHECK
(SETUPHOLD (posedge D) (negedge CLK) (-8) (20))
(SETUPHOLD (negedge D) (posedge CLK) (-8) (20))
)
)
)

wire O1;

$sdf_annotate("./general.sdf");
CLK=0; D=0; #100;
CLK=1; D=0; #100;
CLK=0; D=1; #100;
end
always @(D or CLK or O1)
$monitor($time,,"d=%b, clk=%b, O=%b", D, CLK, O1);
force I1.COND = 0; #4;
force I1.COND = 1;
end

Changing Default Scope of DPI Functions
By default, VCS sets the scope to calling context of DPI function. However, as per
LRM Section H.9.3, scope must be set to declaration context. You can use the
-dpi_lrm_context option at compile time for LRM compliance behavior.
The -dpi_lrm_context option is required only if the declaration context and
the calling context of the DPI function are different.
Use the following option at compile time:
• vcs -sverilog -dpi_lrm_context <filename.sv> <filename.c>
In three step flow, use this option at vcs step.

Changing Default Scope of DPI Functions
Consider the following testcases:
Example 65 test.sv
package mypkg;
import "DPI-C" context function import_a();
export "DPI-C" task export_b;
task automatic export_b();
$display("SV: enter export_b");
$display("SV: leave export_b");
endpackage
mypkg::import_a();
The content of the test.c file is as follows:
#include "svdpi.h"
void import_a()
{
printf("C:enter import_a\n");
printf("scope: %s\n", svGetNameFromScope(svGetScope()));
export_b();
printf("C:leave import_a\n");
}
Run the example using the following commands:
• vcs -sverilog -dpi_lrm_context test.sv test.c -R
The following output is generated:
C:enter import_a
scope: mypkg
SV: enter export_b
SV: leave export_b
C:leave import_a
Without the -dpi_lrm_context option, VCS generates the following error message:
Error-[DPI-DXFNF] DPI export function not found
The DPI export function/task 'export_b' called from a user/external
C/C++/DPI-C code originated from import DPI function 'import_a' at file
'dpi.sv'(line 12) is not defined or visible.
Please check the called DPI export function/task is defined in the
mentioned
module, or check if the DPI declaration of the DPI import function/task
which invokes that DPI export function/task is made with 'context'.
Another

Extensions to SystemVerilog
work-around is using svGetScopeFromName/svSetScope to explicitly set
the
scope to the module which contains the definition of the DPI export
function/task.
In this example, the import DPI-C function is declared in mypkg package and is called
inside the top module. An export DPI-C function is declared in the same package and
called inside the import DPI-C function. Without the -dpi_lrm_context option, VCS
issues the DXFNF -DPI export function not found error message at runtime as it
searches for the export DPI function inside the calling context, that is, the top module.
However, it cannot locate it.
When you use the -dpi_lrm_context option, the declaration context, that is, the mypkg
package is searched.
Extensions to SystemVerilog
Support for Variable-Size Arrays In continuous assignment and
force Statements
VCS supports variable-size arrays in the right side of continuous assignment and force
statements by using the -xlrm dyn_types_in_ca option at compile-time.
The following is an example where variable-size array is used on the right side of
continuous assignment and force statements. The newly supported expressions are
described in the following example.
Example 66 test.v
module m;
logic [6:0] a [string][][$];
logic [6:0] c,d;
int i;
assign d = a["wr"][i][1] ;
static string s[] = '{"wr", "rd"};
#1 foreach(s[i]) begin
a[s[i]] = new[2];
a[s[i]][i] = '{'1,'1};
end
end
#1 force c = a["wr"][i][1] ;
#1 $display("Value of c at %0t is %0d",$time,c);
$display("Value of d at %0t is %0d",$time,d);
end

Extensions to SystemVerilog
Run the example using the following commands:
% vcs test.v -sverilog - xlrm dyn_types_in_ca
The limitation of this feature is as follows:
• Expressions (like function call) which are not allowed/supported inside event control
are not supported with this feature.

Assertion Features
This chapter contains the following feature:
• Signature-Based Control
• Enabling Fail-Only Feature
• Support for Dynamic Data Types in Assertions
VCS provides an enhanced way to control unique-case/priority-case violation checks,
deferred assertions (labeled assertions), immediate and concurrent assertions, initial and
final blocks, using the -assert signature compile-time option.
VCS generates a “signature” in addition to the regular assertion message from the
deferred assertions, unique-case/priority-case violation checks, immediate and concurrent
assertions, initial and final blocks, when you use -assert signature .
A signature is a string made up of tokens extracted from the function call stack trace of
assertions, and is separated by dots. Each signature uniquely determines a path from
where the error/warning occurs, as shown in the following example.
Example 67 Function call stack trace
function f(input a, b);
L: assert final(a > b);
endfunction // function is defined in $unit, used by many
callers as
// intellectual property
reg a, b, c, d;
always_comb begin : block1
f(a, b);
end
always_comb begin : block2
f(c, d);

end
The following output contains the signature (highlighted in bold) for function call stack
trace:
"te1.v", 3: \$unit ::f.L: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending '(a > b)'
#0 in f.L at te1.v:3
#1 in top.block1 at te1.v:10
[Warning/Error Signature: "top.block1.f.L"]

"te1.v", 3: \$unit ::f.L: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending '(a > b)'
#0 in f.L at te1.v:3
#1 in top.block2 at te1.v:13
[Warning/Error Signature: "top.block2.f.L"]
This feature helps you to locate the exact place where the assertion failure occurs. You
can use signature to control assertions, unique-case/priority-case violation checks, and
initial/final blocks. The following section describes how to use signature to achieve the
required control.
Using Signature to Control Assertions
Existing assertion control tasks, including $assertoff()and $asserton(), accept
signature as an argument to perform the control.
The following topics illustrate how to use signature to control the assertions in various
ways:
• Full-signature control (single control)
• Partial-signature control (group control)
• Static Configuration File
• Runtime Control
Full-signature control (single control)
In Example 68, VCS provides all assertion failures and the corresponding signatures for
them, as shown in Output: run.log.ref:
Example 68 Full-signature Control
reg a;
function reg foo (reg a);
for(int i=1;i<2;i++) begin:BL
for(int j=-1;j<1;j++) begin
A1 : assert final (a !== 1'b1);

end
end
foo = 1;
module Top;
reg b;
reg cond;
// here, the signature of each path is presented
a = 1'b1;
#0;
end
always_comb begin : AL
for(int i=0;i<1;i++) begin:BL1
foo(a);
end
for(int i=1;i<2;i++) begin:BL2
foo(a);
end
end
Output: run.log.ref
"cts2.v", 5: \$unit ::foo.BL.A1: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending '(a !== 1'b1)'
#0 in foo.BL.A1 at cts2.v:5
#1 in loop with j=-1 at cts2.v:4
#2 in loop with i= 1 at cts2.v:3
#3 in Top.AL.BL1 at cts2.v:26
#4 in loop with i= 0 at cts2.v:25
[Warning/Error Signature: "Top.AL.BL1[0].foo.BL[1].GenLoop_j_0[-1].A1"]

"cts2.v", 5: \$unit ::foo.BL.A1: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending '(a !== 1'b1)'
#0 in foo.BL.A1 at cts2.v:5
#1 in loop with j= 0 at cts2.v:4
#2 in loop with i= 1 at cts2.v:3
#3 in Top.AL.BL1 at cts2.v:26
#4 in loop with i= 0 at cts2.v:25

You can pass the complete signature produced by VCS in a previous run to turn ON/OFF
a particular assertion failure corresponding to that signature.
$assertoff(0, " Top.AL.BL1[0].foo.BL[1].GenLoop_j_0[-1].A1");

Partial-signature control (group control)
Full-signature can only control assertion failure in one particular path at a time. You can
use partial signature, if you want to turn ON/OFF a set of assertion failures.
Scope-level control
When a partial signature ending with a scope name (including a block or function and
so on) is passed to assert control tasks, assertion failures rooted from that scope are
enabled/disabled.
$assertoff(0, "Top.AL");
All failures in Example 68 will be shut off.
Wildcard character control
This feature supports “*” wildcard character in signature string. The “*” wildcard character
represents zero or many tokens in the signature.
For example, if you apply the above wildcard character by specifying the following system
tasks:
$assertoff(0,"Top.AL.*.A1");
the string, Top.AL.*.A1, matches the following signatures (the matched part of “*” is
highlighted in bold): Top.AL.BL1.A1 and Top.AL.BL2.A1
Instance-level control
You can continue to perform instance level control, using different depth levels. The
behavior is compatible with VCS releases prior to G-2012.09, with the below exception:
Control task Effect
$assertoff(0, "Top") All assertions under "Top" will be shut off (including all
those from grand children instances).
$assertoff(1, "Top") Assertions directly under "Top" will be shut off. Others
remain ON.
$assertoff(2, "Top") Assertions under "Top", "Top.L1" will be shut off.
Others (in “Top.L1.L0") remain ON.
$assertoff(-1, "Top") Invalid level, generates error message.
Even for those assertion failures that do not have signatures generated, due
to one of the reasons listed in Contexts where no Signature is Generated, they

can still be turned on or off by instance-level control. This is to match legacy
semantics.

Static Configuration File
The signature can be used as an argument for static control. You can use the signature
option with the signature string, as shown in this example, to define signature in static
configuration file.
Example 69 Specifying signature in static configuration file
//----sig.cfg-----------------------------------
+signature M.AL.GenLoop_i_0[0].foo.loopA[0].U1
-signature Top.AL.*.A1
//----------------------------------------------
+signature
Enables all assertions represented by the signature.
-signature
Disables all assertions represented by the signature.
The configuration file (sig.cfg in Example 69) can be used to control either assertions or
unique-case/priority-case violation checks, at compile time or at runtime.
You can use the static configuration file with the -assert hier_uniq option, as described
in Table 10.
Table 10 The -assert hier_uniq option commands
Command Effect
vcs -assert hier_uniq=sig.cfg Controls all applicable unique-case/priority-case
violation checks at compile-time.
vcs -assert hier=sig.cfg Controls all applicable assertions at compile-time.
simv -assert hier_uniq=sig.cfg Controls all applicable unique-case/priority-case
violation checks at runtime.
simv -assert hier=sig.cfg Controls all applicable assertions at runtime.
-assert hier and -assert hier_uniq runtime options require -assert
enable_hier at compile time.

If you want to control assertions/ unique-case and priority-case violation checks uniformly,
the same configuration file can be passed to different switches, as shown below:
% vcs -assert signature -assert hier_uniq=sig.cfg -assert hier=sig.cfg
In this way, all assertions and unique-case/priority-case violation checks whose signatures
match those defined in configuration file will be disabled/enabled.
• All existing syntax, such as -assert, -tree, and so on continues to work as before.
• You can use the -signature option in the existing file along with legacy -assert,
-tree.
Runtime Control
You can use the call command, as shown below, to call the signature-based control at
runtime.
call {$assertoff(0, "Top.AL.BL1[0].foo.BL[1].GenLoop_j_0[-1].A1")};
All types of control (single or group) presented in sections Partial-signature control (group
control) and Static Configuration File works using the call command.
Generating Warning Message for Invalid Signature Path
VCS generates a warning message, if the static path of the signature is not valid. Consider
the following example testcase:
Example 70 Testcase test.sv
module Test;

logic a;
mod1 m1(a);

$assertoff(0, "Test.m1.m2.blk2.A1");
end

VCS generates the following warning message for Example 70:
Warning-[RA-INVSTR] Not found in design
"Test.m1.m2.blk2.A1" not found in design. Ignored in "$assertoff".

"tx.v", 21: Test.m1.m2.blk1.A1: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending 'a'
[Signature: "Test.m1.m2.blk1.A1"]
Key points to note
• An XMR that starts with a module name is not supported. For example, mod1.A1 is not
supported.
• This feature is not supported for designs.
Support for Signature-Based Control in Immediate and
Concurrent Assertions
VCS supports these features for immediate and concurrent assertions:
• Block-level exclusion of assertions.
• Using “*” wildcard character in the regular expressions for exclusion of assertions.
For example, consider Example 71.
Example 71 Testcase test.sv
reg a, b, c, d;

always_comb begin : block
L1: assert (a > b);
L2: assert (a < b);
end
$assertoff(0,"top.block");
$assertoff(0,"top.*");
end
In Example 71, all assertions defined inside the block level top.block are excluded.

In the $assertoff(0,"top.*") command, all the assertions matching the wildcard pattern are
excluded.
Support for Signature-Based Control in Initial and Final Blocks
VCS supports signature-based control for assertions in the initial and final blocks. For
example, consider the following code which contains initial block:
Example 72 test.v

initial begin : INI //Behavioral
for(int i=0;i<1;i++) begin : LOOP
A1: assert final (0);
end
end

This is the simulation output for the above code:
"test.v", 5: top.INI.LOOP.A1: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending '0'
#0 in top.INI.LOOP.A1 at test.v:5
#1 in loop with i= 0 at test.v:4
[Signature: "top.INI.LOOP[0].A1"]
In the above simulation output, top.INI.LOOP[0].A1 is the signature generated by VCS for
assertion A1 in the initial block.
Key points to note
• Functions having deferred assertions with the named action block, but called from the
final block, are not supported.
• Function calls from the final block are not supported in the partition compile flow.
• Contexts where no Signature is Generated
The signature is introduced to locate the exact place where the assert failure occurs.
Each signature corresponds to a real hardware unit when the design is synthesized.
If an assertion is not placed in a synthesizable code, or if it is not identifiable, no
signature is generated. As a result, such assertions cannot be controlled using
signatures. Example 73, Example 74, , and Example 75 show contexts where
signatures will not be generated.

$assertoff(0,"top.block1.f.L_simple");
end
In Example 76, VCS does not allow you to exclude the assertion for each function call.
This indicates that you cannot exclude top.block1.f.L_simple.

Enabling Fail-Only Feature
Example 77 Assertion Defined Inside the For Loop
bit a;
int i;
always_comb begin : block1
for(i=0;i<3;i++) begin
C_imm: assert (a);
end
end
initial begin:GenLoop_i_0
#2 $finish;
end
In Example 77, VCS does not allow you to exclude the assertion for each loop iteration.
This indicates that you cannot exclude top.block1. GenLoop_i_0[0].C_imm .
Enabling Fail-Only Feature
VCS supports the -assert failonly compile-time option which enables fail-only mode
for concurrent assertion. The -assert failonly option reports only assertion failures
with their end times. For more information, see the section Fail-Only Assertion Evaluation
Mode in the VCS User Guide. However, VCS also supports
-assert select_failonly
-assert select_failonly
option that can move the selected assertions or covers to fail-only mode. The following are
the options:
• auto
• fastcover
• <filename>
The
failonly
failonly mode improves the runtime performance and decreases the runtime
memory requirement.
The use model is as follows:
• -assert select_failonly=auto
This option automatically identifies the assertions to move to fail-only mode.
• -assert select_failonly=fastcover
This option allows you to move all cover properties to fail-only mode.
• -assert select_failonly=<filename>

• % vcs -sverilog test.v -assert svaext -assert select_failonly=auto
• % vcs -sverilog test.v -assert svaext -assert
select_failonly=fastcover
• % vcs -sverilog test.v -assert svaext -assert select_failonly=test.txt
Where, the content of the test.txt file is as follows:

mod2 A2
Following is the simulation command:
• % simv
Outputs
This section shows the difference in outputs that is generated with default option and with
auto, fastcover, and <test.txt> option.
Output with Default Options
The default flow starts at 99 attempts and each failure is reported with start time and end
time.
"test.v", 30: top.m1.A1: started at 1ns failed at 101ns
Offending 'c'

Offending 'c'
For cover properties, there are 60 attempts and 60 matches,
"test.v", 34: top.m2.A2, 60 attempts, 60 match
Outputs with options
• The -assert select_failonly=auto option reports failure with end times for all
assertions maturing at the same time.
"test.v", 30: top.m1.A1: failed at 101ns
Offending '1'b0'
For covers properties, it reports only one match for all covers maturing at the same
time.
"test.v", 34: top.m2.A2, 10 match

• The -assert select_failonly=fastcover.txt option reports one match for all
covers maturing at the same time.
"test.v", 34: top.m2.A2, 10 match
• The -assert select_failonly=text.txt option reports the following failures for the
modules specified in the text.txt file.
"test.v", 30: top.m1.A1: failed at 101ns
Offending '1'b0'
"test.v", 34: top.m2.A2, 60 attempts, 60 match
VCS supports dynamic data as specified in IEEE Std 1800-2012 Section 16.6 Boolean
expressions. The dynamic data types supported are as follows:
• String data types
• Dynamic array size and static array value
• Functions on queues ( queue.size() and queue.empty() and static queue values)
• Static class functions and members
Use the -assert allow_dynamic option at compile time.
-assert allow_dynamic
% vcs <filename> -assert allow_dynamic -sverilog

Overview
This chapter describes the availability of the VMM-SystemC library (VMM-SC) with VCS
E-2011.03 and later versions. It consists of a set of base classes equivalent to the VMM
library in SystemVerilog (SV). It also describes the use model for the VMM-SC based
verification methodology and how you can use this methodology with VMM SystemVerilog
(VMM-SV).
The VMM-SC implementation is based on VMM D-2010.06 and later versions of VMM-SV.
VMM-SC does not implement all the classes and utilities that are provided with VMM-SV.
The supported classes and utilities are described in detail in this chapter.
Purpose
The purpose of this document is to familiarize you with the VMM-SC class library. The
following section provides a brief introduction to VMM-SC base classes, followed by the
different use model for VMM-SystemC.
The objective of VMM-SC is to provide a unified reference verification methodology in
conjunction with VMM-SV for system-level verification to RTL verification. The system-
level environments primarily use the SystemC/C-based models.

You use VMM-SC to develop a verification environment at the system level and also to
verify the system on a chip (SoC) at the RTL level with VMM-SV effectively. For details,
see the use model section.

vmm_data
The vmm_data class provides some common functions required by any data payload.
User-defined payload can be derived from this class to make use of these functions. The
standard library provides the following macros to use these functions.
Macros Usage
1. VMM_DATA (user payload class)
Use this macro to define a payload class.
2. VMM_DATA_CTOR (user payload class){ …}
Use this macro to define a constructor when the payload is derived from vmm_data.
However, if your payload has multiple base classes, provide your own constructor.
3. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_BEGIN (user payload class)
Call this macro inside a user payload class definition. This macro is mandatory and
should be used before using the following macro.
4. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_BASE_CLASS (base class)

Call this macro for each and every base class of user payload class with the name of
the base class as its argument.
The macros from 5-13 are used based on the type of the member variable
name of the user payload class.
The following arguments are used with these macros:
◦ type: Gives the type of the member variable.
◦ member: Member variable name.
◦ length: Length of the array.
◦ do_what: Is an enum with values DO_PRINT, DO_COPY, DO_COMPARE, DO_PACK,
DO_UNPACK, and DO_ALL. Depending on this value, the variable is involved in the
common functions.
◦ do_how: Is an enum with the following values:
▪ DO_NOCOPY, DO_REFCOPY, DO_DEEPCOPY
▪ HOW_TO_COPY (OR of all DO_*COPY)
▪ DO_NOCOMPARE, DO_REFCOMPARE, DO_DEEPCOMPARE
▪ HOW_TO_COMPARE (OR of all DO_*COMPARE)
▪ DO_NONE (OR of all DO_NO*)
▪ DO_REF (OR of all DO_REF*)
▪ DO_DEEP (OR of all DO_DEEP*)
◦ format: The member variable is printed based on this format. For example, <<hex,
<<dec, and so on. This argument can also be left blank.
5. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_SCALAR (type, member, do_what, format )
Use this macro for any C++/SystemC scalar data types and std::string, but not for
char pointers.
6. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_SCALAR_ARRAY (type, member, length, do_what, format )
Use this macro for C++/SystemC arrays of scalar types and arrays of std::string.
7. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_SCALAR_PTR (type, member, length, do_what, do_how,
format)

Use this macro for any C++/SystemC pointers and std::string pointers. You should
allocate sufficient space for these pointers.
8. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_CHAR_PTR (type, member, do_what, format )
This macro can be used for C++/SystemC char pointers.
9. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_ENUM (type, member, do_what, format )
This macro can be used for enum types.
10. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_ENUM_ARRAY (type, member, length, do_what, format )
This macro can be used for an array of enums.
11. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_VMM_DATA (type, member, do_what, format )
Use this macro for any member objects of type vmm_data and its derivatives.
12. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_VMM_DATA_ARRAY (type, member, do_what, format )
Use this macro for any member which is an array of objects of type vmm_data and its
derivatives.
13. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_VMM_DATA_PTR (type, member, do_what, do_how, format )
Use this macro for any member which is a pointer to type vmm_data and its derivatives.
14. VMM_DATA_MEMBER_END (user payload class)
Call this macro after all the members are covered by the above macros.
All the above macros make every member to get involved in the common functions such
as psdisplay(), copy(), compare(), byte_pack(), and byte_unpack(). If you need to
provide implementation for any of the above functions, then implement do_psdisplay(),
do_copy(), do_compare(), do_byte_pack(), and do_byte_unpack() to overwrite the
corresponding default implementation provided by the standard library.
Because the vmm_data class is an abstract base class, it cannot be instantiated directly.
The default implementations of byte_pack() and byte_unpack() are not provided if the
NON_VCS flag is defined by a non-VCS user.
• vmm_data class is an abstract base class; therefore, it cannot be instantiated
directly.
• The default implementations of byte_pack() and byte_unpack() are not
provided if the NON_VCS flag is defined by a non-VCS user.
• The macros for pointer to char array , array of char pointers, and
containers such as std::map, std::vector, and std::list are also not

implemented. You must write the common functions for these by using do_*
functions.
• For the copy (vmm_data* to ) function, unlike in SystemVerilog (SV), you
should either allocate the to object or set to NULL before calling the copy
function.
• For byte packing/unpacking, the VMMSCBytes class creates and allocates
the bytearray. You can get the size and pointer of the byte array by using
the functions getByteArraySize() and getBytesPtr().
• The float, double, and sc_bit data types are not supported.

The vmm_log feature in VMM-SC provides an exception reporting facility to report an

Macros
• VMM_VERBOSE
• VMM_DEBUG

The usage of all the above macros is the same as in VMM-SV.
Controlling Log Report

1. SET_SEVERITY(severity)
Call this macro to set the severity. The expected values are as follows:
◦ ERROR_MSG_TYPE: Prints only VMM_ERROR messages.
◦ WARNING_MSG_TYPE: Prints VMM_WARNING and VMM_ERROR messages.
◦ NOTE_MSG_TYPE: Prints VMM_WARNING, VMM_ERROR, and VMM_NOTE messages.
◦ TRACE_MSG_TYPE: Prints VMM_WARNING, VMM_ERROR, VMM_NOTE, and VMM_TRACE
messages.
◦ DEBUG_MSG_TYPE: Prints VMM_WARNING, VMM_ERROR, VMM_NOTE, VMM_TRACE, and
VMM_DEBUG messages.
VERBOSE_MSG_TYPE: Prints all messages.
By default, the severity is set to NOTE_MSG_TYPE.
2. STOP_AFTER_N_ERRORS(limit)
Call this macro to set a limit on the number of reports (ERROR types) that can cause
simulation to call sc_stop () .
For example, STOP_AFTER_N_ERRORS(10);
This macro sets the default error count to 10.

You can now use VMM-SC in a pure SystemC environment or with SystemC-

of using verification constructs like constraints, randomization, and coverage that are

The following important components for a verification environment are listed:
• Transaction data classes to specify the payload data
• Multiple verification components implemented as transactors
• Transaction-level interfaces to connect various transactors
• One or more sub-blocks instantiating lower-level transactors
• Top-level verification environment
• Multiple test cases
VMM provides base classes to implement each verification component and guidelines to
implement robust and reusable testbenches. A few other base classes and utilities like
vmm_opts are provided for ease of use and controlling the testbench behavior from the
test-case level. VMM-SC provides a message service utility for issuing message reports
from the testbench.
A verification environment developed in VMM-SC can be used to verify a transaction-level
reference model. This can also be reused to verify the pin-level RTL. The pin-level RTL
can be in SystemC, Verilog-HDL, VHDL, or a combination of these HDLs.

Defining Transaction Data Objects Using vmm_data
VMM-SC provides a vmm_data base class for defining the packet data. User extensions
of the vmm_data class. This specifies the member fields of the payload data class. The
shorthand macros available with vmm_data provide an implementation of basic functions
such as byte_pack, byte_unpack, print, compare, and copy. These are required for
most payload classes.
You can also use the OSCI-TLM2 tlm_generic_payload class as a payload class in a
VMM-SC environment.
Example 80 Transaction Class Defined Using vmm_data
VMM_DATA(my_payload)
{
VMM_DATA_CTOR(my_payload){};
int addr;
int data;

VMM_DATA_MEMBER_BEGIN(my_payload)
VMM_DATA_MEMBER_BASE_CLASS(vmm_data)
VMM_DATA_MEMBER_SCALAR(int,addr,DO_ALL,<<hex)
VMM_DATA_MEMBER_SCALAR(int,data,DO_ALL,<<hex)
VMM_DATA_MEMBER_END(my_payload)
};
Example 80 shows the transaction data class extended from vmm_data. There
are two member variables, addr and data. The use of shorthand macros,
'vmm_data_member_scalar for each member variable provides the implementation of
member functions. For example, byte_pack, byte_unpack, and others.
For the complete list and functionality of the methods implemented by the shorthand
macros, see the VMM User Guide.
Issuing Message Reports Using VMM Log Macros
The macros provided in VMM-SC match the different severity-level macros provided in
VMM (Verification Methodology Manual) SystemVerilog. In pure VMM-SC, the messages
are internally issued by sc_report_handler. The messages are issued on standard
output by default. If the sc_report_handler is set to issue the messages into another log
file, the VMM log messages are also redirected to the same log file.

Communication Between Transactors
VMM-SC does not specifically provide any transaction-level interface. The OSCI-TLM 2.0
is the recommended transaction-level interface that you should use to connect various
verification components. You can also use other transaction-level interfaces like TLM1.0 or
sc_fifo.
Defining Verification Environment Using vmm_group
A verification environment or sub-environment instantiates, connects, and controls the
underlying lower-level transactors. A verification environment is implemented in VMM-SC
by extending the vmm_group or vmm_subenv class.

title: 0 d=0, clk=0, O=0 0 d=0, clk=0, O=0
text:
The vmm_group and vmm_subenv classes have the same phases as those in the
vmm_xactor. The vmm_group is an implicitly phased environment class. The phases of
the children of the vmm_group class are also called implicitly in a top-down or bottom-up
manner. That is depending on the phase.
The vmm_subenv provides both implicit and explicit phase methods. In implicit phasing, the
children of vmm_subenv are not called implicitly. The particular phase method of the child
must be called in the appropriate phase method of vmm_subenv.
For more details on vmm_group and vmm_subenv, see the VMM User Guide.

Coordinating Simulation Using vmm_timeline
Use the vmm_timeline class to coordinate simulation through a user-defined timeline.
A verification environment can have a single timeline controlling the top-level verification
components. This can also have multiple timelines in different verification sub-
environments connected hierarchically to a top-level timeline.
The top-level timeline is instantiated in the verification top, which is usually an sc_module
extension. This verification top instantiates a top-level timeline. This instantiates the
verification environment and connects the timeline to the verification environment. This
also executes the timeline by calling the run_phase() method of vmm_timeline.
For more details on vmm_timeline, see the VMM User Guide.

You can synchronize VMM-SC transactors with VMM-SV transactors using the interop
solution (that is, you can synchronize the phases in the VMM-SC and VMM-SV worlds).
The interop use model depends on whether vmm_timeline or vmm_simulation is a top
level. It is recommended to use vmm_simulation as a top level.
Interconnects in Interop Flow
The interop flow interconnects to communicate between the two languages (SC and SV).
For this purpose you have two interconnect classes, one in SC and the other in SV.

• Interconnect class in SC: vmm_interop
• Interconnect class in SV: vmm_interop
Interconnect class in SC: vmm_interop:
Use this SC class to call phases in SV-SC interop mode using the following static
methods:
1. run_phase(interop_dir dir, vmm_timeline* top_timeline):
This method is called when you have vmm_timeline as a top level and need to run SV
and SC phases in sync.
The first argument is an enum which takes the direction. Valid values are as follows:
◦ vmm_interop::SV_DRV (when the direction is SV->SC)
◦ vmm_interop::SC_DRV (when the direction is SC->SV)
The second argument is a top-level timeline.
2. run_tests (interop_dir dir, string tests):
This method is called when you have vmm_simulation as a top level and want to run
SV and SC phases in sync.
The first argument is an enum which takes the direction. Valid values are as follows:
◦ vmm_interop::SV_DRV (when the direction is SV->SC)
◦ vmm_interop::SC_DRV (when the direction is SC->SV)
The second argument is vmm_test name, which needs to run. By default, it runs all
tests registered.
Interconnect class in SV: vmm_interop:
This SV class is used to call phases in SV-SC interop mode using the following static
methods:
1. run_phase (interop_dir dir, vmm_timeline top_timeline):
This method is called when you have vmm_timeline as a top level and want to run SV
and SC phases in sync.
The first argument is an enum which takes the direction. Valid values are as follows:
◦ vmm_interop::SV_DRV (when the direction is SV->SC)
◦ vmm_interop::SC_DRV (when the direction is SC->SV)
The second argument is a top-level timeline.

2. run_tests(interop_dir dir, string tests):
This method is called when you have vmm_simulation as a top level and want to run
SV and SC phases in sync.
The first argument is an enum which takes the direction. Valid values are as follows:
◦ vmm_interop::SV_DRV (when the direction is SV->SC)
◦ vmm_interop::SC_DRV (when the direction is SC->SV)
The second argument is vmm_test name, which needs to run. By default, it runs all
tests registered.
Use Model When vmm_timeline is a Top Level
In this flow, you should call vmm_interop::run_phase in SV and SC with appropriate
arguments. This synchronizes the phases in SV and SC.
Perform the following steps in SV:
1. Call imported DPI-C function register_dpi_scope() in the program block where
vmm.sv is included.
2. Call vmm_interop::run_phase() to run the phases implicitly, with direction and top
timeline as arguments to the method.
Perform the following steps in SC:
1. In the top-level SystemC module (or sc_main), call vmm_interop::run_phase() with
direction and top timeline as arguments to the method.

• Executing Multiple Tests in SystemC Testbench Flow
Executing Multiple Tests in SystemC Testbench Flow
VCS enables you to have multiple top-level tests (sc_module) in the testbench (SystemC-
on-top) and allows you to compile all the tests at once and then you can select the test you
want to run during runtime.
In addition, VCS also provides you a capability to write all the new tests together even
after creating the executable (simv). VCS then enables you to compile only the new tests
and run the simulation by selecting one of the compiled tests.
This feature enables the runtime selection of a test scenario in a SystemC testbench
(SystemC on top designs). Each test scenario is defined in its own function. The name of
the function can be anything including sc_main. The rest of the design remains constant.
Quick compile turnaround time can be achieved for different test scenarios by compiling
each top level SystemC test as a separate shared library and selecting the test to execute
during runtime.
Perform the following steps to execute multiple tests in SystemC testbench flow:
1. Build the SystemC-on-top design, where initial testbench (bootstrap test) is instantiated
in sc_main. Also, the option -sysc=shared and -sysc=show_sc_main should be
passed during the elaboration. This bootstrap test is the test that you can modify for the
different tests based on the requirement.
//sc_main.cpp
extern "C" int sc_main(int, char **) {
vhdl1 m1("vhdl1");
vlog1 m2("vlog1");
sc_sub m3("sub");

Support for Partition Compile Flow in Mixed-Signal Simulation
VCS supports partition compile flow in mixed-signal simulation.
The feature requires VCS installation. However, you do not need any VCS
licenses or special licenses. The Verilog-only users can use their existing
licenses for this feature.
Partition Compile Flow
VCS supports SystemVerilog SPICE design configuration with VCS-XA in the partition
compile flow. You can create partitions in the following ways:
• User-defined partitions: SPICE cannot be specified as user-defined partitions. By
default, VCS creates single partition for SPICE.
• Auto-partition: The partitions are automatically created by the tool.
Both user-defined partitions and auto-partitions are supported in two-step flow and three-
step flow.
For two-step flow:
%vcs test.v -ad=<InitFile> <vcs_options> -partcomp
<other_partcomp_options>
For three-step flow:
vlogan 1.v 2.v -work lib1 < vlogan options>;
vhdlan vhdl_files -work lib2 < vhdlan options>;
%vcs top/topConfig -ad=<InitFile> <vcs options> -partcomp
<other_partcomp_options_>

The following are the limitations with this feature:
• Verilog-AMS flow is not supported.
• WREAL connectivity is not certified for pure digital usage and across partitions other than
the SPICE boundary in PC flow.
• SPICE parameter override through array instance hierarchy is not supported in PC
flow.
The following sub-sections are supported for this:
• Bidirectional Converter With SPICE and Tran
• Bidirectional Converter Support with UPF
Bidirectional Converter With SPICE and Tran
In the previous releases, VCS supported automatic insertion of converter module to bridge
up two signals of incompatible types by using the -xlrm enable_converter XLRM
Starting with this release, VCS supports bidirectional converter that is compatible with
SPICE and tran. You can enable this feature by using the enable_bidir_converter
option. For example,
Consider a design that contains a set of net segments those are interconnected by INOUT
ports. The types of these segments are NT1, NT2, …, NTn and they are incompatible
with each other. In these segments, consider NTx to be the most accurate. Then, NTx is
considered as the Most Accurate Representative (MAR) of these set of data-types.
If the MAR information is available, then a single bidirectional converter is inserted for this
whole INOUT island that will have n INOUT ports of types NT1, NT2, …, NTn ( one port for
each type ). Out of these ports, one port is of type NTx, and that is the MAR port.
Using unidirectional converters you can convert (NT1 to NTx), (NT2 to NTx), … (NTn to NTx).
The final resolution happens at the NTx port because NTx is the MAR of this set. Once the
final value is computed, then back-convert (NTx to NT1), (NTx to NT2), … (NTx to NTn) using
unidirectional converters of opposite kinds.
Figure 58 shows the bidirectional converter processing where NT1 is the MAR type and
NT2, NT3 are the non MAR types.

title: 0 d=0, clk=0, O=0 0 d=0, clk=0, O=0
text:
Figure 58 Bidirectional Converter Processing
To enable this feature, use the enable_bidir_converter command in the opt
configuration file. A connect-resolveto rule is added in the opt-configuration file to
provide the MAR type information.
1. Connect-resolveto rule
This rule connects non-MAR net segments that are interconnected by INOUT ports to
MAR type. For example, if NT1, NT2, NT3, NT4 are net segments that are incompatible
with each other and NT4 is the MAR type. Then the connect-resolveto rule connects
NT1, NT2, NT3 resolve to NT4
2. Unidirectional converters that converts each non-MAR to MAR, and vice-versa as
shown in the following table:
Non-MAR to MAR MAR to Non-MAR
NT1_to_NT4 NT1_to_NT4

Non-MAR to MAR MAR to Non-MAR
NT1_to_NT4 NT1_to_NT4
NT1_to_NT4 NT1_to_NT4
Bidirectional converter with n ports (based on the n types in the INOUT port) is generated
by VCS using unidirectional converters, those are specified by the type-adaptor rules in
opt-configuration file.
Bidirectional Converter Support with UPF
System-Verilog does not allow designers to connect a signal to a port if their types are
incompatible. For example, VCS issues "Port-Connection Type Mismatch" error if a wreal
net is connected to a logic port. For the ease of use (under -xlrm enable_converter
option), VCS supports automatic insertion of converter module to bridge up a signal with
a port of incompatible types. You need to provide converter modules and converter-rules
through VCS opt-config file.
For unidirectional conversion (such as logic-to-real or real-to-logic), converter modules
can be developed easily. However, if the dataflow is bidirectional, then developing such
converter is challenging.
Bidir-Island in Presence of UPF
In the presence of UPF, the low-power network-gates (such as ISOLATION, SRSN, SPA
and so on) may get inserted at the power-domain boundaries. These network-gates may
break the net-port connectivity in the design.
Hence, at bidir-island determination time the RNM algorithm should honor the presence
of the low-power network-gates. Based on the presence of these network-gates, there
could be multiple bidir-islands in the design instead of a single island that used to be there
without UPF. The following diagram shows example of Bidir-Islands with UPF.

Figure 59 Bidirectional Islands with UPF

UPF):

This section describes the enhancements that fine tunes the Verilog-AMS discipline
resolution and connectmodule insertion algorithms. Also, commands are introduced to
override Verilog-AMS connect-rules and associated connect-module parameters, and
insertion-modes (merge/split), override the supply-voltage parameter and the threshold
parameters of a particular or a set of connectmodule instances in the design.

The details are in the following sections:
• Overriding Connectmodule
• Setting Net Discipline
• Generating connectmodule Report With Parameters Override Information
• Generating connectmodule Activity Report at Runtime
Overriding Connectmodule
ams_cm
Enables the override of connect rules and connect module parameters in the Verilog-AMS-
SPICE flow.
Using this command, you can override the following:
• General parameters of one or more connect module instances
• Connect module insertion mode (split | merge)
• Connect rule for connect module insertion
This command does not change any disciplines in the design (for this, use
ams_set_discipline).
This command is functional only when the Verilog-AMS-SPICE flow is enabled
using the VCS -ams option. If the Verilog-AMS-SPICE flow is not enabled, this
command is ignored and a warning message is output.
ams_cm connect_rule_module_parameter_name=parameter_value
[mode=split | merge]
[crules=connect_module_library_name.connect_rule_name]
[library=library_name]
[cell=cell_name [node=node_name]]
[inst=inst_name [node=node_name]
[node=hier_name]
connect_rule_module_parameter_name=parameter_value
Specifies the connect rule or connect module parameter and the value to which it is set.
The parameter_value can be either real or a string parameter. If you specify override

title: 0 d=0, clk=0, O=0 0 d=0, clk=0, O=0
text:
information for a nonexistent parameter of a connect rule or connect module, then that
override is ignored.
mode=split | merge
Specifies the connect module insertion mode. The default is merge.
crules=connect_module_library_name.connect_rule_name
Specifies the connect rules. The default for the .connect_rule_name extension is
snps_crules.
Multiple connect rules cannot be specified for the same ams_cm command, but
multiple connect rules can be referenced with separate ams_cm commands.
library=library_name
Specifies the name of the logical library for which the connect module is inserted or
connected globally.
cell=cell_name [node=node_name]
Specifies the cell or cell/node names for which the connect module is inserted or
connected. The node name is optional; if it is not specified, the command is applied to all
nodes of the selected cell.
inst=inst_name [node=node_name]
Specifies the hierarchical instance path or instance/node names for which the connect
module is inserted or connected. The node name is optional; if it is not specified, the
command is applied to all nodes of the selected cell.
node=hier_name
Specifies the hierarchical node name for which the connect module is inserted or
connected.
The following examples show different uses of the ams_cm command:
ams_cm vsup=3.3;
This example globally overrides the vsup parameter value (3.3) for all connect modules
connected or inserted throughout the design.
ams_cm vsup=3.2 node=ClockTop.I3.y;

This example overrides the vsup parameter value (3.2) for any connect modules
connected or inserted on node ClockTop.I3.y.
There could be multiple connect modules inserted on the node ClockTop.I3.y
depending on whether the connect module insertion mode is set to split or
merge.
Example 3
ams_cm vsup=3.222 cell=dflop;
This example overrides the vsup parameter value (3.222) for all connect modules
connected or inserted for any cell named dflop in the design.
Example 4
ams_cm vsup=3.333 inst=ClockTop2.I3;
This example overrides the vsup parameter value (3.333) for all connect modules
connected or inserted for the instance ClockTop2.I3 in the design.
Example 5
ams_cm vsup=3.3;
ams_cm vsup=3.222 inst=ClockTop2.I3.I5;
ams_cm vsup=3.444 node=ClockTop2.I3.net18;
This example:
• Globally overrides the vsup parameter value (3.3) for all connect modules connected
or inserted throughout the design.
• Then overrides the vsup parameter value (3.222) for all connect modules connected or
inserted for the instance ClockTop2.I3.I5 in the design.
• Then overrides the vsup parameter value (3.444) for any connect modules connected
or inserted on node ClockTop2.I3.net18.
Example 6
ams_cm vsup=3.3;
ams_cm crules=snpsConnectLib.snps_ana_crules vddnet=top.vdd1
inst=ClockTop.I3;
This example:
• Globally overrides the vsup parameter value (3.3) for all connect modules connected
or inserted throughout the design.
Then overrides the vddnet parameter for dynamic supply on instance ClockTop.I3 in
the design using the connect rules in snpsConnectLib.snps_ana_crules.

Port-based ams_cm is supported under the following options:
• -adopt port_based_ams_cm : To enable the feature regardless of the used

Setting Net Discipline
ams_set_discipline
Enables the override of net disciplines (or setting the discipline of a net that does not have
any declared discipline) in the Verilog-AMS-SPICE flow. .
• Global ams_set_discipline commands override the discipline provided by the switch
-ams_discipline.
• Cell / cell-node / library / global level ams_set_discipline commands:
◦ Can only have discrete discipline
◦ Are applied after discipline resolution on nodes having no declared or resolved
discipline
◦ Cannot influence discipline resolution outcome
• Node / inst-node / inst level ams_set_discipline commands:
◦ Can have either discrete or continuous discipline
◦ Are applied before discipline resolution on nodes having no declared discipline
◦ Can influence discipline resolution outcome
ams_set_discipline discipline=discipline_name
[library=library_name]
[cell=cell_name [node=node_name]]
[inst=inst_name [node=node_name]]
[node=hier_name]
discipline=discipline_name

Specifies the name of the discipline to declare.
library=library_name
Specifies the name of the logical library for which the discipline is declared.
cell=cell_name [node=node_name]
Specifies the cell or cell/node names for which the discipline is declared. The node name

inst=inst_name [node=node_name]
Specifies the hierarchical instance path or instance/node names for which the discipline
is declared. The node name is optional; if it is not specified, the command is applied to all
nodes of the selected cell.
node=hier_name
Specifies the hierarchical node name for which the discipline is declared.

Improved MSV Parameter Override and Optimizations in
Verilog-AMS Flow
Simulating mixed-signal SystemVerilog/Verilog-AMS designs involves cosimulation where
VCS identifies and isolates analog parts for processing by an analog engine. Parameter
overrides for connect module instances and analog components in Verilog-AMS (VAMS)
modules are partitioned to the analog simulator in a partition file. A current challenge in
this process is the inefficient method of providing parameter override information through a
partition file, which requires the analog engine to process numerous long paths, creating a
performance bottleneck during the analog elaboration phase.

Improved MSV Parameter Override and Optimizations in Verilog-AMS Flow
VCS provides the following optimizations that improve mixed-signal elaboration
performance. These optimizations efficiently partition analog parameter override
information from VCS and transfer it to the analog simulator:
• Improved Partitioning for Verilog-AMS Parameter Values
• Improved Partitioning of SPICE Primitive Parameter Values
• Improved Partitioning Format for Sharing Hierarchical Information
Improved Partitioning for Verilog-AMS Parameter Values
VCS resolves all parameters at the compilation stage. In previous releases, the final
analog parameter values are transferred to the analog simulator in a hierarchical format
through a partition file. This may result in performance issues for the analog engine.
To improve simulation performance, VCS partitions the most common parameter value
is partitioned in a "folded" manner (optimization technique) as an instance parameter
override within the partition file. For scenarios requiring hierarchical information, a
flattened hierarchical format is provided. Enable this feature by using the -adopt
sp_param_part_enh compile option.
To optimize performance, parameter information is partitioned via a hierarchical parameter
partition file. Consider the following testcases:
Example 101 Top Module
electrical e1, e2;
wire w1, w2;
mid m1();
mid m2();
mid m3();
Example 102 VAMS Module with Parameter Override
module mid ();
wire pi1, pi2, pi3 ;
wire po1, po2, po3 ;

The details related to the commands are as follows:
The following topics describe the connect-definition commands:
• ams_cdef_net
• ams_cdef_inst
• ams_supply
ams_cdef_net
Connects an electrical net to an analog power or ground electrical net. When the netlist
for the design does not contain the connectivity for the power and ground network, this
command is used to create that connection.
This command is used with the ams_supply and ams_cdef_inst commands to
allow power-aware connect modules in the design.
ams_cdef_net -cell cell_name [-lib library_name]
-net {net_name [, net_name] …}
-default_supply {attribute_name => net_name};
Specifies the cell name.
-lib library_name
Specifies the library name. This is the VCS compiled library.
-net {net_name [, net_name] …}
Specifies a list of net names that are connected to the net specified by the
-default_supply argument. These nets are declared inside the specified cell.
-default_supply {attribute_name => net_name}
Specifies the name of the net associated with the list in the -net argument.

The following example shows one use of the ams_cdef_net command:
• This example electrically connects the net vdd2 in the cell blk02 to the net top.vdd.
ams_cdef_net -cell blk02 -net {vdd2} -default_supply {vdd2_tag =>
top.vdd};
ams_cdef_inst
Overrides connectivity to power and ground nets given from ams_cdef_net commands.
This command is used when specific instances in the designs have different power and
ground connections.
This command is used with the ams_supply and ams_cdef_net commands to
allow power-aware connect modules in the design.
The ams_cdef_inst command accepts the name of a local net, or the name of a global
net specified through a hierarchical path.
The following figure displays a cell developed in isolation of a top level design.

ams_cdef_inst
[ -lib < library_name | WORK > ]
[ -inst { { instance_name }* } ]
-supply { { attribute_name [: new_attribute_name]
=> name_of_the_local_net|name_of_the_global_net }* }
Defines the name of a cell or module to be used for scoping.
-lib library_name
Defines the name of a VCS logical compilation library to be used for scoping. If this option
is not specified, the default value WORK is used.
-inst { { instance_name }* }
Comma-separated list of instance names within a selected cell and library combination.
If the instance name is not specified, the command applies to all instances within the
selected cell.
-supply { { attribute_name [: new_attribute_name]
=> name_of_the_local_net|name_of_the_global_net }* }
Defines the local net or the port of a cell specified with -cell argument or a global net
for establishing a connection to a list of nets specified earlier. The attribute_name
option is used as an identifier of a previously created connection using the ams_cdef_net
command. The connection previously defined by the attribute_name option is overridden
using the new definitions provided in this option. The [: new_attribute_name] option is
used to change the name of the attribute as visible downward in the design hierarchy.
