Use Mode in SystemVerilog
Use Mode in SystemVerilog
This section discusses about the following chapters:
The Entire Design Targets SystemVerilog
To use the SVA Checker Library in VCS with a design written in SystemVerilog (which thus
respects its enlarged set of keywords), you instantiate or bind any number of the checkers
in the design and indicate the placement of the library using the Verilog library mechanism
as follows:
vcs -sverilog +define+ASSERT_ON <design files and options> \
-y $VCS_HOME/packages/sva +libext+.v \
+incdir+$VCS_HOME/packages/sva
Note that +define+ASSERT_ON on the VCS command line is necessary to turn on the
assertions in all checker instances. Alternatively or in addition, by defining COVER_ON the
coverage functionality can be included (it can be controlled at the instance level by the
checker parameter coverage_level_i, where, i = 1, 2, or 3 .
To gather coverage information using the coverage functionality of the checkers, do
not include the -cm assert option. This is because coverage on cover property and
covergroup statements is automatically turned on in VCS.
Some Design Files Are Restricted to Verilog2001
In this case, the Verilog2001 files have names with the .v extensions, while all
SystemVerilog files, including the checkers, have a name with the .sv extension. In the
case of the checkers, it is the symbolic link with the .sv extension that is used. The vcs
compilation command line has the following form:
vcs +define+ASSERT_ON <design files and other options> \
-y $VCS_HOME/packages/sva +libext+.sv -sverilog \
+verilog2001ext+.v+incdir+$VCS_HOME/packages/sva
The compiler uses Verilog2001 syntax for all .v files, and SystemVerilog syntax for all
other files including those with the .sv extension.
SVA Checker Library Enabled With VMM Messaging Service
In VCS, to use the SVA Checker Library with VMM reporting service, you must pass
+define+SVA_VMM_LOG and -ntb_opts rvm at compile-time. You must also include the
sva vmm package file, namely "sva_vmm.sv" defined in $VCS_HOME/packages/sva at
compile-time.

Use Model in VHDL in VCS Mixed-HDL Designs

vcs -sverilog+define+ASSERT_ON+COVER_ON \
<design files and other options> -y
$VCS_HOME/packages/sva_cg \
+libext+.sv +verilog2001ext+.v
+incdir+$VCS_HOME/packages/sva_cg \
+define+SVA_VMM_LOG -ntb_opts rvm
$VCS_HOME/packages/sva_cg/sva_vmm.sv

Recommended Use Model
• • Use -assert quiet option at runtime:
Assertion evaluations by default use the built-in reporting messaging service. To
suppress this messaging service, use the – assert quiet compile-time switch.
• Do not use assertion switches controlling the simulations, such as:
-assert finish_maxfail and -assert global_maxfail
The use of these switches terminates the simulation only from an assertion
perspective, irrespective of the testbench status. If you want to integrate assertion
evaluation with the complete testbench environment, you must avoid using them.

Section 2: SVA Basic Checkers
This chapter contains 31 OVL-like checkers. All checkers, except assert_proposition, are
triggered at the positive edge of a triggering signal or expression clk.
The values of all actual signals or expressions in the ports of the checkers are sampled
just before the positive edge of clk. Therefore, any pulses happening on the signals /
expressions between consecutive positive edges of clk are not observed by the checkers.
Moreover, whenever an edge of a signal / expression on a port of a checker other than the
clock is used in the checker, it is the sampled form of the edge as detected by looking at
two consecutive samples of the signal.
The checker assert_proposition monitors an expression at all times.and triggers at the
falling edge of the test_expr.

Section 1: The SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA)
Checker Library
The SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) Checker Library consists of two parts:
• SVL (described in Chapter 2) consists of checkers that have the same behavior and
controls as those in the Open Verification Library (OVL) - see the Accellera Open
Verification Library Reference Manual available at http://www.accellera.org/downloads/
standards/ovl. These checkers have additional features such as coverage in the SVA
Library.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
those in the Open Verification Library (OVL) - see the Accellera Open
Verification Library Reference Manual available at http://www.accellera.org/downloads/
standards/ovl. These checkers have additional features such as coverage in the SVA
Library.
• SVA Advanced Checkers (described in Chapter 3) contains checkers that generally
verify more complex behaviors. These have similar controls to the SVL checkers, but,
in addition, they allow selecting the sampling clock edge(s), posedge or negedge.
Coverage is also provided.
Note that the header of each checker file also contains a description of the behavior
and parameters.

Overview
The checker library resides in a release in the directory
$VCS_HOME/packages/sva/

Global Controls
The library consists of 53 checker files having the name assert_checker_name.v. There
is also a symbolic link to that file with the name assert_checker_name.sv that can be
used in situations where parts of the Verilog design follow Verilog2001 syntax and should
be compiled with that in mind to avoid keyword clashes with SystemVerilog keywords.
In that way, the extension .sv identifies the checkers to be compiler with SystemVerilog,
while the files with the .vextension compiles with Verilog2001 syntax and keywords.
The checkers have dual functions:
1. As a verification object using assert property statements. This form is employed for
verifying the behavior as specified for the checker.
2. As a coverage objects using cover property and cover points implemented using
the equivalent of covergroup statements. This form is employed to obtain information
about the observed presence of certain behavioral patterns in the design - coverage of
such patterns.
The two forms can coexist or be enabled independently as described later - See “Global
Controls” and “Shared Syntax” . Note also that there is header file sva_std_task.h in the
directory. It contains user-modifiable reporting tasks and is included in each checker using
‘include.
Global Controls
The following symbols are macro’s defined using ‘define and apply to all instances of the
checkers.
ASSERT_ON
When this macro is defined, the assertions and related variables in checkers are included.
I.e., the checking functionality is enabled. or
COVER_ON
When this macro is defined, the coverage items in the checkers are included, that
is, the coverage functionality is enabled. Note that additional per-instance control is
provided using the checker parameters coverage_level_1, coverage_level_=2, and
coverage_level_3.
ASSERT_INIT_MSG
When this macro is defined, the all checker instances display a message to stdout to
indicate their hierarchical name.
ASSERT_GLOBAL_RESET
When this macro is defined its defining expression is taken as the reset signal for all the
checkers. Otherwise, the reset_n port signal is used as reset.

Checker Triggering
ASSERT_MAX_REPORT_ERROR
When this global macro variable is defined, the assertion instance stops reporting
messages if the number of errors for that instance is greater than the value defined
by the macro. Using this macro as described requires modifying the reporting tasks in
sva_std_task.h.
SVA_CHECKER_INTERFACE
If not defined, the interface is a SystemVerilog "module". If defined then the checker
interface is "interface". The parameters and ports remain the same in both cases.
SVA_CHECKER_NO_MESSAGE
Causes the std tasks in sva_std_task.h file that is included in every checker skips over any
user generated messages. So to disable all message, use the -assert quiet option and
define the above symbol.
Checker Triggering
In the SVL library (Chapter 2) all but one checker, assert_proposition, is triggered at
the positive edge of a triggering signal or expression clk.
In the Advanced Checker Library (Chapter 3), all the checkers can select the sampling
edge(s) using a parameter. It can be either the positive or the negative edge of the clock
port expression.
The values of all actual signals or expressions in the ports of the checkers are sampled
just before the sampling edge of clk . Therefore, any pulses happening on the signals /
expressions between consecutive sampling edges of clk are not observed by the
checkers.
Moreover, whenever an edge of a signal / expression on a port of a checker other than
the clock is used in the checker, the value is the sampled form of the edge as detected by
looking at two consecutive samples of the signal.
The checker assert_proposition monitors an expression at all times and triggers by a
change of its value to 0.
Checkers With VMM Reporting Service
All checkers are enhanced to incorporate VMM messaging service. This qualifies the
simulation as PASSED or FAILED based on the assertion result.
Inclusion of VMM messaging service also allows you to control the simulation based on
the severity level of the checker instance. A severity level of 0 would continue with the
simulation, and a severity level other than 0 would terminate the simulation.

Shared Syntax
Inclusion of VMM messaging service is under a global control macro defined using
`define, namely SVA_VMM_LOG.
Custom Reporting:
As in OVL, if you want to have more elaborate error reporting, counting, and so on, you
must edit the sva_std_task.h file that is distributed with the library and also resides in the
directory.

This file is automatically ‘include -ed in each checker. If the location of the header file is
changed, the +incdir+ directive must also be modified accordingly

in each of the parameters when set to 1 enable some specific coverage point, one per
bit. The number of bits used thus depends on the number of cover points in the checker
at each level and varies from checker to checker. Generally, the following levels are
supported (default is 1):
Level 1: Basic coverage, implemented using cover property statements. Used by
simulation and Magellan.
Level 1 coverages are enabled by setting bits in coverage levels to 1. Level 1 coverages
are enabled by setting bits in coverage_level_1 to 1.
Example: The number of Enqueues and Dequeues in a FIFO
Level 2: Usually includes data coverage on ranges of values. These are coverage items
which show certain interesting activities of the RTL behavior in the form of statistics. Used
in simulation only but might also include cover properties on some particular sequences
that can be of interest as search goals for formal tools.
Level 2 coverages are enabled by setting bits in coverage_level_2 to 1.
Example: Range of latency values classified on at-least-once basis.
Level 3: Mostly cover property coverage of specific corner points as specified. Used
primarily by formal tools as goals. These cover properties can be enabled in simulation
too, however, the same information can be obtained from Level 2 range coverages in the
extreme bins. These coverage items ensure that the corner case condition of the RTL/
design block are verified during testing.
Level 3 coverages are enabled by setting bits in coverage_level_3 to 1.
Examples: The number of times FIFO reached HIGH water mark. The number of times
ACK was received at the next clock after REQ was issued. The number of times the
specified Min latency value was reached.

Use Mode in SystemVerilog
Use Mode in SystemVerilog
This section discusses about the following :
The Entire Design Targets SystemVerilog
To use the SVA Checker Library in VCS with a design written in SystemVerilog (which thus
respects its enlarged set of keywords), you instantiate or bind any number of the checkers
in the design and indicate the placement of the library using the Verilog library mechanism
as follows:
vcs -sverilog +define+ASSERT_ON <design files and options> \
-y $VCS_HOME/packages/sva +libext+.v \
+incdir+$VCS_HOME/packages/sva_cg
Note that +define+ASSERT_ON on the VCS command line is necessary to turn on the
assertions in all checker instances. Alternatively or in addition, by defining COVER_ON the
coverage functionality can be included (it can be controlled at the instance level by the
checker parameter coverage_level_i, where, I = 1, 2, or 3 .
To gather coverage information using the coverage functionality of the checkers, do
not include the -cm assert option. This is because coverage on cover property and
covergroup statements is automatically turned on in VCS.
Some Design Files Are Restricted to Verilog2001
In this case, the Verilog2001 files have names with the .v extensions, while all
SystemVerilog files, including the checkers, have a name with the .sv extension. In the
case of the checkers, it is the symbolic link with the .sv extension that is used. The vcs
compilation command line has the following form:
vcs +define+ASSERT_ON <design files and other options> \
-y $VCS_HOME/packages/sva +libext+.sv -sverilog \
+verilog2001ext+.v+incdir+$VCS_HOME/packages/sva_cg
The compiler uses Verilog2001 syntax for all .vfiles, and SystemVerilog syntax for all other
files including those with the .sv extension.
SVA Checker Library Enabled With VMM Messaging Service
In VCS, to use the SVA Checker Library with VMM reporting service, you must pass
+define+SVA_VMM_LOG and -ntb_opts rvm at compile-time. You must also include the
sva vmm package file, namely "sva_vmm.sv" defined in $VCS_HOME/packages/sva at
compile-time.

Recommended Use Model
• • Use -assert quiet option at runtime:
Assertion evaluations by default use the built-in reporting messaging service. To
suppress this messaging service, use the – assert quiet compile-time option.
• Do not use assertion switches controlling the simulations, such as:
-assert finish_maxfail and -assert global_maxfail
The use of these switches terminates the simulation only from an assertion
perspective, irrespective of the testbench status. If you want to integrate assertion
evaluation with the complete testbench environment, you must avoid using them.
Use Model in VHDL in VCS Mixed-HDL Designs
The SVA Checker Library .v files can be found in the $VCS_HOME/packages/sva/
directory.
There is also a VHDL package called sva_lib in this directory, containing the component
definitions for all the checkers in the library. The name of the file is component.
sva_v.vhd.
To use the SVA library in VHDL, the user should proceed as follows:
1. Compile the component package in a library. For example, suppose that the default
WORK library used. The command to compile the package is then:
vhdlan $VCS_HOME/packages/sva/component.sva_v.vhd
2. Compile the selected SVA checkers using vlogan and deposit in a VHDL library. For
example, suppose again that the default WORK library is used and that you want to

the command is:
vlogan +vc -sverilog $VCS_HOME/packages/sva/*.v \
+incdir+$VCS_HOME/packages/sva_cg \

Other macro definitions can be supplied with +define.
Note that if you choose to compile only some specific checkers that are described in
Chapter 2, you also must compile the file sva_std_edge_select.v. This is because

3. To use the compiled checkers in the VHDL design, it must include commands to use
the following libraries:
library IEEE;
use IEEE.STD_LOGIC_1164.all;
library WORK;
use WORK.sva_lib.all;
and instantiate the checker component(s) as any other VHDL entity.

Note that the signals on the checker ports are of the IEEE std_ulogic and unsigned
types.

-- Some design entity instance

Section 2: SVA Basic Checkers
This chapter contains 31 OVL-like checkers. All checkers, except assert_proposition, are
triggered at the positive edge of a triggering signal or expression clk.
The values of all actual signals or expressions in the ports of the checkers are sampled
just before the positive edge of clk. Therefore, any pulses happening on the signals /
expressions between consecutive positive edges of clk are not observed by the checkers.
Moreover, whenever an edge of a signal / expression on a port of a checker other than the
clock is used in the checker, it is the sampled form of the edge as detected by looking at
two consecutive samples of the signal.
The checker assert_proposition monitors an expression at all times.and triggers at the
falling edge of the test_expr.

Section 3: SVA Advanced Checkers
This section describes 22 checkers. These advanced checkers use the same controls as
the OVL-equivalent checkers in the previous section. In addition, they have a clock edge
selection parameter, edge_expr, that allows the user to select posedge or negedge clock
edge selection for sampling in the assertions and cover statements.
In this chapter:
• Checker Descriptions
This section provides syntax and descriptions, and examples for all checkers.
Shared Syntax
Many checkers share the same syntax elements. In addition to using severity_level,
reset_n, clk , and msg described in Chapter 1, the checkers in this chapter can select
the active edge the clock:
edge_expr: Specifies the active edge for the clock signal (clk) in unit syntax. Use the
following values to specify the edge type:
• posedge: 0 (the default)
• negedge: 1
• edge: 2
If edge_expr is not specified, it defaults to posedge.
assert_arbiter
This checker ensures that a resource arbiter provides grants to corresponding requests
within min_lat and max_lat cycles. reqs and grants are vectors of size [no_chnl-1:0]
where the bits correspond to the individual channels. They are assumed to be 1 when
active. The checker can verify a priority arbitration scheme alone or in conjunction with (as

a secondary criterion) round robin, fifo or LRU selection algorithms. The checks are not
enabled unless reset_n evaluates true.

arbitration_rule, min_lat, max_lat,
inst_name ( clk, reset_n, reqs, req_priority, grants );

assert_dual_clk_fifo
This is a checker for a dual-clock, single in- and single out-port FIFO. It assume that
enqueue is enabled when enq is asserted at the active clock edge of enq_clk and
effectively occurs enq_lat cycles later. Dequeue is enabled when deq is asserted at
the active edge of deq_clk and effectively occurs deq_lat cycles later. It can verify that
neither overflow or underflow of the queue occurs, that it reaches a watermark and that the
enqueued data value is the correct one upon dequeue.

assert_fifo
This is a checker for a single-clock, single in- and single out-port FIFO. All signals are
sampled at the active edge of the clock, clk. It assume that enqueue is enabled when enq
is asserted and effectively occurs enq_lat cycles later. Dequeue is enabled when deq is
asserted and effectively occurs deq_lat cycles later. It can verify that neither overflow or
underflow of the queue occurs, that it reaches a watermark and that the enqueued data
value is the correct one upon dequeue. Also, if pass_thru is 1 it allows simultaneous
enqueue and dequeue of data on empty or full queue. Otherwise a dequeue on an empty
queue reports an underflow.

locations are written into before being read, that there is at least one read between two
consecutive writes to an address, or similarly that there is at least one write between two

assert_multiport_fifo
This checker implements a checker for a single-clock, multi-port in and multi-port out
queue. enq and deq are bit vectors of equal size no_ports. Each pair of corresponding
bits in these vectors defines the enqueue and dequeue enable signals for a fifo port.
Their priority is such the bit 0 is the lowest priority, the highest order bit no_ports-1
is the highest priority. The enqueue port and the dequeue port of the highest priority
are processed at every active clk edge. enq_data is a concatenation of the data from
the different ports, dimensioned as [no_ports*elem_size-1:0], with data vectors
appearing in the same order as the enq requests. Whenever a bit in enq is asserted 1,
the corresponding data part in enq_data must be valid after enq_lat clock cycles. Only
the highest priority data is actually enqueued. deq_data is a concatenation of the data
from the different ports. It is assumed that it is dimensioned the same way as enq_data,
with data vectors appearing in the same order as the deq requests. Whenever a bit in
deq is asserted 1, the corresponding data part in deq_data must be valid after deq_lat
clock cycles. Only the data of the highest priority dequeue request is compared with the
reference data when value_chk is 1. Overflow, underflow, watermark, value and pass-
through checks can be enabled as in the assert_fifo checker.

elem_sz, no_ports, hi_water_mark, enq_lat,

coverage_level_3, property_type )]

Introduction
This chapter provides an introduction to VCS SystemC co-simulation interface that
enables VCS and
SystemCcosimulating with Verilog
SystemC modeling environment to work together, when simulating a
system described in Verilog, VHDL, and SystemC languages.
This chapter includes the following topics:
• Supported Topologies
• Supported Platforms in SystemC
• Supported Port Data Types
• Support for SystemC 2.3.3
• Support for SystemC 2.3.4
• Support for SystemC 3.0.1
• VCS Extensions to SystemC Library
• Porting VCS SystemC on the ARM Platform
• Supported Macros
• Installation of UVM-SystemC

Supported Topologies
Supported Topologies
VCS SystemC co-simulation interface supports the following topologies:
• Verilog Design Containing SystemC and Verilog/VHDL Modules
This topology comprises of a Verilog testbench and instances of SystemC and Verilog
and/or VHDL. The design can also have other SystemC modules. To instantiate a
SystemC module in your Verilog design, perform the following:
◦ Create a Verilog wrapper for the SystemC module, using syscan utility.
◦ Instantiate the wrapper in the Verilog testbench.
For the usage model and an example, see “Instantiating SystemC Inside Verilog
Design” .
• SystemC Design Containing Verilog and VHDL Modules
This topology comprises of a SystemC testbench and instances of Verilog and/or
VHDL. The design can also have other SystemC modules. Instantiating Verilog/VHDL
Inside SystemC module, perform the following:
◦ Create a SystemC wrapper for the Verilog and VHDL design units, using the
vlogan/vhdlan executable.
◦ Instantiate the wrapper in the SystemC module.
For the use model and an example, see “Instantiating SystemC Inside VHDL
Design” .
• VHDL Design Containing SystemC and Verilog/VHDL Modules
This topology comprises of a VHDL testbench and instances of SystemC, Verilog and/
or VHDL instances. The design can also contain many other SystemC modules. To
instantiate a SystemC module in the VHDL design, perform the following:
◦ Create a VHDL wrapper for the SystemC module using the syscan utility.
◦ Instantiate the wrapper in the VHDL testbench.
For the usage model and an example, see “Instantiating SystemC Inside VHDL
Design”.
• Support for multiple-top topology.
VCS supports topologies that comprise of multiple top-level modules, that is, a
SystemC top module (under the function sc_main) and one or more Verilog/VHDL top
modules (svtop1, vhdltop2, and so on).
For the usage model and an example, see “Support for Multiple-Top Topology” .

Installing VG GNU Package
Several GNU GCC compiler versions are provided in the VG_GNU_PACKAGEalong

To download the VG GNU package, see section “Downloading and Installing VG GNU

Supported Port Data Types
The Input and output ports that cross the co-simulation boundary between SystemC and
Verilog/VHDL must observe the following restrictions:
• The SystemC types are restricted to sc_clock, sc_bv, sc_logic, sc_lv, sc_int,
sc_uint, sc_bigint, and sc_biguint data types.
• The native C/C++ types are restricted to unsigned int , unsigned char , unsigned

ust observe the following restrictions:
• The SystemC types are restricted to sc_clock, sc_bv, sc_logic, sc_lv, sc_int,
sc_uint, sc_bigint, and sc_biguint data types.
• The native C/C++ types are restricted to unsigned int , unsigned char , unsigned
short, int , bool, short, char, long, long long , unsigned long , and unsigned
long long types.

Support for SystemC 2.3.3
• The Verilog ports are restricted to bit, bit-vector and signed bit-vector types.
• The VHDL ports are restricted to bit, bit-vector, standard logic, standard , signed and
unsigned types.
The In-out ports that cross the co-simulation boundary between SystemC and Verilog/
VHDL must observe the following restrictions:
• SystemC port types must be sc_inout_rv<> or sc_inout_resolved and must be
connected to signals of type sc_signal_rv<> or sc_signal_resolved.
• Verilog port types must be bit_vector or bit.
• VHDL port types must be std_logic_vector or std_logic.
Multidimensional array ports are not supported.
Support for SystemC 2.3.3
VCS supports SystemC 2.3.3 version. SystemC 2.3.3 can be selected by passing the
-sysc=233 option to the syscan and vcs commands. This SystemC version is available
only for the compiler version gcc 9.2.0, and gcc 9.5.0.
When the -sysc=233 option is used, VCS compiles and elaborates the SystemC model
and the design with SystemC 2.3.3. The resulting simv uses the SystemC 2.3.3 library.
SystemC 2.3.3 is deprecated.
Support for SystemC 2.3.4
VCS supports SystemC 2.3.4 version. SystemC 2.3.4 can be selected by passing the
-sysc=234 option to the syscan and vcs commands. This SystemC version is available
only for the compiler version gcc 9.2.0, gcc 9.5.0, gcc12.3 (64 bit only), and gcc13.2 (64 bit
only).
When the -sysc=234 or -sysc=2.3.4 option is used, VCS compiles and elaborates the
SystemC model and the design with SystemC 2.3.4. The resulting simv uses the SystemC
2.3.4 library.
VCS uses the SystemC 2.3.4 version by default.

Support for SystemC 3.0.1
The other options, -sysc=233 (with the compiler version gcc 9.2.0, gcc 9.5.0),
and -sysc=301 (with the compiler version gcc 12.3.0 and gcc 13.2.0) are
available to select the SystemC version 2.3.3 or 3.0.1 respectively.
To switch from SystemC 2.3.3 to SystemC 2.3.4 version, update the compilation flow by
changing all the references from -sysc=233 to -sysc=234, and by changing the include
paths from -I$VCS_HOME/include/systemc233 to -I$VCS_HOME/include/systemc234.
Support for SystemC 3.0.1
VCS supports SystemC 3.0.1 version. SystemC 3.0.1 can be selected by passing the
-sysc=301 option to the syscan and vcs commands. This SystemC version is available
only for the compiler version gcc 12.3.0 (64 bit only), and gcc 13.2.0 (64 bit only).
When the -sysc=301 option is used, VCS compiles and elaborates the SystemC model
and the design with SystemC 3.0.1. The resulting simv uses the SystemC 3.0.1 library.
VCS Extensions to SystemC Library
The following proprietary extensions are available as part of VCS, and not available as
part of OSCI SystemC.
• Runtime functions
The systemc_user.h include file contains the prototypes of functions that can be
called during execution of the simulation. Add the following to the source code to make
the header file visible:
• GetFullName()
It returns the full logical name of the given object or "No Name" on error. The full name
contains hierarchical sub-paths of other domains, such as, Verilog/VHDL:
namespace sc_snps {
const char *GetFullName(sc_object *obj);
}
• sc_object::name()
By default, it returns the physical path name (underscore is used when hierarchy
crosses the language).

Porting VCS SystemC on the ARM Platform
It returns the logical path name (dot is used when hierarchy crosses the language) only
when the following call is made:
sc_snps::sysc_configure(sc_snps::VCS_SYSC_LOGIC_NAME, 1);
The function sysc_configure() is defined in systemc_user.hfile. You must include
this header file to use this function.
The member function sc_core::sc_object::name() defined as part
of the SystemC language usually does not return the same string as
sc_snps::GetFullName(). The sc_object::name() member does not
consider Verilog/VHDL instances and displays only the path name with respect
to the SystemC hierarchy. Alternatively, the GetFullName()function considers
the entire Verilog/VHDL/SystemC instance hierarchy and returns the correct
logical name of the SystemC instance inside this hierarchy.
• GetName()
It returns the instance name (short name) of the given object or returns "No Name" on
error:
namespace sc_snps
{
const char *GetName(sc_object *obj);
}
The corresponding member function sc_core::sc_object::basename(),
defined as part of the SystemC language, may not return the same string as
sc_snps::GetName().
• SystemC standard IEEE 1666-2005 (that is, SystemC 2.3.x) does not support
asynchronous reset. However, VCS supports a subset of the functionality.
Only one asynchronous reset is allowed and it can be specified only for
SC_CTHREADs.
Porting VCS SystemC on the ARM Platform
VCS supports SystemC flow for the ARM (
aarch64
aarch64) platform. To compile a SystemC
design, you must call the syscan command. However, the -full64 option of syscan,
vlogan, and vcs has no effect as 64-bit is the only supported bit width on ARM.

Supported Macros
On the ARM platform, the same SystemC and compiler versions are supported as on
Linux.
All the SystemC features available on Linux are supported on the ARM platform too. This
includes simulation, UCLI interface, FSDB dumping, debug with Cbug and Verdi, and so
on. AMS for entire VCS is not supported for ARM Platform.
Supported Macros
SystemC co-simulation interface supports the following macros for ease of use:
• VCSSYSTEMC
• SNPS_REGISTER_SC_MAIN
• SNPS_REGISTER_SC_MODULE
VCSSYSTEMC
The VCSSYSTEMC macro is used for selective compilation of the VCS- specific SystemC
source code.
#ifdef VCSSYSTEMC
<your VCS-specific code>
#else
<not VCS-specific code>

SNPS_REGISTER_SC_MODULE
The SNPS_REGISTER_SC_MODULE macro can be used to implement the sc_main() function
in a SystemC-on-top design.
Instead of writing a sc_main start up function whenever there is a SystemC-on-top design,
you can use this macro to implement the sc_main function by passing the top-level
sc_module as an argument. As this macro is defined in the systemc_user.h header file,
you must include this file to use this macro.
SC_MODULE(mytopmodule)
{
…
}
SNPS_REGISTER_SC_MODULE(mytopmodule);
Installation of UVM-SystemC
UVM-SystemC is a new standard to develop structured verification environments following
the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM). It is implemented as a class library based
on C++ and SystemC (Accellera).
A directory hierarchy is provided to correspond to the Accellera installation directly in the
VCS installation image. This significantly simplifies the installation and the usage of UVM-
SystemC with VCS.
VCS image contains the following directory which mimics the standard SystemC Accellera
installation:
$VCS_HOME/etc/systemc/accelera_install
This directory hierarchy contains links to the include files and to the SystemC library in the
VCS installation image.

Installation of UVM-SystemC
A typical SystemC Accellera installation has the following (partial) hierarchy:
Table 2 Directory and Their Roles
Signal Constant Type
$SYSTEMC_HOME/include Contains all the SystemC included files
$SYSTEMC_HOME/lib-linux Contains the 32-bit SystemC library files
$SYSTEMC_HOME/lib-linux/libsystemc.a Static 32-bit SystemC library file
$SYSTEMC_HOME/lib-linux64 Contains the 64-bit SystemC library files
$SYSTEMC_HOME/lib-linux64/libsystemc.a Static 64-bit SystemC library file
UVM-SystemC uses the standard compilation process on Linux ./configure … ;
make ; make install . The SystemC home directory must be passed to the configure
command of UVM-SystemC as follows:
./configure --prefix=/path/to/UVMSystemC_install --with-systemc=/path/
to/systemc-233
Following are the steps to install UVM-SystemC with SystemC 2.3.3 and GCC 9 versions:
1. Set the VCS HOME, GNU Package, and GCC.
2. Download the UVM-SystemC tarfile.
3. Untar the tarfile and go to the directory.
4. Create a directory, for example, objdir and go to this directory.
5. Run the following command to install UVM-SystemC:
For 64-bit:
% ./configure --prefix=/path/to/UVMSystemC_install --
with-systemc=$VCS_HOME/etc/systemc/accellera_install/
systemc233-gcc9 LDFLAGS="-pthread"
% make
% make install
For 32-bit:
% ./configure --prefix=/path/to/UVMSystemC_install --
with-systemc=$VCS_HOME/etc/systemc/accellera_install/
systemc233-gcc9 CFLAGS="-m32" CXXFLAGS="-m32"

SystemC Only Designs
SystemC Only Designs
VCS supports running and debugging simulations that contain only SystemC models,
referred to as "Pure SystemC" or “SystemC Only” designs.
Pure SystemC designs do not contain Verilog, VHDL, SVA, and NTB modules. These
designs contain only SystemC and other C/C++ source files. The usage model to simulate
pure SystemC designs is the same as SystemC-on-top designs, except for the wrapper
generation phase, which is not required for pure SystemC designs.
The use model to simulate a pure SystemC design involves the following steps:
1. Analysis
2. Elaboration
3. Simulation
Analysis
% syscan [ syscan_options] all_systemC_source_files
Elaboration
% vcs -sysc [elab _options] sc_main
To run the designs in the 64-bit mode, include the -full64 option in the vcs
command line.
Simulation
% simv [ runtime_options]
Example 1
% syscan adder.cpp
% syscan foo.cpp bar.cpp xyz.cpp main.cpp
% vcs -sysc sc_main
% ./simv -gui=verdi
Example 2
% syscan -cflags -g adder.cpp
% syscan -cflags -g foo.cpp bar.cpp xyz.cpp
% syscan -cflags -g main.cpp
% vcs -sysc sc_main \
-cflags -g \

Supporting Designs With Donut Topologies
extra_file.o -ldflags "-L/u/me/lib -labc"
% ./simv -ucli
For information to debug SystemC source files and any other C/C++ file, refer
to the Debugger Setup With VCS section in the Verdi SystemC Debug User
Guide.
Supporting Designs With Donut Topologies
Donut or “sandwich” topologies are designs in which SystemC models are embedded
into HDL (Verilog/VHDL) models, or vice-versa. These models are embedded into each
other on both top and bottom, or vice-versa. In other words, following the design hierarchy
from a leaf instance toward the root, there are multiple transitions from SystemC to HDL
(Verilog/VHDL), or vice-versa.
For example, a design topology SystemC->Verilog->VHDL->SystemC defines a donut
because there are two transitions between SystemC and HDL.The first transition is from
SystemC->Verilog, and the second transition is from VHDL->SystemC.
However, a design topology SystemC->Verilog->VHDL->Verilog is not a SystemC/HDL
donut because there is only one transition between SystemC and HDL. Transitions inside
HDL between Verilog and VHDL are not relevant in this context.
VCS SystemC generally does not support donuts, with one exception (described as
follows). An attempt to compile a donut structure in VCS triggers an error message.
One specific donut topology is supported: Verilog->SystemC ->Verilog, with no VHDL
models at any level. Multiple layers of Verilog modules at the top and bottom are allowed.
Multiple SystemC layers in the middle are also allowed. That is, a design topology of
Verilog->Verilog->SystemC->SystemC->Verilog is also supported.
This style of donuts are useful for using SystemVerilog assertions for SystemC models in
a Verilog-top design. The assertions must be embedded in a Verilog model, which is then
instantiated under a SystemC model. All signals to be observed by the assertions must be
fed through ports.
This type of donut must be compiled according to the UUM flow. Verilog models must
be analyzed with vlogan, SystemC models with syscan, and elaboration with vcs
-sysc Interface models are created as described before.

Unified Hierarchy for VCS and SystemC
Design topology is V1->S2->S3->V4->V5, with V1, V4, V5 being Verilog models, and S2,
S3 being SystemC models. With this topology, you must compile the simulator as follows:
% vlogan V5.v
% vlogan V4.v -sc_model V4
% syscan S3.cpp
% syscan S2.cpp:S2
% vlogan V1.v
% vcs -sysc V1
SystemC donuts are not supported with Partition Compile flow. For example, if there is a
scenario such as Verilog top -> System C -> Verilog, for Partition Compile flow, it shows
the following error:
Error-[SC-VCS-PARTCOMP-SYSC-DONUT] No SystemC donuts with Part Comp
SystemC donut designs are not supported with Partition Compile.
Unified Hierarchy for VCS and SystemC
Using the –sysc=show_sc_main Option
This is the default option. This is useful for designs with SystemC modules on top and
Verilog or VHDL instantiated within SystemC. This simplifies many flows where the
hierarchical path names to Verilog or VHDL instances have to be specified
Following is an example report:
% Printing Inst 'sc_main.SC_TOP.SC_INST_1.VLOG_INST_A' of Verilog module
VLOG_BOT
Use option -sysc=noshow_sc_main to exclude sc_mainfrom the hierarchy and revert to
use SystemC on Top internally.
It provides the following example $display output for SystemC on Top design.
% Printing Inst 'SC_TOP.SC_INST_1.VLOG_INST_A' of Verilog module VLOG_BOT

Combining SystemC With Verilog Configurations
SystemC Unified Hierarchy Flow Limitations
The following limitations apply for the SystemC unified hierarchy flow:
• Generally, only available for designs that have SystemC on top of the hierarchy and
HDL instantiated below SystemC.
• Not available for designs that have VHDL or Verilog on top and instantiate SystemC
below Verilog/VHDL.
• Not available for donut designs (Verilog-SystemC-Verilog).
• Only available with UUM flow (not with non-UUM flow).
Combining SystemC With Verilog Configurations
SystemC can be used in combination with Verilog configurations. This is supported only in
UUM flow. The SystemC-top, Verilog-top and VHDL-top topologies are supported. These
configurations can be triggered during runtime using -vhdlconf option.
Verilog-on-Top, SystemC and/or VHDL Down
A Verilog-on-Top design with SystemC and/or VHDL down is specified similar to any other
design. Here, the analysis of the Verilog files, with vlogan, must use the libmapoption..
Added to it is a Verilog source file and containing the configurations. A configuration
consists of a config scope.
For example:
config use_A;

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
// name of the Verilog top-entity
design top;

// library where the top-entity is analyzed different
// mappings of verilog instances
default liblist workA;

// Verilog-subtractor
instance top.v_mod.inst1 use workA.v_sub;

// VHDL subtractor
instance top.v_mod.inst2 use workA.h_sub;

// SystemC-subtractor
instance top.v_mod.inst3 use workA.s_sub;
endconfig

Combining SystemC With Verilog Configurations
config use_B;
design top;
default liblist workA;
// no overrule for inst1

// SystemC-subtractor
instance top.v_mod.inst2 use workA.s_sub;
// SystemC-subtractor
instance top.v_mod.inst3 use workA.s_sub;
endconfig
The name of the Verilog top-entity is obligatory. The default liblist statement defines where
this Verilog top-entity is analyzed, by means of the libmap option of vlogan.
The instances are defined by their logical hierarchical name within the design hierarchy.
For setting up a design with Verilog configurations, there must be at least one call to
syscan as follows:
%> syscan s_sub.cpp:s_sub
This command generates an interface model, which has to be instantiated in Verilog.
The libmap option for vlogan requires the correct setting of the synopsys_sim.setup file.
For details, see the VCS and VCS User Guide.
Compiling a Verilog/SystemC Design
To compile a design containing Verilog and SystemC, use the following commands:
%> syscan s_sub.cpp:s_sub
%> vlogan v_sub.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> vlogan v_design.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> vlogan v_configs.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> vcs -sysc -sverilog use_B
The used configuration for the design is specified with the "<config-name>" option.
When a different configuration is used, or a configuration has changed, it is sufficient to
reanalyze the Verilog file that contains the changed configuration. Rerun the elaboration
step.
Compiling a Verilog/SystemC+VHDL Design
To compile such a design, use the following commands:
%> syscan s_sub.cpp:s_sub
%> vlogan v_sub.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> vhdlan h_sub.vhdl
%> vlogan v_design.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> vlogan v_configs.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> vcs use_A -sverilog

Combining SystemC With Verilog Configurations
SystemC-on-Top, Verilog and/or VHDL Down
1.
Specify a SystemC-on-top design with Verilog and VHDL as you specify any other design.
Analyze the Verilog files using the vlogan command with the libmap option. Add a Verilog
source file that contains the configuration details.
The following example shows a configuration with a SystemC-on-top topology:
config use_SysC_A;

design sYsTeMcToP; // name of the default SystemC top entity
default liblist workA; // library where the top-entity is analyzed

// Different mappings of verilog instances:
instance sYsTeMcToP.v_mod.inst1 use workA.v_sub; // verilog subtractor
instance sYsTeMcToP.v_mod.inst2 use workA.v_add; // verilog-adder
instance sYsTeMcToP.\sctop.sc2 .v_mod.inst3 use workA.v_add;

endconfig

config use_SysC_B;

design sYsTeMcToP;
default liblist workA;
instance sYsTeMcToP.v_mod.inst1 use workA.h_sub; //
VHDL-subtractor
instance sYsTeMcToP.v_mod.inst2 use workA.v_sub; //
verilog-subtractor
instance sYsTeMcToP.\sctop.sc2 .v_mod.inst3
use workA.v_add;

endconfig
By default, the name of the SystemC top-entity is sYsTeMcToP..
• Only Verilog modules can be re-configured. it is not possible to reconfigure a
SystemC instance and/or a VHDL instance.
• it is not possible to re-configure a Verilog-instance to a SystemC-instance.
When SystemC top-entity name is sYsTeMcToP,the method to specify the path name for a
Verilog instance depends on the position of the instance within the design hierarchy.

Combining SystemC With Verilog Configurations
• Use a normal path for Verilog modules that are instantiated at the top-level inside the
sc_main() function. These should not a sub-instance of a SystemC model.
"instance sYsTeMcToP.v_mod.inst1"
• Use a partially escaped path name for Verilog instances that are sub-instances of
SystemC modules. The path name must be split into the following two parts:
Here,
◦ The first part contains only SystemC instances.
◦ the second part contains Verilog or VHDL instances
Specify the first part as an extended Verilog identifier. This must start with a backslash
‘\’ and ends with a space ‘ ’.
instance sYsTeMcToP.\sctop.sc2 .v_mod.inst3 use workA.v_add;

The design topology is:
sctop SystemC
sc2 SystemC
v_mod Verilog
inst3 Verilog
The first part consists of two SystemC instances, ‘sctop’ and ‘sc2’. These instances
must be specified as "\sctop.sc2 " . Note that the space at the end is important and
must not be omitted.
The second part consists of two Verilog instances, ‘v_mod’ and ‘inst3’ must not be
escaped.
Writing the configuration as follows is not supported:
instance sYsTeMcToP.sctop.sc2.v_mod.inst3 use workA.v_add;
The name of the SystemC top-entity can be changed when unified hierarchy is enabled.
Compiling a SystemC/Verilog Design
To compile such a design, use the following commands:
%> vlogan v_sub.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> vlogan v_mod.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog -sc_model v_mod
%> vlogan v_configs.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> syscan sc_main.cpp
%> vcs -sysc use_A sc_main -sverilog
The used configuration is specified with the <config-name> option.

Considerations for Export DPI Tasks
The sc_main argument specifies that the design topology is SystemC-on-top.
When a different configuration is used, or a configuration has changed, it is sufficient to re-
analyze the Verilog file containing the changed configuration, and redo the elaboration.
Compiling a SystemC/Verilog+VHDL Design
To compile such a design, use the following commands:
%> vlogan v_sub.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> vhdlan h_sub.vhdl
%> vlogan v_mod.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog -sc_model v_mod
%> vlogan v_configs.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog
%> syscan sc_main.cpp
%> vcs -sysc sc_main use_B -sverilog
The following are the limitations for this feature:

%> vlogan v_mod.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog -sc_model v_mod
%> vlogan v_configs.v -libmap liblist.map -sverilog

%> vcs -sysc sc_main use_B -sverilog
The following are the limitations for this feature:
• A Verilog-on-top design must contain at least one SystemC instance, when no
configurations are used. Then, this SystemC instance can be configured to something.
• The interfaces of the modules must match, if not, the results are unpredictable. Make
sure that the consistency is maintained.
Considerations for Export DPI Tasks
If you have a SystemC design with Verilog instances, and you want to call export DPI
tasks from the SystemC side of the design, you can use either one of the following three
options:
• Use syscan -export_DPI []
• Use syscan -export_DPI [Verilog-file]
• Use Stubs File
Use syscan -export_DPI []
Register the name of all export DPI functions and tasks before the final vcs call to
elaborate the design. You can call syscan using the following command:
syscan -export_DPI function-name1 [[ function-name2] ]

Considerations for Export DPI Tasks
This is necessary for each export DPI task or function that is used by SystemC or C code.
Only the name of function must be specified, and formal arguments are neither required
nor allowed. Multiple space-separated function names can be specified in one call of
syscan -export_DPI . It is allowed to call syscan -export_DPI multiple times. A function
name can be specified multiple times.
Assume that you want to instantiate the following SystemVerilog module inside a SystemC
module:
//myFile.v
module vlog_top;
export "DPI" task task1;
import "DPI" context task task2(input int A);
export "DPI" function function3;

You must use the following steps before you can elaborate the simulation:

Use syscan -export_DPI [Verilog-file]
This is similar to syscan -export_DPI [function-name] . However, you can specify the
name of a Verilog file instead of the name of an export DPI function. The syscan searches
for all export_DPI declarations in that file.
The syntax is as follows:
syscan -export_DPI [ Verilog-file]
For example, (see myFile.vin the earlier mentioned section):
% syscan -export_DPI myFile.v
This locates export_DPI functions task1 and functions3 in the myFile.v file.

Considerations for Export DPI Tasks
syscan does not apply a complete Verilog or SystemVerilog parser, instead it
does a primitive string search in the specified file.
The following restrictions apply:
• The entire export_DPI declaration must be written in one line (no line breaks allowed).
• `include statements are ignored.
• Macros are ignored.
VCS elaborates the design even if the source files do not comply with the restrictions as
mentioned earlier. However, syscan is unable to extract some or all of the export_DPI
declarations. In this case, use syscan -export_DPI [function-name] .
Use Stubs File
An alternative approach is to use stubs located in a library. For each export DPI function,
such as, my_export_DPI, create a C stub with no arguments and store it in an archive that
is linked by VCS:
File: my_DPI_stubs.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

void _attribute_((weak)) my_export_DPI()
{
fprintf(stderr,"Error: stub for my_export_DPI is used\n");
exit(1);
}

more stubs for other export DPI function

Static and Dynamic Linking
You can also compile the SystemC source files with a static library, as shown in the
following commands:
% g++ -03 -Wall -I$VCS_HOME/inclue/systemc233 -c sc_src1.cpp -o sc_src1.o
% g++ -03 -Wall -I$VCS_HOME/inclue/systemc233 -c sc_src2.cpp -o sc_src2.o
% g++ -03 -Wall -I. -c ext_buf.cpp -o ext_buf.o
% ar -r sc_lib.a sc_src1.o sc_src2.o
% vcs TOP -sysc sc_lib.a
Ensure that at least one SystemC source file is compiled once with syscan command
before VCS elaborates the design, if not the SC-VCS-NO-SYSC error message is issued. To
avoid this error, you can compile an empty file, as shown in the following commands:
% touch sc_dummy.cpp
% syscan sc_dummy.cpp
% g++ -03 -Wall -I$VCS_HOME/inclue/systemc233 -c sc_src1.cpp -o sc_src1.o
% g++ -03 -Wall -I$VCS_HOME/inclue/systemc233 -c sc_src2.cpp -o sc_src2.o
% g++ -03 -Wall -I. -c ext_buf.cpp -o ext_buf.o
% ar -r sc_lib.a sc_src1.o sc_src2.o
% vcs TOP -sysc sc_lib.a
Dynamic Linking in VCS (For C/C++ Files)
You can compile C/C++ files into a shared library.
The pre-compiled shared object should be built on the same compiler as
supported by VCS.
The shared object file uses the following naming convention:
lib library_name.so.version
It begins with the lib keyword, followed by any specified name library_name, and then
followed by .so.version.
The version is optional and is user-defined. The linker/loader automatically locates and
picks the shared object file using -L and -l options.
For example, the library name in libfoo.so or libfoo.so.1 is foo. The commands to
create a shared object file are as follows:
% gcc -fPIC -o foo.o -c -I$VCS_HOME/include foo.c
% gcc -shared -o libfoo.so foo.o
You can dynamically link the shared library file using -ldflags with
-Lpath_to_shared_object and -llibrary_name options on the vcs command line.
-ldflags options

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Using -Mlib and -Mdir Options
Specifies the options to the linker/loader.
-L path_to_shared_object
Specifies the path, where shared objects reside.
-l library_name
Specifies the library name of the shared object file.
If there are more than one shared objects located in different directories, you can specify
-Lpath_to_the_shared_object multiple times for each directory and -llibrary_name
multiple times for each shared object file.
% vcs top -ldflags "-L<path_to_libfoo.so> -lfoo -L<path_to_libhello.so>
-lhello"
You can also specify the linker options directly to the vcs command line.
% vcs top -L path_to_libfoo.so -lfoo -L path_to_libhello.so -lhello
Dynamic Linking in VCS (For SystemC Files)
For dynamic linking of SystemC files, see Shared Library Flow.
LD_LIBRARY_PATH Environment Variable
You can set the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable to the directory where the shared
object file resides.
% setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH path_to_shared_objectfile:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
Now, for any change in the C/C++/SystemC files, you need to rebuild the shared object file
with the commands as mentioned above and execute the simvcommand. You do not need
to rebuild simv.
You must make sure to include the path to libstdc++.so provided by your C++ compiler
in your LD_LIBRARY_PATH, typically <path to g++>/lib64:<path to g++>/lib. If you use a
source_me file from the VG GNU package, then LD_LIBRARY_PATH is set automatically.
Using -Mlib and -Mdir Options
You can use the VCS -Mlib and -Mdir options during analysis and elaboration to store
analyzed SystemC files in multiple directories. Files specified with -Mdir within a directory
are not modified during VCS elaboration. This might be helpful if analyzing (compiling) of
SystemC source files takes a long time, and if you want to share analyzed files between
different projects.

Shared or Static SystemC Libraries
The use model is as follows:
syscan -Mdir=<dir1> model1.cpp:model1

syscan -Mdir=<dir2> model2.cpp:model2

vcs -sysc -Mlib=<dir1>,<dir2>
The -Mlib and -Mdir options are available in all configurations, for SystemC designs
containing Verilog/VHDL modules, and also for Verilog/VHDL designs containing SystemC
modules.
Shared or Static SystemC Libraries
Packaging SystemC Libraries in the VCS Installation Image
The SystemC libraries are provided as shared libraries in the VCS installation image in
addition to static libraries. Using the shared SystemC libraries instead of the static libraries
might avoid link errors or potential runtime crashes in some complex cases. For example,
link with a shared library which is in turn linked with the SystemC library, dynamic loading
of another shared library with dlopen() or with the -sv_lib option.
The static library remains default.
• You can use vcs -sysc=shared option to elaborate simv with the shared SystemC
libraries.
• You can use the vcs -sysc=static default option to elaborate simv with the static
SystemC libraries.
SystemC source files are compiled with syscan. VCS supports the incremental compile of
SystemC source files to reduce the re-compilation time. Only the files that have changed
(or the files affected by a change in a header file that they use) are recompiled; all other
files are not recompiled.
You can choose among the following different usage models:
• Full Build From Scratch
• Full Incremental Build
• Partial Build With Object Files

• Partial Build With Shared Libraries
• Dependency Checking of SystemC Source Files
Incremental compile does not require any change in existing compile scripts. VCS
automatically figures out when a syscan command needs to trigger compiling a source file
with GCC.
Full Build From Scratch
When you compile a design for the first time, there are no object files (for SystemC
sources) from a previous compilation. A typical command sequence is as follows:
Analyzing SC source files:
% syscan B1.cpp
% syscan B2.cpp
% syscan A.cpp:A

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Analyzing Verilog/VHDL source files:
% vlogan top.v
% vhdlan middle.vhd

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Elaboration:
% vcs -sysc Top
Here, all SC source files are compiled. Each invocation of syscan triggers a compilation
of the specified SC source files. Object files are stored in csrc/sysc or the mydir/sysc
directory, if you use the -Mdir mydir option.
This is called a "full build" from scratch. It serves as a basis for later incremental builds.
Full Incremental Build
If you specify the same commands again (see Full Build From Scratch), incremental
compilation kicks in. It is important not to remove the csrc/sysc directory; if not, you get
another full build.
Each call of syscan checks if the specified files need to be compiled again.
% syscan B1.cpp
The preceding command compiles B1.cpp only if, either the file B1.cpp or a header file
has changed since the last invocation of syscan. The dependency check to header files
includes any header that is directly or indirectly included by B1.cpp.

Note that any compiler option specified with -cflags (such as -Imydir or -DMODE=1)
is not considered during the dependency check. If the flags change but the source files
remain the same, the files are not recompiled.
Syscan calls can also create a Verilog or VHDL wrapper. For example, you can use the
following command:
% syscan A.cpp:A
Here, source file A.cpp is compiled again if either A.cpp, or a header file is changed.
This syscan call also checks if the signature (the set of interface ports) of the interface is
changed. If (and only if) the signature is changed, then the interface file is generated and
compiled again.
Incremental compilation of SystemC files reduces the time spent in syscan calls. When
the following remaining commands
% vlogan top.v
% vhdlan middle.vhd
% vcs -sysc Top
are issued again, the Verilog or VHDL files are analyzed and elaborated again, therefore,
these phases of the overall compilation do not benefit directly from the SystemC
incremental compilation. However, generation of object code for Verilog or VHDL files may
be skipped by VCS if this feature is enabled.
Partial Build With Object Files
The overall Turn-Around-Time (TAT) to get an updated simulation (simv) after a change in
a SC source file can be further reduced in same cases. If you are sure that only SC source
files have changed, and none of the changes affects the signature of the SC interface file,
then invoke a partial build with the following command:
% vcs -sysc=incr [-full64] [-Mdir=mydir]
(Optional, when used during initial elaboration)
All SC source files that are previously compiled with syscan are checked and
automatically compiled again if necessary. Finally, the simulation (simv) is linked again.
When you use -full64 and/or -MdirVCS options during the initial compilation or
elaboration step, then you must also specify these options for the incremental compilation
or elaboration step.
You can call syscan before calling vcs -sysc=incr .
% syscan B1.cpp
% vcs -sysc=incr

Using this example, if B1.cpp, or a header file is changed, then B1.cpp is compiled again
by the syscan call. The subsequent vcs -sysc=incr does not compile B1.cpp in this
case. That is, issuing the syscan call neither increases nor decreases the TAT; it only
triggers the compilation of B1.cpp earlier.
If the signature of an SC interface file is changed, VCS issues an error message and stops
the compilation. You need to do a full incremental build in this case.
This compile flow applies only when the SC source files change. You must use a full
incremental build in all other situations. For example, in case of the following situations:
• A Verilog or VHDL source file is changed.
• The signature of an SC interface file is changed.
• SC models instantiate VHDL or Verilog models, and the set of instances is changed.
Partial Build With Shared Libraries
By default, syscan creates object files (for example. B1.o) that are part of the final link
command to create the simulation (simv) during elaboration.
g++ -o simv B1.o B2.o A.o
To use shared libraries instead of object files, use the following command:
% syscan [-Mdir mydir] -shared
This command is specified without any other options (except the optional -Mdir
argument). It sets a “sticky” flag which applies to the csrc (or mydir) library. If the flag is
present, the final link command uses a shared library.
g++ -o simv libcsrc_sysc.so
Updating the Shared Library
The shared library is updated whenever necessary, that is, whenever a SystemC source
file is changed and recompiled. The update is triggered when you invoke the following
command:
% syscan -shared
or during elaboration with the following command:
% vcs -sysc Top

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
or, with a partial build:
% vcs -sysc=incr
Using Different Libraries
Each library specified with -Mdir can use either object files or a shared library. For
example,
% syscan -Mdir=lib1 B1.cpp
% syscan -Mdir=lib1 B2.cpp
% syscan -Mdir=lib1 -shared
% syscan -Mdir=lib2 A.cpp
% vcs -sysc -Mlib=lib1,lib2
The above example specifies to use a shared library for lib1, but object files for lib2.
Partial Build Invoked With VCS
You can get a simple use model and short turn-around time by calling vcs -sysc=incr,
after the “sticky” flag is set for one or more libraries.
VCS goes over all SC source files that are previously specified with syscan, recompiles
them as necessary, updates the shared libraries as necessary, and links the simulation.
Partial Build If Only One Shared Library is Updated
If only the SC source files located in one shared library change, but everything else is
not modified, then it is sufficient to update the library. Linking the simulation again is not
needed.
For example, to specify the content of shared library lib1,
% syscan -Mdir=lib1 B1.cpp
% syscan -Mdir=lib1 B2.cpp
% syscan -Mdir=lib1 -shared

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
% vcs -sysc -Mlib=lib1
Now, you can modify B1.cpp and update only the shared library as follows:
edit B1.cpp // modify src code
% syscan -Mdir=lib1 -shared // update shared lib
% ./simv // run simulation
Adding or Deleting SC Source Files in Shared Library
When a new file is specified with syscan, it is compiled and automatically added to the
library later. That is, the library remembers the files that were specified with syscan.
You cannot directly delete a file from a shared library. Instead, remove the entire csrc/
syscdirectory and perform a full build again with the remaining SC source files.

Changing From a Shared Library Back to Object Files
After you specify syscan -shared , this library always remains as a shared library later.
If you want to revert to use object files, remove the csrc/sysc/info-comp file. This
removes the “sticky flag.” The existing object files remain valid.
Dependency Checking of SystemC Source Files
By default, VCS does a dependency check for SystemC source files. Even if no source file
needs to be recompiled, the check itself takes some time. You can speed up the overall
compile time using the
-sysc=nodep
-sysc=nodep option.
To explicitly enable the dependency check for SystemC source files compiled with syscan,
the
-sysc=dep
-sysc=dep option is specified with the call of VCS.
The dependency check works in combination with the -Mlib option also. To enable
dependency checking for one specific library LIB1, the -sysc=dep:LIB1 option must be
used. If the specified library LIB1 does not exist, a warning message is issued mentioning
that the dependency check is skipped due to the non-existence of the specified library.
The behavior of the -sysc=nodep and -sysc=dep options in a VCS-elaboration call and
following incremental compile call (-sysc=incr) is explained in the following scenarios.
Default Setting
When a library is not specified in either -sysc=nodep or -sysc=dep options, the
dependency check for that library is skipped during the elaboration stage. But, at the
incremental compile call, the dependency checking is performed.
% syscan d1.cpp d2.cpp // goes to csrc
% syscan -Mdir AA a1.cpp
% syscan -Mdir BB b1.cpp b2.cpp
% syscan -Mdir AA a2.cpp
% syscan -Mdir DD d3.cpp d4.cpp
VCS Command
% vcs -Mlib=… -sysc=nodep:AA -sysc=dep:BB

BB(explicit on) : Yes
DD(default) : No
csrc : Yes

Check Dependency at Incremental Compile (vcs –sysc=incr)
BB(explicit on) : Yes
DD(default) : Yes
csrc : Yes
–sysc=dep Option Applies to All Libraries
If you use the -sysc=dep option on the VCS command, then the dependency checking is
enabled for all the libraries during elaboration and incremental compilation.
Selecting Specific Libraries
You can disable dependency checking for all the libraries but enable only for specific
libraries. The -sysc=depoption overrides the -sysc=nodep option.
% syscan d1.cpp d2.cpp // goes to csrc
% syscan -Mdir AA a1.cpp
% syscan -Mdir BB b1.cpp b2.cpp
% syscan -Mdir AA a2.cpp
% syscan -Mdir DD d3.cpp d4.cpp
VCS Command
% vcs -Mlib=… -sysc=dep:BB -sysc=nodep
Here the option '-sysc=dep:BB' overrides '-sysc=nodep'

csrc : Yes

DD(explicit off) : No
csrc : Yes
–sysc=nodep Option Applies to All Libraries, Except csrc
It is not possible to disable dependency check for files in csrc directory. For example, the
command vcs -sysc=nodep disables dependency checking for all libraries except csrc.
% syscan d1.cpp d2.cpp // goes to csrc
% syscan -Mdir AA a1.cpp

1. Compiling and linking your SystemC source files.
2. Adding glue to connect SystemC with Verilog/VHDL.
The syscan script is frequently used to achieve these tasks.
// (1) compile source file, link to simulation
% syscan A.cpp

Compiling and Linking the SystemC Source Files
You can decide how and when to compile your source files with GCC. However, you must
use the following GCC flags during compilation:
• Use the SystemC headers from VCS image: g++ -I$VCS_HOME/include/systemc233
…
Or use SystemC 233, 234 or any other supported version. Do not use headers files
from OSCI/Accellera.
• Always add the -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 option. This macro is used in some areas to
distinguish VCS-SystemC from OSCI/Accellera or other third-party SystemC kernels.
• Always use the -fPIC option, which GCC requires for a shared library
• Use -m32 for 32-bit and -m64 for 64-bit simulation.
• Compile the SystemC source file with the debug information ( g++ -g … ) in the
following scenarios:
◦ You want to instantiate the SystemC model in Verilog or VHDL (SC-down interface
model).
◦ You want TLI capabilities for the SystemC model.

Shared Library Flow
◦ You want full debug support for the SystemC model with Verdi or UCLI.
Most of the SystemC/HDL glue requires to know the internals of the SystemC
model which VCS gets from the debug information that GCC creates with -g.
• It is recommended to use both the -g and -O GCC flags, which provides the necessary
debug information and also optimized object code that runs faster: g++ -g -O …
However, you must omit the -O flag when you plan to perform interactive debugging
because stepping through optimized GCC code tends to be confusing.
1. Set the GCC flags using the following commands:
% g++ -c … -fPIC -m32 -g -O -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -I$VCS_HOME/
include/systemc233 A.cpp
% g++ -c … -fPIC -m32 -g -O -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -I$VCS_HOME/
include/systemc233 B.cpp
2. Link all the object files into a shared library using the following syntax:
% g++ -shared -o libSC.so A.o B.o
3. Add the shared library to the VCS elaboration command:
% vcs … libSC.so …
You can also use other methods to specify the shared library. For example, with
the -ldflags, -L or -l options. Set the LD_LIBRARY_PATH as necessary. For more
information, see VCS documentation.
Ensure that use the exact same GCC version that was used to compile your SystemC
source files. It is possible to use multiple shared libraries for your SystemC and other C/C+
+ source files.
Using Makefiles
Makefiles enable you to get all your SystemC source files compiled into a shared library.
You can configure a Makefile using the compile flags as described in the previous section.
A sample makefile is as follows:
SRC = A.cpp B.cpp

CXX = g++
CXXFLAGS = -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -m32 -fPIC -g -O \
-I$(VCS_HOME)/include/systemc233-I$(VCS_HOME)/include/systemc233
OBJS = $(SRC:%.cpp=%.o)
%.o: %.cpp $(DEPS)

Shared Library Flow
$(CXX) -c -o $@ $< $(CXXFLAGS)

libSC.so: $(OBJS)
$(CXX) -o $@ -shared -m32 $(OBJS)

clean:
rm -f $(OBJS)
rm -f $(subst .o,.d,$(OBJS))
rm -fr libSC.so
Generating an SC/HDL Interface model
To create an SC-down interface model, use the shared library instead of a source file
using the following syntax:
% syscan libSC.so:A [other syscan options]
Note that the source code containing SC_MODULE(A) must have been compiled with the
debug information (g++ -g ), if not syscan is not able to locate that model.
Specify other options in the similar method as you do for syscan A.cpp:A .
For example, -Mlib=… or -sysc=opt_if .
If you plan to perform interactive debug, then compile with debug information:
% syscan libSC.so:A -cflags -g

The hdl_connect is used to connect SystemC objects (sc_signals) to Verilog/
VHDL objects, so that value changes on either side propagates to the other side. The
hdl_connect is Synopsys' way of connecting SystemC to HDL simulators, and should
only be used with a Synopsys simulator.

Support for syscan in Parallel Build Environment
VCS supports parallel analysis flow in designs that contain SystemVerilog/VHDL and
SystemC files. This specifically prevents the read/write conflicts of SystemC related files
created during syscan calls that are issued in parallel within the same working directory.
Though SystemC related analysis and I/O file of syscan, vlogan -sc_model, and vhdlan
-sc_model are internally serialized, vlogan, vhdlan calls unrelated to SystemC calls are
parallelized. Thus, accelerating the analysis phase. There is no change in the use model
for compiling and running designs that have SystemVerilog, VHDL, and SystemC files.
• Parallel elaboration in the same working directory is not supported.
For example, vcs TOP -o simv1 …
• Clock time spent on SystemC related analysis calls (that is, syscan or vlogan,
-sc_model or vhdlan -sc_model ) does not reduce as the SystemC related analysis
calls are internally serialized.

Elaboration Scheme
• Ensure that the logical dependencies between analysis calls are executed sequentially.
(1) vlogan bottom.v -sc_model bottom // creates bottom.h
(2) syscan top.cpp // #include "bottom.h"
The top.cpp file need bottom.h, which is generated by step 1. As this is logically
dependent, execute step 2 only after step 1 is completed.
• Two-step flow is not supported (For example, vcs A.v …; syscsim … ). This
enhancement is only supported with the UUM flow.
Elaboration Scheme
When SystemC is at the top of the design hierarchy, you can instantiate Verilog code in the
SystemC code. The elaboration of the simulation is performed in the following two steps:
1. First, VCS creates a temporary simulation executable. This executable contains all
SystemC parts, but does not yet contain any HDL (Verilog, VHDL, ) parts. VCS
then starts this temporary executable to find out which Verilog/VHDL instances
are needed. All SystemC constructors, begin_end_of_elaboration() and
end_of_elaboration() methods are executed during this step. However, simulation
does not start at this point. Information about SystemC or HDL instances is extracted
and stored for the next step.
2. VCS creates the final version of the simv file containing SystemC, and all HDL parts.
The design is now fully elaborated and ready to simulate.
As a side effect of executing the temporary executable during step 1, all
statements located inside the constructors are executed. Statements inside
begin_end_of_elaboration()and end_of_elaboration() methods are also executed.
Additionally, all statements inside sc_main up to the first sc_start() call are executed.
If your simulation contains statements that should not be executed during step 1, you need
to guard these statements. You can use a check for the SYSTEMC_ELAB_ONLY environment
variable or, with the following function:
extern "C" bool hdl_elaboration_only()
Both are set/yield true only during this extra execution of simv during step 1.
For example, guard the statements as follows:
sc_main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
// instantiate signals, modules,
ModuleA my_top_module(); // <-- must always be executed

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Elaboration Scheme
// run simulation
if (! hdl_elaboration_only())
{
open log file for simulation report
}

sc_start(); // <-- must always be executed
if (! hdl_elaboration_only())
{
close log file
}

}
If you guard the statements as mentioned earlier, ensure that all the module constructors
are executed. Also, ensure that at least one call of sc_start() is executed.
VCS needs to know the entire SystemC module hierarchy during step 1. This means that
all SystemC constructors must be executed.
If your simulation checks the command line arguments argc and argv, then you have the
following two options:
• Guard these statements with an IF-statement as shown above.
Or
• Provide the simv command line arguments used during elaboration using the VCS
argument -syscelab. For example,
vcs -sysc sc_main -syscelab A
You can specify the -syscelab option multiple times. White space within the arguments
is not preserved. Instead, the arguments are broken up into multiple arguments. Multiple
arguments can also be enclosed within double quotes. For example, you can use
-syscelab "1 2 3".
If your SystemC design topology (the set of SystemC instances) depends on simv runtime
arguments, you must provide the relevant arguments with -syscelab. The SystemC
design topology during step 1 must be identical during the final execution of simv .
Note that, the -syscelab option is only supported when SystemC is at the top of the
design hierarchy. If Verilog or VHDL is at the top, then -syscelabis neither required nor
supported.

Introduction to Precompiled Header Files
The precompiled header files
systemc.h

use them. The
g++

include paths. In case it finds the header file, the g++ compiler uses the matching
precompiled header file. If not, it parses the specified header file (ASCII version) as usual.
A nonmatch can be caused by the use of different compile options. For example, use
options like
-m32

Using Precompiled Header Files
Use the syscan option to create precompiled header files (systemc.h and systemc).
Compile the given SystemC files. Add a search path to the location of the precompiled
header file:
%syscan -prec[=<target_directory>] <file1>[<file2>]
•
target_directory
<target_directory> is the user-specified path. If specified, this path is the first path
searched for all includes.
• <file1>, <file2> are the SystemC source files.
The earlier mentioned command creates the precompiled header files
systemc.h and systemc, if these do not exist. Otherwise, it uses the
precompiled header files that are already present.

Improving Compilation Speed Using Precompiled C++ Headers
If you mention <target_directory>, then the g++ call first searches this directory for
precompiled header files. This ensures that you get the best performance improvement,
and that the precompiled header files are used if they exist.
If you do not specify a directory, g++ creates a precompiled header file in each of the
following two directories:
./csrc/sysc/prec/$hostname/<SC_version>/<GCC_version>/<VCS_version>/syste

-fPIC).
If -Mdir is specified as an argument to syscan -prec , then the directory structure

and

use -Mdir with -prec with a path, the
-Mdir

The generation of the precompiled header files is done using makefiles. In case of no
change, a precompiled header file is not generated again.
The following example shows how to use precompiled header files:
In this example, assume that a Verilog module my_top instantiates a SystemC module
called my_sc_top.
% syscan -prec -tlm2 my_sc_top.cpp:my_sc_top

% syscan -prec my_sc_module.cpp

% vlogan -sverilog my_top.sv

Invoking the Creation of Precompiled Header Files
If any of the following changes occur, syscan -prec triggers creation of the appropriate
precompiled header files.
• The GCC version is different from the one used for the creation of the precompiled
header files systemc.h and/or systemc .
• Compile flags are not the same.
• SystemC-related defines passed with -D as argument(s) of the -cflags option are not
the same.
• $VCS_HOME (version) changes.
• SystemC version changes.
• Host changes (different system include files).
If the -prec option is called with a user-specified path, then a sanity check is done. This
ensures that the precompiled header files are already generated at the specified location.
If any of the previously mentioned changes occur, an appropriate message is generated.
and the creation and usage of precompiled header files is skipped. This occurs for VCS,
GCC, SystemC version, and host name changes.

This section lists the limitations that apply to the following:
• Limitations of GNU Precompiled Header Files
• Limitations of syscan -prec Option
• Limitations of Using -prec With Path
• Limitations of Sharing Precompiled Header Files

Improving Compilation Speed Using Precompiled C++ Headers
Limitations of GNU Precompiled Header Files
• The option used for creating the precompiled header file and the actual object file must
be the same. If not, the precompiled header file is skipped.
• Only one precompiled header file can be used in one compilation step.
• Any C token before a precompiled header file is skipped.
• The g++ compiler installation to create the precompiled header file and the actual g++
compiler installation must be the same.
• Any macro defined before the precompiled header file must be the same when creating
and using it.
Limitations of syscan -prec Option
• The include statement of a SystemC header file must be on top of a file. Any C/C++
token used before the SystemC header file skips the usage of the precompiled header
file. This also parses the ASCII source file.
A C/C++ token can be any valid C/C++ source code like a typedef or variable
declaration. Preprocessor directives (for example, #define, #include) are not
C/C++ tokens.
• Two precompiled header files are created, one for systemc.h and one for systemc.
• The size of a precompiled header file is at least 2.5 MB. The size depends on the
options passed in a sysc -prec call.
• All syscan calls must use the -prec option to make use of the precompiled header
files.
• A change in compile flags and/or SystemC related defines in a syscan -prec call
creates precompiled header files with those settings.
• If you use SystemC-related defines before a SystemC header file, create the
precompiled SystemC header file with the same defines names and values. Use the -D
option as part of -cflags in the syscan -prec command.
The defines in front of a SystemC header file must match the set of defines used in the
precompiled header file creation step. If matching precompiled files are not found, then
the ASCII version of the SystemC header file is used.

Limitations of Using -prec With Path
This feature has the following limitation:
• If there are already precompiled header files stored in the path-location, a sanity
check is done with respect to changes to hostname, SystemC version , gcc version ,
and VCS version (time stamp).
If one of these does not match, a warning message is generated, and the creation (and
usage) of the precompiled header files is skipped. The result is that the precompiled
header files are not used in the compile step. Putting the host name as part of the path
prevents skipping (and usage) of precompiled header files in case of any host name
changes. All the rest must match.
Limitations of Sharing Precompiled Header Files
• You must call the
-prec
-prec option, along with an absolute path, to share precompiled
header files. You must have read (and maybe write) permissions.
If there is a change with respect to the name of the host, then VCS, GCC, and
SystemC version sharing is not possible. In this case, the sanity check creates a
warning, and the usage of precompiled header files is skipped.
In most cases, the name of the host changes. If the host name is part of the path (such
as, /some_dir/${hostname}/), then the precompiled header files can be used. The
downside is that the precompiled header files are created in this specific directory with
the information used by VCS, SystemC, and GCC version.
• You must call the syscan executable with the -prec option with the same path. Any
change in the compile flags (passed with -cflags) invokes the creation of precompiled
header files, if they do not exist for the changed combination of compile flags.

You can model your designs containing SystemC and SystemC Verification Standard

Modeling SystemC Designs With SCV
SCV Library in VCS
The SCV library is shipped along with the VCS image. SCV library is supported for all
SystemC versions for all the compilers. SCV library is not binary compatible with OSCI-
SystemC, but belongs to the SystemC version shipped with VCS.
The VCS- SystemC flow supports the following SCV versions:
• SCV 1.0p2 (default version)
• SVC 2.0
For the SCV version and its compatible version of GCC compiler, see the VCS Release
Notes.
• To select the default SCV version (1.0p2), you can use the -sysc=scv option on
syscan while compiling the source code containing SCV. This option adds the
required include directories within the VCS image during analysis. Also, use the
-sysc=scvoption on VCS command that selects the correct library to be linked.
syscan -sysc=scv myfile.cpp
vcs -sysc -sysc=scv
You can also use -sysc=scv10 option instead of -sysc=scv option, as both these
options exhibit the same functionality.
syscan -sysc=scv10 myfile.cpp
vcs -sysc -sysc=scv10
• To select SCV 2.0 version, you can use the -sysc=scv20 option on syscan.
syscan -sysc=scv20 myfile.cpp
vcs -sysc -sysc=scv20
It is not allowed to integrate SCV 1.0p2 and SCV 2.0 versions with the same
simulation. You must use the same version consistently throughout all the
calls of syscan and VCS.
