The hdl_param class defines the ::operator() to initialize the parameters. Use
the ::get() function to obtain the final value of the parameter. initialize parameters
only one time. You cannot change parameters after you obtain their value using the

function.::get() function. This means parameters are constant, all get() calls yields the
same result.
Namespace
The hdl_param objects are defined in the sc_snps {} namespace.
namespace sc_snps {
template < class T >
class hdl_param : public sc_object { };
} // namespace sc_snps
For the declaration of the parameters, this namespace must be used:
SC_MODULE(sysc_foo) {
sc_snps::hdl_param<int> i;
};
Parameter Specification as VCS Elaboration Arguments
The parameters can be defined using the VCS elaboration command line arguments. This
is implemented only for a Verilog-on-Top design.
* -pvalue+v_top.foo1.msb=33
This works only for integer and real parameter types. This does not work for string
parameters.
* -parameters param.lst
With param.lst a list of parameter assignments (see the specific vcs part of this guide
discussing parameters).
Debug
The SystemC hdl_param objects are visible as class parameters within a combined
hierarchy view (vpd-file). Although parameters are constant and do not change after time
== 0, these can be traced.
Access with the UCLI get command is supported. Changing the value with the change or
force commands is not supported, since parameters are constant after the construction
time.
The verilog parameters are not compile constants for SystemC. So, these cannot be used
as template arguments for the construction of templatized classes.

SC_CTOR(not_possible) : HDL_PARAM(width, 4)
{
sc_int<width> *pint = new sc_int<width>; // NOT SUPPORTED
}
The same holds for the Verilog and VHDL domains:
module test( data_in1, data_in2 );

Support for Wreal Data Type at the SystemC or Verilog Boundary
SystemC provides support for the wreal data type. The ports of the wreal data type can
also be connected across the SystemC/Verilog boundary. This includes hierarchies in
which Verilog instantiates a SystemC module and vice versa.
The wreal inout ports at the boundary can be driven by multiple drivers across domains,
with the same set of resolution functions. For example, the resolution functions can be
res_def, res_sum, res_min, or res_max that are supported by Verilog.
This feature is enabled through the Synopsys-proprietary extension to the SystemC
kernel. It allows usage of wreal data type in SV boundaries.It includes the sc_wreal data
type to model a wreal data type on the SystemC side with the following new signal and
new ports:
• Signal:
◦ sc_signal_wreal_resolved
• Ports:
◦ sc_in_wreal_resolved
◦ sc_out_wreal_resolved
◦ sc_inout_wreal_resolved
To model the X and Z states, two constant sc_wreal objects SC_WREAL_X and
SC_WREAL_Z are provided for comparison or assignment.
The sc_wreal class currently does not provide arithmetic and logical operators.
However, raw access to an underlying double value is provided through the
to_double member function.

Support for Wreal Data Type at the SystemC or Verilog Boundary
To use the wreal data type at the SystemC or Verilog boundary, analyze models with the
wreal data type at the interface.
To select a resolution function, the -wreal <res_func> VCS flag is used, where
<res_func> defines the resolution function.
The wreal data type at the SystemC/Verilog boundary is only supported with
the HSOPT wrapper generation. You must analyze SystemC/Verilog models
using the -sysc=opt_if command using vlogan/syscan to generate the
interface code.
• Supported with the HSOPT wrapper backend generation -sysc=opt-if.
• The sc_trace mechanism is not supported with sc_wreal.
• TLI access to sc_wreal is not supported.
• VPD dumping of the wreal data type is not supported.

This chapter describes the VCS SystemC capabilities that can be used for transaction
level simulations and includes the following topics:
• Transaction Level Interface

The Transaction Level Interface (TLI) between SystemVerilog and SystemC supports
communication between these languages at the transaction level. At RTL, all the
communication goes through signals. At transaction level, communication goes through
function or task calls.

TLI is an easy-to-use feature that enables integrating transaction level SystemC models
into a SystemVerilog environment seamlessly and efficiently. The automated generation
of the communication code alleviates the difficulties in implementing a synchronized
communication mechanism. This allows you to fully integrate cycle accurate SystemC
models into a SystemVerilog environment.
TLI exploits using the powerful Verification Methodology Manual (VMM methodology)
to verify functional or highly accurate SystemC TLMs. TLI improves mixed language
simulation performance. TLI speeds-up the development of the verification scenarios.
Also, it adds the necessary logic to enable you to debug the transaction traffic using the
waveform viewer in Verdi.
TLI augments the pin-level interface (DKI) to enable both languages to communicate
at different levels of abstraction.

text:
ion scenarios.
Also, it adds the necessary logic to enable you to debug the transaction traffic using the
waveform viewer in Verdi.
TLI augments the pin-level interface (DKI) to enable both languages to communicate
at different levels of abstraction. Using this interface, you can simulate some part of the
design at the transaction-level and the other part at the hardware level. This enables full
control over the level of detail required for your simulation runs. This integration also helps
you to leverage the powerful features of SystemVerilog for transaction-level verification.
You can use the same testbenches for hardware verification.
TLI enables you to perform the following:
• Call interface methods of SystemC interfaces from SystemVerilog.
• Call tasks or functions of SystemVerilog interfaces from SystemC.
Methods and tasks can be blocking or non-blocking. Blocking means the call might not
return immediately, but consumes simulation time before it returns. Non-blocking calls
always return immediately in the same simulation time.
The caller's execution is resumed exactly at the simulation time when the caller returns. A
blocking call consumes the same amount of time in both the language domains. SystemC
and SystemVerilog non-blocking calls always return immediately.
The tasks or functions must be reachable through an interface of the specific language
domain. That is, for SystemVerilog calling SystemC, the TLI can connect to functions that
are members of a SystemC interface class. For SystemC calling SystemVerilog, the TLI
can call functions or tasks that are part of a SystemVerilog interface.
The usage model of the transaction level interface consists of defining the interface by
means of an interface definition file. You can call a code generator to create the TLI
adaptors for each domain. Finally, you instantiate and bind of the adaptors.
Support for Typedefs
SystemC supports user-defined typedefs for the supported types.

Typedefs are supported for:
• All ANSI integer data-types
• Arguments of imported methods
• Return type of imported methods
• Nested typedefs
Typedefs can be declared in any scope.
The following is an example of TLI adapter defining variables with typedefs:
typedef unsigned int MY_TYPE_1;
SC_MODULE(SC_MOD) {
typedef unsigned int MY_TYPE_2;
typedef MY_TYPE_1 MY_TYPE_3;
…
void method_AAA(MY_TYPE_1 a);
MY_TYPE_2 method_BBB();
MY_TYPE_3 member_CCC;
…
};
The TLI adapter imports both methods and member_CCC and represent them in
SystemVerilog as int unsigned , as shown in the following example:
interface SC_MOD;
…
function void method_AAA(input int unsigned param_1);
…

function int unsigned method_BBB();
…
function int unsigned get_member_CCC();
…
function void set_member_CCC(input int unsigned …);
…
Interface Definition File
The interface definition file contains all the necessary information to generate the TLI
adaptors. It consists of a general section and a section specific to a task/function. The
order of lines within the general section is arbitrary, and the first occurrence of a task or

function keyword marks the end of this section. The format of the file is illustrated as
follows:
interface if_name
direction sv_calls_sc
[verilog_adaptor name]
[systemc_adaptor name]
[hdl_path XMR-path]

[#include " file1.h"]
[`include " file2.v"]

task <method1>
input|output|inout|return vlog_type argument_name_1 return
input|output|inout|vlog_type argument_name_2
.
.
.
function [return type] method2
input|output|inout vlog_type argument_name_1
.
.
.
The interface entry defines the name of the SystemVerilog "interface". Similarly,
the class entry defines the name of the SystemVerilog "class". For the direction
SystemVerilog calling SystemC, the if_name argument must match the name of
the SystemC interface class. Specialized template arguments are allowed in this
case, for example, my_interface<int> or my_interface<32>. For SystemC calling
SystemVerilog, if_name must match the SystemVerilog interface name.
The direction field specifies the caller and callee language domains, and defaults to
sv_calls_sc. The SystemC calling SystemVerilog direction is indicated by sc_calls_sv.
The verilog_adaptor and systemc_adaptor fields are optional and define the names
of the generated TLI adaptors and the corresponding file names. The .sv file extension
is used for the verilog_adaptor and .h and .cpp file extensions are used for the
systemc_adaptor.
The optional #include lines are inserted literally into the generated SystemC header file.
The optional `include lines into the generated SystemVerilog file.
The hdl_path field is optional. It binds the generated Verilog adaptor through an XMR to a
fixed Verilog module, Verilog interface, or class instance. Using hdl_path makes it easier
to connect to a specific entity. However, the adaptor can be instantiated only once, not
multiple times. If you want multiple connections, then create multiple adaptors which differ
only by their name.

A SystemC method might or might not be blocking. That is, it might consume simulation
time before it returns or it returns immediately. This distinction is important for the
generation of the adaptor.
Use task for SystemC methods that are blocking or even potentially blocking. Use
function for SystemC methods that are not blocked. Note that functions enable faster
simulation than tasks.
The lines after task or function define the formal arguments of the interface method.
This is performed in SystemVerilog syntax. That is, types of the arguments must be valid
SystemVerilog types. See Supported Data Types of Formal Arguments for more details.
The return keyword is only allowed once for each task. It becomes an output argument
on the Verilog side to a return value on the SystemC side. This feature is required because
blocking functions in SystemC might return values, while Verilog tasks do not have a
return value.
The exception is only if the methods of the SystemC interface class use reference
parameters.

blocking functions in SystemC might return values, while Verilog tasks do not have a
return value.
The exception is only if the methods of the SystemC interface class use reference

allowed for inout parameters. For input parameters, this special marker is not needed

Interface

direction sv_calls_sc
verilog_adaptor simple_bus_blocking_if_adaptor systemc_adaptor
simple_bus_blocking_if_adaptor
#include "simple_bus_blocking_if.h"

task burst_read
input int unsigned priority_
inout int data[32]

input int unsigned length

input int unsigned start_address

Instantiation and Binding
TLI adaptors must always be instantiated in pairs, where each pair forms a point-to-point
connection from one language domain to the other.
If multiple pairs of the same TLI adaptor type are needed in the design, you must
instantiate the adaptor multiple times in each domain. The point-to-point connection must
be set up by assigning a matching ID value to the SystemVerilog interface or class, and
the SystemC module. The ID value is set for SystemC module and the SystemVerilog
class, if generated, as a constructor argument. In case the SystemVerilog adaptor is
generated as an interface, the ID is set through a parameter.
The SystemVerilog TLI adaptor (either as an interface or a class) can be instantiated
and used like any other SystemVerilog interface or class. If you want to call an IMC of a
SystemC interface, you need to call the corresponding member function or task of the TLI
adaptor.
The SystemC part of the TLI adaptor is a plain SystemC module that has a port p over the
specified interface name (sc_port if_name p ). This module can be instantiated in the
SystemC design hierarchy, where you can bind the port to the design interface like any
other SystemC module.
As mentioned earlier, there is an optional constructor argument for the point-to-point ID
of type int that defaults to zero. There is a second optional constructor argument of type
int that specifies the format of debug information that the adaptor prints when an interface
method is called.
If the LSB of this argument is set, the TLI adaptor issues messages to stdout. If the next
bit (LSB+1) is set, this information is written to sc_signal<string>that you can display in
Verdi.
For SystemC calling SystemVerilog, the SystemC part of the TLI adaptor is a sc_module
that you can instantiate within the module where you want to call the Verilog tasks or
functions. You can execute the cross-boundary task or function calls by calling the
corresponding member function of the SystemC TLI adaptor instance.
The SystemVerilog portion of the TLI adaptor depends on whether the hdl_path field and
the following options are used:
• The -idf option used along with the interface entry in the idf file.
• The -idf option used along with the class entry in the idf file.
• The combination -idf used along with the interface entry in the idf file, no
hdl_path:
The Verilog adaptor has a port over the interface type, as defined in the interface
description file. You can instantiate the adaptor module in the Verilog design like any

other Verilog module, and the port should be bound to the SystemVerilog interface that
implements the tasks or functions to be called.
• The combination -idf used along with the interface entry in the idf file, with
hdl_path path :
The Verilog adaptor is a Verilog module with no ports. All calls initiated by SystemC are
routed through the XMR path to some other Verilog module or interface.
• The combination -idf used along with the class entry in the idf file, with hdl_path
path:
The Verilog adaptor is a group of task definitions and other statements that must be
included in a program with the `include "if_name_sc_calls_sv.sv " statement.
Calls initiated by the SystemC side are routed through the XMR path to some class
object of the SV testbench.
• The combination -idf used along with the class entry in the idf file, no hdl-path:
This combination is not supported and displays an error message.
It is important to note that Verilog tasks, in contrast to Verilog functions, must always be
called from within a SystemC thread context.
This is because tasks can consume time, and to synchronize the simulator kernels,
wait() is used in the SystemC adaptor module. The SystemC kernel throws an error
when wait() is called from a non-thread context.

Miscellaneous
The TLI generator uses Perl5 that needs to be installed on the local host machine. Perl5
is picked up in the following order from your installation paths (1=highest priority):
1. Use ${SYSCAN_PERL}, if (defined)
2. /usr/local/bin/perl5
3. perl5 from local path and issues a warning message
Generation of TLI Adaptors
The following command generates SystemVerilog and SystemC source code for the TLI
adaptors from the specified interface definition file:
syscan -idf interface_definition_file
This command generates SystemC and SystemVerilog files that define the TLI adaptors
for each language domain. All generated files can be compiled like any other source file
for the corresponding domain. The files have to be generated again only when the content
of the interface definition file changes.
TLI adaptors for the sv_calls_sc direction can be generated in two different styles.
The SystemC part of the generate adaptor is the same for both styles, however, the
SystemVerilog part is different.
If you use the
-idf
-idf option along with the interface entry in the idf file, then this option
creates a SystemVerilog "interface". Similarly, if you use the -idf option along with the
class entry in the idf file, then this option creates a SystemVerilog "class".
A class is generally easier to connect into the SystemVerilog source code and there are
situations where a SystemVerilog testbench allows you to instantiate a class but not an
interface. However, if a class is generated, then the TLI adaptor can create only one
connection of this type between the SystemVerilog and SystemC side. Alternatively, if an
interface is generated, then multiple connections can be created (which are distinguished
by the integer parameter of the interface).

Pack and unpack functions:
template <typename T>
void tli_conv2_unpack_tlmgp(tli_pack_data& P, T &gp)
{
P >> gp.addr >> gp.data >> gp.RW >> gp.response;
}
template <typename T>
void tli_conv2_pack_tlmgp(tli_pack_data& P, T &gp)
{

P << gp.addr << gp.data << gp.RW << gp.response;
}

template void
tli_conv2_pack_tlmgp<my_payload>(tli_pack_data& ,
my_payload&);
template void
tli_conv2_unpack_tlmgp<my_payload>(tli_pack_data& ,
my_payload&);
On SV VMM side
The pack and unpack methods are created by vmm shorthand macros.
class my_payload extends vmm_data;
rand bit [31:0] addr;
rand bit [31:0] data;
rand bit RW;
bit response;

`vmm_data_member_begin(my_payload)
`vmm_data_member_scalar(addr,DO_ALL)
`vmm_data_member_scalar(data,DO_ALL)
`vmm_data_member_scalar(RW,DO_ALL)
`vmm_data_member_scalar(response, DO_ALL)
`vmm_data_member_end(my_payload)

`vmm_channel(my_payload)
Connecting SystemVerilog UVM with SystemC TLM 2.0
For TLM generic payload, the pack and unpack methods are defined internally in the TLI
adapters. For other payload types, you need to define the pack and unpack methods on
SC and SV side. On SC side, it is same as described in the section User-Defined Payload.
On SV side, the pack/unpack methods can be created by using the UVM shorthand
macros.

This section describes how you can align both VMM or UVM and SC messages with the
same API. It consists of the following topics:
• Aligning VMM and SystemC Messages
• Aligning UVM and SystemC Messages
Aligning VMM and SystemC Messages
SystemC and VMM both contain APIs, which control the functionality of a message (info,
warning, and error). Both concepts are similar, but the APIs and underlying implementation
is completely independent. For example, if you want to skip all warnings or re-direct
warnings into a log file, then you must call both the SystemC and VMM APIs. This is
tedious.
The scenario explained in the use model, enables you to decide if you want to align
SystemC messages with VMM.
To align VMM messages with SystemC, perform the following steps:
1. Instantiate the tli_vmm_sc_msg_align module in the top module.
2. Include the tli_vmm_sc_msg_align.sv file before the SV top module.
For Example,
`include "tli_vmm_sc_msg_align.sv"
tli_vmm_sc_msg_align vmm_msg_align();
test tb();
sc_top sysc();
The SystemC message handler has the capability to suppress specific kinds of SystemC
messages. Only the messages which are not suppressed from SystemC are aligned with
VMM. If you are registering your own sc_report_handler, then the report_handler is
not aligned with VMM messaging, and the user-defined report handler takes precedence.
The default setting for VMM message alignment creates a vmm_log instance for each
SystemC process-id (name for a SystemC process). This process-id is the instName of a
vmm_log instance. You can change this default behavior to use one vmm_log instance for
all SystemC processes and messages, or you can disable the VMM message alignment.

Changing Message Alignment Settings
This section explains how you can change certain settings, using APIs, for aligning
messages.
The following SystemC API is provided to disable VMM message alignment or to change
the type of vmm_log to be used.
// multiple vmm_logs for SystemC-VMM message
sc_snps::align_sc_report_with_VMM( sc_snps::MultipleVMMLogs );
// single vmm_log for all SystemC-VMM messages
sc_snps::align_sc_report_with_VMM( sc_snps::SingleVMMLog );
// switch off VMM message alignment
sc_snps::align_sc_report_with_VMM( sc_snps::NoVMMLog );
You can disable VMM message alignment, or switch to the usage of one vmm_log for all
SystemC processes, only once. If there are multiple calls for changing VMM message
alignment, messages are not generated, and the calls do not have an effect on the VMM
message behavior.
To use the API in SystemC, you must include the systemc_user.h file, as shown in the
following example. This example shows how to disable the VMM message alignment.
Disabling of the VMM message alignment must take place before the start of
the simulation.

sc_main()
{

sc_snps::align_sc_report_with_VMM( sc_snps::NoVMMLog );

sc_start();

}
Mapping SystemC to VMM Severities
The concept of severity applies to both VMM and SystemC. The process of mapping
SystemC severities to VMM are as follows:
• SC_REPORT_INFO message is converted into a vmm_note
• SC_REPORT_WARNING is converted into a vmm_warning

• SC_REPORT_ERROR is converted into a vmm_error
• SC_REPORT_FATAL is converted into a vmm_fatal
SystemC messages consist of an ID, which is turned into a prefix of the VMM message.
For example, if the following message definition is available:
SC_DEFINE_MESSAGE(TLM_PKG_FAIL, 801, "failure in package processing");
Call of this message definition in SystemC:
SC_REPORT_INFO(TLM_PKG_FAIL, "Packet got lost");
It is issued as the following VMM message:
Normal[NOTE] on SystemC(top.sysc.tli1.driver) at 7000:
SC_I_801 [failure in packet processing] : Packet got lost
In file: /u/me/src/my_systemc_src.cpp:42
Filtering Messages
All messages generated with SC_REPORT_INFO or similar calls are aligned with VMM.
The decision on whether a specific SC message is suppressed or not, is not influenced
within the SystemC kernel. If it is normally (no VMM present) suppressed, then it is also
suppressed when VMM is present. If it is normally processed, then this also occurs in
context with VMM.
A SC message triggers a set of actions within the sc_report_handler. If VMM message
alignment is active, and if print to stdout and print to log actions are influenced,
then other actions (such as stopping the simulator) proceed as usual.
If VMM alignment is active, a message is generated, but not suppressed by the
sc_report_handler. Then, this message is forwarded to the VMM message handler,
which decides what to do with it.
The filter setting for VMM messages influence the type of SC messages that
are issued. For example, if you run simv to print only errors, then less severe
messages (for example, warnings) are not printed to stdout. This applies to
both VMM and SC messages.
The following are the two methods for filtering messages:
• Printing messages into a log file.
• Skipping messages with a specific severity, by influencing the simulator runtime options
such as +vmm_log_default and -l.

Perform the following steps to archive the changes in the settings of SystemC-VMM specific
to the vmm_log instantiations:
1. Get the actual vmm_log instantiation of a SystemC-instName (SystemC process-
id(name)).
2. Call the vmm_log related methods with the appropriate arguments.
The following SV-task returns the current vmm_log used by the SystemC-VMM message
alignment as the second argument, depending on the vmm_log settings (single or multiple

title: 1.01 /* factor */,
text:
id(name)).
2. Call the vmm_log related methods with the appropriate arguments.
The following SV-task returns the current vmm_log used by the SystemC-VMM message
alignment as the second argument, depending on the vmm_log settings (single or multiple
vmm_logs).
tli_util_get_sysc_vmm_log_by_instName(<string>, <vmm_log>);
Where, <string> is the process name. If SystemC-VMM alignment is disabled, then the
second task argument, vmm_log, is 0. The task is declared in the tli_vmm_sc_msg_align
module. To use this task, the module must be instantiated within the top module. You can
then access the task using the following command:
<top_module_name>.<instance_name_of_tli_vmm_sc_msg_align>.tli_util_get_sy
sc_vmm_log_by_instName();
For example, if the name of the top SV module is mentioned as top, then the
tli_vmm_sc_msg_align module is instantiated in the top SV module, and the instance
name is vmm_msg_align, as shown in the following example:

vmm_log log;
string process_name = "top.sysc.vmmconn1.driver";
// call task with XMR path starting with top

top.vmm_msg_align.tli_util_get_sysc_vmm_log_by_instName(process_name,lo
g);
if (log)
log.set_verbosity(vmm_log::WARNING_SEV, , , );

If multiple vmm_logs are used (default) and vmm_log is not created, then a vmm_log with
the instName provided in the string parameter is created. If VMM message alignment is
switched-off, then the return value of vmm_log is 0.
The name of the vmm_logs used by SystemC message alignment is SystemC. The
instance name for single vmm_log is reporter, and it is process id (process name) for
multiple vmm_logs.
SystemC can generate messages to stdout, in a specified SystemC log file (see
SystemC LRM, set_log_file_name), to both stdout and SystemC log file. If VMM
message alignment is active, then the messages are not generated in a specified SC-log
file. If the SC-message is not suppressed from SystemC, then the VMM message settings

decide what and how to print. As a result, the messages are printed to stdout only, and
not in a SC-log file.
Calling the VMM message handler requires a valid (and existing) SV scope. If there
is no VMM-scope, then all SystemC messages are generated using the default
sc_report_handler. If you have registered your own report_handler, it is used for
messages even if VMM alignment is active.
The default setting, using multiple vmm_logs, can be changed only once, before start of
simulation. It can be changed either to use single vmm_log or to switch-off the SystemC-
VMM message alignment.
Aligning UVM and SystemC Messages
SystemC and
UVM
UVM both have APIs to produce messages (for example, info, warning,
error) and an API to control what happens with such messages. Both concepts are similar
but the APIs and underlying implementations are totally independent. You must call both
the APIs if you want. For example, to skip all the warnings or re-direct warnings into a log
file.
With the following functionality, you can decide whether you want SystemC messages
aligned with UVM or not.
To enable UVM message alignment, you must either include the provided
tli_uvm_sc_msg_align.sv file before the SV top module or analyze this file. The path
to the SV file is $VCS_HOME/etc/systemc/tlm/tli/tli_uvm_sc_msg_align.sv. The
tli_uvm_sc_msg_align module residing in this file must be instantiated in the top module
to enable UVM message alignment (see Example 20).

`include "tli_uvm_sc_msg_align.sv"
tli_uvm_sc_msg_align uvm_msg_align();
test tb();
sc_top sysc();

can control whether you want message alignment enabled or not at compile time (see
Example 21).

The SystemC message handler has the functionality to suppress specific kinds of
SystemC messages. Only the messages that are aligned with UVM, which are not
suppressed from SystemC. If you are registering your own sc_report_handler, this
report handler does not align with UVM messaging. The user-defined report handler takes
precedence.
Changing Message Alignment Settings
The default setting for UVM message alignment is that for each SystemC process-id,
a UVM report object is created with the process-id as the instName of a UVM report
instance. You can change this default behavior to use one UVM report instance for all
SystemC processes or you can disable the UVM message alignment.
The following API (see Example 22, Example 23, and Example 24) is provided for
SystemC to disable UVM message alignment or change the kind of UVM report object to
be used.
Example 22 Multiple UVM Report Objects for SystemC-UVM Message
sc_snps::align_sc_report_with_UVM(sc_snps::MultipleUVMLogs);
Example 23 Single UVM Report Object for all SystemC-UVM Messages
sc_snps::align_sc_report_with_UVM(sc_snps::SingleUVMLog);
Example 24 Switch off UVM Message Alignment
sc_snps::align_sc_report_with_UVM(sc_snps::NoUVMLog);
Disabling UVM message alignment or switching to one UVM report object for all SystemC
processes can only be performed once. Disabling UVM message alignment can only be
performed before the simulation starts. In this case, messages are not generated. The
calls have no effect on the UVM message behavior.
To use the API in SystemC, include the
systemc_user.h
systemc_user.h file. Example 25 shows how to
disable UVM message alignment. Note that, disabling happens before simulation starts.

title: 1.01 /* factor */,
text:
sc_main()
{

sc_snps::align_sc_report_with_UVM(sc_snps::NoUVMLog);

sc_start();

}
Mapping SystemC to UVM Severities
UVM and SystemC messages both have severities, and the mapping of SystemC
severities to UVM is as follows:
• SC_REPORT_INFO maps to UVM info message.
• SC_REPORT_WARNING maps to UVM warning message.
• SC_REPORT_ERROR maps to a UVM error message.
• SC_REPORT_FATAL maps to a UVM fatal message.
The SystemC messages have an ID. For UVM, this ID is prefixed with SC.
The following are some examples of converted messages. Assume the following SystemC
message definition (as define):
SC_DEFINE_MESSAGE(TLM_PKG_FAIL, 801, "failure in package processing");
Call of this message definition in SystemC, is issued as a UVM message.
SC_REPORT_INFO(TLM_PKG_FAIL, "Package got lost");
In case of single UVM report object, the following message is issued:
UVM_INFO my_sc_file.cpp(18) @ 50000: SystemC(reporter)
SC-801] failure in package processing : Package got lost
In SystemC process:top.sysc.do_transactions
In case of multiple UVM message objects, the following message is issued:
UVM_INFO my_sc_file.cpp(18) @ 50000:
SystemC(top.sysc.do_transactions) [SC-801] failure in
package processing : Package got lost
The following SystemC report handler call with the SC message without an ID in a file
called my_sc_file.cpp:
SC_REPORT_INFO("failure in package processing", "Package got lost");

This generates the following information:
UVM_INFO my_sc_file.cpp(31) @ 50000:
SystemC(top.sysc.do_transactions) [SC-NAN] failure in
package processing : Package got lost
The SC message triggers a set of actions within the sc_report_handler. If UVM
message alignment is active, "print to stdout" and "print to log" action is
influenced. Other actions (such as stopping the simulator) proceed as usual.
If UVM message alignment is active, a message is emitted and not suppressed by the
sc_report_handler
sc_report_handler.Then, it is forwarded to the UVM message handler, which decides
what to do with it.
Note that setting the filter for UVM messages also influences which SC messages
are printed. For example, if you indicate simv to filter uvm_note, then more severe
messages like warnings, errors, and fatal are issued to stdout. This applies to UVM and
SC messages.
There are two methods to filter messages. You can print them into a log file and skip
messages with a specific severity for SC-messages using the
+UVM_VERBOSITY=+UVM_VERBOSITY=
+UVM_VERBOSITY=and -l
simulator runtime options.
Accessing UVM Report Object of SystemC Instance
You can get the actual UVM report object of a SystemC instance (SystemC process-id)
and call the UVM report object related methods.
The following SV task can be used to get the UVM report object of a SystemC instance:
uvm_report_object log = tli_util_uvm_sc_get_log_by_instName(<string>);
where,
<string> is the process name.
If SystemC-UVM alignment is disabled, the returned UVM report object is 0. The function
is declared in the tli_uvm_sc_msg_align_pkgpackage. To use this function, you must
include or analyze the provided tli_uvm_sc_msg_align.svfile previously. You can
access the task explicitly as follows:
uvm_report_object log =
tli_uvm_sc_msg_align_pkg::tli_util_uvm_sc_get_log_by_instName(<string>);
Or by previously importing the package function, as follows:
import tli_uvm_sc_msg_align_pkg::tli_util_uvm_sc_get_log_by_instName;

uvm_report_object log = tli_util_uvm_sc_get_log_by_instName(<string>);

TLI Adaptor
The SystemVerilog Transaction Level Interface (TLI) is created automatically and
represents the SystemC instance inside the SV world. It allows you to directly access
public member variables and member functions of a SystemC instance.
The TLI adaptor is created by calling syscan with specific arguments. It has a collection of
SV functions to access SystemC member variables and call methods. These arguments
and functions are described in the following sections.
Creating a TLI Adapter
Instantiating TLI Adaptor in SV
The TLI adaptor, which is a SV interface, is generated automatically, but it needs to be
instantiated in the SV design to make it accessible. The SV interface has no ports, but it
has one string parameter to specify the hierarchical path of the SystemC instance.
The path refers to the mixed SC or HDL module hierarchy. This path can be absolute or a
relative path name. Consistent with Verilog, a relative path name is resolved relative to the
SV module, where the TLI function call occurs.
Direct Variable Access
The TLI adaptor has a function for each public SystemC member variable for which
access from SV is to be enabled. The function is named get_<member_variable>. The
function has no arguments and returns the value of the member variable. The TLI adaptor

provides a set_<member_variable>() function to write SystemC members from SV with
a value.
Calling SystemC Member Function
The public member functions of the SC instance can be called from SV code. The member
function is represented by a SV function in the TLI adaptor. Both SV and SC functions
have the same signature.
The SC function is represented by a SV task in the TLI adaptor. If the SC member has a
return value other than void, then the SV task has an additional output argument at the
front (beginning) into which the return value is written.
The SC function may be blocking, that is, it is allowed to call the wait() function from the
SC kernel and consume simulation time.
SystemC member functions that take arrays as arguments or return an array
cannot be called from SystemVerilog.
Definition of the SystemC instance is as follows:
class ABC
{
int AAA;
sc_int<10> BBB;
bool CCC(const char* p1);

};
Definition of automatically generated TLI adaptor is as follows:
(* vcs_systemc_1 *)
interface tli_ABC;

title: 1.01 /* factor */,

text:
endinterface
Usage of TLI adaptor in SV code is as follows:

tli_ABC #("top.sysc_a.inst0") sc_inst0();
tli_ABC #("sysc_b.reader.inst1") sc_inst1();

int a;

a = sc_inst0.get_AAA();
a = a + sc_inst1.get_BBB();
sc_inst0.set_AAA( a+10 );
if (sc_inst0.CCC("final test"))

end
Arguments of Type char* Used in Blocking Member Functions
Arguments of type char*, or const char* that are passed from Verilog into a blocking
SystemC method need special attention.
It is not guaranteed that the string remains valid when a blocking statement (a wait()
statement) is executed. You must therefore, make a local copy of the string at the
beginning of the method, and then release the string when the method ends. This can be
performed by using std::string type.
void my_blocking_systemC_method( const char* S_from_sv )
{
std::string S = S_from_sv;
wait(10,SC_NS);
printf("string=%s", S.c_str());
}
Supported Data Types
Basic Types for SC Class Methods
Only a few data types like ANSI integer and unsigned types, bool, std::string, and
char* that are used within the SystemC methods can be accessed.
The data types of SystemC and SV, excluding unsigned are mapped as follows:
SystemC SV

bool bit
char byte

short int shortint
int int
long long longint
long (on 64-bit compiler) longint
double real
float shortreal
std::string string
char* string (copy-by-value)
pointers/references chandle
Basic Types for SC Class Members
Only a few data types like ANSI integer types, native SystemC bit vector types, bool,
sc_logic, std::string, and char* that are used within the SystemC classes can be
accessed.
The data types of SystemC and SV are mapped as follows:
SystemC SV

bool bit
sc_logic wire (4-state)

int int

double real

SystemC char* Type
The created set method for char* type takes optional bool argument which controls
whether to free the current SystemC char* memory or not.
SV Code:
-------
function void set_CCC(input string ccc, \
input bit free_mem=0);

tli_set_CCC(SC_OBJECT_PATH, CD, free_mem);

Plumbing Code:
-------------

title: 1.01 /* factor */,
text:
void tli_set_CCC(const char* id, const char* ccc, \
bool free_mem=false);
{
SCObject* p = tli_adaptor.find_sc_object(id);
if (free_mem && p->ccc) free(p->ccc);
p->ccc = strdup(ccc);
}
The default value for free_mem is false. That is, a potential memory leak. You need to
carefully set this value depending on how the SC object is constructed.
SystemC Channel Types
The following templatized SystemC classes can be accessed if the template type is
supported:
• sc_signal_in_if
• sc_signal_inout_if
Classes derived from these classes are also supported. For example,
• sc_signal
• sc_signal_resolved (datatype is sc_logic)
• sc_signal_rv (datatype is sc_lv)
• sc_in
• sc_out
• sc_inout
• sc_buffer
Read/write accesses go directly to the underlying channel.

SC_MODULE(ABC) {

Currently, there is no protection against such crashes.
Write accesses with invalid indices may corrupt other memory locations, and do not trigger
a signal, therefore they are unnoticed.
To generate a TLI adaptor automatically, call syscan using the following syntax:
% syscan -tli <tli-file> <cpp-source-file> \
[-o <tli-file>] [-cmp]
The C++ file is parsed, and most of the necessary data is extracted from there. The TLI file
has the function to supplement the information; for example, to define for which classes
access functions are to be generated.
If you are using the shared library flow (seeShared Library Flow), call syscan with the
shared library using the following syntax:
% syscan libSC.so -tli A.tli [other syscan options]
Ensure that you compile the relevant source files with the debug information (g++ -g ).
Either of these calls generate the following files:
<tli_file>.sv TLI interface
<tli_file>.cpp helpers for TLI interface
<tli_file>.h helpers for TLI interface
The generated files are not automatically compiled or analyzed and you can control this
step.
You can specify C++ compiler directives, such as include paths. For example:
-cflags -I/some/dir/include
Support for $call_systemc_func API in TLI Flow
An API is provided that allows calling the SystemC method from SystemVerilog through
built-in function $call_systemc_func.
For example, the syntax $call_systemc_func("top.sc_inst.scmember_function",
arg1, arg2)

longint unsigned res_ull;
begin
…..

64'd8446744073709551481, 64'd18446744073709551481);

Th following limitations are applied when an additional API is used to call the SystemC
methods from SystemVerilog:
• The SystemC method must be non-blocking.
• The number and order of argument types must match the SystemC method.
• The arguments to the system function must be of type input or inout.
• Operators are not supported.
• SystemC-bitvectors, for example sc_int<n> and SystemC-fixed point data types are
not supported.
• Component data types (arrays, structs, classes, unions, pointer, references) are not
supported.
• The return value must not be a string (char*), double or float, C-pointer or C-reference.
Creating a TLI Adapter by Simplifying the Compile Flow
To simplify the compile flow, call syscan -tli to replace all the following analyze calls if
specified with the directive tli_compile_mode in the TLI file.
syscan -tli scmodule.tli scmodule.cpp
syscan tli_scmodule.cpp
vlogan -sverilog tli_scmodule.sv

title: 1.01 /* factor */,
text:
This section provides the use model to compile steps for creating an TLI adapter as
follows:
Add tli_compile_mode directive to the TLI file, and then create the TLI adapter using the
following single syscan command:
syscan -tli my.tli scmodule.cpp <syscan_tli_opts> <syscan_comp_opts> <sy
scan_comp_tli_opts> <vlogan_comp_opts>
The tli_compile_mode directive requires an additional argument, manual, auto, or all.
This directive specifies if the call is a synonym for the two or three analyze steps.
If this directive is missing or the tag is manual, then the syscan -tli is handled as the
TLI adaptor code creation call as before. The -cmp option is supported for the directive
tli_compile_mode manual .
The top syscan -tli call splits the passed arguments in single syscan analyze and
vlogan analyze arguments. The split arguments are passed to the sycan and vlogan
analyze call.
The TLI-files, SystemC and SystemVerilog are created by default in the csrc/sysc/tli
directory.
Rules for TLI File/Syntax
The rules for TLI files are as follows:
• One TLI file must be available for each adaptor/ top-level SC_MODULE class.
• Directives:
◦ Adaptor name must match the top-level sc_module class in a cpp file
◦ import member [name|glob_pattern]
◦ skip member [name|glob_pattern] where,
glob_pattern includes a special char *
* matches everything
name can be name.[name|glob_pattern]
• By default, all plain members of the adaptor class are imported.
• By default, all the inner class members ( bar.* in the following example) are skipped.

• Precedence rules:
◦ The order of lines is not important.
◦ For precedence rules, use the following three types of match sequences:
name (plain name without any *)
name can be name.name
match_all (match_all is single * at any level), examples are *, *.* , *.*.* ,
select_pattern (name with a * but not match_all), examples are nam*, *ame, na*e,
name.*ame, and so on
• Precedence from lowest to highest
import member * (match_all)
skip member * (match_all)
import member name* (select_pattern)
skip member name* (select_pattern)
import member name
skip member name
• Rules with the higher precedence override rules with the lower precedence. For
example, skip member * skips all members even if there is an import member *
directive.
• To access SC methods from SV, the method keyword must be used, like import
method * directive.
• The syntax of the TLI option is as follows:
◦ syscan -tli <tli_input_file> <src_file>
◦ syscan does not support multiple files with the -tli option.
The syscan command
--------------

% syscan -tli foo_file.tli foo.cpp
Input files
------------
foo_file.tli
foo.cpp

Output files
------------
foo_file.[h|cpp|sv]
foo_file.idf (intermediate file)
foo.cpp
------------
class Bar
{
int a1, a2, b1, b2, c1, c2;
}

class Foo
{
int aname1, aname2, bname1, bname2, cname1, cname2;
int x1, x2, y1, y2, z1, z2;
Bar* bar;
}
foo_file.tli
---------------
adaptor sc_data
// (implicit) import member *
skip member *

import member *name*
skip member bname*

import member bname1
skip member cname2

// (implicit) skip member bar.*
import member bar.c*
import member bar.b1
skip member bar.c1
Foo.idf
---------------
adaptor Foo
direction sv_to_sc
verilog_module tli_Foo
systemc_module tli_Foo

var int aname1
var int aname2
var int bname1
var int cname1

var int bar.b1
var int bar.c2
Debug Flow
The TLI implementation uses the following existing CBug debug features:
• Displays in a combined HDL or SC design hierarchy.
All access functions are visible on the SV side as functions or tasks of the SV interface.
• Underlying DPI functions of the adaptor are visible in the list of DPI, PLI, or DirectC
functions.
• Cross-step from calling SV statement into an adaptor code, and from the adaptor code
into the C function.

The tli_S interface code of the above example is created with a regular syscan -tli
call, such as syscan -tli packunpack.tli S.h . Extensions to the TLI-input file must
be used to create the additional code required for byte pack/unpack. The additional
functionality is responsible for exchanging a complete struct or class. The pack/unpack
sub-routines are called in the order of the single members of the struct/class declaration.
For details regarding the tli-fileextensions, see the TLI Input File Extensions section.
For a more complex example describing all the single steps, see the "Compile Flow
for VMM" and "Compile Flow for UVM" sections. This interface must be instantiated
by referring to a hierarchical path to an instance of sc_module S in the SystemVerilog
source code. You can change the hierarchical path anytime during the simulation using the
scSetScopeByName()interface function.
A second interface named tli_S_P is generated, which is instantiated in the tli_S
interface as the member name (P) of the struct within a SystemC module. The tli_S_P
interface contains get(ba)and set(ba) functions to set and get the entire struct.
You cannot check whether the C++ struct or class is compliant with the SystemVerilog
class. There is no restriction to use only UVM, OVM, or VMM byte pack/unpack when
passing the packed byte stream as an argument.
You can write your own SystemVerilog byte pack/unpack routines, but these routines must
be VMM, UVM, or OVM byte pack/unpack compatible. The TLI C++ byte pack/unpack
routines with the TLI package support only VMM or UVM or OVM compliant byte pack/
unpack. The set_<member_name>('Value') and get_<member_name> functions are
provided for the scalar members of the struct. For example, to access the member A of a
structure or class, use set_A(val and get_A().
There is no change in the compile steps to generate and compile the generated files as
compared to the adaptor code generation and byte pack or unpack functionality.
Generating the Adaptor Code
The adaptor code is generated using a syscan call and a TLI input file, as shown in the
following command:
% syscan -tli <input_file> <SC/C++_file>

irective:
use <struct_type_name> pack:my_pack unpack:my_unpack /ab/cd/huhu.h
You can specify struct or class members for which the pack/unpack adaptor code should
be generated, using the above directive. In the case of a user-provided C++ byte pack/
unpack, you must specify the function names of pack and unpack routines and the header
file using the function declarations.
The adaptor code is generated using the create adaptor directive. The import member
directive specifies the struct or class members for which the byte pack/unpack adaptor
code should be generated.
The [create VMM|UVM|OVM] and create packunpack directives generate UVM/VMM/
OVM classes and byte pack/unpack routines for the structs or classes specified using the
import member directive. In these cases, the generated pack/unpack routines are used
in the adaptor code for the pack/unpack of struct or class members. This applies to UVM,
VMM, and OVM flows.
The C++ pack/unpack routines reside in a class called tli_pack_data, which has the
byte pack/unpack routines for single types.

The C++ byte pack/unpack functions are void functions, and have two arguments. The
prototypes are as follows:
• For pack functions: tli_pack_data&, const <class_type>&)
• For unpack functions: (tli_pack_data&, <class_type>&)
For details, see the Exchanging Data Between SystemVerilog and SystemC Using Byte
Pack/Unpacksection.
Invoking the Pack or Unpack Adaptor Code Generation
The pack or unpack adaptor code generation is invoked for the following:
• The adaptor code generation is enabled in the TLI input file.
• A member of the type struct or class can be accessed using the import member
directive.
• The use and/or create packunpack directive is available in the TLI file.
The following are the limitations of accessing struct or class members of a SystemC
module from SystemVerilog:
• The structs in method calls are not supported.
• sc_fifo and tlm_fifo are not supported.
• Nested classes or structs are not supported.

Usage Model
You can access the variables of Verilog instances from the SystemC code by calling the tli_get_<type>
tli_get_<type> (path)or
tli_set_<type>
tli_set_<type> (val, path) functions.
<type> = logic|int64|uint64|bv|lv|string , path is the absolute path to the variable
in a Verilog instance.
val is the value to be set on the variable.
The following topic describes the prototypes of these functions.
These functions either get or set the value and return immediately. You can call them
either from SystemC methods or from regular C++ functions.
You can specify the location of the variable in the code using the absolute path. For
example, in tli_get_int64 ("top.inst0.D") , top.inst0 is the absolute path name of
a Verilog instance, and D refers to the variable D of that instance.
All tli_get_<type> or tli_set_<type> APIs are stored in a header file called
systemc_user.h. You should include this header file in the SystemC file that uses these
APIs. Also, you must enable VPI read/write capabilities during VCS elaboration using the
-debug_access+all option.

path) functions:

Supported Data Types
The tli_get_<type> (path)or tli_set_<type> (val, path) functions allow access
only to the certain member variables of Verilog module instances. These functions
internally use VPI calls to get or set a variable. Therefore, any variable which is accessible
through VPI can be accessed using these TLI functions.
The following data types can be accessed through these TLI APIs:
• Signed and unsigned versions of all integer types: bit, reg, logic, byte, shortint,
longint, and integer.
• All net types in Verilog (read-only).
• Vectors/memories of the earlier mentioned supported types.
• SystemVerilog strings.
• Enum types defined as one of the earlier mentioned supported types.
• Typedefs to one of the earlier mentioned supported types.
• Sub members of classes, interfaces, structures, or unions are accessed only if they are
of the earlier mentioned supported types.
• Parameters (read-only).
Unsupported Data Types
The following data types cannot be accessed with the tli_get_<type> (path)or
tli_set_<type> (val, path) functions:
• Double, float, real, and all other floating point types.
• Any type of a SystemVerilog array.
• SystemVerilog event types.

Accessing a variable of an incompatible type using a TLI API results in an error. For
example, accessing a string type using tli_get_int64 or accessing a bit vector using
tli_get_logic results in an error.
The following example shows how you can use TLI APIs to access SystemVerilog
variables:
File: top.v
module bot;
reg [3:0] r = 4'b1100;

int i1 = 100000;
bot b1();

File: sc_bot.h
SC_MODULE(sc_bot)
{
…
void Func();
}

File: sc_bot.cpp
#include "sc_bot.h"
void sc_bot::Func()
{
sc_bv_base bv = tli_get_bv("top.b1.r");
tli_set_bv(bv.reverse(), "top.b1.r");
long long val = tli_get_int64("top.i1");
tli_set_int64(val+1, "top.i1");
}
Follow the regular compile flow and run the steps as follows:
% syscan sc_bot.cpp:sc_bot
% vlogan -sverilog top.v
% vcs -sysc -debug_access+all top
% ./simv
Type Conversion Mechanism
The type of the variable being accessed must match the type of the TLI access function.

You can access the following:
• All single-bit values using the tli_get_logic function.
• All 2-state bit vectors and integer types using the tli_get_bv function.
• All 4-state bit vectors using the tli_get_lv function and its corresponding tli_set*
functions.
If a 4-state value is accessed with a function that accepts only 2-state values (such
as tli_get_bv ), then all X and Z bits are converted to 0. Also, If the source vector
(on SystemC side) passed to a set function (such as tli_set_bv) is smaller than the
destination vector (on Verilog side), then the source vector is padded with 0 bits or sign
extended (if it is signed type).
If the source is larger than the destination vector, the upper bits are removed. The
tli_get_bv
tli_get_bv and
tli_get_lv
tli_get_lv functions preserve bit width; that is, they return a vector
whose size is the same as the actual vector on the Verilog side.
Example 30 Accessing 4-State Value With a Function That Accepts Only 2-State Values
tli_get_bv("top.S2.A")
In Example 30, if top.S2.A refers to a logic vector of size 8, then this function call
converts the 4-state value fetched from the Verilog side to 2-state values (by replacing all
X and Z with 0), and returns sc_bv_base<8>.
If the variable A has the binary value 8'b1x1z0x01, then tli_get_bv() converts all X and
Z to 0, and returns the value 10100001 in the sc_bv_base variable.
padding
Example 31 Padding the Upper Bits
tli_set_lv(val,"top.S2.A")
In Example 31, if val is a logic vector of size 8 and top.S2.A refers to a bit vector of size
20, then this function call first converts all X and Z in val to 0, and then pads the upper 12-
bits with 0 and assigns it to the referred variable.
If the variable has the binary value 8'11xxzz11, then the tli_set_lv() function first
converts all X and Z to 0, and then adds 12 zeros. Therefore, the resulting value is the
binary value 20'b000…00011000011 or the integer value 195.
accessing signed variablesasigned variablesaccessing
Example 32 Accessing Signed Variables
tli_get_bv("top.S2.B")
In Example 32, top.S2.B refers to a 8-bit signed register (reg signed [7:0] B ). It has
the binary value 8'b11111110, which corresponds to the hex value 32'hfe or the decimal
value -2.

The example returns sc_bv<8>, which holds the value 8'b11111110. The assumption
here is that you know the signed value of the referred variable when you call tli_get_bv
and convert the retrieved value appropriately. Instead, you can use tli_get_int64 to
access signed values less than 64-bit.
The tli_get_logic and tli_set_logic functions operate on single-bit variables
only. If you pass a vector value totli_set_logic or try to access a vector value using
tli_get_logic, then it results in an error. You can access SystemVerilog string type
variables using the tli_get_string and tli_set_string functions only.

Using the tli_get_<type> and tli_set_<type> Functions
You can access the members of the SystemC instances from the SystemVerilog code by
calling the following functions:
tli_get_<type> (path [, member_name]) or
tli_set_<type> (val, path [, member_name]) functions:
Here,
• <type> = logic|int64|uint64|string|logic64
• path is the absolute path to the member of a SystemC module instance. For example,
top.S2.D refers to the member D of the SystemC instance top.S2. Only absolute path
names are supported. Relative paths are not supported.
• val is the value to be set on the member variable.
• member_name is optional. It is the name of the member variable in a SystemC object. If
this argument is not specified, then the first argument is considered as the full path of
the variable. For more information on this argument, see Member Variablessection.

The tli_get_<type> and tli_set_<type> functions either get or set the value and
return immediately.

These functions can access only the following:
• Objects of a SystemC module, which are derived from sc_core::sc_module.
• Member variables that are public. You cannot access private and protected members.
You can view all SystemC module instances in the static design hierarchy
shown by Verdi.
Supported Data Types
The tli_get_<type> (path [, member_name]) or tli_set_<type> (val, path [,
member_name]) functions allow access only to the certain member variables of SystemC
module instances. There are restrictions regarding the data type, accessibility, and compile
flow.
The tli_get_<type> (path [, member_name]) or tli_set_<type> (val, path [,
member_name]) functions can access the following data types:
• bool and sc_logic
• All ANSI integer signed and unsigned types of int, signed char , short, int, long,
and long long .
• Native SystemC bit-vectors with a length of not more than 64-bit: sc_int, sc_uint,
sc_bigint, sc_biguint, sc_lv, and sc_bv
• Signals and ports: sc_signal<T>, sc_signal_rv, sc_signal_resolved, sc_in<T>,
sc_inout<T>, sc_out<T>, sc_inout_rv, and sc_inout_resolved
• Strings of type std::string or char*
• Sub-Members that have one of the above types.
• The bool and sc_logic data types are single-bit entities. They are only
accessed using the tli_get_logic and tli_set_logic functions. Z and
X are preserved while accessing the sc_logic variable. Using any other
tli_get_<type> or tli_set_<type> function for these types results in an
error.
• The std::string and char* data types can only be accessed through
the tli_get_string and tli_set_string functions. Using any other TLI
function results in an error.

• The tli_set_string function has a fourth argument free_mem, which
applies only if the SystemC variable is of the char*type. If the type is
free_mem=1, then TLI uses free()type of the current string value before
assigning the new value. You must ensure that the value is freed.
Sub-Members
The tli_get_<type> (path [, member_name]) or tli_set_<type> (val, path [,
member_name]) functions can access the members of sub-classes or sub-structs, if these
members contain supported type as int. This corresponds to an import member *.*
directive within a TLI file.
struct my_struct2 {
int D;
};
struct my_struct1 {
int C;
my_struct2 S2;
};
SC_MODULE(foo) {
sc_int<40> A;
my_struct1 S1;
};
In this example, members A and S1.C of foo are accessible, and are of type int.
Members S1 and S1.S2 are not accessible because they refer to entire user-defined
structs.
Member S1.S2.D is also of type int, but is not accessible if the corresponding source
file is compiled with the -tli_D flag. This flag makes the first-level (A) and second-level
(S1.C) members accessible, but not the third-level (S1.S2.D) or any further levels.
Member S1.S2.Dis accessible if the corresponding source file is compiled with an explicit
TLI file, which specifies to import this third-level member.
Unsupported Data Types
The tli_get_<type> and tli_set_<type> functions cannot access the following data
types:
• Base types of native SystemC bit-vectors: sc_int_base, sc_uint_base, sc_signed,
sc_unsigned, sc_lv_base, and sc_bv_base.
• Resolved input and output ports: sc_in_rv, sc_out_rv, sc_in_resolved, and
sc_out_resolved.
• Other SystemC channel types. For example, sc_fifoandsc_buffer.

• Arrays of fixed or varying size. For example, int[8]and int[].
• Double, float , and all native SystemC fix-point types. For example, sc_fix.
Using any TLI API to access a variable of an incompatible type results in an error. For
example, accessing string types using

Member Variables
The member_name argument is optional. SystemC instance names contain their own name
space. They do not clash with other member variables defined in the same class.
If sub-members are also supported, then you might face difficulties in differentiating
between member variables. You can overcome these difficulties by using the
member_name argument.
For example, consider the following code:
struct mystruct {
int B;
};
SC_MODULE(sub) { // instance top.inst.A
int B;
};
SC_MODULE(foo) { // instance top.inst
sub inst_A;
my_struct A;
SC_CTOR(foo): inst_A("A") {}
};
In the earlier mentioned code, the inst_A member forms sub instance top.inst.A. The
(SC_CTOR) constructor defines the hierarchical name of the C++ member inst_A to be A.
The inst_A member does not clash with the member A within class foo, at least for the C
++ compiler. However, it constitutes a clash for the hierarchy, such that the top.inst.A.B
path which refers to the following:
• The member B of the top.inst.A instance.
• The member A.B of the top.inst instance.
Using any API with the top.inst.A.B path creates ambiguity. This ambiguity is resolved
by the optional member_name argument.
tli_get_int("top.inst.A.B") // ambiguous situation
tli_get_int("top.inst.A", "B") // member "B" of instance "top.inst.A"
tli_get_int("top.inst", "A.B")

tli_set_int(value, "top.inst.A.B")) // ambiguous situation

tli_set_int(value, "top.inst.A", "B")// member "B" of instance
//"top.inst.A"
tli_set_int(value, "top.inst", "A.B")// member "A.B" of instance
//"top.inst"
Type Conversion Mechanism
The type of the variable accessed must match the type of the TLI access function. VCS
generates an error message if the type of the variable accessed is incompatible with the
type of the TLI access function. If the type a of the variable accessed is compatible with
the type of the TLI access function, then you can do appropriate conversions as follows:
• If a 4-state value logic is accessed with a function that accepts only 2-state values,
then all X and Z bits are converted to 0.
• If the source vector passed to a set function is smaller than the destination vector, then
the source vector is padded with 0 bits or sign extended (if it is a signed type). If the
source is larger than the destination vector, then the upper bits are removed.
• Sign extension is performed only when the source is a signed integer type
and is called; (for example, int, signed char, sc_int, sc_bigint ) and
tli_get_int64()or tli_get_uint64(). 0 bits are added in all other cases.
Example 33 Accessing 4-State Value With a Function That Accepts Only 2-State Values
tli_get_int64("top.S2.A")
If the above function refers to sc_lv<8> (a vector of 8 bits of four\u0002valued logic),
it converts the 4-state value to 2-state values (by replacing all X and Z with 0) and the
missing 24 bits are filled with zeros.
If the variable A has the binary value 8'bxxzz1100, then tli_get_in64() first converts
allXand Zto 0 and then adds 24 zeros. Therefore, the resulting value is the binary value
64'b000…0001100 or the integer value 12.

Access for tli_get_<type> or tli_set_<type> must be enabled during the compilation
of SystemC source files with syscan.
Using the tli_D Option
Use the -tli_D option along with syscan using the following syntax:
% syscan -tli_D <source file>
If you are using the shared library flow (see Shared Library Flow), call syscan with the
shared library using the following syntax:
% syscan -tli_D libSC.so
Access is enabled for all SystemC module classes that are present during the compilation
of the source file. If this option is used for compiling the top-most model of an entire
SystemC design tree, then all SystemC modules are supported.

TLI Directive (Create DirectAccess)
The
–tli_D
-tli_D option only creates information needed for the tli_get_<type> or

This section describes how to directly access the SystemVerilog functions and tasks from
the SystemC code.
The existing idf file-based mechanism allows you to access variables or function calls on
the Verilog side from SystemC class methods. However, this mechanism expects you to
write an idf file, to instantiate the corresponding interfaces in SystemC source files, and
to access variables or functions using the interface objects.
You can use the TLI-DirectAccess (TLI-DA) mechanism to directly access SystemVerilog
functions and tasks from SystemC code. This mechanism allows you to easily interact
across language boundaries.
• Usage Model
• Function Declaration Hierarchy
• Passing Arguments
• Supported Types
• Usage Example

• Compile Flow
• Usage Guidelines
• Limitations
Usage Model
To directly access SystemVerilog functions or tasks from the SystemC code, use the
following syntax:
TLI::<Function declaration hierarchy>::<Function_name>
("<design_hierarchy>", <comma separate list of actual arguments>);
Following is an example of a
TLIfunction call
TLI function call:
TLI::Mid::Add("top.m1", arg1, arg2);
You must call a function with the design hierarchy string (xmr) as the first argument,
followed by the list of actual arguments.
The design hierarchy specified in the call should be a string literal (for example,
top.m1). You cannot use a variable of the type string or char*.
You must prefix the function call with the function declaration hierarchy. This hierarchy is
the scope where a function is declared in the SystemVerilog design. For more information,
see Function Declaration Hierarchy.
You must include the generated TLI header file tli_sc_calls_sv.h in SystemC files
which access the TLI function calls.
Function Declaration Hierarchy
The function declaration hierarchy is the scope where a function is declared in the
SystemVerilog design. It consists of a module name which is optionally prefixed by the
enclosing library name, and optionally suffixed by the containing class or interface name.
The function declaration hierarchy performs the following:
• Locates the function in a SystemVerilog design and extract its prototype. This prototype
is required to automatically generate the corresponding DPI wrappers.
• Avoids conflicts with other function calls having the same name, but declared in
different scopes.

To declare the function hierarchy, use the following syntax:
[<lib_name>::]<module_name/program_name/
package_name>::[<class_name>/<interface_name>/
<named_block_name>::]
• If there are any conflicts, then module_name or package_name is the only mandatory
item.
• Use library_name if a module with the same name exists in a different library, and
that module also has a function with the same name.
• Use class_name, interface_name, or named_block_name, if a function with the same
name is present in two different scopes in the same module.
• You must separate all the above-mentioned strings with a scope resolution operator
(::).
Passing Arguments
The type of actual arguments passed to the TLI functions should match the corresponding
SystemVerilog type used in the function declaration. Following is the list of compatible
types:
Table 7 Compatible Types
SystemVerilog Data Type SystemC Data Type
bit bool
logic sc_logic
reg sc_logic
reg vector sc_lv
logic vector sc_lv
bit vector sc_bv
int int
shortint short int
longint long long
byte char

• The SystemC compiler generates an error if the sizes of the vectors passed as actual
arguments do not match the sizes of the formal parameters.
• Use plain types for input arguments and pointers for output or inout arguments. You
must allocate enough space for these pointers. Also, use pointers to collect the return
values from these function calls.
• Functions can have reference arguments, which are treated as inout types on the
SystemC side.The SystemVerilog ref semantics are not maintained on the SystemC
side. That is, any change to the ref variable in the function or task is not immediately
visible on the SystemC side.
Supported Types
The following types are supported:
• Functions having arguments of basic data types from the SystemC code. Supported
argument types include: all integral types, reg, logic, bit, string, and so on.
• Bit vectors of basic types are allowed in the argument list.
• In Verilog-top designs, the design hierarchy should only consist of Verilog instances.
• In SystemC top designs, the design hierarchy should start in SystemC and end in
Verilog. Donuts are not allowed.

In the previous example, consider the following points:
• The int* i = TLI::Mid::Add("top.m1", arg1, arg2, arg3); function call is
equivalent to the top.m1.Add(arg1, arg2) XMR function call. This function call refers
to the function Add in the module Mid.
• The int* i = TLI::Mid::C::Add("top.m1.c1", arg1, arg2, arg3); function
call is equivalent to the top.m1.c1.Add(arg1, arg2) XMR function call. This function
call refers to the Add function in class C of the Mid module. Here, you must mention the
class name along with the module name because the module has another function with
the same name.
• The int* i = TLI::Mid::Sub("top.m1.c1", arg1, arg2); function call refers to
the Sub function in class C of the Mid module. Since the function name is unique in the
given module scope, there is no need to prefix the function call with the class name.
However, you can use the class name to call this function, as follows:
res3 = TLI::Mid::C::Sub("top.m1.c1", arg1, arg2);

• The int* i = TLI::$unit::C::Add("top.c1", arg1, arg2); function call calls
the Add function in class C. This class resides in $unit scope , which is outside all
modules.
• The int* i = TLI::P::Sub("top.c2", arg1, arg2); function call refers to the Sub
function in the P package.
To enable direct function access using TLI, perform the following steps:
1. Compile Verilog or VHDL files using vlogan or vhdlan:
% vlogan -sverilog top.v
2. Run syscan using the -tli_F option, and then pass all the SystemC files to it
(especially the files having TLI function calls). Also, pass all the required include
directories using -cflags.
% syscan -tli_F sc_top.cpp
3. Note:
This is an extra step required to automatically generate the TLI adaptor
code.
4. Compile all SystemC files:
% syscan sc_top.cpp:sc_top
5. Run VCS elaboration:
% vcs -sysc top
Usage Guidelines
The following are the guidelines for accessing SystemVerilog functions or tasks from
SystemC:
• You must compile all Verilog files before the SystemC compilation (with
–tliF
syscan
-tli_F).
• You must analyze SystemC source files containing TLI function calls with the syscan
-tli_F command before they are compiled with syscan.
• You should specify all files that contain TLI function calls together to the syscan
-tli_F command. You may observe some slowdown if this command is run on each
file separately.

Generating C++ Struct Definition From SystemVerilog Class Definition
• If there are any changes to the TLI function calls in any of the source files, then you
must process the files with the syscan -tli_F command before compiling them with
syscan.
• You must include the tli_sc_calls_sv.h file in all source files that access TLI
function calls.
• The widths of the formal arguments should match the widths of actual arguments. Also,
the types of arguments should be compatible as per SystemC semantics. For example,
you cannot pass a sc_bv vector to a function that expects a logic vector.
• You must specify an appropriate declaration hierarchy to handle conflicting function
calls.
The following limitations apply when accessing SystemVerilog functions or tasks from
SystemC:
• Compound data types ( arrays, structures, classes, and so on), enums, and
typedefs are not allowed in function arguments.
• Floating point types are not allowed as function arguments.
• Functions declared in nested modules cannot be called from SystemC.
• Donuts (design hierarchies, such as Verilog-SC-Verilog) are not supported.
• The TLI function call and its first argument must be on the same line. That is, the
function name and its first argument must not spread over multiple lines.

Generating C++ Struct Definition From SystemVerilog Class Definition
Use Model for Generating C++ Struct From SystemVerilog Class
Exchanging the content of a struct or a class from SV to SC or vice versa requires a class/
struct with matching members on both the language sides. Not only the type must match,
even the order of the members which need to be exchanged must match. A SV class
is created from a SC/C++ class with a syscan-tli call if the target is VMM, UVM, or
OVM. Creating a C++ struct from a SV class with the -tli option is not possible. You can
use the
tli_gen_struct
-tli_gen_struct option to invoke the C++ struct generation, as shown in the
following command:
% syscan -tli_gen_struct [-v] <file_name> -class <class_name> [-o
<output_header_file>]
where,
• -v is the verbose switch. The generated C++ struct is also printed to stdout.
• <file_name> is the SystemVerilog input file.
• -class <class_name> specifies the SystemVerilog class, for which a corresponding C
++ struct is generated.
• -o <output_header_file> is an optional argument. If specified, the C++ struct is
created in this file.
In the earlier mentioned command example, the struct generator requires a SystemVerilog
file and the class name, for which the corresponding C++ struct should be created, as
inputs. Therefore, a SystemVerilog class is required in the specified SystemVerilog file.
The SystemVerilog file is read for all data members in the class, and the corresponding C+
+ data types are generated in a struct.
The name of the C++ struct is tli_struct_<class_name>.

The SystemVerilog file is read for all data members in the class, and the corresponding C+

The name of the C++ struct is tli_struct_<class_name>. If you do not specify an output

A comment is printed in the preceding line of each C++ struct data member. This comment

of the corresponding SystemVerilog class data member.

Example for Generating C++ Struct From SystemVerilog Class
The following example shows how the SystemVerilog class my_payload in the
SystemVerilog file my_payload.sv is converted into a C++ struct:
class my_payload;
byte my_byte[3]; // holds 3 byte values
shortint myshort; /* some short */
The following call generates a C++ struct named tli_struct_my_payload in the
tli_struct_my_payload.h file:
% syscan -tli_gen_struct my_payload.sv -class my_payload
The following are the contents of the tli_struct_my_payload.h file:
#ifndef tli_struct_my_payload_H
#define tli_struct_my_payload_H
#include "string"
struct tli_struct_my_payload {
// SV declaration
(my_payload.sv, 2): byte my_byte[3];
(my_payload.sv, 3): shortint myshort;
char my_byte[3];
/* some short */
short int myshort;
};

The following limitations apply for creating a C++ struct from a SystemVerilog class:
• The syscan -tli_gen_struct option cannot recognize all the legal SystemVerilog
class definitions. For example, the following types are not supported:
◦ User-defined structs
◦ enums
◦ Multidimensional arrays
Data members that cannot be converted are created in a comment. By default,
the data type is void and appears as follows:
// TODO: void <variable_name>;
• The typedef, function, and task constructs cannot be converted to any C++
construct. The syscan script ignores these constructs if they are specified in
the SystemVerilog class definition.
• Splitting data member definitions over multiple lines is not supported.
• Preprocessor directives are not supported.
Exchanging Data Between SystemVerilog and SystemC Using
Byte Pack/Unpack
Transaction-Level Interface (TLI) allows you to exchange user-defined C++ classes or
data in struct objects between SystemVerilog and SystemC/C++ using the byte packing
and unpacking mechanism. This mechanism allows you to put bits of all the class
members into an array of bytes. That is, the values of data types are packed in a byte
stream for exchanging the data between SystemVerilog and SystemC/C++. These packed
values of data types can be retrieved or unpacked from the byte stream at the other end.
SystemVerilog uses built-in byte pack/unpack routines from VMM, UVM, or OVM for byte
packing/unpacking of a complete instance of a SystemVerilog class. SystemC uses the
tli_pack_data class object, which contains APIs to pack and unpack the data type
values.

• Use Model
• Supported Data Types
• Unsupported Data Types
• Mapping of SystemC/C++ and SystemVerilog Data Types
To pack and unpack the data type values using the APIs in SystemC or C++, perform the
following steps:
1. Include the tli_packunpack.h header file.
2. Create a class object tli_pack_data that contains API to provide the pack and
unpack functionality.
3. Use the pack operator ( << ) or the pack() function to put data into the byte array. This
operator converts data into a byte stream. Similarly, use the unpack operator ( >> ) or
the unpack() function to extract data from the byte array. This operator converts the
data of the byte stream into the type along with the variable declaration.
The tli_pack_data class provides pack and unpack functionality using the
following:
• The << and >> operators for basic data types.
• The pack() and unpack() functions for 1-dimensional array (fixed size and dynamic)
of the supported basic data types.
To exchange the byte stream buffer between SystemVerilog and SystemC, you can
use the SV and SC APIs listed as follows. The packed data in the byte streams can
be exchanged between SystemC and SystemVerilog using the upload and download
functions/tasks.
• The C++ upload/download functions are part of the tli_pack_data_classclass. The
<tli_pack_data>.download(0) method loads a byte buffer sent from SV into an
instance of tli_pack_data. The <tli_pack_data>.upload(0) method is used to
send a byte buffer to SV.
• The SV tasks tli_upload and tli_download are part of the tli_packunpack.sv
SV package. The tli_download(<byte_buffer_var>, null) task loads a byte
buffer sent from SC into <byte_buffer_var>. The tli_upload(<byte_buffer_var>,
null) task is used to send the contents of <byte_buffer_var> to SC.

Supported Data Types
The following basic integral and SystemC data types are supported:
• bool
• enum
• Native C/C++ Integer Data Types: char, signed char , short, int, long, long long ,
sc_int, and sc_bigint
• Unsigned Data Types: unsigned ( char, short, int, long, long long), sc_uint, and
sc_biguint
• String Types: const char* , char*, and std::string
• std::vector<T>
• sc_dt::sc_bv<W>
• sc_dt::sc_logic sc_dt::sc_lv<W>
• 1-dimensional fixed-size array of the base types listed earlier mentioned.
• 1-dimensional dynamic array (pointers) of the base types listed earlier mentioned,
except std::vector.
Unsupported Data Types
The following data types are not supported:
• floatanddouble
• sc_fixedand sc_fix
• sc_ufixedand sc_ufix
• Struct or Classes
These types cannot be supported by the API. The pack or unpack routines must be written
with the knowledge of a single member.
• Unions
• Pointers

Byte-packing cannot perform type checking between byte pack/unpack routines
from VMM, or UVM, or OVM on one side and the corresponding pack/unpack
routines on the SystemC/C++ side.
Once the data is packed into bytes and sent across, only the actual values of
data members exist without any information about the structure. The function
that unpacks the data must match exactly to the one that packed it. If both the
functions do not match, then an invalid object results after unpacking. It is not
possible to automatically detect this and no error message is issued.
Usage Examples
This section provides examples to use pack and unpack operators and functions.

Usage Examples
Using the Pack Operator
You can use the pack operator << to put data into the byte array. You can also use this
operator for the data types listed in the preceding section.
The following example illustrates how to use the pack operator using int, std::string,
and a sc_bv variable.
Example 36 Packing Using the Pack Operator
// variable declaration for variables supposed to be packed
int my_int = 42;
std::string my_str = "This is a string";
sc_bv<9> my_sc_bv = 127;

Class Refers to a user-defined C++ class or C struct on the C side. On the

Complex Data types Complex data types are the types which require additional arguments
in the pack/unpack routines. For example, enum, length of a dynamic

Simple Data Types Simple data types are non-pointer built-in data types, such as,
